sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The Greek alphabet has twenty-four letters. Form Name Equivalents Sound as in *a a a)/lfa alpha a ă: aha; ā: father *b b bh=ta bēta b beg *g g ga/mma gamma g go *d d de/lta delta d dig *e e ei)=, e)/ (e)\ yi_lo/n） ĕpsīlon ĕ met *z z zh=ta zēta z daze *h h h)=ta ēta ē Fr. fête *q q, u qh=ta thēta th thin *i i i)w=ta iōta i ĕ: meteor; ī: police *k k ka/ppa kappa c, k kin *l l la/mbda lambda l let *m m mu= mu m met *n n nu= nu n net *c c cei= (ci=） xi x lax *o o ou)=, o)/ (o)\ mi_kro/n） ŏmīcron ŏ obey *p p pei= (pi=） pi p pet *r r r(w= rho r run *s s, s si/gma sigma s such *t t tau= tau t tar *u u u)= (u)= yi_lo/n） üpsīlon （u) y ŭ: Fr. tu; ū: Fr. sûr *f f fei= (fi=） phi ph graphic *x x xei= (xi=） chi ch Germ. machen *y y yei= (yi=） psi ps gypsum *w w w)= (w)= me/ga） ōmĕga ō note a. Sigma (not capital) at the end of a word is written s, elsewhere s1. Thus, seismo/s earthquake. b. The names in parentheses, from which are derived those in current use, were given at a late period, some as late as the Middle Ages. Thus, epsilon means ‘simple e,’ upsilon ‘simple u,’ to distinguish these letters from ai, oi, which were sounded like e and u. c. Labda is a better attested ancient name than lambda.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The Greek alphabet as given above originated in Ionia, and was adopted at Athens in 403 B.C. The letters from A to T are derived from Phoenician and have Semitic names. The signs *u to *w were invented by the Greeks. From the Greek alphabet are derived the alphabets of most European countries. The ancients used only the large letters, called majuscules (capitals as *e, uncials as [Eunc ]); the small letters (minuscules), which were used as a literary hand in the ninth century, are cursive forms of the uncials. a. Before 403 B.C. in the official Attic alphabet E stood for e, h, spurious ei (6), O for o, w, spurious ou (6), H for the rough breathing, *x*s for *c, *f*s for *y. *l was written for g, and [lins ] for l. Thus: *e*d*o*x*s*e*n*t*e*i*b*o[lins ]*e*i*k*a*i*t*o*i*d*e*m*o*i e)/docen th=| boulh=| kai\ tw=| dh/mw|. *x*s*u*l*l*r*a*f*e*s*x*s*u*n*e*l*r*a*f*s*a*n cuggrafh=s cune/grayan. *e*g*i*t*e*d*e*i*o*n*e*n*a*i*a*g*o*t*o*a*r*l*u*r*i*o e)pith/deion ei)=nai a)po\ tou= a)rguri/ou.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: In the older period there were two other letters: (1) *v: vau=, uau, called digamma (i.e. double-gamma) from its shape. It stood after e and was pronounced like w. v was written in Boeotian as late as 200 B.C. (2) ϟ: ko/ppa, koppa, which stood after p. Another s, called san, is found in the sign [sampi ], called sampi, i.e. san + pi. On these signs as numerals, see 348.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: There are seven vowels: a, e, h, i, o, u, w. Of these e and o are always short, and take about half the time to pronounce as h and w, which are always long; a, i, u are short in some syllables, long in others. In this Grammar, when a, i, u are not marked as long (a_, i_, u_) they are understood to be short. All vowels with the circumflex (149) are long. On length by position, see 144. a. Vowels are said to be open or close according as the mouth is more open or less open in pronouncing them, the tongue and lips assuming different positions in the case of each.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: A diphthong (di/fqoggos having two sounds) combines two vowels in one syllable. The second vowel is i or u. The diphthongs are: ai, ei, oi, a_|, h|, w|; au, eu, ou, hu, and ui. The i of the so-called improper diphthongs, a_|, h|, w|, is written below the line and is called iota subscript. But with capital letters, i is written on the line (adscript), as *t*h*i *w*i*d*h*i = th=| w)|dh=| or *)widh=| to the song. All diphthongs are long. a. In a|, h|, w| the i ceased to be written about 100 B.C. The custom of writing i under the line is as late as about the eleventh century.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: ei, ou are either genuine or spurious (apparent) diphthongs (25). Genuine ei, ou are a combination of e + i, o + u, as in lei/pw I leave (cp. le/loipa I have left, 35 a), ge/nei to a race (49), a)ko/louqos follower (cp. ke/leuqos way). Spurious ei, ou arise from contraction (50) or compensatory lengthening (37). Thus, e)fi/lei he loved, from e)fi/lee, qei/s placing from qent-s; e)fi/loun they loved from e)fi/leon, plou=s voyage from plo/os, dou/s giving from dont-s.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The figure of a triangle represents the relations of the vowels and spurious diphthongs to one another. From a_ to i and from a^ to ou the elevation of the tongue gradually increases. w, o, ou, u are accompanied by rounding of the lips.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Diaeresis.—A double dot, the mark of diaeresis (diai/resis separation), may be written over i or u when these do not form a diphthong with the preceding vowel: proi+/sthmi I set before, nhi+/ to a ship.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Every initial vowel or diphthong has either the rough (‘) or the smooth (’) breathing. The rough breathing (spiritus asper) is pronounced as h, which is sounded before the vowel; the smooth breathing (spiritus lenis) is not sounded. Thus, o(/ros hóros boundary, o)/ros óros mountain.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Initial u (u^ and u_) always has the rough breathing.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Diphthongs take the breathing, as the accent (152), over the second vowel: ai(re/w hairéo I seize, ai)/rw aíro I lift. But a|, h|, w| take both the breathing and the accent on the first vowel, even when i is written in the line (5): a)/|dw = *)/aidw I sing, a(/|dhs = *(/a_idhs Hades, but *ai)nei/a_s Aeneas. The writing a)i/dhlos (*)ai/dhlos) destroying shows that ai does not here form a diphthong; and hence is sometimes written ai+ (8).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: In compound words (as in proora=n to foresee, from pro/ + o(ra=n) the rough breathing is not written, though it must often have been pronounced: cp. e)ce/dra_ a hall with seats, Lat. exhedra, exedra, polui/stwr very learned, Lat. polyhistor. On Attic inscriptions in the old alphabet (2 a) we find *e*u*h*o*r*k*o*n eu)o(/rkon faithful to one's oath.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Every initial r has the rough breathing: r(h/twr orator (Lat. rhetor). Medial rr is written r)r( in some texts: *pu/r)r(os Pyrrhus.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The sign for the rough breathing is derived from H, which in the Old Attic alphabet (2 a) was used to denote h. Thus, HO o( the. After H was used to denote h, one half ([rough ]) was used for h (about 300 B.C.), and, later, the other half ([smooth]) for the smooth breathing. From [rough ] and [smooth] come the forms ‘and’.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The seventeen consonants are divided into stops (or mutes), spirants, liquids, nasals, and double consonants. They may be arranged according to the degree of tension or slackness of the vocal chords in sounding them, as follows: a. Voiced (sonant, i.e. sounding) consonants are produced when the vocal chords vibrate. The sounds are represented by the letters b, d, g (stops), l, r (liquids), m, n, g-nasal (19 a) (nasals), and z. (All the vowels are voiced.) r with the rough breathing is voiceless. b. Voiceless (surd, i.e. hushed) consonants require no exertion of the vocal chords. These are p, t, k, f, q, x (stops), s (spirant or sibilant), and y and c. c. Arranged according to the increasing degree of noise, nearest to the vowels are the nasals, in sounding which the air escapes without friction through the nose; next come the semivowels [uglide] and [iglide] (20 a), the liquids, and the spirant s, in sounding which the air escapes with friction through the cavity of the mouth; next come the stops, which are produced by a removal of an obstruction; and finally the double consonants.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Stops (or mutes). Stopped consonants are so called because in sounding them the breath passage is for a moment completely closed. The stops are divided into three classes (according to the part of the mouth chiefly active in sounding them) and into three orders (according to the degree of force in the expiratory effort). Classes Labial (lip sounds) p b f Dental (teeth sounds) t d q Palatal (palate sounds) k g x Orders Smooth p t k Middle b d g Rough f q x a. The dentals are sometimes called linguals. The rough stops are also called aspirates (lit. breathed sounds) because they were sounded with a strong emission of breath (26). The smooth stops are thus distinguished from the rough stops by the absence of breathing. ( (h) is also an aspirate. The middle stops owe their name to their position in the above grouping, which is that of the Greek grammarians.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Spirants.—There is one spirant: s (also called a sibilant). a. A spirant is heard when the breath passage of the oral cavity is so narrowed that a rubbing noise is produced by an expiration.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Liquids.—There are two liquids: l and r. Initial r always has the rough breathing (13).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Nasals.—There are three nasals: m (labial), n (dental), and g-nasal (palatal). a. Gamma before k, g, x, c is called g-nasal. It had the sound of n in think, and was represented by n in Latin. Thus, a)/gku_ra (Lat. ancora) anchor, a)/ggelos (Lat. angelus) messenger, sfi/gc sphinx. b. The name liquids is often used to include both liquids and nasals.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Semivowels.—i, u, the liquids, nasals, and the spirant s are often called semivowels. ([iglide] becoming z, and v are also called spirants.) a. When i and u correspond to y and w (cp. minion, persuade) they are said to be unsyllabic; and, with a following vowel, make one syllable out of two. Semivocalic i and u are written [iglide] and [uglide]. Initial [iglide] passed into ( (h), as in h(=par liver, Lat. jecur; and into z in zugo/n yoke, Lat. jugum (here it is often called the spirant yod). Initial [uglide] was written v (3). Medial [iglide], [uglide] before vowels were often lost, as in ti_ma/-（[iglide]) w I honour, bo（[uglide]）-o/s, gen. of bou=-s ox, cow (43). b. The form of many words is due to the fact that the liquids, nasals, and s may fulfil the office of a vowel to form syllables (cp. bridle, even, pst). This is expressed by l?o?, m?o?, n?o?, r?o?, s?o?, to be read ‘syllabic l,’ etc., or ‘sonant l’ (see 35 b, c).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Double Consonants.—These are z, c, and y. z is a combination of sd (or ds) or di (26). c is written for ks, gt, xt; y for ps, bs, fs.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: No consonant except n, r, or s (including c and y) can stand at the end of a Greek word. All other consonants are dropped. a. Exceptions are the proclitics (179) e)k out of, derived from e)c (cp. 104, 136), and ou)k not, of which ou) is another form (137). b. Examples of dropped final consonants: sw=ma body for swmat (gen. sw/matos); pai= oh boy for paid (gen. paid-o/s); ga/la milk for galakt (gen. ga/lakt-os); fe/ron bearing for feront (gen. fe/ront-os); kh=r heart for khrd, cp. kard-i/a_; a)/llo for a)l[iglide]od (110), cp. Lat. aliud; e)/fere- (t) was carrying, e)/fero-n (t) were carrying (464 c, e). c. An original final m preceded by a vowel becomes n, cp. i(/ppon with Lat. equum. So e(/n one from e(m (349 a), Lat. sem-el, a(/ma once.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: There are three accents in Greek. No Greek accent can stand farther back than the antepenult. 1. Acute (/): over short or long vowels and diphthongs. It may stand on ultima, penult, or antepenult: kalo/s, dai/mwn, a)/nqrwpos. 2. Circumflex (=): over vowels long by nature and diphthongs. It may stand on ultima or penult: gh=, qeou=, dw=ron, tou=to. 3. Grave (\): over short or long vowels and diphthongs. It stands on the ultima only: to a)/ndra, th tu/xhn, oi( qeoi\ th=s ( *ella/dos.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The acute marks syllables pronounced in a raised tone. The grave is a low-pitched tone as contrasted with the acute. The circumflex combines acute and grave.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Accented syllables in Ancient Greek had a higher pitch (to/nos) than unaccented syllables, and it was the rising and falling of the pitch that made Ancient Greek a musical language. The Greek word for accent is prosw|di/a_ (Lat. accentus: from ad-cano), i.e. ‘song accompanying words.’ Musical accent (elevation and depression of tone) is to be distinguished from quantity (duration of tone), and from rhythmic accent (stress of voice at fixed intervals when there is a regular sequence of long and short syllables). N.—The accent heard in Modern Greek and English is a stress-accent. Stress is produced by strong and weak expiration, and takes account of accented syllables to the neglect of the quantity of unaccented syllables. Thus, shortly after Christ, a)/nqrwpos was often pronounced like a dactyl, fi/los like a trochee; and pro/swpon, e)nne/a, were even written pro/sopon, e/nnh/a.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The marks of accent are placed over the vowel of the accented syllable. A diphthong has the accent over its second vowel (tou=to), except in the case of capital a|, h|, w| (as (/ *aidhs, 5), where the accent stands before the first vowel.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: A breathing is written before the acute and grave (oi(/, h)/), but under the circumflex (w)=, ou(=tos). Accents and breathings are placed before capitals: (/ *omhros, (= *wrai. The accent stands over a mark of diaeresis (8): klhi+=di.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The grave is written in place of a final acute on a word that is followed immediately by another word in the sentence. Thus, meta\ th ma/xhn after the battle (for meta/ th/n ma/xhn). It is also sometimes placed on ti\s, ti\ (334), to distinguish these indefinite pronouns from the interrogatives ti/s, ti/. a. An oxytone (157) changes its acute to the grave when followed by another word, except: (1) when the oxytone is followed by an enclitic (183 a); (2) in ti/s, ti/ interrogative, as ti/s ou(=tos; who's this? (3) when an elided syllable follows the accented syllable: nu/xq' o(/lhn (124), not nu\xq' o(/lhn (174 a); (4) when a colon or period follows. (Usage varies before a comma.)

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The ancients regarded the grave originally as belonging to every syllable not accented with the acute or circumflex; and some Mss. show this in practice, e.g. pa\gkra\th/s. Later it was restricted to its use as a substitute for a final acute.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The circumflex is formed from the union of the acute and the grave (/\ = ^), never from \/. Thus, pai=s = pa/i\s, eu)= = e)/u\. Similarly, since every long vowel may be resolved into two short units (morae), tw=n may be regarded as = to/o. The circumflex was thus spoken with a rising tone followed by one of lower pitch. mou=sa, dh=mos are thus = mo/u\sa, de/e\mos; mou/shs, dh/mou are = mo\u/shs, de\e/mou. In didou=sa (i.e. dido/u\sa) compared with didou/s the accent has receded (159) one mora. a. The whole vowel receives the acute when the second short unit of a vowel long by nature is accented: *di/_ = *di\i/.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Words are named according to their accent as follows: Oxytone (acute on the ultima): qh/r, kalo/s, lelukw/s. Paroxytone (acute on the penult): lu/_w, lei/pw, leluko/tos. Proparoxytone (acute on the antepenult): a)/nqrwpos, paideu/omen. Perispomenon (circumflex on the ultima): gh=, qeou=. Properispomenon (circumflex on the penult): pra=cis, mou=sa. Barytone (when the ultima is unaccented, 158): mou=sa, mh/thr, po/lemos.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: A word is called barytone (baru/-tonos deep-toned, low-toned) when it has no accent on the ultima. All paroxytones, proparoxytones, and properispomena are also barytones.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: An accent is called recessive when it moves back as far from the end of the word as the quantity of the ultima permits (166). The quantity of the penult is here disregarded (tre/pwmen). Cp. 178.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Oxytone (o)cu/s, sharp + to/nos) means ‘sharp-toned,’ perispomenon (perispw/menos) ‘turned-around’ (circumflectus, 156). Paroxytone and proparoxytone are derived from o)cu/tonos with the prepositions para/ and pro/ respectively. Acute corresponds to Lat. acutus (o)cei=a, scil. prosw|di/a_).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The invention of the marks of accent is attributed to Aristophanes of Byzantium, librarian at Alexandria about 200 B.C. The use of signs served to fix the correct accentuation, which was becoming uncertain in the third century B.C.; marked the variation of dialect usage; and rendered the acquisition of Greek easier for foreigners. The signs for the accents (and the breathings) were not regularly employed in Mss. till after 600 A.D.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The position of the accent has to be learned by observation. But the kind of accent is determined by the following rules.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The antepenult, if accented, can have the acute only (a)/nqrwpos, basi/leia queen, oi)kofu/lakos of a house-guard). If the ultima is long, either by nature or by position (144), the antepenult cannot take an accent: hence a)nqrw/pou (176 a), basilei/a_ kingdom, oi/kofu/lac. a. Some nouns in -ews and -ewn admit the acute on the antepenult. Thus, the genitive of nouns in -is and -us (po/lews, po/lewn, a)/stews), the forms of the Attic declension, as i(/_lews (289). So the Ionic genitive in -ew (poli/_tew); also some compound adjectives in -ws, as du/serws unhappy in love, u(yi/kerws lofty antlered. On w(=ntinwn see 186.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The penult, if accented and long, takes the circumflex when the ultima is short by nature (nh=sos, tau=ta). In all other cases it has the acute (fo/bos, leluko/tos, tou/tou). a. Apparent exceptions are w(/ste, ou)/tis, h(/de (properly h(=de). See 186. b. A final syllable containing a vowel short by nature followed by c or y does not permit the acute to stand on the antepenult (oi)kofu/lac); but the circumflex may stand on the penult (kh=ruc).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The ultima, if accented and short, has the acute (potamo/s); if accented and long, has either the acute (lelukw/s), or the circumflex (*periklh=s).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: When the ultima is long, the acute cannot stand on the antepenult, nor the circumflex on the penult. Thus, a)/nqrwpou and dw=rou are impossible.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: When the ultima is short, a word, if accented a. on the ultima, has the acute: sofo/s. b. on a short penult, has the acute: no/mos. c. on a long penult, has the circumflex: dw=ron. d. on the antepenult, has the acute: a)/nqrwpos.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: When the ultima is long, a word, if accented a. on the ultima, has the acute or the circumflex: e)gw/, sofw=s. b. on the penult, has the acute: le/wn, dai/mwn.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Final -ai and -oi are regarded as short: mou=sai, bou/lomai, pro/palai, a)/nqrwpoi. But in the optative -ai and -oi are long (lu/_sai, bouleu/oi), as in contracted syllables. So also in the locative oi)/koi at home (but oi)=koi houses). a. The difference in the quantitative treatment of -ai and -oi depends on an original difference of accentuation that may have vanished in Greek. -ai and -oi, when short, were pronounced with a clipped, or simple, tone; when long, with a drawled, or compound, tone.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The quantity of a, i, u (147) may often be learned from the accent. Thus, in qa/latta, h(/misus, ph=xus, du/namis, mh=nis, the vowel of the last syllable must be short; in fi/los the i must be short (otherwise fi=los). Cp. 163.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: ACCENT AS AFFECTED BY CONTRACTION, CRASIS, AND ELISION
sections.en: Contraction.—If either of the syllables to be contracted had an accent, the contracted syllable has an accent. Thus: a. A contracted antepenult has the acute: fileo/menos = filou/menos. b. A contracted penult has the circumflex when the ultima is short; the acute, when the ultima is long: file/ousi = filou=si, fileo/ntwn = filou/ntwn. c. A contracted ultima has the acute when the uncontracted form was oxytone: e(staw/s = e(stw/s; otherwise, the circumflex: file/w = filw=. N. 1.—A contracted syllable has the circumflex only when, in the uncontracted form, an acute was followed by the (unwritten) grave (155, 156). Thus, *perikle/h\s = *periklh=s, ti_ma/w\ = ti_mw=. In all other cases we have the acute: file\o/ntwn = filou/ntwn, beba\w/s = bebw/s. N. 2.—Exceptions to 171 are often due to the analogy of other forms (236 a, 264 e, 279 a, 290 c, 309 a).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: ACCENT AS AFFECTED BY CONTRACTION, CRASIS, AND ELISION
sections.en: If neither of the syllables to be contracted had an accent, the contracted syllable has no accent: fi/lee = fi/lei, ge/nei+ = ge/nei, peri/ploos = peri/plous. For exceptions, see 236 b.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: ACCENT AS AFFECTED BY CONTRACTION, CRASIS, AND ELISION
sections.en: Crasis.—In crasis, the first word (as less important) loses its accent: ta)_gaqa/ for ta\ a)gaqa/, ta)_n for ta\ e)n, ka)_gw/ for kai\ e)gw/. a. If the second word is a dissyllabic paroxytone with short ultima, it is uncertain whether, in crasis, the paroxytone remains or changes to properispomenon. In this book tou)/rgon, ta)/_lla are written for to\ e)/rgon, ta\ a)/lla; but many scholars write tou)=rgon, ta)=lla.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: ACCENT AS AFFECTED BY CONTRACTION, CRASIS, AND ELISION
sections.en: Elision.—In elision, oxytone prepositions and conjunctions lose their accent: par' (for para\) e)mou=, a)ll' (for a)lla\) e)gw/. In other oxytones the accent is thrown back to the penult: po/ll' (for polla\) e)/paqon. a. Observe that in po/ll' e)/paqon the acute is not changed to the grave (154 a, 3). A circumflex does not result from the recession of the accent. Thus, fh/m' (not fh=m') e)gw/ for fhmi\ e)gw/. tina/ and pote/, after a word which cannot receive their accent (183 d), drop their accent: ou(/tw pot' h)=n.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Anastrophe (a)nastrofh/ turning-back) occurs in the case of oxytone prepositions of two syllables, which throw the accent back on the first syllable. a. When the preposition follows its case: tou/twn pe)ri (for peri\ tou/twn) about these things. No other preposition than peri/ follows its case in prose. N. 1.—In poetry anastrophe occurs with the other dissyllabic prepositions (except a)nti/, a)mfi/, dia/). In Homer a preposition following its verb and separated from it by tmesis (1650) also admits anastrophe (lou/sh| a)/po for a)polou/sh|). N. 2.—When the final vowel of the preposition is elided, the accent is dropped if no mark of punctuation intervenes: xersi u(f' h(mete/rh|sin B 374. b. When a preposition stands for a compound formed of the preposition and e)sti/. Thus, pa/ra for pa/resti it is permitted, e)/ni for e)/nesti it is possible (e)ni/ is a poetic form of e)n). N.—In poetry, pa/ra may stand for pa/reisi or pa/reimi; and a)/na arise! up! is used for a)na/sthqi. Hom. has e)/ni = e)/neisi.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: CHANGE OF ACCENT IN DECLENSION, INFLECTION, AND COMPOSITION
sections.en: When a short ultima of the nominative is lengthened in an oblique case a. a proparoxytone becomes paroxytone: qa/latta qala/tths, a)/nqrwpos a)nqrw/pou. b. a properispomenon becomes paroxytone: mou=sa mou/shs, dw=ron dw/ron. c. an oxytone becomes perispomenon in the genitive and dative of the second declension: qeo/s qeou= qew=| qew=n qeoi=s.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: CHANGE OF ACCENT IN DECLENSION, INFLECTION, AND COMPOSITION
sections.en: When, for a long ultima, a short ultima is substituted in inflection a. a dissyllabic paroxytone (with penult long by nature) becomes properispomenon: lu/_w lu=e. b. a polysyllabic paroxytone (with penult either long or short) becomes proparoxytone: paideu/w pai/deue, ple/kw ple/komen.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.group: CHANGE OF ACCENT IN DECLENSION, INFLECTION, AND COMPOSITION
sections.en: In composition the accent is usually recessive (159) in the case of substantives and adjectives, regularly in the case of verbs: ba/sis a)na/basis, qeo/s a)/qeos, lu=e a)po/lu_e. a. Proper names having the form of a substantive, adjective, or participle, usually change the accent: *)/elpis (e)lpi/s), *glau=kos (glauko/s), *ge/lwn (gelw=n). b. Special cases will be considered under Declension and Inflection.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Ten monosyllabic words have no accent and are closely connected with the following word. They are called proclitics (from prokli/_nw lean forward). They are: The forms of the article beginning with a vowel (o(, h(, oi(, ai(); the prepositions e)n, ei)s (e)s), e)c (e)k); the conjunction ei) if; w(s as, that (also a preposition to); the negative adverb ou) (ou)k, ou)x, 137).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: A proclitic sometimes takes an accent, thus: a. ou) at the end of a sentence: fh/|s, h)\ ou)/; do you say so or not? pw=s ga\r ou)/; for why not? Also ou)/ no standing alone. b. e)c, e)n, and ei)s receive an acute in poetry when they follow the word to which they belong and stand at the end of the verse: kakw=n e)/c out of evils *c 472 . c. w(s as becomes w(/s in poetry when it follows its noun: qeo\s w(/s as a god. w(s standing for ou(/tws is written w(/s even in prose (ou)d' w(/s not even thus). d. When the proclitic precedes an enclitic (183 e): e)/n tisi. N.—o( used as a relative (for o(/s, 1105) is written o(/. On o(/ demonstrative see 1114.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Enclitics (from e)gkli/_nw lean on, upon) are words attaching themselves closely to the preceding word, after which they are pronounced rapidly. Enclitics usually lose their accent. They are: a. The personal pronouns mou=, moi/, me/; sou=, soi/, se/; ou(=, oi(=, e(/, and (in poetry) sfi/si. b. The indefinite pronoun ti\s, ti\ in all cases (including tou=, tw=| for tino/s, tini/, but excluding a)/tta = tina/); the indefinite adverbs pou/ (or poqi/), ph/|, poi/, poqe/n, pote/, pw/, pw/s. When used as interrogatives these words are not enclitic (ti/s, ti/, pou= (or po/qi), ph=|, poi=, po/qen, po/te, pw=, pw=s). c. All dissyllabic forms of the present indicative of ei)mi/ am and fhmi/ say (i.e. all except ei)= and fh/|s). d. The particles ge/, te/, toi/, pe/r; the inseparable -de in o(/de, toso/sde, etc. N.—Enclitics, when they retain their accent, are called orthotone. See 187.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The accent of an enclitic, when it is thrown back upon the preceding word, always appears as an acute: qh/r te (not qh=r te) from qh/r + te/.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: The word preceding an enclitic is treated as follows: a. An oxytone keeps its accent, and does not change an acute to a grave (154 a): do/s moi, kalo/n e)sti. b. A perispomenon keeps its accent: filw= se, ti_mw=n tinwn. c. A proparoxytone or properispomenon receives, as an additional accent, the acute on the ultima: a)/nqrwpo/s tis, a)/nqrwpoi/ tines, h)/kousa/ tinwn; sw=so/n me, pai=de/s tines. d. A paroxytone receives no additional accent: a monosyllabic enclitic loses its accent (xw/ra_ tis, fi/los mou), a dissyllabic enclitic retains its accent (xw/ra_s tino/s, fi/loi tine/s) except when its final vowel is elided (174 a). N.—Like paroxytones are treated properispomena ending in c or y when followed by a dissyllabic enclitic: kh=ruc e)sti/; and so probably kh=ruc tis. e. A proclitic (179) takes an acute: e)/n tini, ei)/ tines.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Since an enclitic, on losing its accent, forms a part of the preceding word, the writing a)/nqrwpos tis would violate the rule (149) that no word can be accented on a syllable before the antepenult. A paroxytone receives no additional accent in order that two successive syllables may not have the acute (not fi/lo/s e)stin).

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: When several enclitics occur in succession, each receives an accent from the following, only the last having no accent: ei)/ pou/ ti/s tina i)/doi e)xqro/n if ever any one saw an enemy anywhere T. 4.47 .

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: Sometimes an enclitic unites with a preceding word to form a compound (cp. Lat. -que, -ve), which is accented as if the enclitic were still a separate word. Thus, ou)/te (not ou)=te), w(/ste, ei)/te, kai/toi, ou(=tinos, w(=|tini, w(=ntinwn; usually per (e(/sper); and the inseparable -de in o(/de, tou/sde, oi)/kade; and -qe and -xi in ei)/qe (poetic ai)/qe), nai/xi. ou)/te, w(=|tini, etc., are not real exceptions to the rules of accent (163, 164). a. oi(=o/s te able is sometimes written oi(=o/ste. ou)k ou)=n is usually written ou)/koun not therefore , and not therefore? in distinction from ou)kou=n therefore. e)gw/ ge and e)moi/ ge may become e)/gwge, e)/moige.

sections.part: Part I: Letters, Sounds, Syllables, Accent
sections.en: An enclitic retains its accent (is orthotone, cp. 181 N.): a. When it is emphatic, as in contrasts: h)\ soi\ h)\ tw=| patri/ sou either to you or to your father (e)mou=, e)moi/, e)me/ are emphatic: ei)pe\ kai\ e)moi/ tell me too), and at the beginning of a sentence or clause: fhmi\ ga/r I say in fact. b. e)sti/ is written e)/sti at the beginning of a sentence; when it expresses existence or possibility; when it follows ou)k, mh/, ei), w(s, kai/, a)lla/ (or a)ll'), tou=to (or tou=t'); and in e)/stin oi(/ some, e)/stin o(/te sometimes. Thus, ei) e)/stin ou(/tws if it is so, tou=to d e)/sti that which exists. c. In the phrases pote\ me . . . pote\ de/, tine\s me . . . tine\s de/. d. After a word suffering elision: polloi\ d' ei)si/n (for de/ ei)sin), tau=t' e)sti/. e. When a dissyllabic enclitic follows a paroxytone (183 d). N. 1.—When they are used as indirect reflexives in Attic prose (1228), the pronouns of the third person ou(= and sfi/si are orthotone, oi(= is generally enclitic, while e(/ is generally orthotone. N. 2.—After oxytone prepositions and e(/neka enclitic pronouns (except ti\s) usually keep their accent (e)pi\ soi/, not e)pi/ soi; e(/neka sou=, not e(/neka/ sou; e(/neka/ tou, not e(/neka tou=). e)mou=, e)moi/, e)me/ are used after prepositions (except pro/s me; and in the drama a)mfi/ moi).
Declension deals with variations of number, gender, and case.

Number.—There are three numbers: singular, dual, and plural. The dual speaks of two or a pair, as tw\ o)fqalmw/ the two eyes; but it is not often used, and the plural (which denotes more than one) is frequently substituted for it (oi( o)fqalmoi/ the eyes).

Gender.—There are three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter. a. Gender strictly marks sex-distinction. But in Greek, as in German and French, many inanimate objects are regarded as masculine or feminine. Such words are said to have ‘grammatical’ gender, which is determined only by their form. Words denoting objects without natural gender usually show their grammatical gender by the form of the adjective, as makro\s lo/gos a long speech, makra\_ nh=sos a long island, makro tei=xos a long wall. b. The gender of Greek words is usually indicated by means of the article: o( for masculine, h( for feminine, to/ for neuter.

Rule of Natural Gender.—Nouns denoting male persons are masculine, nouns denoting female persons are feminine. Thus, o( nau/ths seaman, o( stratiw/ths soldier, h( gunh/ woman, h( ko/rh maiden. a. A whole class is designated by the masculine: oi( a)/nqrwpoi men, i.e. men and women. b. EXCEPTIONS TO THE RULE OF NATURAL GENDER.—Diminutives in -ion are neuter (199 d), as to\ a)nqrw/pion manikin (o( a)/nqrwpos man), to\ paidi/on little child (male or female, o( or h( pai=s child), to\ gu/naion little woman (h( gunh/ woman). Also the words te/knon, te/kos child (strictly ‘thing born’), a)ndra/podon captive.

Common Gender.—Many nouns denoting persons are either masculine or feminine. Thus, o( pai=s boy, h( pai=s girl, o( qeo/s god, h( qeo/s (h( qea/_ poet.) goddess. So with names of animals: o( bou=s ox, h( bou=s cow, o( i(/ppos horse, h( i(/ppos mare. a. Some names of animals have only one grammatical gender without regard to sex, as o( lagw/s he-hare or she-hare, h( a)lw/phc he-fox or she-fox.

Gender of Sexless Objects.—The gender of most nouns denoting sexless objects has to be learned by the endings (211, 228, 255) and by observation. The following general rules should be noted. a. Masculine are the names of winds, months, and most rivers. Thus, o( *bore/a_s the North Wind, o( *(ekatombaiw/n Hecatombaeon, o( *khfisso/s Cephissus. N.—The gender of these proper names is made to correspond to o( a)/nemos wind, o( mh/n month, o( potamo/s river. In the case of winds and rivers the gender may be due in part to personification. b. Feminine are the names of almost all countries, islands, cities, trees, and plants. Thus, h( *)attikh/ Attica, h( *dh=los Delos, h( *ko/rinqos Corinth, h( pi/tus pine, h( a)/mpelos vine. The gender here follows that of h( gh= or h( xw/ra_ land, country, h( nh=sos island, h( po/lis city, h( dru=s, originally tree in general, but later oak (to\ de/ndron is the ordinary word for tree). c. Feminine are most abstract words, that is, words denoting a quality or a condition. Thus, h( a)reth/ virtue, h( eu)/noia good-will, h( taxu/ths swiftness, h( e)lpi/s hope. d. Neuter are diminutives (197 b), words and expressions quoted, letters of the alphabet, infinitives, and indeclinable nouns. Thus, to\ u(_mei=s the word ‘you,’ to\ gnw=qi seauto/n the saying ‘learn to know thyself,’ to\ a)/lfa alpha, to\ paideu/ein to educate, to\ xrew/n necessity. N.—But some names of women end in -ion (197 b): h( *gluke/rion Glycerium.

Remarks.—a. Most of the exceptions to 199 a-b are due to the endings; e.g. h( *lh/qh Lethe, h( *stu/c Styx (rivers of the Lower World), to\ *)/argos Argos, o( *kaludw/n Calydon, to\ *)/i_lion Ilium, oi( *delfoi/ Delphi, o( lwto/s lotus. b. Change in gender is often associated with change in form: o( lu/kos he-wolf, h( lu/kaina she-wolf, o( poihth/s poet, h( poih/tria poetess, o( bi/otos and h( bioth/ life, o( tro/pos manner, h( troph/ rout. c. The gender of one word may influence that of another word of like meaning. Thus h( nh=sos island and h( li/qos stone are feminine probably because of h( gh= land and h( pe/tra_ rock.

Cases.—There are five cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative. The genitive denotes from as well as of, the dative denotes to or for and also by, with, on, in, at, etc. The other cases are used as in Latin. a. The genitive, dative, and accusative are called oblique cases to distinguish them from the nominative and vocative.

The vocative is often like the nominative in the singular; in the plural it is always the same. Nominative, vocative, and accusative have the same form in neuter words, and always have a in the plural. In the dual there are two forms, one for nominative, accusative, and vocative, the other for genitive and dative.

Lost Cases.—Greek has generally lost the forms of the instrumental and locative cases (which have become fused with the dative) and of the ablative. The Greek dative is used to express by, as in bi/a|, Lat. ui_ ; with, as in li/qois with stones; and in, on, as in gh=| on the earth. From may be expressed by the genitive: po/rrw *spa/rths far from Sparta. When the genitive and dative do duty for the ablative, prepositions are often used. Instances of the forms of the lost cases are given in 341.

Declensions.—There are three declensions, which are named from the stems to which the case endings are attached. 1. First or Â-declension, with stems in a_) Vowel Declension. 2. Second or O-declension, with stems in o) 3. Third or Consonant declension, with stems in a consonant or in i and u. The nominative and accusative are alike in the singular and plural of all neuter nouns. The nominative and vocative are alike in the plural.
Stems in a_ are masculine or feminine. The feminine nominative singular ends in -a_, -a^, or -h; the masculine nominative singular adds -s to the stem, and thus ends in -a_s or -hs.

V. a_ Gen. a_-s or h-s h-s a_-io (Hom. a_-o） w=n (for e/-wn, a/_-wn） G. D. a-in Dat. a_-i or h-i h-i a_-i h-i a-is or a-isi（n） Acc. a_-n or a^-n h-n a_-n h-n a_s (for a-ns） Voc. a_ or a^ h a_ a^ or h a-i Observe the shortening of the stem in vocative singular and plural, in nominative and dative plural, and genitive and dative dual.

Accent.—For special rule of accent in the genitive plural, see 208. The genitive plural is always perispomenon since -w=n is contracted from -e/-wn derived from original (and Hom.) -a/_-wn (51). Final -ai is treated as short (169). a. The form of the gen. pl. is taken from the pronominal adjective, i.e. (Hom.) qea/_wn goddesses follows the analogy of (Hom.) ta/_wn (332 D.) for ta_- (s）wn, cf. Lat. istā-rum deā-rum.
The dialects show various forms.

Dative Plural.—The ending -aisi（n) occurs in Attic poetry (di/kaisi from di/kh right, despo/taisi from despo/ths lord). a. Attic inscriptions to 420 B. C. have -h|si (written -hisi), -hsi, and (after e, i, r) -a|si (written -aisi) and -a_si. Thus, draxmh=|si and draxmh=si drachmas, tami/a|si and tami/a_si stewards. -hsi and -a_si are properly endings of the locative case (341).

I. FEMININES SINGULAR h( xw/ra_ h( ni/_kh h( fugh/ h( moi=ra h( glw=tta h( qa/latta （xwra_-） （ni_ka_-） （fuga_-） （moira_-） （glwtta_-） （qalatta_-） land victory flight fate tongue sea Nom. xw/ra_ ni/_kh fugh/ moi=ra glw=tta qa/latta Gen. xw/ra_s ni/_khs fugh=s moi/ra_s glw/tths qala/tths Dat. xw/ra| ni/_kh| fugh=| moi/ra| glw=tth| qala/tth| Acc. xw/ra_-n ni/_kh-n fugh/-n moi=ra-n glw=tta-n qa/latta-n Voc. xw/ra_ ni/_kh fugh/ moi=ra glw=tta qa/latta DUAL N. A. V. xw/ra_ ni/_ka_ fuga/_ moi/ra_ glw/tta_ qala/tta_ G. D. xw/rain ni/_kain fugai=n moi/rain glw/ttain qala/ttain PLURAL N. V. xw=rai ni=kai fugai/ moi=rai glw=ttai qa/lattai Gen. xwrw=n ni_kw=n fugw=n moirw=n glwttw=n qalattw=n Dat. xw/rais ni/_kais fugai=s moi/rais glw/ttais qala/ttais Acc. xw/ra_s ni/_ka_s fuga/_s moi/ra_s glw/tta_s qala/tta_s w(/ra_ season, h(me/ra_ day, skia/_ shadow, ma/xh battle, te/xnh art, gnw/mh judgment, ti_mh/ honor, a)reth/ virtue, mou=sa muse, prw=ra prow, a(/maca wagon, do/ca opinion.

RULES.—a. If the nominative singular ends in alpha preceded by a vowel (skia/_ shadow) or r (moi=ra), alpha is kept throughout the singular. b. If the nominative singular ends in alpha preceded by a consonant not r, alpha is changed to h in the genitive and dative singular. c. If the nominative singular ends in h, h is kept in all the cases of the singular. d. When the genitive singular has -hs, final a of the nominative singular is always short; when the genitive singular has -a_s, the final a is generally long. Feminines fall into two classes:

(I) Feminines with a_ or h in all the cases of the singular. After e, i, or r, a_ appears in all the cases of the singular, as in genea/_ race, oi)ki/a_ house, xw/ra_ land. Otherwise, h throughout the singular, as ni/_kh victory. a. After o, we find both a_ and h, as stoa/_ porch, boh/ shout, a)koh/ hearing, o(|oh/ current, r(o/a_ pomegranate. After r we have h in ko/rh girl, de/rh neck (31).

(II) Feminines with a^ in the nominative, accusative, and vocative singular. The quantity of the vowel is generally shown by the accent (163, 164). In this class are included: 1. Substantives having s (c, y, tt, or ss), z, ll, or ain before the final a show a^ in nom., accus., and voc. sing., and h in gen. and dat. sing. Thus, mou=sa muse, mou/shs, mou/sh|, a(/maca wagon, tra/peza table, glw=tta tongue, r(i/za root, a(/milla contest, le/aina lioness. Others are to/lma daring, di/aita mode of life, a)/kanqa thorn, mui=a fly. 2. Substantives in a^ in nom., accus., and voc. sing., and a_ in gen. and dat. sing. a. Substantives in -eia and -tria denoting females, as basi/leia queen (but basilei/a_ kingdom), ya/ltria female harper; so the fem. of adj. in -us, as gluku/s, glukei=a sweet. b. Abstracts in -eia and -oia from adjectives in -hs and -oos, as a)lh/qeia truth (from a)lhqh/s true), eu)/noia good will (from eu)/nous, eu)/noos kind, 290). c. Most substantives in -ra after a diphthong or u_, as moi=ra fate, ge/fu_ra bridge.

Exceptions to 219, 1: ko/rsh temple (later ko/rrh), e(/rsh dew; to 2 b: in Attic poetry, a)lhqei/a_, eu)noi/a_, a)gnoi/a_ ignorance, which owe their a_ to the influence of the genitive and dative a)lhqei/a_s, a)lhqei/a|, etc.

Most, if not all, of the substantives in a^ are formed by the addition of the suffix [iglide]a or ia (20); thus, glw=tta from glwx-[iglide]a (cp. glwxi=n-es points), ge/fu_ra from gefur-[iglide]a, do/teira giver from doter-[iglide]a (and so fe/rousa bearing from feront[iglide]a), moi=ra from mor-[iglide]a, ya/ltr-ia.

II. MASCULINES SINGULAR o( nea_ni/a_s o( poli/_ths o( krith/s *)atrei/dhs （nea_nia_-） （poli_ta_-） （krita_-） （*)atreida_-） young man citizen judge son of Atreus Nom. nea_ni/a_-s poli/_th-s krith/-s *)atrei/dh-s Gen. nea_ni/ou poli/_tou kritou= *)atrei/dou Dat. nea_ni/a_| poli/_th| krith=| *)atrei/dh| Acc. nea_ni/a_-n poli/_th-n krith/-n *)atrei/dh-n Voc. nea_ni/a_ poli=ta krita/ *)atrei/dh DUAL N. A. V. nea_ni/a_ poli/_ta_ krita/_ *)atrei/da_ G. D. nea_ni/ain poli/_tain kritai=n *)atrei/dain PLURAL N. V. nea_ni/ai poli=tai kritai/ *)atrei=dai Gen. nea_niw=n poli_tw=n kritw=n *)atreidw=n Dat. nea_ni/ais poli/_tais kritai=s *)atrei/dais Acc. nea_ni/a_s poli/_ta_s krita/_s *)atrei/da_s tami/a_s steward, *ai)nei/a_s Aeneas,—nau/ths sailor, toco/ths bowman, stratiw/ths soldier, despo/ths ruler,—maqhth/s pupil, poihth/s poet—*pe/rshs Persian.
Accent.—The vocative of despo/ths lord is de/spota.
a_ and h.—In the final syllable of the singular a_ appears after e, i, and r; otherwise we find h. Cp. 218. a. Exceptions are compounds in -me/trhs: gew-me/trhs measurer of land.

Genitive singular.—The form in -ou is borrowed from the genitive singular of the second declension. A few words in -a_s, generally names of persons not Greeks, have -a_, the Doric genitive (214 D. 5): *)anni/ba_s Hannibal, gen. *)anni/ba_.

Vocative singular.—Masculines in -a_s have the vocative in -a_ (nea_ni/a_); those in -ths have -a^ (poli=ta), all others in -hs have -h (*)atrei/dh, *kroni/dh son of Kronos) except names of nations and compounds: *pe/rsa^ Persian, *sku/qa^ Scythian, gew-me/tra^ (nom. gew-me/trhs measurer of land), paido-tri/ba^ gymnastic master.
Contracts in a_ or h from ea_ or aa_ have the circumflex in all the cases: nominative feminine -a=, -h=, masculine -a=s, -h=s.

O stems in the nominative add -s to the stem in masculines and feminines; -n in neuters. The feminines, of which there are few, are declined like the masculines. In the neuters, nominative, vocative, and accusative singular have the same form (in -o-n); in the plural these cases end in -a.

The dat. sing. in -w| represents the union of the stem vowel -o and ai, the original case ending in the I. E. languages. Forms in -oi, as oi)/koi at home, may be locatives (-o + i, the locative ending).—The stem vowel o varies with e, which appears in the vocative sing., and in pandhmei/ (locative) in full force.— N. A. V. dual -w is for I. E. ōu.—The genitive pl. -wn is due to the union of -o + wn, which contracted to -wn in the earliest period of the language.—The neuter plural is probably the relic of a feminine collective ending in -a_, which was shortened to -a^.
The dialects show various forms.

Feminines.—a. See 197 for nuo/s daughter-in-law; see 199 for nh=sos island (cp. 200 c), *dh=los (the island of) Delos, *ko/rinqos Corinth, fhgo/s (acornbearing) oak, a)/mpelos vine. b. Some are properly adjectives used substantively: dia/lektos (scil. glw=tta speech) dialect, dia/metros (scil. grammh/ line) diameter, au)/leios (scil. qu/ra_ door) house-door, su/gklhtos (scil. boulh/ council) legislative body, e)/rhmos and h)/peiros (scil. xw/ra_ country) desert and mainland. c. Words for way: o(do/s and ke/leuqos way; and a(macito/s carriage-road, a)trapo/s foot-path, which may be adjectival (b) with o(do/s omitted. d. Various other words: ba/sanos touch-stone, bi/blos book, ge/ranos crane, gna/qos jaw, gu/yos chalk, de/ltos writing-tablet, doko/s beam, dro/sos dew, ka/mi_nos oven, ka/rdopos kneading-trough, ki_bwto/s chest, ko/pros dung, lhno/s wine-press, li/qos stone (200 c), no/sos disease, pli/nqos brick, r(a/bdos rod, soro/s coffin, spodo/s ashes, ta/fros trench, xhlo/s coffer, ya/mmos sand, yh=fos pebble.
Vocative.—The nominative qeo/s is used instead of the vocative. a)delfo/s brother retracts the accent (a)/delfe).
Dative Plural.—The ending -oisi（n) often appears in poetry, rarely in Attic prose (Plato). a. In Old Attic inscriptions -ois displaces -oisi（n) about 444 B.C.

Stems in eo and oo are contracted according to 50, 51. ea in the neuter becomes a_ (56). Accent.—a. The nominative dual is irregularly oxytone: nw/, o)stw/, not nw=, o)stw= according to 171, N. 2. b. kanou=n (ka/neon) basket receives its accent (not ka/noun) from that of the genitive and dative kanou=, kanw=|. Cp. 290 c. c. Compounds retain the accent on the syllable that has it in the nominative singular: e)/kplous from e)/kploos; e)/kplou (not e)kplou=) from e)kplo/ou; e)/kplwn (not e)kplw=n) from e)kplo/wn.

Some substantives ending in -ews are placed under the Second Declension because they are derived from earlier o stems preceded by a long vowel (-ews from -hos, 34). A few others have a consonant before -ws. The vocative has no special form. N.—This declension is called “Attic” because the words in question generally show -ws in Attic and -os in the Koinè dialect (p. 3, F).

o( new/s temple SINGULAR DUAL PLURAL Nom. new/-s (Ionic nho/-s） N. A. new/ (Ionic nhw/） Nom. new/| (Ionic nhoi/） Gen. new/ (“ nhou=） G. D. new/|n (“ nhoi=n） Gen. new/n (“ nhw=n） Dat. new/| (“ nhw=|） Dat. new/|s (“ nhoi=s） Acc. new/n (“ nho/-n） Acc. new/s (“ nhou/s） a. So o( lew/s people, o( *mene/lews Menelaus, o( lagw/s hare. Observe that w is found in every form, and that it takes i subscript in the dative of all numbers where an ordinary o stem has i. b. There are no neuter substantives belonging to the Attic declension in standard classical literature; but neuter adjectives (289) end in -wn. c. new/s and most words of this declension owe their forms to transfer of quantity (34) or to shortening (39). Thus, new/s is from nho/s ( = Doric na_o/s), new/n from nho/n; new/| is from nhw=|. lagw/s is contracted from lagwo/s. d. In the accusative singular some words end in -w or -wn, as lagw/ or lagw/n hare. So o( *)/aqws, h( *ke/ws, h( *te/ws, h( *kw=s, o( *mi/_nws. h( e(/ws dawn always has e(/w.

Accent.—a. The accent of the nominative is kept in all cases. *mene/0ews (163 a) retains the accent of the earlier *mene/la_os. b. The genitive and dative are oxytone when the final syllable is accented. N.—The accentuation of the words of this declension is doubtful. Some of the ancients accented lagw/s, lagw/n, others lagw=s, lagw=n, etc.

This declension includes stems ending in a consonant, in i, u, or a diphthong, and some in w and o, representing wv and oi. N.—To determine whether a noun belongs to the third declension it is necessary in most cases to know the stem, which is usually found by dropping -os of the genitive singular. Stems in i and u are classed under the consonant declension because neither of these vowels admits contraction with the case endings beginning with a vowel, herein being like a consonant.

Masculine and feminine stems not ending in n, r, s and ont, add s. a. A labial (p, b, f) + s becomes y (97). b. A dental (t, d, q) + s becomes ss (98), which is reduced to s (107). c. A palatal (k, g, x) or kt + s becomes c (97). (The same changes occur in the dative plural.) gu/_y vulture gu_p-o/s, *)/aray Arab *)/arab-os; kako/ths baseness kako/tht-os, e)lpi/s hope e)lpi/d-os, o)/rni_s bird o)/rni_q-os; fu/lac guard fu/lak-os, ma/sti^c scourge ma/sti_g-os, sa/lpigc trumpet sa/lpigg-os, o)/nuc nail o)/nux-os, nu/c night nukt-o/s; a(/l-s salt a(l-o/s, i)xqu/_s fish i)xqu/-os; e)le/fa_s elephant e)le/fant-os.

Masculine and feminine stems ending in n, r, and s reject s and lengthen a preceding vowel if short (e to h, o to w). dai/mwn divinity dai/mon-os, xeimw/n winter xeimw=n-os, limh/n harbour lime/n-os, *(/ellhn Greek *(/ellhn-os; r(h/twr orator r(h/tor-os, a)h/r air a)e/r-os, fw/r thief fwr-o/s, trih/rhs trireme (stem trihres-, 263 b), ai)dw/s shame (stem ai)dos-, 266). On mh/n see 259 end. For stems in es, nominative -os, see 263 c.
Masculine stems in ont drop t (133) and lengthen o to w: ge/rwn old man ge/ront-os, le/wn lion le/ont-os.

Neuters show the pure stem, from which final t and other consonants not standing at the end of a word (133) are dropped: a(/rma chariot a(/rmat-os, pra=gma thing pra/_gmat-os, ga/la milk ga/lakt-os (133 b).

Summary.—s is added to stems ending in a labial, dental, palatal, and in ant, ent, unt; to some stems in n (as ei(=s one e(n-o/s, me/la_s black me/lan-os); to stems in eu, au, ou; and to masc. and fem. stems in i and u. s is not added to most stems ending in n, nor to those in ont, r, es, as, os, u (neut.), w（v), o（i).

Masculines and feminines usually add a to stems ending in a consonant; n to stems ending in i or u. gu=p-a, o)/nux-a, e)le/fant-a, lime/n-a, r(h/tor-a, le/ont-a; po/li-n, i)xqu/_-n, bou=-n from po/li-s city, i)xqu/_-s fish, bou=-s ox, cow. Stems in eu take a (275).

Barytone stems of two syllables ending in it, id, i_q usually drop the dental and add n. xa/ris grace (stem xarit-) xa/rin, e)/ris strife (e)rid-) e)/rin, o)/rni_s bird (o)rni_q-) o)/rni_n. So eu)/elpis hopeful (eu)elpid-) eu)/elpin (292). Oxytones end in a: e)lpi/d-a, sfra_gi=da (sfra_gi/_s seal). a. klei=s key (kleid-), Old Att. klh/|s, has klei=n (late klei=da), acc. pl. klei=s (late klei=das).

The vocative of masculines and feminines is usually the pure stem. po/li (po/li-s city), bou= (bou=-s ox, cow), *sw/krates (*swkra/ths). Stems in id and nt cannot retain final d and t (133), hence *)/artemi from *)/artemis (*)artemid-), pai= from pai=s boy, girl (paid-), nea=ni from nea=nis maiden (nea_nid-); ge/ron from ge/rwn old man (geront-), gi/gan from gi/ga_s giant (gigant-).

The vocative is the same as the nominative: a. In stems ending in a stop (16) consonant (except those in it, id, i_q; nt in nouns): w)= fu/lac watchman. (*ai)/a_s Ajax (*ai)ant-) is nom. and voc.) b. In oxytone stems ending in a liquid and not taking s to form their nominative (242): w)= poimh/n shepherd (poimen-); but a)nh/r man, path/r father have a)/ner, pa/ter (262). Barytones use the stem as the vocative: dai=mon, r(h+tor from dai/mwn divinity, r(h/twr orator. c. In all participles.

The dative plural adds -si to the stem. *)/aray (*)arab-) *)/arayi, ma/sti^c (masti_g-) ma/stici, fu/lac (fulak-) fu/laci, sw=ma (swmat-) sw/masi (98), e)lpi/s (e)lpid-) e)lpi/si (98), o)/rni_s (o)rni_q-) o)/rni_si (98), e)le/fa_s (e)lefant-) e)le/fa_si, qh/r (qhr-) qhrsi/. a. Stems in nt drop nt and lengthen the preceding vowel (100): le/wn (leont-) le/ousi, gi/ga_s (gigant-) gi/ga_si. b. Stems in n drop n without lengthening the preceding vowel (if short): dai/mwn (daimon-) dai/mosi, poimh/n (poimen-) poime/si, frh/n mind (fren-) fresi/. N.—Strictly n is not dropped, but since the stem of the dat. pl. is weak in form (253 a) the n stood originally between two consonants and should become a (35 b). Thus, frasi/ in Pindar is for frṇsi. Attic fresi/ borrows its e from fre/nes, frenw=n, etc. So poime/si, for poimasi from poimṇsi, because of poime/nes, etc. c. rs is not changed to rr (79 a).

a. The ending -as is produced by adding ns to the stem (n becoming a between two consonants by 35 b). Thus fu/lak-as is from fulak-ṇs. This -as may be added even to i and u stems: Hom. po/li-as, i)xqu/-as, Hdt. ph/xe-as. Hom. po/li_s is from po/li-ns (Cretan). b. The nominative pl. masc. or fem. is sometimes used instead of the accusative pl.: trih/reis 264, po/leis and ph/xeis 268.

Accent.—Stems of one syllable accent the case ending in the genitive and dative of all numbers; and -wn and -oin take the circumflex accent. Thus, fle/y vein, fleb-o/s, fleb-w=n; qh/r wild beast, qhr-o/s, qhr-oi=n, qhr-w=n; qri/c hair, trix-o/s, trix-w=n. a. Exceptions. The ending of the gen. dual and pl. is not accented in the case of o(, h( pai=s boy, girl, o( dmw/s slave, o( qw/s jackal, o( *trw/s Trojan, h( da/|s torch, to\ fw=s light, to\ ou)=s ear. Thus, pai/dwn (but paisi/), *trw/wn, w)/twn, etc. So w)/n being, o)/ntwn (305). b. A trisyllabic form, if contracted, does not show the accent on the case ending: h)=r-os for e)/ar-os, h)=r-i for e)/ar-i, from to\ e)/ar spring.

Variation of Stem Formation.—Many words of the third declension show traces of an original variation of stem that is due to the influence of a shifting accent which is seen in some of the cognate languages. In Greek this variation has often been obscured by the analogy of other forms. Thus pate/rwn, in comparison with Hom. patrw=n, Lat. patrum, gets its e from pate/res. a. Variation of stem is seen in wn, on (259); hr, er, ra (262); hs, es- (264); in stems in i, ei (270); u, eu (270); eu, hu (278); oi, w (279), etc. Words in wn, hn show a middle form on, en, and a weak form in n (250 N.). b. Several words ending in r show a parallel stem in t; thus, u(/dwr water u(/dat-os, h(=par liver h(/pat-os, fre/a_r tank fre/a_t-os (but poet. da/ma_r wife da/mart-os). The reason for this change is uncertain, but at is derived from nt after a consonant (35 b): u(dntos, h(pntos, cp. Lat. jecinoris, nom. jecur. h(=par is probably derived from h(part (133). c. -atos was transferred from such genitives as o)no/matos, h(/patos to other neuter words: go/natos from go/nu knee, instead of gonv-os, whence Hom. gouno/s. fw=s light, for fa/os (stem faes-), has taken on the t inflection (fwt-o/s, etc.). d. Neuter stems in -es show -os in the nominative. Cp. e)/tos year (stem e)tes-) with Lat. vetus, veter-is (for vetes-is).

Variation of Quantity.—a. In poetry the quantity of i in words in -is may differ from that of prose; as in tragedy o)/rni^s bird, ko/ni_s dust, o)/fi_s serpent (in prose o)/rni_s, ko/ni^s, o)/fi^s); so in Pind. i)xqu^/s (prose i)xqu/_s) fish. b. kh=ru^c herald, *foi=ni^c Phoenician, ma/sti^c whip have long u and i in the oblique cases except the dat. pl. (kh/ru_kos, *foi/ni_ki, ma/sti_ga, etc.). a)lw/phc fox has e in the gen. a)lw/pekos, etc., by analogy to such words as poimh/n, poime/nos (a)lwph/kwn occurs in Ionic). pu=r fire has pu^ro/s, pu^ri/, etc. (285, 25).

Gender.—The gender of substantives of the third declension is frequently known by the last letters of the stem. 1. Masculine are stems ending in a. nt: o)dou/s tooth (o)dont-), dra/kwn serpent (drakont-). b. ht, wt: pe/nhs day-labourer (penht-), ge/lws laughter (gelwt-). Exceptions. Stems in -tht (2, b): h( e)sqh/s dress (e)sqht-), to\ fw=s light (fwt-). c. n: leimw/n meadow (leimon-). Exceptions. Fem.: stems in gon, don (2, a), and frh/n mind (fren-), i)/_s strength (i)_n-), r(i/_s nose (r(i_n-), a)kti/_s ray (a)kti_n-), glwxi/_s arrow-point (glwxi_n-), w)di/_s birth-pang (w)di_n-), ei)kw/n image (ei)kon-), h)i+w/n shore (h)i+on-), xqw/n earth (xqo/n-), xiw/n snow (xion-), a)lkuw/n halcyon (a)lkuon-), etc., o(, h( xh/n goose (xhn-). d. r: qh/r wild beast (qhr-), fw/r thief (fwr-). Exceptions. Fem.: xei/r hand (xer-), kh/r fate (khr-), gasth/r belly (gaster-); neut.: stems in ar (3, a), pu=r fire (pur-), and the indeclinable pe/lwr monster, te/kmwr (Hom) token, etc. e. eu: goneu/s parent, foneu/s murderer. 2. Feminine are stems ending in a. gon, don: stagw/n drop (stagon-), xeli_dw/n swallow (xeli_don-). b. tht, d, q: kako/ths baseness (kakotht-), e)/ris strife (e)rid-), e)lpi/s hope (e)lpid-). Exceptions. Masc.: pou/s foot (pod-), o(, h( o)/rni_s bird (o)rni_q-). c. i, u with nom. in -is, -us: po/li-s city, i)sxu/_-s strength. Exceptions. Masc.: o)/fi-s serpent, e)/xi-s viper, o)/rxi-s testicle; bo/tru-s cluster of grapes, i)xqu/_-s fish, mu=-s mouse, ne/ku-s corpse, sta/xu-s ear of corn, pe/leku-s axe, ph=xu-s fore-arm; and o(, h( su=-s or u(=-s swine. d. oi: h)xw/ echo, peiqw/ pèrsuasion. 3. Neuter are stems ending in a. at, ar: pra=gma thing (pra_gmat-), ne/ktar nectar (nektar-). But o( ya/_r starling. b. as, es (with nom. in -os): kre/as flesh (kreas-), genos race (genes-). c. i, u with nom. in -i, -u: si/na_pi mustard, a)/stu city. N.—No stem ending in p, b, f or k, g, x is neuter.

Accusative Sing.—*)apo/llw and *poseidw= are found as well as *)apo/llwna, *poseidw=na. The shorter forms are regular in inscriptions, and occur especially in expressions of swearing after nh\ to/n, ma\ to/n (1596 b).

Vocative.—swth/r preserver, *)apo/llwn, *poseidw=n (from *poseide/wn, -a/_wn, -a_vwn) have voc. sw=ter, *)/apollon, *po/seidon with recessive accent. Recessive accent also occurs in compound proper names in -wn; as *)agame/mnwn, *)aga/memnon; *au)tome/dwn, *au)to/medon; *filh/mwn, *filh=mon; but not in those in -frwn (*eu)qu/fron). *lakedai/mwn has *lakedai=mon.

Several words in -thr show three forms of stem gradation: -thr strong, -ter middle, -tr weak. r between consonants becomes ra (35 b). The vocative has recessive accent. a)nh/r man has the weak form in r even before vowels; between n and r, d is inserted by 130. Stems in sigma are contracted where s falls out between the vowel of the stem and the vowel of the ending (120). Thus, ge/nos race, gen. gene（s）-os ge/nous, dat. gene（s）-i ge/nei, cp. Lat. genus gener-is (for genes-is), gener-i. a. The masculine and feminine accusative plural, when it is contracted, borrows the form of the contracted nominative plural. -eis is not derived from -eas. In the dative plural the union of s of the stem and s of the ending produces ss, which is reduced to s without lengthening the preceding vowel (107). b. Masculine stems in es with the nominative in -hs are proper names; the feminine trih/rhs trireme is an adjective used substantively (properly, triply fitted; h( trih/rhs (nau=s) ‘ship with three banks of oars’). c. Neuters with stems in es have -os in the nominative, accusative, and vocative singular; neuters with stems in as have -as in these cases. d. Some stems in as have also a stem in at or a_t (258).

Stems in i and u are of two kinds:— 1. a. Stems in i, with genitive in -ews, as (masc.) ma/ntis seer, e)/xis viper; (fem.) po/lis city, poi/hsis poetry, du/namis power, sta/sis faction, u(/bris outrage. Neuter nominatives in -i are not used in classical prose. b. Stems in i, with genitive in -ios, as o( ki/_s weevil, gen. ki_-o/s, dat. ki_-i/; and so in proper names in -is, as *lu/gdamis Lygdamis, gen. *lugda/mios. 2. a. Stems in u, with genitive in -uos; as (masc.) mu=s mouse, bo/trus cluster of grapes, i)xqu/_s fish; (fem.) dru=s oak, o)fru/_s eyebrow, i)sxu/_s force. b. Stems in u, with genitive in -ews: (masc.) ph=xus forearm, pe/lekus axe; (neut.) a)/stu town. N. 1.—In the nom., acc., and voc. sing. barytone stems in u have short u; oxytone substantives (usually) and monosyllables have u_; and monosyllables circumflex the u_ (su=s, su=n, su=). N. 2.—h( e)/gxelus eel follows i)xqu/_s in the singular (e)gxe/lu-os, etc.), but ph=xus in the plural (e)gxe/leis, etc.). But this does not hold for Aristotle.

Stems in i and u vary with stronger stems, of which e in the cases other than nom., acc., and voc. sing. is a survival. Thus: a. i, u, as in po/li-s, ph=xu-s. b. ei, eu, which before vowels lost their i and u (43), as in pole（[iglide]）-i, pole（[iglide]）-es, phxe（[uglide]）-es; which contract to po/lei, po/leis, ph/xeis. c. There is also a stem in h, as in Hom. po/lh-os (268 D. 1, c), whence po/le-ws. N. 1.—po/le-os in Attic poetry for the sake of the metre is due to the analogy of u stems with gen. in -e-os (h(de/-os, 297). Hom. ph/xe-os is the regular form (from phxe（[uglide]）-os). Attic ph/xe-ws follows po/lews. po/le-si and ph/xe-si for po/li-si and ph/xu-si are due to the analogy of forms from stems in ei, eu (po/le-wn, ph/xe-wn, etc.). N. 2.—The dual po/lee occurs in some Mss.

Accent.—Final -ws of the genitive singular does not prevent the acute from standing on the antepenult (163 a). Thus po/le-ws, ph/xe-ws, a)/ste-ws. po/le-ws retains the accent of the earlier po/lh-os, which, by transference of quantity (34), became po/le-ws. The accent of the gen. pl. follows that of the gen. sing.
Accusative plural.—po/leis, ph/xeis are borrowed from the nominative. i)xqu=s is from i)xqun-s. i)xqu/as occurs in late Greek. Cp. 251 a.

Contraction.—i)xqu= (once) for i)xqu/e and i)xqu=s for i)xqu/es occur in comedy. i)xqu= is not a legitimate contraction, as u cannot contract with e (51 c). i)xqu=s (for i)xqu/es) is the accus. form used as the nom. (251 b).

oi)=s sheep is declined as follows: oi)=s, oi)-o/s, oi)-i/, oi)=-n, oi)=; dual, oi)=-e, oi)-oi=n; pl. oi)=-es, oi)-w=n, oi)-si/, oi)=-s. Here the stem is oi', representing o)vi, which is properly an i stem: o)vi-s, Lat. ovi-s.

Substantives in -eu/s preceded by a vowel may contract in the gen. and acc. sing. and pl. Thus, a(lieu/s fisherman has gen. a(lie/ws or a(liw=s, acc. a(lie/a_ or a(lia=, gen. pl. a(lie/wn or a(liw=n, acc. pl. a(lie/a_s or a(lia=s. All other forms are regular. The contracted forms were in use in the fifth century, but in the fourth (especially after 350 B.C.) the open forms are common. So are declined *eu)boeu/s Euboean from *eu)boieu/s, *pairaieu/s Peiraeus, *plataieu/s Plataean.

Other Forms.—a. In the drama from words in -eu/s we find rarely -e/a^ in acc. sing., -e/a^s in acc. pl. -e/os and -h=os, -h=es, -h=as are occasionally found. b. The nom. pl. in older Attic ended in -h=s (basilh=s), derived either from -h=es by contraction or from -e/hs (once on an inscription) by 34. -h=s occurs on inscriptions till about 350 B.C., and is the form to be adopted in the texts of authors of the fifth century and in Plato. -e/es occurs rarely, but is suspected. basilei=s (regular on inscriptions after 329 B.C.) is from analogy to h(dei=s. c. The acc. pl. basilei=s was not used till the end of the fourth century. -h=s (the nom. form) is used for the acc. in a few passages (251 b).

Stem Variation.—Stems ending in eu, au, ou lose u before case endings beginning with a vowel, [uglide] passing into v (43). Stems in eu show the pure form only in the vocative; other forms are derived from the stronger stem hu. hu and a_u before a consonant become eu, a^u (40) as in basileu/s, basileu=si, nau=s, nausi/ from basilhus, na_us, etc. From basilh=（v）-os, -h=（v）-i, -h=（v）-a, -h=（v）-as come, by transfer of quantity (34), the Attic forms. So new/s is derived from nh（v）-o/s. In basile/wn, new=n, e is shortened from the h of basilh/wn, nhw=n by 39. bo-o/s, etc. are from the stem bou- bov-, cp. Lat. bovis.

Stems in oi, with nominative in -w/, turn i into unwritten [iglide] (y) (43) before the endings beginning with a vowel. h( peiqw/ persuasion is thus declined: N. peiqw/. G. peiqou=s (peiqo/-os). D. peiqoi= (peiqo/-i). A. peiqw/ (peiqo/-a). V. peiqoi=. Dual and plural are wanting. So h)xw/ echo, eu)estw/ well-being, feidw/ sparing, *sapfw/, *lhtw/, *kaluyw/. oi stems are chiefly used for women's names. a. A stronger form of the stem is wi, seen in the earlier form of the nominative (*sapfw/|, *lhtw/|). The accusative has the accent of the nominative. b. When dual and plural occur, they are of the second declension: nom. lexoi/ (late) from lexw/ woman in child-bed, acc. gorgou/s from gorgw/ gorgon. c. h( ei)kw/n image, h( a)hdw/n nightingale, properly from stems in on, have certain forms from this declension (ei)kou=s, ei)kw/, voc. a)hdoi=).

Cases in -fi（n).—-fi（n) is often added to noun stems in Hom. to express the relations of the lost instrumental, locative, and ablative, both singular and (more commonly) plural; rarely to express the relations of the genitive and dative cases. From a_ stems are made singulars, from o stems singulars or plurals, from consonant stems almost always plurals. Except in qeo/-fin with the gods -fi（n) is not added to a stem denoting a person. (a) Instrumental: bi/h-fi by might, e(te/rh-fi with the other (hand), dakruo/-fin with tears; (b) Locative: qu/rh-fi at the door, o)/res-fi on the mountains; (c) Ablative: kefalh=-fin from off the head; especially with prepositions, as e)k ponto/-fin from off the sea, a)po\ nau=-fin from the ships.

The gender in the singular and in the plural may not be the same: o( si=tos grain, ta\ si=ta; o( desmo/s chain, ta\ desma/ chains (oi( desmoi/ cases of imprisonment); to\ sta/dion stade, race-course, pl. ta\ sta/dia and oi( sta/dioi.

Usually the irregularity consists in a word having two different stems. a. Both stems have a common nominative singular: sko/tos darkness, sko/tou sko/tw|, etc. (like i(/ppou i(/ppw|) or sko/tous sko/tei (like ge/nous ge/nei). So to *)/aqw, and to *)/aqwn from *)/aqws (238 d), to *swkra/th and to *swkra/thn (264 b). These are called heteroclites (e(tero/klita differently declined). N. Many compound proper names in -hs (especially names of foreigners) have forms of the 1 and 3 decl., as *tissafe/rnhs, -nous, -nh| and -nei. So *qeokri/_nh (voc.) in Demosth., *lewni/dhn and *lewni/dea in Hdt. b. Certain cases are formed from another stem than that of the nom. singular: o( o)/neiro-s dream, gen. o)nei/rat-os (as if from to\ o)/neirar), or (less freq.) o)nei/rou; so to *)apo/llwna and to *)apo/llw (260), tou= ui(e/os and tou= ui(ou= (285, 27). These are called metaplastic forms (metaplasmo/s change of formation).

Defectives are substantives having, by reason of their meaning or use, only one number or only certain cases. Thus, sing. only: o( a)h/r air, o( ai)qh/r upper air; plur. only: ta\ *dionu/_sia, ta\ *)olu/mpia the Dionysiac (Olympic) festival, oi( e)thsi/ai annual winds; in some cases only: w)= me/le my good sir or madam; o)/nar dream; o)/felos use only in nom.; libo/s li/ba from *li/y stream, libation.

Indeclinables are substantives having one form for all cases: to\ xrew/n, tou= xrew/n, etc. fatality, to\ a)/lfa alpha, to\ le/gein to speak, most cardinal numbers (to\ de/ka ten), several foreign words, as *)iakw/b Jacob, *dabi/d David.

LIST OF THE PRINCIPAL IRREGULAR SUBSTANTIVES 1. *)/arhs (o() Ares, stems *)ares-, *)areu- from *)ares v-. G. *)/arews (poet. *)/areos), D. *)/arei, A. *)/arh (poet. *)/area), *)/arhn. Epic G. *)/arhos, *)/areos, D. *)/arhi, *)/arei+, A. *)/arha, *)/arhn. Hdt. *)/areos, *)/arei, *)/area. Aeolic *)/areus, *)/areuos, etc. 2. a)rh/n (o(, h() lamb, sheep, stems a)ren-, a)rn-, a)rna-. Thus, a)rn-o/s, a)rn-i/, a)/rn-a, a)/rn-es, a)rn-w=n, a)rna/-si (Hom. a)/rn-essi), a)/rn-as (declined like a subst. in -hr). Nom. a)rh/n occurs on inscript. but a)mno/s (2 decl.) is commonly used. 3. ga/la (to/) milk (133), ga/lakt-os, ga/lakt -i, etc. 4. ge/lws (o() laughter, ge/lwt-os, etc. Attic poets A. ge/lwta or ge/lwn. Hom. has D. ge/lw|, A. ge/lw, ge/lwn or ge/loi (?) from Aeol. ge/los. Cp. 257 D. 5. go/nu (to/) knee, go/nat-os, etc. Ionic and poetic gou/nat-os, gou/nat-i, etc. Epic also goun-o/s, goun-i/, gou=n-a, pl. gou/n-wn, gou/n-essi (250 D. 2). The forms in ou are from gonv- (37 D. 1, 253 c); cf. Lat. genu. 6. gunh/ (h() woman, gunaik-o/s, gunaik-i/, gunai=k-a, gu/nai (133); dual gunai=k-e, gunaik-oi=n; pl. gunai=k-es, gunaik-w=n, gunaici/, gunai=k-as. The gen. and dat. of all numbers accent the last syllable (cp. a)nh/r). Comic poets have A. gunh/n, guna/s, N. pl. gunai/. 7. da/kruon (to/) tear, dakru/ou, etc., in prose and poetry. da/kru (to/) is usually poetic, D. pl. da/krusi. 8. de/ndron (to/) tree, de/ndrou, etc. Also D. sing. de/ndrei, pl. de/ndrh, de/ndresi. Adjectives of Three Endings.—Most adjectives of the vowel declension have three endings: -os, -h (or -a_), -on. The masculine and neuter are declined according to the second declension, the feminine according to the first. a. When e, i, or r (30, 218) precedes -os the feminine ends in -a_, not in -h. But adjectives in -oos (not preceded by r) have h. Thus, o)/gdoos, o)gdo/h, o)/gdoon eighth, a)qro/os, a)qro/a_, a)qro/on crowded. See 290 e.

Adjectives of Two Endings.—Adjectives using the masculine for the feminine are called adjectives of two endings. Most such adjectives are compounds.

Such adjectives as belong only to the consonant declension have two endings. Most such adjectives have stems in es (nominative -hs and -es) and on (nominative -wn and -on). For the acc. of stems in it and id see 247. Neut. eu)/xari and eu)/elpi for eu)xarit, eu)elpid (133).

Adjectives of the consonant declension having a separate form for the feminine inflect the feminine like a substantive of the first declension ending in -a^ (216).

Participles of the active voice (except the perfect, 309), and the aorist passive participle have stems in nt. The masculine and neuter follow the third declension, the feminine follows the first declension. a. Most stems in ont make the nom. sing. masc. without s, like ge/rwn (243). But stems in ont in the present and second aorist of mi-verbs (didou/s, dou/s), and all stems in ant, ent, unt, add s, lose nt (100), and lengthen the preceding vowel (-ous, -a_s, -eis, -u_s, 37). In like manner the dat. pl. is formed: -ont-si = -ousi, etc. N.—The stem of participles in -wn, -ontos was originally wnt. ge/rwn was orignally a participle. b. The nominative neuter of all participles drops final t of the stem (133). c. The perfect active participle (stem ot) has -ws in the masculine, -os in the neuter. -ws and -os are for -vwt-s, -vot-s. d. The feminine singular is made by adding [iglide]a to the stem. Thus, lu/_ousa (lu_ont-[iglide]a), ou(=sa (o)nt-[iglide]a), i(sta=sa (i(stant-[iglide]a), tiqei=sa (tiqent-[iglide]a). The perfect adds -u（s）-[iglide]a, as in ei)d-ui=a.
The vocative of all participles is the same as the nominative.
Participles in -wn, -a_s, -eis, -ous, -u_s frequently use the masculine for the feminine in the dual.
The accent of monosyllabic participles is an exception to 252: w)/n, o)/ntos (not o)nto/s), sta/_s, sta/ntos.

Thus pra=|os, pra_ei=a, pra=|on, G. pra/|ou, pra_ei/a_s, pra/|ou, etc. In the plural we have N. V. pra=|oi or pra_ei=s pra_ei=ai pra=|a or pra_e/a Gen. pra/|wn or pra_e/wn pra_eiw=n pra/|wn or pra_e/wn Dat. pra/|ois or pra_e/si（n） pra_ei/ais pra/|ois or pra_e/si（n） Acc. pra/|ous pra_ei/a_s pra=|a or pra_e/a d. Some compounds of pou/s foot (pod-) have -oun in the nom. sing. neut. and sometimes in the acc. sing. masc. by analogy to a(plou=s (290). Thus, tri/pous three-footed, tri/poun (but acc. tri/poda tripod).

Adjectives of one ending have the same termination for masculine and feminine. The neuter (like masc. and fem.) sometimes occurs in oblique cases. Examples: a)gnw/s a)gnw=t-os unknown or unknowing, a)/pais a)/paid-os childless, a)rgh/s a)rgh=t-os white, a(/rpac a(/rpag-os rapacious, ma/kar ma/kar-os blessed, a)ka/ma_s a)ka/mant-os unwearied. Here belong also certain other adjectives commonly used as substantives, as gumnh/s gumnh=t-os light armed, pe/nhs pe/nht-os poor, fuga/s fuga/d-os fugitive, h(=lic h(/lik-os comrade, a)lazw/n a)lazo/n-os flatterer. Some are masculine only, as e)qelonth/s (-ou=) uolunteer. Adj. in -i/s -i/dos are feminine only. *(ellhni/s Greek, patri/s (scil. gh=) fatherland, summaxi/s (po/lis) an allied state.

Comparison by -teros, -tatos.—The usual endings are: For the comparative: -teros m. -tera_ f. -teron n. For the superlative: -tatos m. -tath f. -taton n. The endings are added to the masculine stem of the positive. Comparatives are declined like a)/cios, superlatives like a)gaqo/s (287). dh=los (dhlo-) clear, dhlo/-teros, dhlo/-tatos; i)sxu_ro/s (i)sxu_ro-) strong, i)sxu_ro/teros, i)sxu_ro/-tatos; me/la_s (melan-) black, mela/n-teros, mela/n-tatos; baru/s (baru-) heavy, baru/-teros, baru/-tatos; a)lhqh/s (a)lhqes-) true, a)lhqe/s-teros, a)lhqe/s-tatos; eu)kleh/s (eu)klees-) famous, eu)klee/s-teros, eu)klee/s-tatos. a. xarie/steros, -e/statos are from xariet-teros, -tatos (83, 299 b), from xari/eis graceful. Compounds of xa/ris grace add o to the stem (xarit-o-), whence e)pixaritw/teros more pleasing. pe/nhs poor has pene/s-teros from penet-teros, with e for h. b. Originally -teros had no other force than to contrast one idea with another, and this function is retained in deci/teros right) (a)ri/steros left, h(me/teros our) ( u(_me/teros your. Hom. has several such words: a)gro/teros wild) (tame, qhlu/terai gunai=kes) (men, cp. Arcadian a)rre/nteros from a)/rrhn male. Cp. 1082 b.

Adjectives in -os with a short penult lengthen o to w: ve/o-s new, vew/-teros, new/-tatos, xalepo/-s difficult, xalepw/-teros, xalepw/-tatos. An undue succession of short syllables is thus avoided. a. If the penult is long either by nature or by position (144), o is not lengthened: lepto/s lean, lepto/teros, lepto/tatos. A stop and a liquid almost always make position here (cp. 145); as pikro/s bitter, pikro/teros, pikro/tatos. keno/s empty and steno/s narrow were originally kenvos, stenvos (Ionic keino/s, steino/s, 37 D. 1), hence keno/teros, steno/teros.

The following drop the stem vowel o: geraio/-s aged, gerai/-teros, gerai/tatos; palaio/-s ancient, palai/-teros, palai/-tatos; sxolai=o-s slow, sxolai/-teros, sxolai/-tatos; fi/lo-s dear, fi/l-teros (poetic), fi/l-tatos (319, 11). a. Some other adjectives reject the stem vowel o and end in -aiteros, -aitatos, as h(/suxos quiet, i)/sos equal, o)/rqrios early. These, like sxolai/teros and gerai/teros, imitate palai/teros, which is properly derived from the adverb pa/lai long ago. So mesai/teros, -ai/tatos imitate mesai- in Hom. mesai-po/lios middle-aged.

-esteros, -estatos.—By imitation of words like a)lhqe/s-teros, a)lhqe/statos (313), -esteros, -estatos are added to stems in on and to some in oo (contracted to ou). Thus, eu)dai/mwn happy, eu)daimon-e/steros, -e/statos; a(plou=s simple, a(plou/steros (for a(plo-esteros), a(plou/statos; eu)/nous well-disposed, eu)nou/steros, -ou/statos, and so in all others in -nous from nou=s mind. (Others in -oos have -owteros: a)qrow/teros more crowded from a)qro/os.) a. Some stems in on substitute o for on; as (from e)pilh/smwn forgetful, e)pilhsmone/s-teros) e)pilhsmo/-tatos; pi/_wn fat, pi_o/teros, pi_o/tatos; pe/pwn ripe has pepai/teros, pepai/tatos. Cp. 315 a. b. Other cases: (with loss of o) e)rrwme/no-s strong, e)rrwmene/steros, -e/statos, a)/kra_to-s unmixed, a)kra_te/statos, a)/smeno-s glad, a)/fqono-s abundant.

-isteros, -istatos.—By imitation of words like a)xari/steros for a)xaritteros (83) from a)/xaris disagreeable, -isteros, -istatos are used especially with adjectives of a bad meaning, as klept-i/statos (kle/pths thief, 321), kakhgori/steros (kakh/goros abusive), lal-i/steros (la/los talkative).

Comparison by -i_wn, -istos.—Some adjectives add to the root of the positive the endings -i_wn for the masculine and feminine, -i_on for the neuter to form the comparative, and -istos -h -on to form the superlative. The vowel (or the syllable ro) standing before s of the nominative is thus lost.
