Poetic or Ionic forms are in ( ). 1. a)gaqo/s good a)mei/nwn (from a)men-i_wn） （a)rei/wn） a)/ristos (a)r-eth/ vir- tue） belti/_wn be/ltistos （be/lteros, not in Hom.) （be/ltatos, not in Hom.) （kratu/s powerful） krei/ttwn, krei/sswn kra/tistos (cp. kra/tos strength） （kre/sswn） （ka/rtistos） （fe/rteros） （fe/rtatos, fe/ristos） lw/|wn (lwi/wn, lwi/teros） lw=|stos 2. kako/s bad kaki/_wn (kakw/teros) peior ka/kistos xei/rwn (xerei/wn) meaner, de- xei/ristos terior (xeiro/teros, xereio/- teros） h(/ttwn, h(/sswn (for h(k-i_wn） （h(/kistos, rare), adv. weaker, inferior (e(/sswn） h(/kista least of all 3. kalo/s beautiful kalli/_wn ka/llistos (ka/ll-os beauty） 4. makro/s long makro/teros (ma/sswn） makro/tatos (mh/ki- stos） 5. me/gas great mei/zwn 318 (me/zwn） me/gistos 6. mi_kro/s small mi_kro/teros mi_kro/tatos （e)la/xeia, f. of e)laxu/s） e)la/_ttwn, e)la/_sswn (for e)la- e)la/xistos xi_wn） mei/wn （mei=stos, rare) 7. o)li/gos little, pl. few o)lei/zwn (inscriptions) o)li/gistos （u(p-o)li/zwn Hom. rather less） 8. polu/s much, pl. many plei/wn, ple/wn, neut. ple/on, plei=stos plei=n 9. r(a/|dios easy r(a/|wn (Ion. r(hi/wn） r(a=|stos （r(hi/dios） （r(hi/teros） （r(hi/tatos, r(h/istos） 10. taxu/s quick qa/_ttwn, qa/_sswn ta/xistos （taxu/teros） （taxu/tatos） 11. fi/los dear （fi/lteros） fi/ltatos filai/teros (Xenoph.) filai/tatos(Xenoph.) （fili/wn, rare in Hom.) a. a)mei/nwn, a)/ristos express aptitude, capacity or worth (able, brave, excellent); belti/_wn, be/ltistos, a moral idea (virtuous); krei/ttwn, kra/tistos, force and superiority (strong) (h(/ttwn is the opposite of krei/ttwn); lw/|wn means more desirable, more agreeable (w)= lw=|ste my good friend); kaki/_wn, ka/kistos express moral perversity, cowardice; xei/rwn, xei/ristos, insufficiency, lack of a quality (less good) (worthless, good fo

Defectives.—Some comparatives and superlatives are derived from prepositions or adverbs: （pro/ before） pro/teros former prw=tos first （u(pe/r over, beyond） u(pe/rteros (poetic) higher, u(pe/rtatos (poetic) high- superior. est, supreme. （plhsi/on near） plhsiai/teros plhsiai/tatos （prou)/rgou serviceable） prourgiai/teros u(/steros later, latter u(/statos latest, last a. -atos appears in u(/patos highest, e)/sxatos farthest, extreme (from e)c).

In poetry and sometimes in prose comparatives and superlatives are formed from substantives and pronouns. Hom. has basileu/teros more kingly, -tatos (basileu/s king), e(tairo/tatos a closest companion (e(tai=ros comrade), ku/nteros more doglike, -tatos (ku/wn dog), kouro/teros more youthful (kou=ros a youth). Aristophanes has klepti/statos most thievish (kle/pths thief, 317), and au)to/tatos his very self, ipsissimus.
Double Comparison.—A double comparative occurs sometimes to produce a comic effect, as kunterw/teros (321). A double superlative is prw/tistos.

Comparison by ma=llon, ma/lista.—Instead of the forms in -teros, -tatos or -i_wn, -istos the adverbs ma=llon more, ma/lista most, may be used with the positive; as ma=llon fi/los more dear, dearer, ma/lista fi/los most dear, dearest. This is the only way of comparing participles and words that do not take the comparative and superlative endings (ma=llon e(kw/n more willing). a. Comparison by ma=llon, ma/lista is common in the case of compound adjectives, adjectives with a prepositional prefix, verbal adjectives in -to/s, and adjectives in -ios.

To express equality or inferiority ou(/tw as (often in correlation with w(/sper), h(=tton less, may be placed before the positive. Thus, as good as handsome may be expressed by ou(/tws a)gaqo\s w(/sper kai\ kalo/s, w(/sper a)gaqo\s ou(/tw kai\ kalo/s, ou)=x h(=tton kalo\s h)\ kai\ a)gaqo/s.

The Personal Pronouns.—The pronouns of the first, second, and third person are declined as follows: SINGULAR Nom. e)gw/ I su/ thou — he, she, it (325 d） Gen. e)mou=; mou enclitic sou=; sou enclitic ou(=; ou( enclitic Dat. e)moi/; moi enclitic soi/; soi enclitic oi(=; oi( enclitic Acc. e)me/; me enclitic se/; se enclitic e(/; e( enclitic DUAL N. A. nw/ we two sfw/ you two G. D. nw=|n sfw=|n PLURAL Nom. h(mei=s we u(_mei=s you sfei=s they Gen. h(mw=n u(_mw=n sfw=n Dat. h(mi=n u(_mi=n sfi/si（n） Acc. h(ma=s u(_ma=s sfa=s a. The enclitic forms mou, moi, me; sou, soi, se are used when the pronoun is unemphatic, the longer forms e)mou=, e)moi/, e)me/ and the accented sou=, soi/, se/ are used when the pronoun is emphatic. Thus, do/s moi to\ bibli/on give me the book, ou\k e)moi/, a)lla\ soi\ e)pibouleu/ousi they are plotting not against me, but against you. See 187 a. On the use after prepositions see 187 N. 2. b. The Greek verb shows distinctions of voice, mood, verbal noun, tense, number, and person.

Voices.—There are three voices: active, middle, and passive. a. The middle usually denotes that the subject acts on himself or for himself, as lou/omai wash myself, a)mu/_nomai defend myself (lit. ward off for myself). b. The passive borrows all its forms, except the future and aorist, from the middle. c. Deponent verbs have an active meaning but only middle (or middle and passive) forms. If its aorist has the middle form, a deponent is called a middle deponent (xari/zomai gratify, e)xarisa/mhn); if its aorist has the passive form, a deponent is called a passive deponent (e)nqu_me/omai reflect on, e)nequ_mh/qhn). Deponents usually prefer the passive to the middle forms of the aorist.

Moods.—Four moods, the indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative, are called finite, because the person is defined by the ending (366). The infinitive, strictly a verbal noun (358), is sometimes classed as a mood.

Verbal Nouns.—Verbal forms that share certain properties of nouns are called verbal nouns. There are two kinds of verbal nouns. 1. Substantival: the infinitive. N.—The infinitive is properly a case form (chiefly dative, rarely locative), herein being like a substantive. 2. Adjectival (inflected like adjectives): a. Participles: active, middle, and passive. b. Verbal adjectives: In -to/s, denoting possibility, as filhto/s lovable, or with the force of a perfect passive participle, as grapto/s written. In -te/os, denoting necessity, as grapte/os that must be written.

Tenses.—There are seven tenses in the indicative: present, imperfect, future, aorist, perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect. The future perfect commonly has a passive force, but it may be active or middle in meaning (see 581). The subjunctive has three tenses: present, aorist, and perfect. The optative and infinitive have five tenses: present, future, aorist, perfect, and future perfect. The imperative has three tenses: present, aorist, and perfect.

Primary and Secondary Tenses.—There are two classes of tenses in the indicative: (1) Primary (or Principal) tenses, the present and perfect expressing present time, the future and future perfect expressing future time; (2) Secondary (or Historical) tenses, the imperfect, pluperfect, and aorist expressing past time. The secondary tenses have an augment (428) prefixed.

Second Aorists, etc.—Some verbs have tenses called second aorists (active, middle, and passive), second perfects and pluperfects (active only), and second futures (passive). The meaning of these tenses ordinarily corresponds to that of the first aorist, etc.; but when a verb has both forms in any tense (which is rarely the case), the two forms usually differ in meaning. Sometimes one form is poetical, the other used in prose.
No single Greek verb shows all the tenses mentioned in 359 and 361; and the paradigms are therefore taken from different verbs.
Number.—There are three numbers: the singular, dual, and plural.

Person.—There are three persons (first, second, and third) in the indicative, subjunctive, and optative. The imperative has only the second and third persons. a. Except in a few cases in poetry (465 c) the first person plural is used for the first person dual.
Inflection.—The inflection of a verb consists in the addition of certain endings to the different stems.

Endings.—The endings in the finite moods (357) show whether the subject is first, second, or third person; and indicate number and voice. See 462 ff. a. The middle has a different set of endings from the active. The passive has the endings of the middle except in the aorist, which has the active endings. b. The indicative has two sets of endings in the active and in the middle: one for primary tenses, the other for secondary tenses. c. The subjunctive uses the same endings as the primary tenses of the indicative; the optative uses the same as those of the secondary tenses.

A Greek verb has two kinds of stems: (1) the tense-stem, to which the endings are attached, and (2) a common verb-stem (also called theme) from which all the tense-stems are derived. The tense-stem is usually made from the verb-stem by prefixing a reduplication-syllable (439), and by affixing signs for mood (457, 459) and tense (455). A tense-stem may be identical with a verbstem.

The Tense-stems.—The tenses fall into nine classes called tense-systems. Each tense-system has its own separate tense-stem. SYSTEMS. TENSES. I. Present, including present and imperfect. II. Future, “ future active and middle. III. First aorist, “ first aorist active and middle. IV. Second aorist, “ second aorist active and middle. V. First perfect, “ first perfect, first pluperfect, and fut. perf., active. VI. Second perfect, “ second perfect and second pluperfect active. VII. Perfect middle, “ perfect and pluperfect middle (pass.), future perfect. VIII. First passive, “ first aorist and first future passive. IX. Second passive, “ second aorist and second future passive. The tense-stems are explained in detail in 497-597. a. Since few verbs have both the first and second form of the same tense (361), most verbs have only six of these nine systems; many verbs do not even have six. Scarcely any verb shows all nine systems. b. There are also secondary tense-stems for the future passive, the pluperfect, and the future perfect. c. The tense-stems assume separate forms in the different moods.

The principal parts of a verb are the first person singular indicative of the tense-systems occurring in it. These are generally six: the present, future, first aorist, first (or second) perfect active, the perfect middle, and the first (or second) aorist passive. The future middle is given if there is no future active. The second aorist (active or middle) is added if it occurs. Thus: lu/_w loose, lu/_sw, e)/lu_sa, le/luka, le/lumai, e)lu/qhn. lei/pw leave, lei/yw, le/loipa, le/leimmai, e)lei/fqhn, 2 aor. e)/lipon. gra/fw write, gra/yw, e)/graya, ge/grafa, ge/grammai, 2 aor. pass. e)gra/fhn. skw/ptw jeer, skw/yomai, e)/skwya, e)skw/fqhn.

The principal parts of deponent verbs (356 c) are the present, future, perfect, and aorist indicative. Both first and second aorists are given if they occur. bou/lomai wish, boulh/somai, bebou/lhmai, e)boulh/qhn (passive deponent). g/gnomai become, genh/somai, gege/nhmai, 2 aor. e)geno/mhn (middle deponent). e)rga/zomai work, e)rga/somai, ei)rgasa/mhn, ei)/rgasmai, ei)rga/sqhn.

Verb-stem (or Theme).—The tense-stems are made from one fundamental stem called the verb-stem (or theme). This verb-stem may be a root (193) as in ti/_-w honour, or a root to which a derivative suffix has been appended, as in ti_-ma/-w honour.

A verb forming its tense-stems directly from a root is called a primitive verb. A denominative verb forms its tense-stems from a longer verb-stem, originally a noun-stem; as doulo/w enslave from dou=los slave. Verbs in mi (379), and verbs in w of two syllables (in the present indicative active, as le/g-w speak) or of three syllables (in the middle, as de/xomai receive) are generally primitive. Others are denominative.

The verb-stem may show numerous modifications in form. Thus, corresponding to the gradations in sing, sang, sung (35), the verb lei/p-w leave shows the stems leip-, loip- (2 perf. le/-loip-a), lip- (2 aor. e)/-lip-o-n); the verb feu/g-w flee shows feug- and fug- (2 aor. e)/-fug-o-n). In r(h/gnu_mi break we find the three stems r(hg, r(wg (2 perf. e)/rrwga), r(ag (2 aor. pass. e)rra/ghn). ste/ll-w send has the stems stel- and stal- (perf. e)/-stal-ka, 2 fut. pass. stal-h/somai). a. When the fundamental stem shows modifications, it is customary for convenience to call its shorter (or shortest) form the verb-stem, and to derive the other forms from it. The student must, however, beware of assuming that the short forms are older than the other forms.

The verb-stem may also show modifications in quantity, as present lu/_-w loose, perfect le/-lu^-ka. N.—Various causes produce this variation. lu/_w has u_ from analogy to lu/_-sw, e)/-lu_-sa where the verb-stem lu^ has been regularly lengthened (534, 543). For Attic fqa/nw anticipate Hom. has fqa/_nw for fqanvw (28, 147 D.).

w Inflection and mi Inflection.—There are two slightly different methods of inflecting verbs, the first according to the common, the second according to the mi system. The names w-verbs and mi verbs (a small class) refer to the ending of the first person singular active of the present tense indicative only: lu/_-w loose, ti/qh-mi place. a. In the w inflection the tense-stem ends in the thematic vowel. To this form belong all futures, and the presents, imperfects, and second aorists showing the thematic vowel.

According to the ending of the verb-stem, w-verbs are termed: 1. Vowel (or pure) verbs: a. Not contracted: those that end in u or i, as lu/_-w loose, paideu/-w educate, xri/_-w anoint. Such verbs retain the final vowel of the stem unchanged in all their forms. b. Contracted: those that end in a, e, o, as ti_mw= honour from ti_ma/-w, poiw= make from poie/-w, dhlw= manifest from dhlo/-w. 2. Consonant verbs, as: Liquid or nasal verbs: de/r-w flay, me/n-w remain. Verbs ending in a stop (or mute), as a)/g-w lead, pei/q-w persuade. N.—Verbs ending in a stop consonant are called labial, dental, or palatal verbs. Consonant verbs do not retain the final consonant of the stem unchanged in all their forms. The final consonant may be assimilated to a following consonant, or may form with it a double consonant.

Thematic Vowel.—Some tense-stems end in a vowel which varies between o and e (or w and h) in certain forms. This is called the thematic (or variable) vowel. Thus lu/_o-men lu/_e-te, lu/_w-men lu/_h-te, lu/_so-men lu/_se-te. The thematic vowel is written o/e or w/h, as lu_o/e-, grafw/h-. See 456.
o is used before m or n in the indicative, and in the optative, w before m or n in the subjunctive, elsewhere e is used in the indicative (h in the subjunctive).

In the mi inflection no thematic vowel is employed, and the endings are attached directly to the tense-stem. The mi form is used only in the present, imperfect, and second aorist. In the other tenses, verbs in mi generally show the same inflection as w-verbs. For further explanation of the w and the mi inflection see 602ff., 717ff.

Meanings of the Tenses and Moods.—In the synopsis (382) meanings are given wherever these are not dependent on the use of the various forms in the sentence. The meanings of the subjunctive and optative forms and the difference between the tenses can be learned satisfactorily only from the syntax. Some of these meanings may here be given: a. Subjunctive: lu/_wmen or lu/_swmen let us loose, (e)a\_n) lu/_w or lu/_sw (if) I loose, (i(/na) gra/fw (that) I may write. b. Optative: (ei)/qe) lu/_oimi or lu/_saimi (would) that I may loose! (ei)) lu/_oimen or lu/_saimen (if) we should loose.

The periphrastic third plural is used instead of the forms derived directly from the union of the stem with the ending. Thus, gegramme/noi ei)si/ is used for gegraf-ntai which would become gegra/fatai by 35 b, n between consonants passing into a. The periphrastic form is also used in verbs adding s to their stems, as tetele-s-me/noi ei)si/ for tetele-s-ntai. Stems in n that drop n in the perfect system form their perfect and pluperfect regularly; thus, kri/_nw (krin-) judge has ke/krintai, e)ke/krinto. N.—On the retention of -atai, -ato see 465 f.

Euphonic Changes.—For the euphonic changes in these forms see 82-87, 103. a. Labial Stems.—le/leim-mai is for leleip-mai, le/leif-qon is for leleip-sqon, le/leifqe is for leleip-sqe (103). In the same manner are inflected other labial stems, as tri/_bw (tri_b-) rub, r(i/_ptw (r(i_p-) throw: te/tri_m-mai for tetri_b-mai, te/tri_yai for tetri_b-sai, etc. Stems ending in mp drop p before m, but retain it before other consonants. Thus, pepemp-mai becomes pe/pemmai pepemp-meqa becomes pepe/mmeqa pepemp-sai “ pe/pemyai pepemp-sqe “ pe/pemfqe (103） pepemp-tai “ pe/pemptai b. Dental Stems.—pe/peis-tai is for pepeiq-tai (83), pe/peis-qon is for pepeiqqon (83), pe/peisqe is for pepeiq-（s）qe (83, 103). The s thus produced was trans ferred to the first persons pe/peismai, pepei/smeqa (86, 87). Like pe/peismai, etc., are formed and inflected e)/yeusmai from yeu/dw (yeud-) deceive, pe/frasmai from fra/zw (frad-) declare, e)/speismai (100) from spe/ndw (spend-) pour a libation.
The forms pe/fansai, e)pe/fanso, and pe/fanso are not attested. Cp. 707 a.

The conjugation of mi-verbs differs from that of w-verbs only in the present, imperfect, and second aorist active and middle; and (rarely) in the second perfect. The mi forms are made by adding the endings directly to the tense-stem without any thematic vowel, except in the subjunctive of all verbs, and in the optative of verbs ending in -nu_mi.

Verbs having second aorists and second perfects of the mi form are, as a rule, w-verbs, not mi-verbs, in the present. Thus, the second aorists: e)/bhn (bai/nw go), e)/gnwn (gignw/skw know); the second perfect: te/qnamen (qnh/|skw die).

There are two main classes of mi-verbs. A. The root class. This class commonly ends in -h-mi or -w-mi (from stems in e, a, or o). The present stem is usually reduplicated, but may be the same as the verb-stem, which is a root. The -nu_mi class. This class adds nu (nu_), after a vowel nnu (nnu_), to the verb-stem. In the subjunctive and optative regularly, and sometimes in the indicative, verbs in -nu_mi are inflected like verbs in -w. All the possible mi forms do not occur in any single verb. ti/qhmi and di/dwmi are incomplete and irregular in the second aorist active; and e)/sbhn went out from sbe/nnu_mi is the only second aorist formed from nu_mi-verbs. e)pria/mhn I bought, second aorist middle (from the stem pria- with no present), is given in the paradigms in place of the missing form of i(/sthmi; and e)/du_n I entered from du/_w (but formed as if from du=mi) in place of a second aorist of the nu_mi-verbs.

Simple or compound verbs usually throw the accent as far back as the quantity of the last syllable permits (recessive accent, 159). lu/_w, lu/_omen, e)lu_o/mhn; paideu/w, paideu/ousi, e)paideue/thn; a)poba/llw, a)po/balle; a)polu/_w, a)pe/lu_on; a)/peimi, su/nesmen, su/mfhmi, pa/resti.

To this general rule there are exceptions. a. Enclitics.—All the forms of fhmi/ say, and ei)mi/ am, except fh/|s and ei)=. b. Imperatives.—(1) The second person sing. of the second aorist active imperative of five verbs is oxytone: ei)pe/ say, e)lqe/ come, eu(re/ find, i)de/ see, labe/ take. Their plurals are accented ei)pe/te, e)lqe/te, etc.; compounds have recessive accent: ka/teipe, a)/pelqe, e)/feure, para/labe. (2) The second aorist middle (2 sing.) is perispomenon, as labou=, parabalou=, kaqelou=. c. Contracted verbs are only apparent exceptions: thus, e.g., ti_ma=| for ti_ma/ei, dhlou=si for dhlo/ousi, filei=n for file/ein. So the subjunctive of the first and second aorist passive luqw= for luqe/w, fanw= for fane/w; the optatives luqei=men from luqe/-i_-men, didoi=men from dido/-i_-men; the futures fanw= for fane/w, fanoi=mi for fane/oimi, fanei=n for fane/ein, fanw=n for fane/wn; lipei=n for lipe/en; and the present and second aorist active and middle subjunctive of most mi-verbs, as tiqw= for tiqe/w, i(stw=mai, qw=mai, perf. kektw=mai. On didou=si, tiqei=si, see 463 d. N. 1.—In athematic optatives the accent does not recede beyond the diphthong containing -i_-, the sign of the optative mood: i(stai=o, i(stai=men, i(stai=to, didoi=to; and so in luqei=men, luqei=en. N. 2.—du/namai am able, e)pi/stamai understand, kre/mamai hang, o)ni/nhmi profit, and e)pria/mhn bought (749 b, 750 b, 757 a) have recessive accent in the subjunctive and optative (du/nwmai, e)pi/stwmai, du/naito, kre/maito). d. Poetic forms sometimes fail to follow the rule, as e)w/n being.

Infinitives, participles, and verbal adjectives are verbal nouns (358), and hence do not regularly show recessive accent. a. Infinitives.—The following infinitives accent the penult: all infinitives in -nai, as leluke/nai, luqh=nai, i(sta/nai, sth=nai (except Epic -menai, as sth/menai); in verbs in w the first aorist active, as lu=sai, paideu=sai, the second aorist middle, as lipe/sqai, the perfect (middle) passive, as lelu/sqai, pepaideu=sqai, pepoih=sqai.

Exceptions to the recessive accent of compound verbs.—a. The accent cannot precede the augment or reduplication: a)/peimi am absent, a)ph=n was absent, ei)s-h=lqon they entered, a)p-h=san they were absent; a)f-i=ktai arrived (cp. i(=ktai). N.—A long vowel or diphthong not changed by the augment receives the accent: u(p-ei=ke was yielding (indic. u(p-ei/kw, imper. u(/p-eike). b. The accent cannot precede the last syllable of the preposition before the simple verb nor move back to the first of two prepositions: peri/qes put around, sune/kdos give up together (not su/nekdos), sugka/qes put down together (not su/gkaqes). Compounds of the second aorist active imperatives do/s, e(/s, qe/s, and sxe/s are thus paroxytone: e)pi/qes set on, peri/qes put around, e)pi/sxes hold on. c. When compounded with a monosyllabic preposition, monosyllabic second aorist middle imperatives in -ou= from mi-verbs retain the circumflex: prodou= betray, e)nqou= put in. But the accent recedes when these imperatives prefix a dissyllabic preposition: a)po/dou sell, kata/qou put down. The open forms always have recessive accent, as e)/nqeo, kata/qeo. d. The accent of uncompounded infinitives, participles, aorist passive, perfect passive, and of the second aorist middle imperative (2. p. sing., but see 426 c) is retained in composition. e. a)pe/stai will be far from, e)pe/stai will be upon do not have recessive accent. f. Compound subjunctives are differently accentuated in the Mss.: a)podw=mai and a)po/dwmai, e)piqh=tai and e)pi/qhtai; the aorist of i(/_hmi has prow=mai and pro/wmai. a)pe/xw has a)po/sxwmai. Compound optatives retain the accent of the primitives: a)podoi=to, as doi=to. For sunqoi=to, prosqoi=sqe (746 c) the Mss. occasionally have su/nqoito, pro/sqoisqe; and so pro/oito.

Final -ai (and -oi) are regarded as long in the optative (169), elsewhere as short. Hence distinguish the forms of the first aorist. 3. Sing. Opt. Act. Infin. Act. 2. Sing. Imper. The augment (increase) denotes past time. It appears only in the secondary or past tenses of the indicative mood, namely, imperfect, aorist, and pluperfect. The augment has two forms, the syllabic and the temporal.

Syllabic Augment.—Verbs beginning with a consonant prefix e as the augment, which thus increases the word by one syllable. In the pluperfect e is prefixed to the reduplication. lu/_w loose e)/-lu_on e)/-lu_sa e)-lelu/kh paideu/w educate e)-pai/deuon e)-pai/deusa e)-pepaideu/kh a. Verbs beginning with r double the r after the augment. r(i/_ptw throw, e)/-rri_pton, e)/-rri_ya, e)-rri/_fqhn; r(h/gnu_mi break, e)/-rrhca, e)-rra/ghn. N.—rr is here due to assimilation of vr, as in Hom. e)/rreca did (and e)/reca); of sr in e)/rreon flowed. Cp. 80 a.

bou/lomai wish, du/namai am able, me/llw intend augment with e or with h (especially in later Attic); thus, e)boulo/mhn and h)boulo/mhn, e)duna/mhn and h)duna/mhn, e)dunh/qhn and h)dunh/qhn. a. These forms seem to be due to parallelism with h)/qelon (from e)qe/lw wish) and e)/qelon (from qe/lw).

Some verbs beginning with a vowel take the syllabic augment because they formerly began with a consonant. Thus, a)/gnu_mi break (*va/gnu_mi), e)/a_ca, aor. pass. e)a/_ghn. a(li/skomai am captured (*vali/skomai), imperf. h(lisko/mhn, aor. e(a/_lwn (with temporal augment) or h(/lwn. a(nda/nw please (*vanda/nw), aor. e(/adon (Ionic). a)n-oi/gw open (*voi/gnu_mi), imperf. a)n-e/w|gon. e)a/w permit (se*vaw), ei)/wn, ei)/a_sa, ei)a/_qhn. e(zo/mai sit (for sediomai), ei(sa/mhn. e)qi/zw accustom (s*veqi/zw, cp. 123), ei)/qizon, ei)/qisa, ei)qi/sqhn. e)li/ttw roll (*veli/ttw), ei)/litton, ei)/lica, ei)li/xqhn. e(/lkw or e(lku/w draw (selkw), ei(=lkon, ei(/lkusa, ei(lku/sqhn. e(/pomai follow (sepomai), ei(po/mhn. e)rga/zomai work (*verga/zomai), ei)rgasa/mhn. e(/rpw creep (serpw), ei(=rpon. e(stia/w entertain (*vesti/aw), ei(sti/wn, ei(sti/a_sa, ei(stia/_qhn. e)/xw hold (sexw), ei)=xon. i(/hmi send (sishmi), aor. du. ei(=ton for e)-e(-ton, ei(/qhn for e)-e(-qhn. i(/sthmi put (sisthmi), plup. ei(sth/kh for e)-se-sthkh. o(ra/w see (*vora/w), e(w/rwn, e(w/ra_ka or e(o/ra_ka. w)qe/w push (*vwqe/w), e)w/qoun, e)/wsa, e)w/sqhn. w)ne/omai buy (*vwne/omai), e)wnou/mhn, e)wnh/qhn. ei)=don saw, 2 aor. of o(ra/w (for e)-*vidon). ei(=lon took, 2 aor. of ai(re/w (for e)-e(lon).
Some forms of some verbs in 431 are augmented as if no consonant had preceded the first vowel, as h)rgazo/mhn (and ei)rgazo/mhn).

Since v disappeared early, many augmented forms show no trace of its existence, as, w)/|koun from oi)ke/w dwell (voi=kos). Besides e, h was also used as the syllabic augment. This appears in Hom. h)-ei/deis (-hs?), Attic h)/|deis you knew.

The verbs a)/gnu_mi, a(li/skomai, (a)n）oi/gnu_mi, o(ra/w, which began originally with v, show forms that appear to have a double augment; as e)a/_ghn, e(a/_lwn, (a)n）e)w|gon (rarely h)/noigon), e(w/rwn, e(w/ra_ka (and e(o/ra_ka). These forms appear to be due to transference of quantity (34) from h)-va^ghn, h)-voigon, h)-vorwn (cp. 433).

Temporal Augment.—Verbs beginning with a vowel take the temporal augment by lengthening the initial vowel. The temporal augment is so called because it usually increases the time required to pronounce the initial syllable. Initial a| becomes h|: a)/|dw sing, h)=|don. Initial h, i_, u_, w remain unchanged. Initial a_ usually becomes h: a)_rista/w breakfast, h)ri/sthsa. a)na_li/skw and a)na_lo/w expend form a)na/_lwsa and a)nh/lwsa, a)na_lw/qhn and a)nhlw/qhn.

Initial diphthongs are sometimes unaugmented: au in au(ai/nomai dry; ei: ei)/kazon, h)/|kazon; eu: eu(re/qhn and hu(re/qhn from eu(ri/skw find, eu)ca/mhn and hu)ca/mhn from eu)/xomai pray; ou is never augmented, since it is never a pure diphthong when standing at the beginning of a verb-form.

Omission of the Augment.—a. In Attic tragedy the augment is sometimes omitted in choral passages, rarely in the dialogue parts (messengers' speeches), which are nearer akin to prose. b. In xrh=n (from xrh\ + h)=n) the augment is strictly unnecessary, but is often added (e)xrh=n) since the composition of xrh=n was forgotten. c. In Homer and the lyric poets either the syllabic or the temporal augment is often absent; as fa/to and e)/fato, bh=n and e)/bhn, e)/xon and ei)=xon. Iteratives (495) in Hom. usually have no augment (e)/xeskon). N.—In Homer the absence of the augment represents the usage of the parent language, in which the augment was not necessarily added to mark past time. It is therefore erroneous, historically, to speak of the omission of the augment in Homer. d. In Herodotus the syllabic augment is omitted only in the case of pluperfects and iteratives in skon; the temporal augment is generally preserved, but it is always omitted in verbs beginning with ai, au, ei, eu, oi, and in a)gi_ne/w, a)eqle/w, a)nw/gw, e)/rdw, e)a/w, o(rme/w, etc.; in others it is omitted only in some forms (as a)goreu/w, a)/gw, e(/lkw, o(rma/w), and in others it is variable (a)gge/llw, a(/ptw, a)/rxw, e)pi/stamai, a)ne/xomai); in cases of Attic reduplication the augment is never added. Hdt. omits the augment for the reduplication in the above verbs.

Reduplication is the doubling of the sound standing at the beginning of a word. It is used in the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect tenses in all the moods, to denote completed action. It is sometimes found also in the present and second aorist.

Verbs beginning with a simple consonant (except r) or with a stop and a liquid (l, m, n, r) place the initial consonant with e before the stem. lu/_w loose, le/-luka, le-luke/nai, le/-lumai, le-lu/_somai; gra/fw write, ge/-grafa; kli/_nw incline, ke/-klika; bla/ptw injure, be/-blafa; pri/_w saw, pe/-pri_smai. a. Exceptions: verbs beginning with gn, most of those with gl, and some with bl. Thus, gnwri/zw recognize, e)-gnw/rika; gi-gnw/skw know, e)/-gnwka; glu/fw carve, e)/-glufa; blasta/nw sprout, e)-bla/sthka (usu. bebla/sthka).
An initial aspirate is reduplicated by the corresponding smooth stop: foneu/w murder, pe-fo/neuka; qu/_w sacrifice, te/-quka; xoreu/w dance, ke-xo/reuka.

In all other cases the reduplication is formed like the augment. a. Verbs beginning with a short vowel lengthen the vowel, as a)/gw lead, h)=xa; o)rqo/w set upright, w)/rqwka; a)gge/llw announce, h)/ggelka. b. Verbs beginning with two or more consonants (except a stop with a liquid), a double consonant, and r simply prefix e. r is here doubled (cp. 429 a). Thus, kti/zw found, e)/-ktika; spei/rw sow, e)/-sparmai; strathge/w am general, e)-strath/ghka; zhte/w seek, e)-zh/thka; yau/w touch, e)/-yauka; r(i/_ptw throw, e)/rri_fa. N.—mimnh/|skw remind and kta/omai acquire are exceptions: me/-mnhmai, e)-memnh/mhn; ke/-kthmai, e)-ke-kth/mhn.

The verbs mentioned in 431 which originally began with a consonant now lost, reduplicate regularly. Since the reduplicated consonant has disappeared only e is left, and this often contracts with the initial vowel of the theme. Thus, e)/a_ga for ve-va_ga from va/gnu_mi break; e)/wsmai for ve-vwsmai from vwqe/w push; e(/sthka for sesthka from i(/sthmi set; ei(=ka for seseka from i(/_hmi (si-shmi) send.

Pluperfect.—The pluperfect prefixes the syllabic augment e to the reduplicated perfect beginning with a consonant; when the perfect stem begins with a vowel the pluperfect retains the prefix of the perfect. Thus perf. le/luka, le/lumai, plup. e)-lelu/kh, e)-lelu/mhn; perf. e)/-stalka, e)/-stalmai, plup. e)-sta/lkh, e)-sta/lmhn from ste/llw send; perf. h)go/reuka, plup. h)goreu/kh from a)goreu/w harangue; perf. h(/|rhka, plup. h(|rh/kh from ai(re/w seize. a. Verbs showing ‘Attic’ reduplication (446), in almost all cases augment the pluperfect. b. The verbs of 431 follow the perfects of 443; as e)a/_gh (a)/gnu_mi), e)w/smhn (w)qe/w), ei(/mhn (i(/_hmi), e)rrw/gh from (v）rh/gnu_mi. i(/sthmi forms ei(sth/kh ( = e)-（s）esthkh), Ion. and poet. e(sth/kh (rare in Att. prose). e)/oika am like forms e)w/|kh.

Some verbs beginning with a liquid or m take ei instead of the reduplication: lamba/nw (lab-) take, ei)/-lhfa, ei)/-lhmmai, ei)-lh/fh; lagxa/nw (lax-) obtain by lot, ei)/-lhxa, ei)-lh/xh; le/gw collect (in composition) -ei)/-loxa, -ei)-lo/xh, -ei)/-legmai (rarely le/-legmai); mei/romai receive a share, ei(/-martai it is fated, ei(/-marto with rough breathing; also the stems ep, rh say, ei)/-rhka, ei)-rh/kh.

Attic Reduplication.—Some verbs whose themes begin with a, e, or o, followed by a single consonant, reduplicate by repeating the initial vowel and the consonant and by lengthening a and e to h, o to w. Thus a)gei/rw collect, a)g-h/gerka, a)g-h/germai; e)gei/rw awaken, e)g-h/germai; e)le/gxw confute, e)l-h/legmai; o)ru/ttw dig, o)r-w/ruxa, o)r-w/rugmai; o)/m-nu_mi swear, o)m-w/moka; o)/l-lu_mi destroy, o)l-w/leka. So also fe/rw bear, e)n-h/noxa, e)n-h/negmai. a. The name ‘Attic’ was given by the Greek grammarians to this form of reduplication though it occurs in Homer and in the other dialects. b. a)kou/w hear has a)k-h/koa for a)k-h/ko（[uglide]）a; a)/gw has a)g-h/oxa for a)g-h/（g）oxa. The pluperfect augments except in the case of verbs with initial e: h)k-hko/h, w)m-wmo/kh, a)pwlw/lh; but e)l-hlu/qh, e)n-hne/gmhn.

Reduplication in the Present.—A few verbs reduplicate in the present by prefixing the initial consonant and i, as gi/-gnomai, gi-gnw/skw, mi-mnh/|skw, ti/-ktw for ti-t（e）kw, pi/_-ptw for pi-p（e）tw, i(/-sthmi for si-sthmi, ti/-qhmi for qi-qhmi (125 a), di/-dwmi. pi/m-plh-mi fill (pla-, plh-) and pi/mprhmi burn (pra-, prh-) insert m. a. In some verbs the reduplication belongs to the verbal stem: biba/zw make go e)bi/basa, dida/skw teach e)di/daca.
Reduplication in the Second Aorist.—a)/gw lead forms the second aorist h)/g-agon, a)g-a/gw, a)g-a/goimi, a)g-agei=n, middle h)g-ago/mhn. So also h)/n-egka and h)/n-egkon from fe/rw.

In verbs compounded with a preposition, augment and reduplication stand between the preposition and the verb. Thus, u(perbai/nw pass over, u(pere/bainon, u(perbe/bhka; ei)sba/llw throw into, ei)se/ballon, ei)sbe/blhka. a. Before e of the augment e)k regains its fuller form e)c (133 a), and e)n and su/n reappear in their proper forms which were modified in the present. Thus e)kba/llw throw out, e)ce/ballon, e)kbe/blhka; e)mba/llw throw into, e)ne/ballon; sulle/gw collect, sune/legon, sunei/loxa; surri/_ptw throw together, sune/rri_ya, sune/rri_fa; suskeua/zw pack together, suneskeu/azon, suneskeua/sqhn. b. Prepositions (except peri/ and pro/) drop their final vowel: a)poba/llw throw away, a)p-e/ballon; but periba/llw throw around, perie/ballon, probai/nw step forward, proe/bhn. But pro/ may contract with the augment (prou)/bhn).

But some verbs, which are not often used except as compounds, are treated like uncompound verbs and take the augment before the preposition, as e)kaqh/mhn sat from ka/qhmai, e)ka/qizon set, sat from kaqi/zw, h)mfi/esa clothed from a)mfie/nnu_mi, e)ka/qeudon (and kaqhu_don) slept from kaqeu/dw, h)pista/mhn, h)pisth/qhn from e)pi/stamai understand. i(/_hmi forms a)fi/_ei and h)fi/_ei. The simple verbs occur mostly in poetry. But a)polau/w enjoy makes a)pole/lauka, e)ceta/zw review e)ch/taka.

Double Augment.—Some verbs take two augments, one before and the other after the preposition, as h)n-eixo/mhn, h)n-esxo/mhn from a)n-e/xomai endure, h)n-w/xloun from e)noxle/w annoy, e)phnw/rqwmai from e)panorqo/w set upright. So also, by analogy to the foregoing, a few verbs derived from compound words: h)mfesbh/toun from a)hfisbhte/w dispute, h)ntede/kei from a)ntidike/w go to law (a)nti/dikos).

Compounds of dus- ill and eu)= well. (1) dustuxe/w am unhappy, e)-dustu/xoun, de-dus-tu/xhka. dus-hre/stoun, dus-hre/sthka from dus-areste/w do not occur. (2) eu)ergete/w do good, eu)erge/thsan, eu)erge/thka (inscrip.) eu)hrge/thka (texts).

Verbs derived from compound nouns take the augment and the reduplication at the beginning; as e)mu_qolo/goun, memu_qolo/ghka from mu_qologe/w tell legends (mu_qolo/gos teller of legends); w)|kodo/moun, w)|kodo/mhka from oi)kodome/w build (oi)kodo/mos house-builder); h)mpo/lwn, h)mpo/lhka from e)mpola/w traffic in (e)mpolh/ traffic). a. e)kklhsia/zw hold an assembly (e)kklhsi/a_) makes h)k-klhsi/azon or e)c-e-klhsi/azon. e)ggua/w pledge makes e)negu/wn, e)negu/hsa and (better) h)ggu/wn, h)ggu/hsa.

Verbs derived from compound nouns whose first part is a preposition are commonly treated as if compounded of a preposition and a simple verb; as kathgore/w accuse (kath/goros), kathgo/roun, kathgo/rhka; e)nqu_me/omai ponder (e)/nqu_mos) e)nequ_mh/qhn, e)ntequ_mh=sqai; e)piorke/w swear falsely (e)pi/orkos), e)piw/rkhka; e)gxeiri/zw entrust (e)n xeiri/), e)nexei/risa. a. But several verbs are not treated as compounds, such as a)pata/w deceive, a)piste/w distrust, a)pore/w am in difficulty, parrhsia/zomai speak freely.

Tense-Suffixes.—The tense-suffixes, which are added to the verb-stem to form the tense-stems, consist of the thematic vowel and certain other letters. No tense-suffixes are added to the verb-stem (1) in the second aorist active and middle, and second perfect and pluperfect, of mi-verbs; (2) in the perfect and pluperfect middle of verbs in -w and -mi. The tense-suffixes are as follows:— 1. Present system, -o/e-, -to/e-, -[iglide]o/e-, -no/e-, -ano/e-, -neo/e-, -na-, -nu-, -（i）sko/e; or none, as in fa-me/n. 2. Future system, -so/e-. 3. First aorist sytem, -sa-. 4. Second aorist system, -o/e-; or none, as in e)/-sth-n. 5. First perfect system, -ka- (plupf. -kh- from -kea-; -kei- from -kee-; -ke-). 6. Second perfect system, -a- (plupf. -h-, -ei-, or -e-); or none, as in e(/-sta-te. 7. Perfect middle system, none (future perfect -so/e-). 8. First passive system, qh-, -qe- (future passive -qhso/e-). 9. Second passive system, h, -e- (future passive -hso/e-). N.—-a in the aorist is properly a relic of the personal ending (666).

Thematic Vowel.—The thematic, or variable, vowel appears at the end of the tense-stems in the present, imperfect, and second aorist active and middle of w-verbs, and in all futures and future perfects. The thematic vowel in the indicative is o before m or n (and in the optative of the tenses mentioned); elsewhere it is e. Thus, lu_o/e-, lipo/e-, lu_so/e-, luqhso/e-, lelu_so/e-; lu/_o-i_-mi. In the subjunctive it is w/h. a. Attic inscriptions have both -esqwn and -osqwn in the imperative.
Subjunctive.—In the subjunctive of all verbs the thematic vowel is w/h-. Thus, lu/_w-men, lu/_h-te, lu/_sw-men, stei/lh-te. a. Verbs in -nu_mi form their subjunctive like w-verbs.
In the present and second aorist of mi-verbs, and in the aorist passive, w/h is added to the tense stem. Thus tiqw=men from tiqe/-w-men, qw= from qe/-w, tiqh=te from tiqe/-h-te, luqw= from luqe/-w.

Suffix of the Optative.—The optative adds the mood suffix -i_-, or -ih- which contracts with the final vowel of the tense-stem: lu/_oimi for lu/_o-i_-mi, filoi/hn for fileo-i/h-n, tiqei/hn for tiqe-i/h-n. -ih- occurs only before active endings. When the suffix is -ih-, the 1 pers. sing. ends in -n; as ti_mao-i/h-n = ti_mw/|hn; when it is -i_-, the 1 pers. sing. ends in -mi, as ti_ma/o-i_-mi = ti_mw=|mi.

ih is used as follows (in all other cases -i_-):— a. In contracted verbs in the singular, rarely in the dual and plural. -i_- appears in the dual and plural, rarely in the singular. b. In liquid verbs in the future active singular: fanoi/h-n for faneo-i/h-n. In the dual and plural -i_-: fanoi=ton, fanoi=men for faneo/-i_-ton, faneo/-i_-men. c. In the singular of mi-verbs: tiqei/hn for tiqe-i/h-n, didoi/hn for dido-i/h-n, qei/hn for qe-i/h-n. Here the modal sign is added to the tense-stem without any thematic vowel. -i_- is more common in the dual and plural: tiqei=men for tiqe/-i_-men, didoi=men for dido/-i_-men, qei=te for qe/-i_-te. Verbs in -nu_mi make their optatives like lu/_w. d. In the aorist passive: luqei/hn for luqe-i/h-n, fanei/hn for fane-i/h-n. In the dual and plural -i_- is more common: luqei=men for luqe/-i_-men, fanei=te for fane/-i_-te. e. In some second perfects, as proelhluqoi/hs, and in the second aorist sxoi/hn from e)/xw (but -sxoi=mi in composition). N.—In the 3 pl. -ie- is regular before -n: lu/_o-ie-n, tiqe-i=e-n, luqe-i=e-n.

a. In the 1 aor. opt. act. of w-verbs the endings -eias, -eie, and -eian are more common than -ais, -ai, -aien. b. In the aor. opt. passive of all verbs and in the opt. of mi-verbs and of contract verbs -iton, -ithn, -imen, -ite, -ien are commoner than -ihton, -ihthn, -ihmen, -ihte, -ihsan. Prose writers use either the shorter or the longer forms; poets use only the shorter forms. Except in contract verbs -ihte is very common in the 2 pl. and is sometimes the only form in the Mss., as doi/hte, qei/hte, gnoi/hte, -bai/hte, luqei/hte, fanei/hte; but the forms in question occur in prose writers and their genuineness is therefore unsupported by metrical evidence.

To make the complete verbal forms, to the tense-stems in the various moods are attached the personal endings in the finite moods and other endings in the infinitives, participles, and verbal adjectives. See 366. The personal endings of the four finite moods are given below. In many forms only the mi-verbs preserve distinct endings. Some of the endings are due to analogy of others and many are still unexplained. The first person dual, when it is used, has the form of the first person plural. ACTIVE MIDDLE INDICATIVE INDICATIVE INDICATIVE INDICATIVE (primary tenses) (secondary tenses) (primary tenses) (secondary tenses) AND AND AND AND SUBJUNCTIVE OPTATIVE SUBJUNCTIVE OPTATIVE Sing. 1.—or -mi -n -mai -mhn 2. -s (for -si), -qa (-sqa） -s, -sqa -sai -so 3. -si (for -ti） — -tai -to Dual 2. -ton -ton -sqon -sqon 3. -ton -thn -sqon -sqhn Plur. 1. -men -men -meqa -meqa 2. -te -te -sqe -sqe 3. -nsi (for -nti） -n, -san, -ntai -nto ACTIVE MIDDLE IMPERATIVE Sing. 2. —,-qi, -s -so 3. -tw -sqw Dual 2. -ton -sqon 3. -twn -sqwn Plur. 2. -te -sqe 3. -ntwn (-twsan） -sqwn (-sqwsan）

PRIMARY ENDINGS OF THE ACTIVE (IND. AND SUBJ.) a. 1 Sing.—-mi is found only in mi-verbs. Verbs in -w have no ending and simply lengthen the thematic vowel (lu/_w, lei/pw). The perfect has no personal ending, -a taking the place of a thematic vowel.

SECONDARY ENDINGS OF THE ACTIVE (IND. AND OPT.) The optative usually has the endings of the secondary tenses of the indicative. a. 1 Sing.—-n stands for m (133 c), cp. e)/fero-n, Skt. ábhara-m. After a consonant m (sonant nasal, 20 b, 35 c) became a: e)/lu_sa for e)lu_sṃ, Epic h)=a was for h'（s）a from h)sṃ. In the pluperfect -h is from e-a (467). -n is found in the optative when the mood suffix is -ih-; elsewhere the optative has -mi.

ENDINGS OF THE MIDDLE (INDIC., SUBJ., OPT.) a. 2 Sing.—Primary -sai retains its s in the perfect of all verbs (le/lu-sai), and in the pres. of mi-verbs (ti/qe-sai). Elsewhere s drops between vowels, as in lu/_h| or lu/_ei from lu/_e-sai, luqh/sh| or -ei, fanh=| from fane/e-sai, ti_ma=| from ti_ma/e-sai; subj. lu/_h| from lu/h-sai, fh/nh| from fh/nh-sai, qh=| from qh/e-sai, dw=| from dw/h-sai, h(=| from e(/h-sai, filh=| from file/h-sai, dhloi= from dhlo/h| = dhlo/h-sai. N. 1.—The forms -h| and -ei are found in the present, future, and future perfect. See 628. N. 2.—du/na| and du/nh| for du/nasai, e)pi/sta| and e)pi/sth| for e)pi/stasai, e)fi/_ei for e)fi/_esai, are poetic and dialectic or late.

ENDINGS OF THE IMPERATIVE 1. Active. a. 2 Sing.—lu=e, li/pe, ti/qei (for ti/qe-e) have not lost -qi. -qi is found in 2 aor. pass. fa/nh-qi; in sth=-qi and e(/sta-qi; in some 2 aorists, like gnw=-qi, tlh=-qi, pi=-qi, which are mi forms though they have presents of the w form (687). Also in i)/s-qi be or know, i)/qi go, fa/qi or faqi/ say. lu/qhti is for luqhqi by 125 b.
Endings of the Pluperfect Active.—-h, -hs, -ei（n) are derived from -e（s）a, -e（s）as, -e（s）e. In later Greek the endings are -ein, -eis, -ei（n), -eiton, -eithn, -eimen, -eite, and very late -eisan.

The Endings -sqe, etc.—The s of the endings -sqe, -sqw, -sqon, -sqwn, -sqai (409 N.) has no exact parallel in cognate languages, and seems to have spread in Greek from forms like tete/les-qe, e)/zws-qe, etc., where a sigma-stem was followed by original -qe.

Infinitive.—The following are the endings added to the tense-stem to make the infinitive. a. -en: in present and 2 aorist active of w-verbs, all futures active. Thus, lu/_ein, ti_ma=n, lipei=n, lu/_sein, fanei=n from lu/_e-en, ti_ma/e-en, lipe/-en, lu/_se-en, fane/e-en. b. -ai: in 1 aor. active, as lu=sai, paideu=sai, dei=cai. c. -nai: (1) present, 2 perf. of mi-verbs, the two passive aorists, as tiqe/-nai, e(sta/nai, luqh=-nai, fanh=-nai; (2) perfect active, leluke/-nai, and ei)de/-nai from ei)d-e (oi)=da). N. 1.—The ending enai appears in the 2 aor. of mi-verbs, as dou=nai from do/-enai, qei=nai from qe/-enai. d. -sqai: in other cases. N. 2.—The infinitives are old cases of substantives, those in -ai being datives, the others locatives.

Participles.—The stem of the participle is formed by adding the following endings to the tense stem. a. -nt-: in all active tenses except the perfect, and in 1 and 2 aor. passive (301). b. -ot-: in the perfect active (for -vot-); masc. -w/s, fem. -ui=a, neut. -o/s (301 c). c. -meno-: in the middle, and in the passive except in the aorist.

Verbal Adjectives.—Most of the verbals in -to/s and -te/os are formed by adding these suffixes to the verbal stem of the aorist passive (first or second). Thus, filhto/s, -te/os (e)-filh/-qhn); peisto/s, -te/os (e)-pei/s-qhn); telesto/s, -te/os (e)-tele/s-qhn); stalto/s, -te/os (e)-sta/l-hn); blhto/s, -te/os (e)-blh/-qhn). On the accent of compound verbals, see 425 c. a. Some are derived from other stem forms (pres. and fut.), as fer-to/s, i/-te/on, duna-to/s; meneto/s (cp. mene/-w = menw= fut.).

Verbals in -to/s, -th/, -to/n either (1) have the meaning of a perfect passive participle, as krupto/s hidden, paideuto/s educated, or (2) express possibility, as nohto/s thinkable, o(ra_to/s visible. Many have either signification, but some are passive only, as poihto/s done. See 425 c. N. a. Usually passive in meaning are verbals from deponent verbs, as mi_mhto/s imitated. b. Usually active in meaning are compounds derived from transitive active verbs; but some intransitive verbs make active verbals, as r(uto/s flowing. c. Many are active or passive, others only active: mempto/s blamed, blamable, blaming, pisto/s trusting in (rare), trusted, a)/pra_ktos doing nothing, not done, fqegkto/s sounding.
Verbals in -te/os, -te/a_, -te/on express necessity (cp. the Lat. gerundive in -ndus), as dote/os that must be given, paideute/os educandus.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: From the verb-stem (or theme) each tense-stem is formed by the addition of a tense-suffix (455) or of a prefix, or of both. In 475-495 certain modifications of the verb-stem are considered.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Variation in Quantity.—Many verbs of the first class (498 ff.) show variation in the quantity of the vowel of the verb-stem, which is commonly long in the present but fluctuates in other tenses, as lu/_-w, lu/_-sw, e)/lu_-sa, but le/lu^-ka, le/lu^-mai, e)lu^/-qhn. (Other examples, 500.) a. Some verbs of the Fourth Class (523 c) lengthen a short vowel of the present in some other tenses. Thus, lamba/nw (lab-) take, lh/yomai, ei)/lhfa, ei)/lhmmai, e)lh/fqhn, but 2 aor. e)/labon.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Vowel Gradation (35, 36).—Verbs of the first class show a variation between a strong grade (or two strong grades) and a weak grade. The weak grades, i^, u^, a^, appear especially in the second aorist and second passive systems; the corresponding strong grades, ei (oi), eu (ou), h (w), appear usually in the other systems (oi, ou, w, in the second perfect). a. Expulsion of a short vowel between consonants (so-called syncope 493) produces a weak form of the stem of the same grade as i, u, a (36). Cp. gi/-gn-omai become (aor. e)-gen-o/-mhn), e)-pt-o/-mhn (pres. pe/t-o-mai fly) with e)/-lip-o-n, e)/-fug-o-n, e)-ta/k-h-n (477 c). So e)/-sx-o-n got from e)/x-w have. b. a is the weak form of h (a_), as in th/kw e)ta/khn; and of e, when e has l, m, n, r before or after it, as in tre/pw, e)tra/phn (479).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: The following examples illustrate the principles of 476. a. ei oi i: lei/pw leave, lei/yw, 2 perf. le/loipa, le/leimmai, e)lei/fqhn, 2 aor. e)/lipom N.—The weak form appears when the verb undergoes Attic reduplication (446); as in a)lei/fw anoint, 2 perf. a)lh/lifa, a)lh/limmai; e)rei/kw tear (Ionic and poetic), 2 perf. e)rh/rigmai, 2 aor. h)/rikon; e)rei/pw overthrow, Epic e)rh/ripa; but e)rei/dw prop, e)rh/reismai. b. eu ou u: e)leu/（q）somai I shall go, 2 perf. e)lh/luqa (Epic e)lh/louqa), 2 aor. (Epic h)/luqon); feu/gw flee, feu/comai or feucou=mai, 2 perf. pe/feuga, 2 aor. e)/fugon; r(e/w flow (for r(eu-w, 43), r(eu/somai, e)rru/hka (r(ue-), 2 aor. pass. e)rru/hn. N.—xe/w pour (for xeu-w, 43), e)/xea (for e)/xeua), has u in ke/xuka, ke/xumai, e)xu/qhn; seu/w (poetic) urge, e)/sseua, e)/ssumai, e)ssu/qhn or e)su/qhn rushed. See also teu/xw in the List of Verbs. c. h w a: r(h/g-nu_mi break, r(h/cw, e)/rrhca, 2 perf. e)/rrwga, 2 aor. pass. e)rra/ghn; th/k-w melt, th/cw, e)/thca, te/thka, e)th/xqhn, 2 aor. pass. e)ta/khn. N.—Verbs of class c usually have a^ in the 2 aorist, w in the 2 perfect (if there is one), elsewhere h. w occurs in the present in trw/gw gnaw, 2 aor. e)/tragon.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Change of e to o in the Second Perfect.—In the second perfect e of the verb-stem is changed to o. kle/p-t-w steal ke/klofa, (a)po-) ktei/nw kill (kten-, 519) -e/ktona, le/g-w collect ei)/loxa, pa/sxw, fut. pei/somai (from penqsomai, 100) pe/ponqa, pe/mp-w send pe/pomfa, ste/rg-w love e)/storga, ti/ktw beget te/toka, tre/p-w turn te/trofa, tre/f-w nourish te/trofa, fqei/r-w corrupt e)/fqora. So in gi/g（e）nomai become e)geno/mhn, ge/gona; e)gei/rw awaken e)grh/gora (446). This change corresponds to that of ei to oi (477 a).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Change of e to a.—In verb-stems containing l, m, n, r, an e is usually changed to a in the first perfect, perfect middle, and second passive systems. tre/p-w turn, te/trammai, e)tra/phn (1 aor. e)tre/fqhn); tre/f-w feed, te/qrammai, e)tra/fhn (1 aor. e)qre/fqhn); spei/rw (sper-) sow, e)/sparmai, e)spa/rhn; fqei/rw (fqer-) destroy, e)/fqarmai, e)fqa/rhn; ste/llw (stel-) send, e)/stalka, e)/stalmai, e)sta/lhn; tei/nw (ten-) stretch, te/taka, te/tamai, e)ta/qhn (1 aor.). a. Also in the 2 aor. pass. of kle/ptw steal (e)kla/phn), ple/kw weave (e)pla/khn), te/rpw gladden (Epic e)ta/rphn). Many of these verbs also show o in the second perfect (478).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: This a^ is also found in the second aorist active and middle of ktei/nw kill (e)/ktanon poetic), te/mnw cut (dialectal e)/tamon), tre/pw turn (e)/trapon poetic), te/rpw gladden (e)tarpo/mhn poetic), poetic de/rkomai see (e)/drakon). Also pe/rqw, pth/ssw.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: e in the perfect middle in ke/klemmai (kle/ptw steal), pe/plegmai (ple/kw weave) is introduced from the present.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: The a^ in 479, 480 is developed from a liquid or nasal brought between two consonants (35 b). Thus, e)/stalmai, te/tamai from e)stḷmai, tetṇmai, e)ta/qhn from e)tṇqhn (20 b). Here stl, tn represent weak grades of the stem.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: a. The variations e, o, a, w appear in tre/pw turn, tre/yw, e)/treya, 2 perf. te/trofa, te/trammai, e)tre/fqhn, 2 aor. pass. e)tra/phn; frequentative trwpa/w (867). b. The variations e, o, w appear in pe/tomai fly, pote/omai (poet.) and frequentative pwta/omai (poet., 867) fly about.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: h, a in the Second Perfect.—In the second perfect a^ of the verb-stem is lengthened to h (a_): qa/llw (qal-) bloom, te/qhla; fai/nw (fan-) show, pe/fhna; mai/nw (man-) madden, me/mhna; kra/_zw (krag-) cry out, ke/kra_ga.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Addition of e.—a. To the verb-stem e is added to make the present stem in doke/w seem, fut. do/cw, aor. e)/doca (dok-); so in game/w marry, w)qe/w push. Usually e is added in some stem other than the present. b. In many verbs e is added to the verb-stem to form the tense-stems other than present, second aorist, and second perfect, e.g. ma/xomai (max-) fight, maxou=mai ( = maxe（s）omai), e)maxesa/mhn, mema/xhmai. So a)/xqomai am grieved, bou/louai wish, gi/gnomai become, de/w want, (e'）qe/lw wish, me/llw intend, me/lei is a care, oi)/omai think. c. In some verbs e is added to form one or more tense-stems, as me/nw (men-) remain, meme/nhka (mene-) to avoid -n-ka in the perfect. So, ne/mw distribute, e)/xw have, oi)/xomai am gone. So also darqa/nw, o)sfai/nomai, r(e/w, stei/bw (poetic), tugxa/nw. d. Some verbs have alternative presents with or without e. Here sometimes one is used in prose, the other in poetry, sometimes both are poetic or both used in prose. Thus, e(/lkw draw (Hom. also e(lke/w), i)a/xw i)axe/w sound (both poetic), me/dw mede/w (both poetic), r(i/_ptw and r(i_pte/w throw (both in prose).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Addition of a and o.—a or o is added to the verb-stem in some verbs. Thus, mu_ka/omai bellow (Epic 2 aor. mu/kon), e)mu_khsa/mhn; a(li/skomai (a(l-) be captured, a(lw/somai from a(lo-; o)/mnu_-mi swear (o)m-) w)/mosa, o)mw/moka etc. (o)mo-); oi)/xomai am gone, Epic oi)/xwka or w)/|xwka.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Lengthening of Short Final Vowel.—Verb-stems ending in a short vowel generally lengthen that vowel before the tense-suffix in all tenses (except the present and imperfect) formed from them. Here a (except after e, i, and r) and e become h, o become w. ti_ma/-w (ti_ma-) honour, ti_mh/-sw, e)ti/_mh-sa, teti/_mh-ka, teti/_mh-mai, e)ti_mh/-qhn; qhra/-w (qhra-) hunt, qhra/_-sw, e)qh/ra_-sa, etc. (389); poie/w (poie-) make, poih/-sw, e)poi/h-sa, pepoi/h-ka, pepoi/h-mai, e)poih/-qhn; dhlo/w (dhlo-) manifest, dhlw/-sw, e)dh/lw-sa, etc.; e)a/w permit, e)a/_sw, etc. a. Note a)kroa/_somai, h)kroa_sa/mhn, etc., from a)kroa/omai hear; xrh/sw, e)/xrhsa from xra/w give oracles; xrh/somai, e)xrhsa/mhn from xra/omai use; trh/sw and e)/trhsa from tetrai/nw bore are from tre-. b. Verb-stems adding e or o (486), and stems apparently receiving a short final vowel by metathesis (128), lengthen the short final vowel, as bou/lomai (boul-) wish, boulh/-somai (boule-, 485), ka/mnw (kam-) am weary, ke/kmh-ka (kma-).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Retention of Short Final Vowel.—Many verb-stems ending apparently in a short vowel retain the short vowel, contrary to 487, in some or all the tenses. gela^/-w laugh, gela^/somai, e)ge/la^sa, e)gela^/sqhn; tele/w finish, telw= from tele/-w, e)te/lesa, tete/leka, tete/lesmai, e)tele/sqhn; a)nu/w accomplish, a)nu^/sw, h)/nu^sa, h)/nu^smai. a. The following verbs retain the final short vowel of the verb-stem in all tenses: a)/ga-mai, ai)de/-omai, a)ke/-omai, a)le/-w, a)nu/-w, a)re/skw (a)re-), a)rke/-w, a)ro/-w, a)ru/-w, gela/-w, e)lau/nw (e)la-), e(lku/-w, and e(/lk-w (e(lk-e-), e)me/-w, e)ra/-w, e)/ra-mai (poet.), e)sqi/w (e)sqi-, e)d-e-, e)do-), ze/-w, qla/-w, i(_la/skomai (i(_la-), kla/-w break, mequ/skw (mequ-), ce/-w, ptu/_-w (ptu_-, ptu^-), spa/-w, tele/-w, tre/-w, fqi/nw (fqi-), fla/-w, xala/-w, xe/-w (xu-). Also all verbs in -annu_mi and -ennu_mi (except e)/sbhka from sbe/nnu_mi extinguish), and o)/llu_mi (o)l-e-), o)/mnu_mi (o)m-, o)me-, o)mo-), sto/rnu_mi (stor-e). b. The following verbs keep short the final vowel in the future, but lengthen it in one or more other tense-systems, or have double future forms, one with the short vowel, the other with the long vowel: ai)ne/w (ai)ne/sw, h)/|nesa, h)/|neka, h)|ne/qhn, h)/|nhmai), a)/xqomai (a)xq-, a)xqe-), kale/-w, ma/xomai (max-e-), mu/_w, pi/_nw (pi-, po-), poqe/-w, pone/-w, e)ru/-w (Epic), fqa/nw (fqa-). c. In some verbs the final short vowel of the verb-stem remains short in one or more tense-stems, but is lengthened in the future, as de/-w bind, dh/sw, e)/dhsa, de/deka, de/demai, e)de/qhn. So ai(re/w, bai/nw (ba-), bu_ne/w (bu-), di/dwmi (do-, dw-), du/na-mai, du/_w (du^-, du_-), eu(ri/skw (eu(r-e-), e)/xw (sex-, sxe-), qu/_w (qu^-, qu_-), i(/hmi (e(-, h(-), i(/sthmi (sta^-, sth-), lu/_w (lu^-, lu_-), ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-), ti/nw (ti-), fu/_w (fu^-, fu_-), and the root e)r-, r(e- (ei)=pon). d. Most of the verbs refusing to lengthen a final short vowel have verb-stems originally ending in s (624); as tele/w from

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Insertion of s.—In the perfect middle and first aorist passive systems, verbs which retain a short final vowel and some others usually insert s before the personal ending. Thus, tele/w (488 d), tete/lesmai, e)tele/sqhn; spa/w draw, e)/spasmai, e)spa/sqhn; keleu/w order, keke/leusmai, e)keleu/sqhn; gignw/skw know, e)/gnwsmai, e)gnw/sqhn. a. If the aorist passive ends in -qhn and not in -sqhn, the perfect middle does not insert s. Thus -qhn, not -sqhn, occurs in all verbs in -euw except leu/w stone to death, in all verbs in -ew which have -qhn preceded by h, in all verbs in -ow except xo/w heap up, and in all verbs in -aw except those that retain a^. Stems originally ending in s (624) properly show s. b. If the aorist passive ends in -sqhn, the perfect middle may or may not insert s. Verbs in -azw and -izw (stems -ad, -id) regularly have s by 83, 587. In the case of other verbs some always show s, some never show s, and some are doubtful. In many cases the later usage with s has crept into the Mss. of the classical authors (so with the perfect of a)le/w, bai/nw, dra/w, zw/nnu_mi, klei/w (klh/|w), sw/|zw, xri/_w, and with the aorist of pau/w). c. The following verbs show an inserted s both in the perfect middle and the aorist passive in classical Greek: ai)de/omai, gignw/skw, e(lku/w, qla/w, qrau/w, keleu/w, kla/w, kna（i/）w, kore/nnu_mi, kuli/_w, cu/_w, pi/mplhmi, pri/_w, pti/ttw, sbe/nnu_mi, sei/w, skeda/nnu_mi, spa/w, tanu/w, tele/w, ti/nw, u(/_w, fla/w, xo/w, xrw/|zw. d. The following form only the perfect middle with s in classical Greek: bu_ne/w, e(/nnu_mi (ei(=mai, but e(/sto Hom.), e)ru/w, zw/nnu_mi, ce/w, *o)du/ssomai, ple/w, fleu/w (Hdt.). e. The following form only the aorist passive with s in classical Greek: a)/gamai, a)kou/w, a)nu/w, a)re/skw, a)/xqomai, gela/w, dai/nu_mi, dra/w, e)lu/w, e)/ramai, e)ra/w, i(_la/skomai, klei/w (klh/|w), leu/w, mequ/skw, mimnh/|skw, o)i/_w, o)/nomai (Hdt.), pai/w, palai/w, peta/nnu_mi, pi/mprhmi, r(ai/w, r(w/nnu_mi, sto/rnu_

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Addition of q.—The present stems of some poetical verbs are made by the addition of q; as nh/-q-w spin, plh/-q-w am full (pi/m-plh-mi). Cp. 832. a. Most of the indicative forms seem to be imperfects, but since some have the force of aorists (e.g., Soph. O. C. 862, 1334, O. T. 650), in certain editions they are regarded as second aorists, and the infinitives and participles are accented (against the Mss.) on the ultima (diwkaqei=n, ei)kaqw/n).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Omission of n.—Some verbs in -nw drop the n of the verbal stem in the first perfect, perfect middle, and first passive systems. kri/_nw (krin-), judge, ke/kri-ka, ke/kri-mai, e)kri/-qhn. So also kli/_nw incline, plu/_nw wash.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Metathesis.—The verbal stem may suffer metathesis (128). a. In the present: qnh/|skw die, 2 aor. e)/qanon, perf. te/qnhka. b. In other tenses: ba/llw throw (bal-), perf. be/blhka, e)blh/qhn (blh-); te/mnw cut (tem-n-), 2 aor. e)/temon, perf. te/tmhka; de/rkomai (derk-) see, 2 aor. e)/drakon; te/rpw delight, 2 aor. pass. e)ta/rphn and e)tra/phn (both poetical).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Syncope.—Some verbs suffer syncope (44 b). a. In the present: pi/_ptw fall for pi-p（e）t-w, i)/sxw hold for (s）i-s（e）x-w (125 e), mi/mnw for mi-men-w. b. In the future: pth/somai from pe/tomai fly. c. In the second aorist: e)/sxon for e)-sex-on from e)/xw (e)x- for sex-, 125 e). d. In the perfect: pe/-pta-mai have expanded from peta/-nnu_mi. N.—Syncopated forms are properly weak stems (476 a).

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Reduplication.—The verb-stem may be reduplicated. a. In the present with i: gi-gnw/-skw (gnw-) know, ti/-qh-mi place, i(/-sth-mi set, di/-dw-mi give. The present reduplication may be carried over to other tenses: dida/ (k) skw teach (99), dida/cw. With e: te-trai/nw bore. b. In the second aorist: a)/gw (a)g-) lead, h)/g-ag-on; e(/pomai follow, e(spo/mhn (for se-sp-omhn). c. Regularly with e in the perfect.

sections.group: FORMATION OF THE TENSE-SYSTEMS (*w AND MI-VERBS)
sections.en: Iterative Imperfects and Aorists in -sko/e-.—Homer and Herodotus have iterative imperfects and aorists in -skon and -skomhn denoting a customary or repeated past action. Homer has iterative forms in the imperfect and 1 and 2 aorist active and middle. Herodotus has no iteratives in the 1 aorist and few in the 2 aorist; and only from w-verbs. Herodotus regularly and Homer usually omit the augment. -aw verbs have -aa-skon or -a-skon; -ew verbs -ee-skon, in Hom. also -e-skon. -a-skon is rare in other verbs than those in -aw. The vowel preceding the suffix is always short. a. The suffix -sko/e- is added to the tense-stem. Imperf.: feu/ge-ske (feu/gw flee), e)/xe-skon (e)/xw have), ni_ka/-skomen (ni_ka/w conquer), goa/a-ske (goa/w bewail), kru/pta-ske (kru/ptw hide), kale/e-skon (kale/w call), zwnnu/sketo (zw/nnu_mi gird) ; 1 aor.: a)po-tre/ya-ske (a)potre/pw turn away）; 2 aor.: fu/ge-ske, sta/-ske stood.

From the verb-stem (or theme) the present stem is formed in several ways. All verbs are arranged in the present system according to the method of forming the present stem from the verbstem. Verbs are named according to the last letter of the verb-stem (376): 1. Vowel Verbs, 2. Liquid Verbs (including liquids and nasals), 3. Stop Verbs.

The present stem is formed from the verb-stem in five different ways. There are, therefore, five classes of present stems. The verb-stem is sometimes the present stem, but usually it is strengthened in different ways. A sixth class consists of irregular verbs, the present stem of which is not connected with the stem or stems of other tenses.
Presents of the Simple Class are formed from the verb-stem with or without the thematic vowel.

(I) Presents with the thematic vowel (w-verbs). The present stem is made by adding the thematic vowel o/e- to the verb-stem, as lu/_-w, paideu/-w, pau/-w, me/n-w, pei/q-w, feu/g-w, and the denominative verbs ti_ma/-w, file/-w, basileu/-w. For the personal endings, see 463 ff. For the derivation of many of these verbs, see 522.

The final vowel of the verb-stem is long in the present indicative, but either long or short in the other tense-stems, of the following verbs in -uw or -iw. 1. a. Verbs in -uw generally have u_ in Attic in the present; as lu/_w loose, du/_w go under, qu/_w sacrifice (almost always), fu/_w make grow (usually). Also in a)lu/_w, a)rtu/_w, brenqu/_omai, ghru/_omai, dakru/_w (once u^), i(dru/_w, i)sxu/_w, kattu/_w, knu/_w,, kwku/_w, kwlu/_w (usually), mhnu/_w, o)pu/_w (o)pui/w), ptu/_w, r(u/_omai, stu/_omai, tru/_w, u(/_ei; possibly in ei)lu/omai, h)mu/w, mu/w, cu/w, flu/w; e)linu/w, mhru/omai, plhqu/w (once u^), fi_tu/w. w)ru/w (u_^) is doubtful. b. -uw has u short in a)nu/w, a)ru/w, bru/w, klu/w (but klu=qi), mequ/w, and in all verbs in -nuw.

Several verbs with medial i_, u_ in the present, show i^ or i_, u^ or u_ in some other tense or tenses. Thus, qli/_bw press te/qlifa, pni/_gw choke e)pni/ghn, tri/_bw rub te/trifa e)tri/bhn, tu/_fw raise smoke e)tu/fhn, yu/_xw cool e)yu/xhn.

Verb-stems having the weak grades a, i, u, show the strong grades h, ei, eu in the present; as th/k-w (ta^k-) melt, lei/pw (lip-) leave, feu/gw (fug-) flee. a. To this class belong also lh/qw, sh/pw, te/qhpa am astonished, 2 aor. e)/tafon, a)lei/fw, (de/doika, 703), ei)/kw (e)/oika), (ei)/wqa, 563 a), e)rei/kw, e)rei/pw, pei/qw, stei/bw, stei/xw, fei/domai; e)reu/gomai, keu/qw, peu/qomai, teu/xw.

Present Stems in -eo/e- for euo/e-.—The strong form eu before the thematic vowel became ev (eu) and then e (20 a, 43) in the verbs qe/w run qeu/somai, ne/w swim e)/neusa, ple/w sail e)/pleusa, pne/w breathe e)/pneusa, r(e/w flow r(eu/somai, xe/w pour ke/xuka, ke/xumai, e)xu/qhn.

(II) Presents without the thematic vowel (mi-verbs). The personal ending is added directly to the verb-stem, which is often reduplicated. The verb-stem shows different vowel grades, strong forms h, w in the singular, weak forms e (a), o in the dual and plural. Thus ti/-qh-mi, ti/-qe-men; i(/-sth-mi for si-sth-mi (= si-sta_-mi), i(/-sta-men; di/-dw-mi, di/-do-men. a. All verbs in mi (enumerated 723 ff) belong to this class except those in -nu_mi (523 f) and -nhmi (523 g).

The present stem is formed by adding -to/e- to the verbstem, which ends in p, b, or f. The verb-stem is ascertained from the second aorist (if there is one) or from a word from the same root. ko/ptw cut, verb-stem kop- in 2 aor. pass. e)-ko/p-hn. bla/ptw injure, “ “ blab- “ “ “ e)-bla/b-hn. kalu/ptw cover, “ “ kalub- “ kalu/b-h hut. r(i/_ptw throw, “ “ r(if-, r(i_f- “ 2 aor. pass. e)-rri/f-hn. a. a)stra/ptw lighten, xale/ptw oppress may be from -p[iglide]w (117, 507).
Some of the verbs of this class add e in the present or other tenses, as r(i_pte/w throw, pekte/w comb, tu/ptw strike tuph/sw.

The present stem is formed by adding -[iglide]o/e- to the verb-stem and by making the necessary euphonic changes (109-116). I. PRESENTS IN -zw Dental Verb-stems.—Verb-stems in d unite with [iglide] to form presents in -zw (116), as fra/zw tell (frad-[iglide]w), e)lpi/zw hope (e)lpid-), komi/zw carry (komid-h/ a carrying), o)/zw smell (o)d-mh/ odour), kaqe/zomai seat myself (e(/d-os seat). a. sw/|zw save (for sw-izw) forms its tenses partly from the verb-stem sw-, partly from the verb-stem swi-. Aeolic has -sdw for -zw. Stems in g.—Some verbs in -zw are derived from stems in g preceded by a vowel; as a(rpa/zw seize for a(rpag-[iglide]w (cp. a(rpag-h/ seizure), kra/_zw cry out (2 aor. e)/kragon). See 116, other examples 623 g III. a. ni/zw wash makes its other tenses from the verb-stem ni/b- (fut. ni/yw, cp. Hom. ni/ptomai). A few verbs with stems in gg lose one g and have presents in -zw; as kla/zw scream (klagg-h/), fut. kla/gcw; salpi/zw sound the trumpet e)sa/lpigca (also lu/zw sob, pla/zw cause to wander). r(eg[iglide]w, e)rg[iglide]w yield r(e/zw do (poetic) and e)/rdw (Ionic and poetic). See 116. Most verbs in -zw are not formed from stems in d or g, but are due to analogy. See 516, 623 g III, 866. 6. II. PRESENTS IN -ttw (IONIC AND LATER ATTIC -ssw, 78） Palatal Verb-stems.—Stems ending in k or x unite with [iglide] to form presents in -ttw (-ssw). fula/ttw guard from fulak-[iglide]w (fulak-h/ guard (112)); khru/_ttw proclaim from khru_k-[iglide]w (kh=ruc, kh/ru_k-os); tara/ttw disturb from tarax-[iglide]w (tarax-h/ confusion). a. pe/ttw cook is for pek-[iglide]w; all other tenses are made from pep-. Several verbs showing forms in g seem to unite g with [iglide] to form presents in -ttw (-ssw.) Thus a)lla/ttw change, ma/ttw knead, plh/ttw strike (with the 2 aorists passive h)lla/g-hn, e)ma/g-hn, e)plh/g-hn), pra/_ttw do (2 perf. pe/pra_ga, 571), ta/ttw arrange (ta_g-o/s commander). a. So dra/ttomai grasp, na/ttw compress (515 b), nu/ttw push, ptu/ssw fold, sa/t

Dental Verb-stems.—Verb-stems in d unite with [iglide] to form presents in -zw (116), as fra/zw tell (frad-[iglide]w), e)lpi/zw hope (e)lpid-), komi/zw carry (komid-h/ a carrying), o)/zw smell (o)d-mh/ odour), kaqe/zomai seat myself (e(/d-os seat). a. sw/|zw save (for sw-izw) forms its tenses partly from the verb-stem sw-, partly from the verb-stem swi-.

Stems in g.—Some verbs in -zw are derived from stems in g preceded by a vowel; as a(rpa/zw seize for a(rpag-[iglide]w (cp. a(rpag-h/ seizure), kra/_zw cry out (2 aor. e)/kragon). See 116, other examples 623 g III. a. ni/zw wash makes its other tenses from the verb-stem ni/b- (fut. ni/yw, cp. Hom. ni/ptomai).
A few verbs with stems in gg lose one g and have presents in -zw; as kla/zw scream (klagg-h/), fut. kla/gcw; salpi/zw sound the trumpet e)sa/lpigca (also lu/zw sob, pla/zw cause to wander).
r(eg[iglide]w, e)rg[iglide]w yield r(e/zw do (poetic) and e)/rdw (Ionic and poetic). See 116.
Most verbs in -zw are not formed from stems in d or g, but are due to analogy. See 516, 623 g III, 866. 6.

Palatal Verb-stems.—Stems ending in k or x unite with [iglide] to form presents in -ttw (-ssw). fula/ttw guard from fulak-[iglide]w (fulak-h/ guard (112)); khru/_ttw proclaim from khru_k-[iglide]w (kh=ruc, kh/ru_k-os); tara/ttw disturb from tarax-[iglide]w (tarax-h/ confusion). a. pe/ttw cook is for pek-[iglide]w; all other tenses are made from pep-.

Several verbs showing forms in g seem to unite g with [iglide] to form presents in -ttw (-ssw.) Thus a)lla/ttw change, ma/ttw knead, plh/ttw strike (with the 2 aorists passive h)lla/g-hn, e)ma/g-hn, e)plh/g-hn), pra/_ttw do (2 perf. pe/pra_ga, 571), ta/ttw arrange (ta_g-o/s commander). a. So dra/ttomai grasp, na/ttw compress (515 b), nu/ttw push, ptu/ssw fold, sa/ttw load, su_ri/ttw pipe, sfa/ttw kill, fra/ttw fence. pra/_ttw has the late perf. pe/pra_xa.

Some presents in -ttw (-ssw) are formed from stems in t, q like those from k, x. Poet. e)re/ssw row (e)re/t-hs rower) aor. h)/resa; poet. koru/ssw arm (ko/rus ko/ruq-os helmet), imperf. e)ko/russe. a. So also bli/ttw take honey, pa/ttw sprinkle, pti/ttw pound, and perhaps pla/ttw form; also a)fa/ssw Hdt., and poetic i(_ma/ssw, lafu/ssw, li/ssomai. b. na/ttw compress (nag-, nad-) e)/naca, ne/nasmai and ne/nagmai. Cp. 514 a.

Formations by Analogy.—a. As g + [iglide] and d + [iglide] unite to form z, none of the verbs in -ttw can be derived from -g[iglide]w or -d[iglide]w. Since the future and aorist of verbs in -zw might often seem to be derived from stems in k, x, or t, q, uncertainty arose as to these tenses: thus the future sfa/cw (sfag-sw) from Epic sfa/zw slay (sfag-[iglide]w) was confused in formation with fula/cw (fulak-sw), and a present sfa/ttw was constructed like fula/ttw. Similarly, Attic a(rpa/sw (-omai) for Epic a(rpa/cw; and so in place of (poetic) a(rmo/zw fit (a(rmod-) the form a(rmo/ttw was constructed.
(I) Presents in -llw are formed from verb-stems in l, to which [iglide] is assimilated (110). Thus, a)gge/llw announce (a)ggel-[iglide]w), ste/llw send (stel-[iglide]w).

(II) Presents in -ainw and -airw are formed from verb-stems in -an and -ar, the [iglide] being thrown back to unite with the vowel of the verb-stem (111). Thus, fai/nw show (fan-[iglide]w), o)nomai/nw name (o)noman-[iglide]w), xai/rw rejoice (xar-[iglide]w). a. Many verbs add -[iglide]w to the weak form of the stem, as o)nomai/n-w for o)noman-[iglide]w from o)nomṇ-[iglide]w, cp. nomen (35 b). b. Hom. has ku_dai/nw and ku_da/nw honour, melai/nw blacken and mela/nw grow black. o)lisqai/nw slip is late for o)lisqa/nw. c. The ending ainw has been attached, by analogy, in qermai/nw make hot, etc. (620 III, 866.7). Likewise -u_nw (519) in poetic a)rtu/_nw prepare, parallel to a)rtu/_w (in composition), by analogy to baru/_nw weigh down, h(du/_nw sweeten.

(III) Presents in -einw, -eirw, -i_nw, -i_rw, -u_nw, and -i_rw are formed from stems in en, er, i^n, i^r, u^n, u^r with [iglide]o/e- added. Here [iglide] disappears and the vowel preceding n or r is lengthened by compensation (e to ei; i to i_; u to u_). See 37 a, 111. tei/nw stretch (ten-[iglide]w), fqei/rw destroy (fqer-), kri/_nw (krin-), oi)kti/_rw pity (oi)ktir-) generally written oi)ktei/rw, a)mu/_nw ward off (a)mun-), martu/_romai call to witness (martur-). a. o)fei/lw (o)fel-) owe, am obliged is formed like tei/nw, fqei/rw in order to distinguish it from o)fe/llw (o)fel-) increase formed regularly. Hom. has usually Aeolic o)fe/llw in the sense of o)fei/lw. dei/rw flay (der-[iglide]w) is parallel to de/r-w (499).

Verb-stems in -au- for (a[uglide], -a*v-）.—Two verbs with verb-stems in -au have presents in -aiw from -aivw out of -av-[iglide]w (38 a) : kai/w burn (kau-, kav-), fut. kau/-sw; and klai/w weep (klau-, klav-), fut. klau/-somai. Others 624 b. a. Attic prose often has ka/_w and kla/_w, derived from aiv before ei (ka/_eis, and, with a_ extended to the 1 person, ka/_w). Cp. 396.
Addition of e.—The following verbs add e in one or more tense-stems other than the present: ba/llw throw, kaqi/zw sit, klai/w weep, o)/zw smell, o)fei/lw owe, am obliged, xai/rw rejoice.

Contracted Verbs and Some Verbs in -iw, -uw.—a. Verbs in -aw, -ew, -ow, which for convenience have been treated under the first class, properly belong here, [iglide] (y) having been lost between vowels. Thus, ti_ma/w from ti_ma-[iglide]w (ti_ma_-), oi)ke/w dwell from oi)ke-[iglide]w (oi)ke- alternate stem to oi)ko-, 229 b), dhlo/w from dhlo-[iglide]w. So in denominatives, as poetic mhni/w am wroth (mhni-[iglide]w), fi_tu/_w sow (fi_tu-[iglide]w). Primitives in -i_w, -u_w are of uncertain origin. Cp. 608, 624. N.—The rare spellings a)lui/w, qui/w, mequi/w, fui/w indicate their origin from -[iglide]w. b. So with stems in long vowels: drw= do from dra_-[iglide]w, zw= live from zh-[iglide]w (cp. zh=qi), xrw= give oracles from xrh-[iglide]w (2 pers. xrh=|s, 394).

The present stem of the N class is formed from the verbstem by the addition of a suffix containing n. a. -no/e- is added: da/k-nw bite, te/m-nw cut. So du/_nw, ka/mnw, pi/_nw, pi/tnw poet., ti/nw, fqa/nw, fqi/nw. b. -ano/e- is added: ai)sq-a/n-omai perceive, a(mart-a/n-w err. So au)ca/nw, blasta/nw, darqa/nw, a)pexqa/nomai, oi)da/nw, o)lisqa/nw, o)fliska/nw (526). c. -ano/e- is added and a nasal (m, n, or g nasal) inserted in the verb-stem: la-m-b-a/n-w (lab-) take, la-n-q-a/n-w escape notice (laq-), tu-g-x-a/n-w happen (tux-). So a(nda/nw please (a(d-), qigga/nw touch (qig-), kigxa/nw find (kix-), lagxa/nw obtain by lot (lax-), manqa/nw learn (maq-), punqa/nomai inquire (puq-). d. -neo/e- is added: bu_-ne/-w stop up (also bu/w), i(k-ne/-o-mai come (also i(/_kw), ku-ne/-w kiss, a)mp-isx-ne/-o-mai have on, u(p-isx-ne/-o-mai promise (cp. i)/-sx-w for si-sx-w, 493 a). e. -uno/e- is added: e)lau/nw drive for e)la-nu-w. f. -nu (-nnu after a short vowel) is added (second class of mi-verbs, 414): dei/k-nu_-mi show (deik-, present stem deiknu_-), zeu/g-nu_-mi yoke (zeug-), o)/llu_mi destroy (for o)l-nu_mi, 77 a); kera/-nnu_-mi mix (kera-), skeda/-nnu_-mi scatter (skeda-). Others 729 ff. Some of these verbs have presents in -uw (746). N. 1.—The forms in -nnu_mi spread from e(/nnu_mi, sbe/nnu_mi, which are derived from e(s-nu_mi, sbes-nu_mi. N. 2.—Some verbs in -nw are formed from -nvo/e- for -n[uglide]o/e-; as Hom. ti/_nw, fqi/_nw, fqa/_nw, a)/_nomai from ti-nv-w, etc., (37 D. 1). Attic ti^/nw, etc. dropped the v. g. -na, -nh are added (third class of mi-verbs 412); as in (poetic) da/m-nh-mi I conquer, da/m-na-men we conquer (dam-), and in ski/d-nh-mi (rare in prose for skeda/nnu_mi) scatter. The verbs of this class are chiefly poetic (Epic), and most have alternative forms in -aw. See 737. In two further divisions there is a transition to the Iota Class. h. -ino/e- for -n-[iglide]o/e is added: bai/nw go (ba-n-[iglide]w), kerdai/nw gain (kerda-n-[iglide]w) tetrai/nw bore (te

A short vowel of the verb-stem is lengthened in the case of some verbs to form one or more of the tense-stems other than the present. Thus, lamba/nw (lab-) take lh/yomai (lhb-); da/knw (dak-) bite dh/cw (dhk-). So lagxa/nw, lanqa/nw, tugxa/nw, punqa/nomai (puq-) inquire, fut. peu/somai (peuq-). a. zeu/gnu_mi yoke, ph/gnu_mi fasten, r(h/gnu_mi break have the strong grade in all tenses except the 2 pass. system. mei/gnu_mi mix (commonly written mi/_gnu_mi) has mi^g- only in the 2 perf. and 2 pass. systems.

Addition of e and o.—a. Many verbs add e to the verb-stem to form all the tenses except present, 2 aorist, and 2 perfect; as ai)sqa/nomai, a(marta/nw, a(nda/nw, au)ca/nw, a)pexqa/nomai, blasta/nw, darqa/nw, kigxa/nw, manqa/nw, o)lisqa/nw, o)fliska/nw. One or more tenses with e added are formed by kerdai/nw, o)/llu_mi, o)sfrai/nomai, sto/rnu_mi, tugxa/nw. b. o)/mnu_mi swear has o)mo- in all systems except the present and future, as w)/mosa, o)mw/moka, but fut. o)mou=mai from o)meomai.

The present stem is formed by adding the suffix -sko/e- to the verb-stem if it ends in a vowel; -isko/e- if it ends in a consonant. Thus, a)re/-skw please, eu(r-i/skw find. a. This class is called inceptive (or inchoative) because some of the verbs belonging to it have the sense of beginning or becoming (cp. Lat. -sco); as ghra/skw grow old. But very few verbs have this meaning. b. In qnh/|skw die, mimnh/|skw remind, -iskw was later added to verb-stems ending in a vowel. The older forms are qnh/skw, mimnh/skw. c. The verb-stem is often reduplicated in the present; as gi-gnw/-skw know, bi-brw/-skw eat, di-dra/_-skw run away. Poetic a)r-ar-i/skw fit, poetic a)p-af-i/skw deceive, have the form of Attic reduplication. mi/sgw may stand for mi-（m）sgw.

The following verbs belong to this class (poetic and Ionic forms are starred): a. Vowel stems: a)ldh/skw* (a)ldh-), a)nabiw/skomai* (bio-), a)re/skw (a)re-), ba/skw* (ba- for bṇ-, 35 b), bibrw/skw (bro-), blw/skw* (mol-, mlo-, blo-, 130 D.), bo/skw (bo-), geneia/skw (cp. geneia/w), ghra/skw (ghra-), gignw/skw (gno-), dedi/skomai frighten, didra/_skw (dra-), h(ba/_skw (h(ba-), h)la/skw* (h)la-), qnh/|skw (qan-, qna-), qrw/|skw* (qor-, qro-), i(_a/skomai (i(_la-), kiklh/skw* (kale-, klh-), kui+/skomai* (ku-), mequ/skw (mequ-), mimnh/|skw (mna-), pipi/skw* (pi-), pipra/_skw (pra-), pinu/skw* (pinu-), pifau/skw* (fau-), titrw/skw (tro-), fa/skw (fa-), xa/skw* (xa-). b. Consonant stems: a(li/skomai (a(l-o-), a)lu/skw* (a)luk-), a)mbli/skw (a)mbl- a)mblo-), a)mplaki/skw* (a)mplak-), a)na_li/skw (a)n-a_l-o-), a)pafi/skw* (a)p-af-), a)rari/skw* (a)r-), dedi/skomai* welcome (de-dik-) and dhdi/skomai (usually written deid-) welcome, dida/skw (didax-), e)i+/skw (e)i+k-), e)pauri/skw* (au)r-), eu(ri/skw (eu(r-e-), la/skw* (lak-), mi/sgw* (mig-), o)fliska/nw (o)fl-e-), pa/sxw (paq-), steri/skw (ster-e-), titu/skomai* (ti-tuk-), u(la/skw* (u(lak-), xrhi+/skomai* (xrh-).

Addition of e and o.—steri/skw deprive (cp. ste/romai) makes all the other tense-stems from stere-; eu(ri/skw has eu(re- except in the present and 2 aorist. —a(li/skomai am captured (a(l-) adds o in other tense-stems.

This class includes some irregular verbs, one or more of whose tense-stems are quite different from others, as Eng. am, was, be, Lat. sum, fui. For the full list of forms see the List of Verbs. 1. ai(re/w (ai(re-, e(l-) take, fut. ai(rh/sw, h(/|rhka, etc., 2 aor. ei(=lon. 2. ei)=don (vid-, i)d-) saw, vidi, 2 aorist (with no present act.); 2 pf. oi)=da know (794). Middle ei)/domai (poetic). ei)=don is used as 2 aor. of o(ra/w (see below). 3. ei)=pon (ei)p-, e)r-, r(e-) spoke, 2 aor. (no pres.); fut. (e)re/w) e)rw=, perf. ei)/-rh-ka, ei)/rhmai, aor. pass. e)rrh/qhn. The stem e)r- is for ver-, seen in Lat. ver-bum. (Cp. 492.) r(e- is for vre, hence ei)/rhmai for ve-vrh-mai. 4. e)/rxomai (e)rx-, e)leuq-, e)luq-, e)lq-), go. Fut. e)leu/somai (usually poet.), 2 perf. e)lh/luqa, 2 aor. h)=lqon. The Attic future is ei)=mi shall go (774). The imperf. and the moods of the pres. other than the indic. use the forms of ei)=mi. 5. e)sqi/w (e)sq-, e)d-, fag-) eat, fut. e)/domai (541), pf. e)dh/doka, -e)dh/desmai, h)de/sqhn, 2 aor. e)/fagon. 6. o(ra/w (o(ra-, o)p-, vid-) see, fut. o)/yomai, perf. e(w/ra_ka or e(o/ra_ka, perf. mid. e(w/ra_mai or w)=mmai (w)p-mai), w)/fqhn, 2 aor. ei)=don (see 2 above). 7. pa/sxw (paq-, penq-) suffer, fut. pei/somai for penq-somai (100), 2 pf. pe/ponqa, 2 aor. e)/paqon.
