(See 526 d.) 8. pi/_nw (pi-, po-) drink, from pi(_-n-w (523 a), fut. pi/_omai (541), pf. pe/pwka, 2 aor. e)/pion, imp. pi=qi (466. 1, a, 687). 9. tre/xw (trex- for qrex- (125 g), dram-, drame-) run, fut. dramou=mai, pf. dedra/mhka, 2 aor. e)/dramon. 10. fe/rw (fer-, oi)-, e)nek-, by reduplication and syncope e)n-enek and e)negk-) bear; fut. oi)/sw, aor. h)/negka, perf. e)n-h/nox-a (446, 478), e)n-h/neg-mai, aor. pass. h)ne/xqhn. 11. w)ne/omai (w)ne-, pria-) buy, fut. w)nh/somai, perf. e)w/nhmai, e)wnh/qhn. For e)wnhsa/mhn the form e)pria/mhn is used.
Apart from the irregularities of Class VI, some verbs may, by the formation of the verb-stem, belong to more than one class, as bai/nw (III, IV), o)sfrai/nomai (III, IV), o)fliska/nw (IV, V).

Many verbs have alternative forms, often of different classes, as ku_da/nw ku_dai/nw honour, i(/_kw i/ka/_nw come, mela/n-w grow black, melai/nw (melan-[iglide]w) blacken, kla/zw (klagg-) klagg-a/n-w scream, sfa/zw sfa/ttw slay (516). Cp. also a)nu/w a)nu/tw accomplish, a)ru/w a)ru/tw draw water, Hom. e)ru/_kw, e)ru_ka/nw, e)ru_kana/w restrain. Cp. 866. 10.

Many, if not all, future forms in s are in reality subjunctives of the first aorist. lu/_sw, paideu/sw, lei/yw, sth/sw are alike future indicative and aorist subjunctive in form. In poetry and in some dialects there is no external difference between the future indicative and the aorist subjunctive when the latter has (as often in Hom.) a short mood-sign (457 D.); e.g., Hom. bh/somen, a)mei/yetai, Ionic inscriptions poih/sei.

The future stem is formed by adding the tense-suffix -so/e- (-eso/e- in liquid stems, 535) to the verb-stem: lu/_-sw, I shall (or will) loose, lu/_somai; qh/-sw from ti/-qh-mi place; dei/cw from dei/k-nu_-mi show. a. In verbs showing strong and weak grades (476) the ending is added to the strong stem: lei/pw lei/yw, th/kw th/cw, pne/w pneu/somai (503), di/dwmi dw/sw.

Vowel Verbs.—Verb-stems ending in a short vowel lengthen the vowel before the tense suffix (a to h except after e, i, r). Thus, ti_ma/w, ti_mh/sw; e)a/w, e)a/_sw; file/w, filh/sw. a. On xra/w give oracles, xra/omai use, a)kroa/omai hear, see 487 a. b. For verbs retaining a short final vowel, see 488.

Liquid Verbs.—Verb-stems ending in l, m, n, r, add -eso/e-; then s drops and e contracts with the following vowel. fai/nw (fan-) show, fanw=, fanei=s from fan-e/（s）w, fan-e/（s）eis; ste/llw (stel-) send, stelou=men, stelei=te from stel-e/（s）omen, stel-e/（s）ete. See p. 128.

s is retained in the poetic forms ke/lsw (ke/llw land, kel-), ku/rsw (ku/_rw meet, kur-), qe/rsomai (qe/romai warm myself, qer-), o)/rsw (o)/rnu_mi rouse, o)r-). So also in the aorist. See a)rari/skw, ei)/lw, kei/rw, fqei/rw, fu/_rw in the List of Verbs.

Stop Verbs.—Labial (p, b, f) and palatal (k, g, x) stops at the end of the verb-stem unite with s to form y or c. Dentals (t, d, q) are lost before s (98). ko/p-t-w (kop-) cut, ko/yw, ko/yomai; bla/p-t-w (blab-) injure, bla/yw, bla/yomai; gra/f-w write, gra/yw, gra/yomai; ple/k-w weave, ple/cw, ple/comai; le/g-w say, le/cw, le/comai; tara/ttw (tarax-) disturb, tara/cw, tara/comai; fra/zw (frad-) say, fra/sw; pei/qw (piq-, peiq-) persuade, pei/sw, pei/somai. a. When e or o is added to the verb-stem, it is lengthened to h or w: as bou/lomai (boul-e-) wish boulh/somai, a(li/skomai (a(l-o-) am captured a(lw/somai. So also in the first aorist and in other tenses where lengthening is regular.

Attic Future.—Certain formations of the future are called Attic because they occur especially in that dialect in contrast to the later language; they occur also in Homer, Herodotus, and in other dialects.

These futures usually occur when s is preceded by a^ or e and these vowels are not preceded by a syllable long by nature or position. Here s is dropped and -a/w and -e/w are contracted to -w=. When i precedes s, the ending is i-（s）e/w which contracts to -iw=. a. kale/w call, tele/w finish drop the s of kale/sw kale/somai, tele/sw tele/somai and the resulting Attic forms are kalw= kalou=mai, telw= (telou=mai poetic). b. e)lau/nw (e)la-) drive has Hom. e)la/w, Attic e)lw=.—kaqe/zomai (kaqed-) sit has Attic kaqedou=mai.—ma/xomai (max-e-) fight has Hom. maxe/somai (and maxh/somai), Attic maxou=mai.—o)/llu_mi (o)l-e-) destroy has Hom. o)le/sw, Attic o)lw=.

Doric Future.—Some verbs, which have a future middle with an active meaning, form the stem of the future middle by adding -seo/e-, and contracting -se/omai to -sou=mai. Such verbs (except ne/w, pi/_ptw) have also the regular future in -somai. klai/w (klau-, 520) weep klausou=mai, ne/w (nu-, neu-) swim neusou=mai (doubtful), ple/w (plu-, pleu-) sail pleusou=mai, pne/w (pnu-, pneu-) breathe pneusou=mai, pi/_ptw (pet-) fall pesou=mai, punqa/nomai (puq-, peuq-) peusou=mai (once), feu/gw (fug-, feug-) feucou=mai, xe/zw (xed-) xesou=mai. a. The inflection of the Doric future is as follows:— lu_sw=, -sou=mai lu_sou=mes, -sou/meqa lu_sw=n, -sou/menos lu_sei=s, -sh=| lu_sei=te, -sei=sqe lu_sei=n, -sei=sqai lu_sei=, -sei=tai lu_sou=nti, -sou=ntai b. These are called Doric futures because Doric usually makes all futures (active and middle) in -se/w -sw=, -se/omai -sou=mai. c. Attic pesou=mai (Hom. pese/omai) from pi/_ptw fall comes from peteomai. Attic e)/peson is derived from 2 aor. e)/peton (Dor. and Aeol.) under the influence of pesou=mai.

Futures with Present Forms.—The following verbs have no future suffix, the future thus having the form of a present: e)/domai (e)d-) eat, pi/_omai (pi-) drink, xe/w (xu-) and xe/omai, pour. See 529. 5, 8. a. These are probably old subjunctives which have retained their future meaning. In e)/domai and pi/_omai the mood-sign is short (457 D.). Hom. has be/omai or bei/omai live, dh/w find, kh/w (written kei/w) lie, e)canu/w achieve, e)ru/w draw, tanu/w strelch, and a)leu/etai avoid. ne/omai go is for nesomai.

The first aorist stem is formed by adding the tense suffix -sa to the verb-stem: e)/-lu_-sa I loosed, lu/_sw, lu/_saimi; e)/-deica I showed, from dei/k-nu_-mi. See 666. a. In verbs showing strong and weak grades (476), the tense-suffix is added to the strong stem: pei/qw e)/peisa, th/kw e)/thca, pne/w e)/pneusa, i(/sthmi (sta-, sth-) e)/sthsa, e)sthsa/mhn. N.—ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-) place, di/dwmi (do-, dw-) give, i(/_hmi (e(-, h(-) send have aorists in -ka (e)/qhka, e)/dwka, h(=ka in the singular: with k rarely in the plural). See 755.

Vowel Verbs.—Verb-stems ending in a vowel lengthen a short final vowel before the tense-suffix (a to h except after e, i, r). Thus, ti_ma/w e)ti/_mhsa, e)a/w ei)/a_sa (431), file/w e)fi/lhsa. a. xe/w (xu-, xeu-, xev-) pour has the aorists e)/xea, e)xea/mhn (Epic e)/xeua, e)xeua/mhn) from e)xeusa, e)xeusamhn.

Liquid Verbs.—Verb-stems ending in l, m, n, r lose s and lengthen their vowel in compensation (37): a to h (after i or r to a_), e to ei, i^ to i_, u^ to u_. fai/nw (fan-) show, e)/fhna for e)fansa; perai/nw (peran-) finish, e)pe/ra_na for e)peransa; ste/llw (stel-) send, e)/steila for e)stelsa; kri/_nw (krin-) judge, e)/kri_na for e)krinsa; a(/llomai (a(l-) leap, h(la/mhn for h(lsamhn. a. Some verbs in -ainw (-an-) have -a_na instead of -hna; as glukai/nw sweeten e)glu/ka_na. So i)sxnai/nw make thin, kerdai/nw gain, koilai/nw hollow out, lipai/nw fatten, o)rgai/nw be angry, pepai/nw make ripe. Cp. 30 a. b. The poetic verbs retaining s in the future (536) retain it also in the aorist. c. ai)/rw (a)r-) raise is treated as if its verb-stem were a)_r- (contracted from a)er- in a)ei/rw): aor. h)=ra, a)/_rw, a)/_raimi, a)=ron, a)=rai, a)/_ras, and h)ra/mhn, a)/_rwmai, a)_rai/mhn, a)/_rasqai, a)_ra/menos. d. h)/negka is used as the first aorist of fe/rw bear. ei)=pa is rare for ei)=pon (549).

Stop Verbs.—Labial (p, b, f) and palatal (k, g, x) stops at the end of the verb-stem unite with s to form y or c. Dentals (t, d, q) are lost before s (cp. 98). pe/mp-w send e)/pemya, e)pemya/mhn; bla/ptw (blab-) injure e)/blaya; gra/f-w write e)/graya, e)graya/mhn; ple/k-w weave e)/pleca, e)pleca/mhn; le/g-w say e)/leca; tara/ttw (tarax-) disturb e)ta/raca, e)taraca/mhn; poetic e)re/ssw (e)ret-) row h)/resa; fra/zw (frad-) tell e)/frasa, e)frasa/mhn; pei/q-w (piq-, peiq-, poiq-) persuade e)/peisa. a. On forms in s from stems in g see 516.
The second aorist is formed without any tense-suffix and only from the simple verb-stem. Only primitive verbs (372) have second aorists.

(I) *w-Verbs.—*w-verbs make the second aorist by adding o/e- to the verb-stem, which regularly ends in a consonant. Verbs showing vowel gradations (476) use the weak stem (otherwise there would be confusion with the imperfect). lei/pw (lip-, leip-) leave e)/lipon, -e)lipo/mhn; feu/gw (fug-, feug-) flee e)/fugon; pe/tomai fly e)pto/mhn (476 a); lamba/nw (lab-) take e)/labon.

a. Vowel verbs rarely form second aorists, as the irregular ai)re/w seize (ei)=lon, 529. 1), e)sqi/w eat (e)/fagon), o(ra/w (ei)=don). e)/pion drank (pi/_nw) is the only second aorist in prose from a vowel stem and having thematic inflection. b. Many w-verbs with stems ending in a vowel have second aorists formed like those of mi-verbs. These are enumerated in 687.

Verbs of the First Class (499) adding a thematic vowel to the verbstem form the second aorist (1) by reduplication (494), as a)/gw lead h)/gagon, and ei)=pon probably for e)-ve-vep-on; (2) by syncope (493), as pe/tomai fly e)pto/mhn, e)gei/rw (e)ger-) rouse h)gro/mhn, e(/pomai (sep-) jollow e)spo/mhn, imperf. ei/po/mhn from e)-sepomhn, e)/xw (sex-) hare e)/sxon; (3) by using a for e (476 b) in poetic forms (480), as tre/pw turn e)/trapon; (4) by metathesis (492), as poet. de/rkomai see e)/drakon.

(II) *mi-Verbs.—The stem of the second aorist of mi-verbs is the verb-stem without any thematic vowel. In the indicative active the strong form of the stem, which ends in a vowel, is regularly employed. The middle uses the weak stem form. i(/-sth-mi (sta-, sth-) set, second aorist e)/sthn, e)/sths, e)/sth, e)/sthton, e)sth/thn, e)/sthmen, e)/sthte, e)/sthsan; middle e)-qe/-mhn from ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-) place, e)-do/-mhn from di/dwmi (do-, dw-) give.

Originally only the dual and plural showed the weak forms, which are retained in the second aorists of ti/qhmi, di/dwmi, and i(/_hmi: e)/qemen, e)/domen, ei(=men (e)-e/men), and in Hom. ba/thn (also bh/thn) from e)/bhn went. Elsewhere the weak grades have been displaced by the strong grades, which forced their way in from the singular. Thus, e)/gnon, e)/fu^n in Pindar (= e)/gnw-san, e)/fu_-san), which come from e)gnwn（t), e)fu_n（t) by 40. So Hom. e)/tla^n, e)/ba^n. Such 3 pl. forms are rare in the dramatic poets. a. For the singular of ti/qhmi, di/dwmi, i(/_hmi, see 755; for the imperatives, 759; for the infinitives, 760.
No verb in -u_mi has a second aorist in Attic from the stem in u.

The difference between an imperfect and an aorist depends formally on the character of the present. Thus e)/-fh-n said is called an ‘imperfect’ of fh-mi/: but e)/-sth-n stood is a ‘second aorist’ because it shows a different tense-stem than that of i(/sthmi. Similarly e)/-fer-on is ‘imperfect’ to fe/rw, but e)/-tek-on ‘second aorist’ to ti/ktw because there is no present tekw. e)/stixon is imperfect to sti/xw, but second aorist to stei/xw. Cp. 546 D.

a. The second aorist and the second perfect are usually formed only from primitive verbs (372). These tenses are formed by adding the personal endings (inclusive of the thematic or tense vowel) to the verb-stem without any consonant tense-suffix. Cp. e)/lipo-n with e)/lu_-s-a, e)tra/p-hn with e)tre/f-q-hn (tre/pw turn), ge/-graf-a with le/lu-k-a. b. The second perfect and second aorist passive are historically older than the corresponding first perfect and first aorist. c. tre/pw turn is the only verb that has three first aorists and three second aorists (596). d. Very few verbs have both the second aorist active and the second aorist passive. In cases where both occur, one form is rare, as e)/tupon (once in poetry), e)tu/phn (tu/ptw strike). e. In the same voice both the first and the second aorist (or perfect) are rare, as e)/fqasa, e)/fqhn (fqa/nw anticipate). When both occur, the first aorist (or perfect) is often transitive, the second aorist (or perfect) is intransitive (819); as e)/sthsa I erected, i.e. made stand, e)/sthn I stood. In other cases one aorist is used in prose, the other in poetry: e)/peisa, poet. e)/piqon (pei/qw persuade); or they occur in different dialects, as Attic e)ta/fhn, Ionic e)qa/fqhn (qa/ptw bury); or one is much later than the other, as e)/leiya, late for e)/lipon.

The stem of the first perfect is formed by adding -ka to the reduplicated verb-stem. le/-lu-ka I have loosed, e)-le-lu/kh I had loosed. a. The k-perfect is later in origin than the second perfect and seems to have started from verb-stems in -k, as e)/-oik-a (= ve/-voik-a) from ei)/kw resemble. b. Verbs showing the gradations ei, eu: oi, ou: i, u (476) have ei, eu; as pei/qw (piq-, peiq-) persuade pe/peika (560). But de/doika fear has oi (cp. 564).
The first perfect is formed from verb-stems ending in a vowel, a liquid, or a dental stop (t, d, q).

Vowel Verbs.—Vowel verbs lengthen the final vowel (if short) before -ka, as ti_ma/-w honour te-ti/_mh-ka, e)a/-w permit ei)/a_-ka, poie/-w make pe-poi/h-ka, ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-) place te/-qh-ka, di/dwmi (do-, dw-) give de/-dw-ka.
This applies to verbs that add e (485). For verbs that retain a short final vowel, see 488. (Except sbe/nnu_mi (sbe-) extinguish, which has e)/sbhka.)

Liquid Verbs.—Many liquid verbs have no perfect or employ the second perfect. Examples of the regular formation are fai/nw (fan-) show, pe/fagka, a)gge/llw (a)ggel-) announce, h)/ggelka. a. Some liquid verbs drop n; as ke/krika, ke/klika from kri/_nw (krin-) judge, kli/_nw (klin-) incline. tei/nw (ten-) stretch has te/taka from tetṇka. b. Monosyllabic stems change e to a; as e)/stalka, e)/fqarka from ste/llw (stel-) send, fqei/rw (fqer-) corrupt. N. For a we expect o; a is derived from the middle (e)/stalmai, e)/fqarmai). c. All stems in m and many others add e (485); as ne/mw (nem-e-), distribute nene/mhka, me/lw (mel-e-) care for meme/lhka, tugxa/nw (tux-e) happen tetu/xhka. d. Many liquid verbs suffer metathesis (492) and thus get the form of vowel verbs; as ba/llw (bal-) throw be/blhka; qnh/|skw (qan-) die te/qnhka; kale/w (kale-, klh-) call ke/klhka; ka/mnw (kam-) am weary ke/kmhka; te/mnw (tem-) cut te/tmhka. Also pi/_ptw (pet-, pto-) fall pe/ptwka. See 128 a.
Stop Verbs.—Dental stems drop t, d, q before -ka; as pei/qw (piq-, peiq-, poiq-) persuade pe/peika, komi/zw (komid-) carry keko/mika.
The stem of the second perfect is formed by adding a to the reduplicated verb-stem: ge/-graf-a I have written (gra/f-w).
The second perfect is almost always formed from stems ending in a liquid or a stop consonant, and not from vowel stems. a. a)kh/koa (a)kou/w hear) is for a)khko（v）-a (a)kov- = a)ko[uglide]-, 43).

Verb-stems showing variation between short and long vowels (476) have long vowels in the second perfect (a^ is thus regularly lengthened). Thus, th/kw (tak-, thk-) melt te/thka, kra/_zw (krag-) cry out ke/kra_ga, fai/nw (fan-) show pe/fhna have appeared (but pe/fagka have shown), r(h/gnu_mi (r(ag-, r(hg-, r(wg-, 477 c) break e)/rrwga. a. ei)/wqa am accustomed ( = se-svwq-a) has the strong form w (cp. h)=qos custom, 123); Hom. e)/qw (Attic e)qi/zw accustom).

The second perfect has o, oi when the verb-stem varies between a, e, o (478, 479) or i, ei, oi (477 a): tre/f-w (tref-, trof-, traf-) nourish te/trofa, lei/pw (lip-, leip-, loip-) leave le/loipa, pei/qw (piq-, peiq-, poiq-) persuade pe/poiqa trust.
Similarly verbs with the variation u, eu, ou (476) should have ou; but this occurs only in Epic ei)lh/louqa ( = Att. e)lh/luqa); cp. e)leu/（q）-somai. Other verbs have eu, as feu/gw flee pe/feuga.
After Attic reduplication (446) the stem of the second perfect has the weak form; a)lei/fw (a)leif-, a)lif-) anoint a)lh/lifa.
Apart from the variations in 563-566 the vowel of the verb-stem remains unchanged: as ge/grafa (gra/fw write), ke/ku_fa (ku/_ptw stoop, ku_f-).

The meaning of the second perfect may differ from that of the present; as e)grh/gora am awake from e)gei/rw wake up, se/shra grin from sai/rw sweep. The second perfect often has the force of a present; as pe/poiqa trust (pe/peika have persuaded). See 819.

Aspirated Second Perfects.—In many stems a final p or b changes to f: a final k or g changes to x. (f and x here imitate verb-stems in f and x, as tre/fw, o)ru/ttw.) ko/ptw (kop-) cut ke/kofa, pe/mp-w send pe/pomfa, bla/ptw (blab-) injure be/blafa, tri/_bw (tri_b-) rub te/tri^fa, fula/ttw (fulak-) guard -pefu/laxa; tre/f-w (tref-) nourish te/trofa; o)ru/ttw (o)rux-) dig o)rw/ruxa.

Most such stems have a short vowel immediately before the final consonant; a long vowel precedes e.g. in dei/k-nu_-mi de/deixa, khru/_ttw (khru_k-) -kekhru_xa, pth/ssw (pthk-) e)/pthxa. te/trifa and te/qlifa show i^ in contrast to i_ in the present (tri/_bw, qli/_bw). ste/rgw, la/mpw do not aspirate (e)/storga, poet. le/lampa).

The following verbs have aspirated second perfects: a)/gw, a)lla/ttw, a)noi/gw, bla/ptw, dei/knu_mi, diw/kw (rare), qli/_bw, khru/_ttw, kle/ptw, ko/ptw, lagxa/nw, lamba/nw, la/ptw, le/gw collect, ma/ttw, mei/gnu_mi, pe/mpw, ple/kw, pra/_ttw, pth/ssw, ta/ttw, tre/pw, tri/_bw, fe/rw (e)nh/noxa), fula/ttw. a)noi/gw or a)noi/gnu_mi has two perfects: a)ne/w|xa and a)ne/w|ga. pra/_ttw do has pe/pra_ga have done and fare (well or ill), and (generally later) pe/pra_xa have done.

Second Perfects of the mi-form.—Some verbs add the endings directly to the reduplicated verb-stem. Such second perfects lack the singular of the indicative. i(/sthmi (sta-, sth-) set, 2 perf. stem e(sta-: e(/sta-men, e(/sta-te, e(sta=si, inf. e(sta/-nai; 2 plup. e(/sta-san (417). The singular is supplied by the forms in -ka; as e(/sthka. These second perfects are enumerated in 704.

Stem Gradation.—Originally the second perfect was inflected throughout without any thematic vowel (cp. the perfect middle), but with stem-gradation: strong forms in the singular, weak forms elsewhere. -a (1 singular) was introduced in part from the aorist and spread to the other persons. Corresponding to the inflection of oi)=da (794) we expect pe/poiqa, pe/poisqa, pe/poiqe, pe/piston, pe/piqmen, pe/piste, pepi/qati (from pepiqṇti). Traces of this mode of inflection appear in Hom. gega/thn (from gegṇthn, 35 b) ge/gamen from ge/gona; e)/i+kton, e)i+/kthn, e)i+kw/s from e)/oika; e)pe/piqmen; me/mamen from me/mona; pe/pasqe (for pepaqte = pepṇqte) from pe/ponqa (other examples 704, 705). So the masc. and neut. participles have the strong forms, the feminine has the weak forms (memhkw/s, memakui=a as ei)dw/s, i)dui=a).

The stem of the perfect and pluperfect middle and passive is the reduplicated verb-stem, to which the personal endings are directly attached. le/lu-mai I have loosed myself or have been loosed, e)-lelu/-mhn; de/do-mai (di/-dw-mi give), de/deig-mai (dei/k-nu_-mi show). On the euphonic changes of consonants, see 409.

The stem of the perfect middle is in general the same as that of the first perfect active as regards its vowel (557), the retention or expulsion of n (559 a), and metathesis (559 d). ti_ma/-w honour teti/_mh-mai e)teti_mh/mhn; poie/-w make pepoi/h-mai e)pepoih/mhn; gra/f-w write ge/gram-mai; kri/_nw (krin-) judge ke/kri-mai; tei/nw (ten-) stretch te/tamai; fqei/rw (fqer-) corrupt e)/fqar-mai; ba/llw (bal-) throw be/blh-mai e)beblh/mhn; pei/qw (piq-, peiq-, poiq-) persuade pe/peismai e)pepei/smhn.

The vowel of the perfect middle stem should show the weak form when there is variation between e (ei, eu): o (oi, ou): a (i, u). The weak form in a appears regularly in verbs containing a liquid (479): that in u, in pe/pusmai from punqa/nomai (puq-, peuq-) learn, poet. e)/ssumai hasten from seu/w (su-, seu-) urge.
The vowel of the present has often displaced the weak form, as in pe/plegmai (ple/k-w weave), le/leimmai (lei/p-w leave), pe/peismai (pei/q-w persuade), e)/zeugmai (zeu/g-nu_-mi yoke).
A final short vowel of the verb-stem is not lengthened in the verbs given in 488 a. e is added (485) in many verbs. For metathesis see 492; for Attic reduplication see 446.

n is retained in endings not beginning with m, as fai/nw (fan-) show, pe/fantai, pe/fanqe. Before -mai, we have m in w)/cummai from o)cu/_nw (o)cun-) sharpen, but usually n is replaced by s. On the insertion of s, see 489.

Future Perfect.—The stem of the future perfect is formed by adding -so/e- to the stem of the perfect middle. A vowel immediately preceding -so/e- is always long, though it may have been short in the perfect middle. lu/_-w loose, lelu/_-somai I shall have been loosed (perf. mid. le/lu^-mai), de/-w bind dedh/-somai (perf. mid. de/de-mai), gra/f-w write gegra/y-omai, kale/w call keklh/somai.

The future perfect usually has a passive force. The active meaning is found where the perfect middle or active has an active meaning (1946, 1947). kekth/somai shall possess (ke/kthmai possess), kekra/_comai shall cry out (ke/kra_ga cry out), kekla/gcomai shall scream (ke/klagga scream), memnh/somai shall remember (me/mnhmai remember), pepau/somai shall have ceased (pe/paumai have ceased).

Not all verbs can form a future perfect; and few forms of this tense occur outside of the indicative: diapepolemhso/menon Thuc. 7. 25 is the only sure example of the participle in classical Greek. The infinitive memnh/sesqai occurs in Hom. and Attic prose.
The periphrastic construction (601) of the perfect middle (passive) participle with e)/somai may be used for the future perfect, as e)yeusme/nos e)/somai I shall have been deceived.

Future Perfect Active.—The future perfect active of most verbs is formed periphrastically (600). Two perfects with a present meaning, e(/sthka I stand (i(/sthmi set) and te/qnhka I am dead (qnh/|skw), form the future perfects e(sth/cw I shall stand, teqnh/cw I shall be dead.

The stem of the first aorist passive is formed by adding -qh- (or -qe-) directly to the verb-stem: e)-lu/-qh-n I was loosed, e)-fa/n-qh-n I was shown (fai/nw, fan-), e)-do/-qh-n I was given (di/dwmi, do-, dw-). a. -qh- appears in the indicative, imperative (except the third plural), and infinitive; -qe- appears in the other moods. -qh- is found before a single consonant, -qe- before two consonants or a vowel except in the nom. neuter of the participle.

The verb-stem agrees with that of the perfect middle herein: a. Vowel verbs lengthen the final vowel of the verb-stem, as te-ti/_mh-mai, e)-ti_mh/-qhn. On verbs which do not lengthen their final vowel, see 488. b. Liquid stems of one syllable change e to a, as te/-ta-mai, e)-ta/-qhn (tei/nw stretch, ten-). But stre/fw turn, tre/pw turn, tre/fw nourish have e)stre/fqhn, e)tre/fqhn, e)qre/fqhn (rare), though the perfect middles are e)/strammai, te/trammai, te/qrammai.

Before q of the suffix, p and b become f; k and g become x (82 c); t, d, q become s (83). f and x remain unaltered. lei/p-w e)lei/f-qhn, bla/ptw (blab-) e)bla/f-qhn; fula/ttw (fulak-) e)fula/x-qhn, a)/g-w h)/x-qhn; komi/zw (komid-) e)komi/s-qhn, pei/q-w e)pei/s-qhn; gra/f-w e)gra/f-qhn, tara/ttw (tarax-) e)tara/x-qhn.
q of the verb-stem becomes t in e)-te/-qhn, and in e)-tu/-qhn for e)-qu-qhn from ti/qhmi (qe-, qh-) place and qu/_w (qu-, qu_-) sacrifice. See 125 c.

The stem of the first future passive is formed by adding -so/e- to the stem of the first aorist passive. It ends in -qhsomai. Thus, paideuqh/-somai I shall be educated, luqh/-somai I shall be loosed. ti_ma/w, e)ti_mh/qhn ti_mhqh/somai; e)a/w, ei)a/_qhn e)a_qh/somai; lei/pw, e)lei/fqhn leifqh/somai; pei/qw, e)pei/sqhn peisqh/somai; tei/nw, e)ta/qhn taqh/somai; ta/ttw, e)ta/xqhn taxqh/somai; ti/qhmi, e)te/qhn teqh/somai; di/dwmi, e)do/qhn doqh/somai; dei/knu_mi, e)dei/xqhn deixqh/somai.

The stem of the second aorist passive is formed by adding -h- (or -e-) directly to the verb-stem. Thus, e)bla/bhn I was injured from bla/ptw (blab-). a. -h- appears in the indicative, imperative (except the third plural), and infinitive; -e- appears in the other moods. -h- is found before a single consonant, -e- before two consonants or a vowel except in the nom. neut. of the participle.
The second aorist passive agrees in form with the second aorist active of mi-verbs; cp. intransitive e)xa/rhn rejoiced with e)/sthn stood. The passive use was developed from the intransitive use.

Primitive verbs showing in their stems the grades e: o: a have a. Thus an e of a monosyllabic verb-stem becomes a, as in ple/k-w weave e)pla/khn, kle/p-t-w steal e)kla/phn, fqei/rw (fqer-) corrupt e)fqa/rhn, ste/llw (stel-) send e)sta/lhn. But le/gw collect has e)le/ghn.

Primitive verbs showing in their stems a variation between a short and long vowel have, in the second aorist passive, the short vowel. Thus th/kw (tak-, thk-) melt e)ta/khn, r(h/gnu_mi (r(ag-, r(hg-, r(wg-) break e)rra/ghn. a. But plh/ttw (plag-, plhg-) strike has e)pla/ghn only in composition, as e)cepla/ghn; otherwise e)plh/ghn.

The second aorist passive is the only aorist passive formed in Attic prose by a)/gnu_mi (e)a/_ghn), gra/fw (e)gra/fhn), de/rw (e)da/rhn), qa/ptw (e)ta/fhn), ko/ptw (e)ko/phn), mai/nw (e)ma/nhn), pni/_gw (e)pni^/ghn), r(a/ptw (e)rra/fhn), r(e/w (e)rru/hn active), r(h/gnu_mi (e)rra/ghn), sh/pw (e)sa/phn), ska/ptw (e)ska/fhn), spei/rw (e)spa/rhn), ste/llw (e)sta/lhn), sfa/zw or sfa/ttw (e)sfa/ghn), sfa/llw (e)sfa/lhn), tu/_fw (e)tu/fhn), fqei/rw (e)fqa/rhn pass. and intr.), fu/_w (in subj. fuw=), xai/rw (e)xa/rhn active).

Both the first aorist passive and the second aorist passive are formed by a)lei/fw (h)lei/fqhn), a)lla/ttw (-hlla/xqhn, h)lla/ghn), ba/ptw (e)ba/fhn), bla/ptw (e)bla/fqhn, e)bla/bhn), bre/xw (e)bre/xqhn), zeu/gnu_mi (e)zu/ghn), qli/_bw (e)qli/_fqhn), kle/ptw (e)kla/phn), kli/_nw (-ekli/nhn), kru/ptw (e)kru/fqhn), le/gw collect (diele/xqhn, but sunele/ghn), ma/ttw (e)ma/ghn), mei/gnu_mi (e)mi/ghn), ph/gnu_mi (e)pa/ghn), ple/kw (e)pla/khn), plh/ttw (e)plh/ghn and -epla/ghn), r(i/_ptw (e)rri/_fqhn, e)rri/fhn), steri/skw (e)sterh/qhn), stre/fw (e)stra/fhn), ta/ttw (e)ta/xqhn), th/kw (e)ta/khn), tre/pw (e)tra/phn pass. and intr.), tre/fw (e)tra/fhn pass. and intr.), tri/_bw (e)tri/bhn, e)tri/_fqhn), fai/nw (e)fa/nqhn was shown, e)fa/nhn appeared), fra/gnu_mi (e)fra/xqhn), yu/_xw (e)yu/xhn). Most of these verbs use either the one in prose and the other in poetry, the dialects, or late Greek. Only the forms in common prose use are inserted in brackets.

Only those verbs which have no second aorist active show the second aorist passive; except tre/pw, which has all the aorists: active e)/treya and e)/trapon turned; middle e)treya/mhn put to flight, e)trapo/mhn turned myself, took to flight; passive e)tre/fqhn was turned, e)tra/phn was turned and turned myself.

The stem of the second future passive is formed by adding -s o/e- to the stem of the second aorist passive. It ends in -hsomai. Thus, blhbh/somai I shall be injured from bla/ptw (blab-) e)-bla/bh-n. ko/p-t-w, e)ko/phn koph/somai; gra/fw, e)gra/fhn grafh/somai; fai/nw, e)fa/nhn appeared, fanh/somai; fqei/rw, e)fqa/rhn fqarh/somai; ph/gnu_mi fix, e)pa/ghn pagh/somai.

Most of the verbs in 594, 595 form second futures passive except a)/gnu_mi, a)lei/fw, ba/ptw, bre/xw, zeu/gnu_mi, qli/_bw, kle/ptw, mai/nw, ma/ttw, r(a/ptw. But many of the second futures appear only in poetry or in late Greek, and some are found only in composition.

Perfect.—For the simple perfect and pluperfect periphrastic forms are often used. a. For the perfect or pluperfect active indicative the forms of the perfect active participle and ei)mi/ or h)=n may be used: as lelukw/s ei)mi for le/luka, lelukw\s h)=n for e)lelu/kh. So bebohqhko/tes h)=san for e)bebohqh/kesan (bohqe/w come to aid); ei)mi\ teqhkw\s for te/qhka I have placed; gegrafw\s h)=n for e)gegra/fh I had written; peponqw\s h)=n I had suffered. Such forms are more common in the pluperfect and in general denote state rather than action. b. For the perfect active a periphrasis of the aorist participle and e)/xw is sometimes used, especially when a perfect active form with transitive meaning is lacking; as sth/sa_s e)/xw I have placed (e(/sthka, intransitive, stand), e)rasqei\s e)/xw I have loved. So often because the aspirated perfect is not used, as e)/xeis tara/ca_s thou hast stirred up. Cp. habeo with the perfect participle. c. In the perfect active subjunctive and optative the forms in -kw and -koimi are very rare. In their place the perfect active participle with w)= and ei)/hn is usually employed: lelukw\s (leloipw\s) w)=, ei)/hn. Other forms than 3 sing. and 3 pl. are rare. Cp. 691, 694. d. The perfect or pluperfect passive is often paraphrased by the perfect participle and e)sti/ or h)=n; as gegramme/non e)sti/ it stands written, e)sti\ dedogme/non it stands resolved, parhggelme/non h)=n = parh/ggelto (paragge/llw give orders). e. In the third plural of the perfect and pluperfect middle (passive) the perfect middle participle with ei)si/ (h)=san) is used when a stem ending in a consonant would come in direct contact with the endings -ntai, -nto. See 408. f. The perfect subjunctive and optative middle are formed by the perfect middle participle with w)= or ei)/hn: lelume/nos w)=, ei)/hn. g. The perfect imperative of all voices may be expressed by combining the perfect participle with i)/sqi, e)/stw (697). lelukw\s i)/sqi loose, etc., ei)rhme/non e)/stw let

Future Perfect Active.—The future perfect active of most verbs is formed by combining the perfect active participle with e)/somai shall be. Thus, gegrafw\s e)/somai I shall have written, cp. scriptus ero. For the two verbs which do not use this periphrasis, see 584. a. The perfect middle participle is used in the case of deponent verbs: a)poleloghme/nos e)/somai And. 1.72.
Future Perfect Passive.—The future perfect passive may be expressed by using the perfect middle (passive) participle with e)/somai shall be. Thus, e)yeusme/noi e)/sesqe you will have been deceived.

Verbs in -w have the thematic vowel -o/e (-w/h-) between the tense-stem and the personal endings in the present system. The name “w-conjugation,” or “thematic conjugation,” is applied to all verbs which form the present and imperfect with the thematic vowel.

Inflected according to the w-conjugation are all thematic presents and imperfects; those second aorists active and middle in which the tense-stem ends with the thematic vowel; all futures, all first aorists active and middle; and most perfects and pluperfects active.

Certain tenses of verbs ending in -w in the first person present indicative active, or of deponent verbs in which the personal endings are preceded by the thematic vowel, are inflected without the thematic vowel, herein agreeing with mi-verbs. These tenses are: all aorists passive; all perfects and pluperfects middle and passive; a few second perfects and pluperfects active; and those second aorists active and middle in which the tense-stem does not end with the thematic vowel. But all subjunctives are thematic.

Verbs in -w fall into two main classes, distinguished by the last letter of the verb-stem: 1. Vowel verbs: a. Uncontracted verbs. b. Contracted verbs. 2. Consonant verbs: a. Liquid verbs. b. Stop (or mute) verbs. N. Under 2 fall also (c) those verbs whose stems ended in s or v (624).

Vowel Verbs.—Vowel verbs usually do not form second aorists, second perfects, and second futures in the passive. A vowel short in the present is commonly lengthened in the other tenses. Vowel verbs belong to the first class of present stems (498-504; but see 612).

Vowel Verbs not contracted.—Vowel verbs not contracted have verb-stems ending in i_^, u_^, or in a diphthong (ai, ei, au, eu, ou). （i) e)sqi/w eat, pri/_w saw, xri/_w anoint, poet. di/w fear, ti/_w honour (500. 2); (u) a)nu/w accomplish, mequ/w am intoxicated, lu/_w loose, qu/_w sacrifice, fu/_w produce, kwlu/_w hinder (and many others, 500. 1 a); (ai) knai/w scratch, pai/w strike, ptai/w stumble, palai/w wrestle, a)gai/omai am indignant, dai/w kindle, dai/omai divide, lilai/omai desire eagerly, poet. mai/omai desire, nai/w dwell, r(ai/w strike; (ei) klh/w (later klei/w) shut, sei/w shake, Epic kei/w split and rest; (au) au(/w kindle, qrau/w break, a)polau/w enjoy, pau/w make cease (pau/omai cease), poet. i)au/w rest; (eu) basileu/w am king, bouleu/w consult (bouleu/omai deliberate), qhreu/w hunt, keleu/w order, leu/w stone, paideu/w educate, xoreu/w dance, foneu/w slay. Most verbs in -euw are either denominatives, as basileu/w from basileu/s; or are due to the analogy of such denominatives, as paideu/w. geu/omai taste is a primitive. qe/w run, ne/w swim, ple/w sail, pne/w breathe, r(e/w flow, xe/w pour have forms in eu, u; cp. poet. seu/w urge, a)leu/w avert, a)xeu/w am grieved; (ou) a)kou/w hear, kolou/w dock, krou/w beat, lou/w wash.

Some primitive vowel verbs in -iw, -uw (522) formed their present stem by the aid of the suffix [iglide] (y), which has been lost. Denominatives in -iw, -uw, -euw regularly added the suffix, as poet. mhni/-w am wroth from mhni-[iglide]w (mh=ni-s wrath), poet. dakru/_w weep (da/kru tear), poet. fi_tu/_-w beget from fi_tu-[iglide]w, mequ/w am drunk, basileu/w am king. Poet. dhri/_omai, masti/w, mhti/omai, khki/w, a)xlu/w, ghru/w, i)qu/w.
The stem of some of the uncontracted vowel verbs originally ended in s or v (624).
Some verbs with verb-stems in vowels form presents in -nw (523), as pi/_nw drink, fqi/_nw perish; and in -skw (526).
Vowel Verbs contracted.—Vowel verbs that contract have verb-stems ending in a, e, o, with some in a_, h, w.
All contracted verbs form their present stem by the help of the suffix [iglide] (y), and properly belong to the Third Class (522).
Some contracted verbs have verb-stems which originally ended in s or v (624).

Liquid Verbs.—Liquid verbs have verb-stems in l, m, n, r. The present is rarely formed from the simple verb-stem, as in me/n-w remain; ordinarily the suffix [iglide] (y) is added, as in ste/llw (stel-[iglide]w) send, kri/_nw (kri^n-[iglide]w) judge, ktei/nw (kten-[iglide]w) slay, fai/nw (fan-[iglide]w) show.

A short vowel of the verb-stem remains short in the future but is lengthened in the first aorist (544). Thus: a. a in the future, h in the aorist: fai/nw (fan-) show, fanw=, e)/fhna. In this class fall all verbs in -ainw, -airw, -allw. b. e in the future, ei in the aorist: me/n-w remain, menw=, e)/meina; ste/llw (stel-) send, stelw=, e)/steila. Here belong verbs in -ellw, -emw, -emnw, -erw, -eirw, -enw, -einw. c. i^ in the future, i_ in the aorist: kli/_nw (klin-) incline, kli^nw=, e)/kli_na. Here belong verbs in -illw, -i_nw, -i_rw. d. u^ in the future, u_ in the aorist: su/_rw (sur-) drag, su^rw=, e)/su_ra. Here belong verbs in -u_rw, -u_nw. For the formation of the future stem see 535, of the aorist stem see 544.

For the perfect stem see 559. Few liquid verbs make second perfects. On the change of e, a of the verb-stem to o, h in the second perfect, see 478, 484. Liquid verbs with futures in -w= do not form future perfects.

Monosyllabic verb-stems containing e have a in the first perfect active, perfect middle, first aorist and future passive and in all second aorists, but o in the second perfect. Thus, fqei/rw (fqer-) corrupt, e)/fqarka, e)/fqarmai, e)fqa/rhn, but di-e/fqora have destroyed (819).

A few monosyllabic stems do not change e to a in the 2 aor., as te/mnw cut e)/temon (but e)/tamon in Hom., Hdt. etc.), gi/gnomai (gen-) become e)geno/mhn. See also qei/nw, qe/romai, ke/lomai, root fen-. Few liquid verbs form second aorists.
Stems of more than one syllable do not change the vowel of the verb-stem.

Stop Verbs.—Many verb stems end in a stop (or mute) consonant. The present is formed either from the simple verb-stem, as in ple/k-w weave, or by the addition of t or [iglide] (y) to the verb-stem, as in bla/ptw (blab-) injure, fula/ttw (fulak-[iglide]w) guard. All tenses except the present and imperfect are formed without the addition of t or i= to the verb-stem; thus, bla/yw from blab-s-w, fula/cw from fulak-s-w.

Some monosyllabic stems show a variation in the quantity of the stem vowel i or u, as tri/_bw rub perf. te/tri^fa, yu/_xw cool 2 aor. pass. e)yu^/xhn, th/kw melt (Doric ta/_kw) 2 aor. pass. e)ta^/khn. Cp. 475, 477 c, 500. Many monosyllabic stems show qualitative vowel gradation: i ei oi; u eu ou; a h w; a e o. For examples see 477-484.

Verbs in s or *v（[uglide]).—Some verb-stems ended originally in s or v. a. Sigma-stems (cp. 488 d) with presents either from -s-w or -s-[iglide]w. Thus (1) from -s-w: a)kou/w, au(/w burn, geu/w, eu(/w, ze/w, qrau/w, krou/w, ni/_somai* (nins-omai, cp. no/s-tos), ce/w, sei/w, tre/w*; (2) from -s-[iglide]w (488 d): a)gai/omai*, ai)de/omai, a)ke/omai (Hom. a)kei/omai), a)rke/w, gela/w, kei/w* split, klei/w* (i.e. klee/w) celebrate, koni/_w*, lilai/omai*, mai/omai*, nai/w* dwell, neike/w (Hom. neikei/w), oi)nobarei/w*, oi)/omai (from o)i+/omai), penqe/w (Hom. penqei/w), pti/ttw (ptins-[iglide]w), tele/w (Hom. telei/w), and some others that do not lengthen the vowel of the verb-stem (488). Also others, such as a)re/skw (a)res-), e(/nnu_mi, zw/nnu_mi, sbe/nnu_mi (732).—s is retained in te/rsomai*. b. v-stems (from -[uglide]-[iglide]w): gai/w*, dai/w* kindle, kai/w (520), klai/w (520), nai/w* swim, flow i 222.—For the loss of v in qe/w, etc., see 43, 503.

Verbs which end in w in the first person present indicative active, and deponent verbs in which the personal endings are preceded by the thematic vowel, have the following peculiarities of inflection: a. The thematic vowel usually appears in all tenses except the perfect and pluperfect middle (passive) and the aorist passive (except in the subjunctive). These three tenses are inflected like mi-verbs. b. The present and future singular active end in -w, -eis, -ei (463). The ending -mi appears only in the optative. c. The thematic vowel o unites in the indicative with the ending -nti, and forms -ousi (463 d). d. The third plural active of past tenses ends in -n. e. The imperative active has no personal ending in the second person singular except -o-n in the first aorist. f. Except in the perfect and pluperfect the middle endings -sai and -so lose s and contract with the final vowel of the tense-stem (465 a, b). In the optative contraction cannot take place (lu/_oi-（s）o, lu/_sai-（s）o). g. The infinitive active has -ein (for -e-en) in the present, future, and second aorist; -e-nai in the perfect; and -ai in the aorist. h. Active participles with stems in -ont- have the nominative masculine in -wn.

In 627-716 the method of inflection of all w-verbs, both vowel and consonant, is described. The examples are generally taken from vowel verbs, but the statements hold true of consonant verbs. Forms of w-verbs which are inflected according to the non-thematic conjugation are included under the w-verbs.

Indicative.—Vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the present by attaching the primary endings (when there are any) to the present stem in -o/e (-w/h-). lu/_w, ti_mw= (ti_ma/-w), fai/nw, lei/pw. The imperfect attaches the secondary endings to the present stem with the augment. See the paradigms, pp. 114, 120. For the active forms -w, -eis, -ei, see 463.

-h| and -ei are found in the pres. fut. mid. and pass., fut. perf. pass. e-（s）ai yields h| (written EI in the Old Attic alphabet, 2 a), which is usually given as the proper spelling in the texts of the tragic poets, whereas ei is printed in the texts of prose and comedy. ei was often written for hi (h|) after 400 B.C., as in a)gaqei= tu/xei, since both had the sound of a close long e. It is often impossible to settle the spelling; but bou/lei wishest, oi)/ei thinkest, and o)/yei shalt see (from o(ra/w) have only the -ei forms. -ei is sometimes called Attic and Ionic in contrast to -h| of the other dialects, including the Koiné.

Subjunctive.—The present subjunctive adds the primary endings to the tense-stem with the long thematic vowel. For the endings -h|s, -h| see 463. Thus, lu/_w, -h|s, -h|, ti_ma=|s ( = ti_ma/-h|s), ti_ma=| ( = ti_ma/-h|), fai/nwmen, -hte, -wsi (from -wnti). Middle lu/_w-mai, lu/_h| ( = lu/_h-sai), lu/_h-tai; ti_ma=-sqon ( = ti_ma/h-sqon); fainw/-meqa, fai/nh-sqe, fai/nw-ntai.

Optative.—To the tense-stem ending in the thematic vowel (always o) are added the mood-sign -i_- (-ie-) or -ih- (459, 460) and the secondary personal endings (except -mi for -n, where the mood sign is -i_-, 459). In the 3 pl. we have -ie-n. a. The final vowel of the tense-stem (o) contracts with the mood suffix (i_), o-i_ becoming oi. Thus lu/_oimi (lu/_o-i_-mi), lu/_ois (lu/_o-i_-s), lu/_oien (lu/_o-ie-n), lu_oi/mhn (lu_o-i/_-mhn), lu/_oio (lu/_o-i_-so).

Imperative.—The present imperative endings are added to the tensestem with the thematic vowel e (o before -ntwn). The 2 pers. sing. active has no ending, but uses the tense-stem instead (pai/deue, fai=ne). In the middle -so loses its s (466, 2 a); lu/_ou from lu/_e-so, fai/nou from fai/ne-so. On the forms in -etwsan and -esqwsan for -ontwn and -esqwn, see 466, 2 b.
Infinitive.—The present stem unites with -en: lu/_e-en = lu/_ein, lei/pe-en = lei/pein. In the middle (passive) -sqai is added: lu/_e-sqai, lei/pe-sqai.

Participle.—The present participle adds -nt- to the present stem ending in the thematic vowel o. Stems in -o-nt have the nominative singular in -wn. Thus masc. lu/_wn from lu_ont-s, fem. lu/_ousa from lu_ont-[iglide]a, neut. lu=on from lu_on（t). See 301 a and N.

A few w-verbs in the present and imperfect show forms of the mi-conjugation. These are usually Epic. de/xomai, 3 pl. de/xatai await for dexṇtai, part. de/gmenos, imperf. e)de/gmhn. But these are often regarded as perfect and pluperfect without reduplication. e)de/gmhn in some passages is a second aorist (688).—e)/dw eat (529. 5), inf. e)/dmenai.—e)ru/w (or ei)ru/w) in ei)ru/atai.—lou=tai wash is from lo/etai, not from lou/w (cp. 398 a).— oi)=mai think is probably a perfect to oi)/omai (oi)-o-).—ou)ta/w wound in ou)=ta, ou)ta/menai is 2 aor.—fe/rw bear, imper. fe/rte. CONTRACT VERBS Verbs in -aw, -ew, -ow contract the final a, e, o of the verb-stem with the thematic vowel -o/e (-w/h) in the present and imperfect tenses. Thus, ti_ma/w ti_mw=, poie/w poiw=, dhlo/w dhlw=; e)ti/_maon e)ti/_mwn, e)poi/eon e)poi/oun, e)dh/loon e)dh/loun. The rules of contraction are given in 4955; the paradigms, p. 120. a. Open forms of -ew verbs occur in the lyric parts of tragedy. Subjunctive.—The subjunctive adds the primary endings. For the contractions see 59. Optative.—a/oi becomes w=|, e/oi and o/oi become oi=. Thus. -a/o-i_-mi = -w=|mi, -ao-i/h-n = -w/|hn, -ao-i/_-mhn = -w/|mhn; -e/o-i_-mi = -oi=mi, -eo-i/h-n = -oi/hn, -eo-i/_-mhn = -oi/mhn; -o/o-i_-mi = -oi=mi, -o-i/h-n = -oi/hn, -oo-i/_-mhn = -oi/mhn. Thus, ti_mw/|hn (ti_mao-i/h-n), ti_mw/|hs (ti_mao-i/h-s), ti_mw/|h (ti_mao-i/h), ti_mw/|mhn (ti_mao-i/_-mhn), poioi=o (poie/o-i_-so), poioi=to (poie/o-i_-to). In the singular -aw verbs usually end in -w/|hn, -w/|hs, -w/h|, rarely in -w=|mi, -w=|s, -w=|. -ew verbs usually end in -oi/hn, -oi/hs, -oi/h, rarely in -oi=mi, -oi=s, -oi= (-oi= chiefly in Plato). In the dual and plural -aw verbs usually end in -w=|ton, -w/|thn, -w=|men, -w=|te, -w=|en, rarely in -w/|hton, -w|h/thn, -w/|hmen, -w/|hte, -w/|hsan. -ew verbs usually end in -oi=ton, -oi/thn, -oi=men, -oi=te, -oi=en, rarely in -oi/hton, -oih/thn, -oi/hmen, -oi/hte, -oi/hsan. Few cases of the optative of -ow verbs occur. In the sing

Verbs in -aw, -ew, -ow contract the final a, e, o of the verb-stem with the thematic vowel -o/e (-w/h) in the present and imperfect tenses. Thus, ti_ma/w ti_mw=, poie/w poiw=, dhlo/w dhlw=; e)ti/_maon e)ti/_mwn, e)poi/eon e)poi/oun, e)dh/loon e)dh/loun. The rules of contraction are given in 4955; the paradigms, p. 120. a. Open forms of -ew verbs occur in the lyric parts of tragedy.
Subjunctive.—The subjunctive adds the primary endings. For the contractions see 59.

Optative.—a/oi becomes w=|, e/oi and o/oi become oi=. Thus. -a/o-i_-mi = -w=|mi, -ao-i/h-n = -w/|hn, -ao-i/_-mhn = -w/|mhn; -e/o-i_-mi = -oi=mi, -eo-i/h-n = -oi/hn, -eo-i/_-mhn = -oi/mhn; -o/o-i_-mi = -oi=mi, -o-i/h-n = -oi/hn, -oo-i/_-mhn = -oi/mhn. Thus, ti_mw/|hn (ti_mao-i/h-n), ti_mw/|hs (ti_mao-i/h-s), ti_mw/|h (ti_mao-i/h), ti_mw/|mhn (ti_mao-i/_-mhn), poioi=o (poie/o-i_-so), poioi=to (poie/o-i_-to).
In the singular -aw verbs usually end in -w/|hn, -w/|hs, -w/h|, rarely in -w=|mi, -w=|s, -w=|. -ew verbs usually end in -oi/hn, -oi/hs, -oi/h, rarely in -oi=mi, -oi=s, -oi= (-oi= chiefly in Plato).

In the dual and plural -aw verbs usually end in -w=|ton, -w/|thn, -w=|men, -w=|te, -w=|en, rarely in -w/|hton, -w|h/thn, -w/|hmen, -w/|hte, -w/|hsan. -ew verbs usually end in -oi=ton, -oi/thn, -oi=men, -oi=te, -oi=en, rarely in -oi/hton, -oih/thn, -oi/hmen, -oi/hte, -oi/hsan.
Few cases of the optative of -ow verbs occur. In the sing. both -oi/hn and -oi=mi are found; in the plur. -oi=men, -oi=te, -oi=en. For r(i_gw/|hn from r(i_go/w shiver see 641.

Several contract verbs have stems in -a_, -h, -w. These are the verbs of 394, 398 with apparently irregular contraction, and drw= do; with presents made from -a_-[iglide]w, -h-[iglide]w, -w-[iglide]w. Thus, from zh/w, zh/eis, zh/ei and xrh/omai, xrh/e（s）ai, xrh/etai come zw=, zh=|s, zh=| and xrw=mai, xrh=|, xrh=tai; so diyh=n, peinh=n from diyh/-en, peinh/-en. i/dro/w, r(i_go/w (398) derive the forms in w and w| from i(drw-, r(i_gw- (i(drw/w, r(i_gw/w from i(drws-[iglide]w, r(i_gws-[iglide]w). The forms in -ow are from the weaker stems i)dros-, r(i_gos-.

-aw Verbs in Homer.—Hom. leaves -aw verbs open 64 times, as naieta/w, -a/ousi, u(la/ei, a)oidia/ousa, goa/oimen, thleqa/ontas. When contracted, -aw verbs have the Attic forms, as o(rw=, o(ra=|s, o(ra=|; as peira=| makest trial from peira/e-（s）ai from peira/omai; h)rw= didst pray from h)ra/e-（s）o from a)ra/omai.

When uncontracted, verbs in -aw often show in the Mss. of Hom., not the original open forms, but “assimilated” forms of the concurrent vowels, ae, aei, ah giving a double a sound by a prevailing over the e sound; ao, aw, aoi, aou giving a double o sound by the o sound prevailing over the a. One of the vowels is commonly lengthened, rarely both. ae = (1) aa: o(ra/esqai = o(ra/asqai, a)ga/- esqe = a)ga/asqe. = (2) a_a: mna/esqai = mna/_asqai, h)ga/- esqe = h)ga/_asqe. aei = (1) aa|: o(ra/eis = o(ra/a|s, e)a/ei = e)a/a|. = (2) a_a|: menoina/ei = menoina/_a|. ah| = (1) aa|: e)a/h|s = e)a/a|s. = (2) a_a|: mna/h| wooest 2 sing. mid. = mna/_a|. ao = (1) ow: o(ra/ontes = o(ro/wntes. = (2) wo: h(ba/ontes = h(bw/ontes, mna/- onto = mnw/onto. aw = (1) ow: o(ra/w = o(ro/w, boa/wn = boo/wn. = (2) ww: menoina/w = menoinw/w. aoi = (1) ow|: o(ra/oite = o(ro/w|te. = (2) woi:h(ba/oimi = h(bw/oimi. aou = (1) ow: o(ra/ousa = o(ro/wsa, o(ra/- ousi = o(ro/wsi, a)la/ou (from a)la/eo imper. of a)la/omai) = a)lo/w. = (2) ww: h(ba/ousa = h(bw/wsa, dra/- ousi = drw/wsi. ou here is a spurious diphthong (6) derived from -ont-: o(ra- ont-[iglide]a, h(baont-[iglide]a, dra/_onti; or by contraction in a)la/ou from a)la/eo. N.—a)lo/w from a)la/eo wander is unique. gelw/ontes is from gelw/w (641).

The assimilated forms are used only when the second vowel (in the unchanged form) stood in a syllable long by nature or position. Hence o(rowmen, o(raate, o(raato, do not occur for o(ra/omen, etc. (mnwo/menos for mna_o/menos is an exception.) The first vowel is lengthened only when the metre requires it, as in h(bw/ontes for h(ba/ontes ¯ ˘ ¯ ˘. Thus two long vowels do not occur in succession except to fit the form to the verse, as menoinw/w for menoina/w; but h(bw/oimi, not h(bw/w|mi. When the first vowel is metrically lengthened, the second vowel is not lengthened, though it may be long either in a final syllable (as in menoina/_a|) or when it represents the spurious diphthong ou from -ont- (as in h(bw/wsa, drw/wsi for h(ba/ousa, dra/_ousi from -ont[iglide]a, -onti).
The assimilated forms include the “Attic” future in -aw from -asw (539); as e)lo/wsi ( = e)la/ousi), kremo/w, dama/a|, damo/wsi.

The assimilated forms are found only in the artificial language of Homer, Hesiod, and their imitators, and nowhere in the living speech. They are commonly explained as derived from the contracted forms by a process of ‘distraction,’ and as inserted in the text for the sake of the metre. Thus o(ra=|s, bow=ntes, the spoken forms which had taken the place of original o(ra/eis, boa/ontes, in the text, were expanded into o(ra/a|s, boo/wntes, by repetition of the a and o. While the restoration of the original uncontracted forms is generally possible, and is adopted in several modern editions, a phonetic origin of many of the forms in question is still sought by some scholars who regard o(ro/w as an intermediate stage between o(ra/w and o(rw=. It will be observed, however, that the forms in 648 can be derived only from the unassimilated forms.
In the imperfect contraction generally occurs, and assimilation is rare.
Some verbs show eo for ao, as h)/nteon, tro/peon, menoi/neon, pote/ontai. Cp. 649, 653.

-aw verbs in Herodotus.—Hdt. contracts -aw verbs as they are contracted in Attic. In many cases before an o sound the Mss. substitute e for a (tolme/w, o(re/wn, e)foi/teon). This e is never found in all the forms of the same verb, and the Mss. generally disagree on each occurrence of any form.—Hdt. always has -w/|hn, -w/|mhn, in the optative.

-ew verbs in Homer.—a. Hom. rarely contracts ew and eo (except in the participle). In a few cases eu appears for eo, as poieu/mhn; rarely for eou, as teleu=si. When the metre allows either -ee and -eei, or -ei, the open forms are slightly more common. ei is often necessary to admit a word into the verse (as h(gei=sqai, e)fi/lei), and is often found at the verse-end. -e/-e-ai, -e/-e-o, in the 2 sing. mid. may become -ei=ai, -ei=o, or -e/ai, -e/o, by the expulsion of one e; as mu_qei=ai or mu_qe/ai sayest, ai)dei=o show regard. b. neikei/w, telei/w, from -es-[iglide]w (neikes-, teles-) are older forms than neike/w, tele/w. See 488 d, 624. qei/w, plei/w, pnei/w show metrical lengthening (28 D.). c. On -hmenai in Hom. see 657.

-ew verbs in Herodotus.—a. Hdt. generally leaves eo, ew, eou, open, except when a vowel precedes the e, in which case we find eu for eo (a)gnoeu=ntes). In the 3 plur. -e/ousi is kept except in poieu=si. For -e/-eo in the 2 sing. mid. we find e/-o in ai)te/o. ee, eei, in stems of more than one syllable, are usually uncontracted in the Mss., but this is probably an error. dei= it is necessary and dei=n are never written otherwise.—The Ion. eu for eo, eou, occurs rarely in tragedy. b. In the optative Hdt. has -e/oi after a consonant, as kale/oi, but -oi= after a vowel, as poioi=mi, poioi=.

Verbs in -ow.—a. Hom. always uses the contracted forms except in the case of such as show assimilation like that in -aw verbs. oo = (1) ow : dhi+o/onto = dhi+o/wnto. ooi = ow| : dhio/oien = dhio/w|en. (2) wo : u(pno/ontas = u(pnw/ontas. oou = ow : a)ro/ousi = a)ro/wsi. b. Hdt. contracts -ow verbs as in Attic. Forms with eu for ou, as dikaieu=si, e)dikai/eun, are incorrect.

Doric.—Doric (59 D.) contracts ae and ah to h; aei and ah| to h|; ao, aw, to a_ except in final syllables: ti_mw=, ti_mh=|s, ti_mh=|, ti_ma=mes, ti_mh=te, ti_ma=nti, ti/_mh, ti_mh=n. Monosyllabic stems have w from a + o or a + w. Some verbs in -aw have alternative forms in -ew (648), as o(re/w, ti_me/w.

The contractions of -ew verbs in Doric may be illustrated thus: Severer Doric Milder Doric file/w, filw=, fili/w file/w, filw= filei=s, file/s(?) filei=s, file/s(?) filei= filei= file/omes, fili/omes, fili/wmes, filw=mes file/omes, filou=mes, fileu=mes filh=te filei=te file/onti, fili/onti, filo/nti file/onti, filou=nti, fileu=nti a. iw for eo is a diphthong. eu for eo is common in Theocritus. In Cretan i ( = y) for e is often expelled (kosmo/ntes = kosme/ontes).
Verbs in -ow contract oo and oe to w in Severer Doric and to ou in Milder Doric.

Aeolic.—In Aeolic contract verbs commonly pass into the mi-conjugation: ti/_maimi, -ais, -ai, ti/_ma_men, ti/_ma_te, ti/_maisi, imperfect, e)ti/_ma_n, e)ti/_ma_s, e)ti/_ma_, etc. inf. ti/_ma_n, part. ti/_mais, -antos, mid. ti/_ma_mai, inf. ti_ma/_menai. So fi/lhmi, fi/lhmen, fi/lhte, fi/leisi, e)fi/lhn, inf. fi/lhn, part. fi/leis, -entos. Thus o)/rhmi from o)re/w = Att. o(ra/w, ka/lhmi, ai)/nhmi. So also dh/lwmi, 3 pl. dh/loisi, inf. dh/lwn. Besides these forms we find a few examples of the earlier inflection in -aw, -ew, -ow, but these forms usually contract except in a few cases where e is followed by an o sound (pote/ontai). From other tenses, e.g. the fut. in -hsw, h has been transferred to the present in a)dikh/w, poqh/w.

Hom. has several cases of contract verbs inflected according to the mi- conjugation in the 3 dual: su_lh/-thn (su_la/w spoil), prosaudh/-thn (prosauda/w speak to), a)peilh/-thn (a)peile/w threaten), o(marth/-thn (o(marte/w meet); also sa/w 3 sing. imperf. (sao/w keep safe). In the infinitive -hmenai, as goh/menai (goa/w), peinh/menai (peina/_w, 641), filh/menai (file/w), forh/menai and forh=nai (fore/w). But a)gi_ne/w has a)gi_ne/menai.
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the future alike.

Indicative.—The future active and middle add the primary endings, and are inflected like the present; as lu/_sw, lu/_somai. On the two endings of the second singular middle, see 628. Liquid verbs, Attic futures (538), Doric futures (540) are inflected like contract verbs in -ew; thus fanw= fanou=mai, kalw= kalou=mai, and pesou=mai, follow poiw= poiou=mai (385). a. The only future perfect active from an w-verb is teqnh/cw shall be dead (584), which is inflected like a future active. Ordinarily the periphrastic formation is used: leleukw\s e)/somai shall have loosed. The future perfect passive (lelu/_somai shall have been loosed) is inflected like the future middle. The periphrastic forms and the future perfect passive rarely occur outside of the indicative.

Optative.—The inflection is like the present: lu/_so-i_-mi, lu_so-i/_-mhn. In the optative singular of liquid verbs, -ih-n, -ih-s, -ih, in the dual and plural -i_-ton, -i_-thn, -i_-men, -i_-te, -ie-n, are added to the stem ending in the thematic vowel o; thus faneo-i/hn = fanoi/hn, fane/o-i_-men = fanoi=men. So in Attic futures in -a/zw, as biba/zw (539 d) cause to go: bibw/|hn, -w/|hs, -w/|h, pl. bibw=|men.
Infinitive.—The future infinitive active adds -en, as lu/_sein from lu/_se-en, fanei=n from fane/（s）e-en. The infinitive middle adds -sqai, as lu/_se-sqai, fanei=sqai, from fane/（s）e-sqai.
Participle.—The future participle has the same endings as the present: lu/_swn lu/_sousa lu=son, fanw=n fanou=sa fanou=n; middle, lu_so/menos, fanou/menos.
All verbs inflect the first and second future passive alike, that is, like the future middle.

The indicative adds -mai to the stem ending in -qhso- or -hso-, as luqh/so-mai, fanh/-so-mai. For the two forms of the second person singular see 628. The optative adds -i_-mhn, as luqhso-i/_-mhn, fanhso-i/_-mhn. The infinitive adds -sqai, as luqh/-se-sqai, fanh/-se-sqai. The participle adds -menos, as luqhso/-menos, fanhso/-menos.
All vowel and consonant w-verbs inflect the first aorist alike.

Indicative.—The secondary endings of the first aorist active were originally added to the stem ending in -s-; thus, e)lu_sṃ, e)lu_s-s, e)lu_s-t, e)lu_s-men, e)lu_s-te, e)lu_s-nt. From e)lu_sṃ came e)/lu_sa (by 35 c), the a of which spread to the other forms except in the 3 sing., where e was borrowed from the perfect. a. In the middle the secondary endings are added to the stem ending in -sa-. For the loss of s in -so, see 465 b.

Subjunctive.—In the subjunctive the long thematic vowel -w/h- is substituted for the a of the indicative, and these forms are inflected like the present subjunctive: lu/_sw lu/_swmai, fh/nw fh/nwmai. For the loss of s in -sai see 465 a.

Optative.—To the stem ending in a the mood-suffix i_ is added, making ai, to which the same endings are affixed as in the present: lu/_sa-i_-mi = lu/_saimi, lu_sa-i/_-mhn = lu_sai/mhn, fh/na-i_-mi = fh/naimi. The inflection in the middle is like that of the present. For the loss of s in -so see 465 b.—In the active -eias, -eie, -eian are more common than -ais, -ai, -aien.

Imperative.—The regular endings (462) are added to the stem in -sa (or -a in liquid verbs) except in the active and middle 2 sing., in which -on and -ai take the place of -a: lu=son lu_sa/tw, lu=sai lu_sa/sqw, fh=non fhna/tw, fh=nai fhna/sqw.
Infinitive.—The aorist active infinitive ends in -ai, which is an old dative: the middle ends in -sqai: lu=sai lu/_sa-sqai, fh=nai fh/na-sqai, ple/cai ple/ca-sqai.

Participle.—The active participle adds -nt like the present: masc. lu/_sa_s from lu_sant-s, fem. lu/sa_sa from lusa_nt-[iglide]a, neut. lu=san from lu_san（t). See 301. The middle ends in -menos: lu_sa/-menos, fhna/-menos.

All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the aorists passive alike, that is, according to the mi-conjugation, except in the subjunctive. a. Vowel verbs rarely form second aorists that are passive in form, as r(e/w flow, e)rru/hn (803). But r(e/w is properly not a vowel verb (see 503).

Indicative.—The indicative adds the active secondary endings directly to the tense stem ending in -qh- (first aorist) or -h- (second aorist). The inflection is thus like that of the imperfect of a verb in -mi. e)lu/qh-n e)ti/qh-n e)lu/qh-men e)ti/qe-men e)lu/qh-s e)ti/qh-s e)lu/qh-ton e)ti/qe-ton e)lu/qh-te e)ti/qe-te e)lu/qh e)ti/qh e)luqh/-thn e)tiqe/-thn e)lu/qh-san e)ti/qe-san a. For -san we find -n from -n（t) in poetical and dialectic forms before which h has been shortened to e (40), thus w(/rmhqen for w(rmh/qhsan from o(rma/w urge.

Subjunctive.—The subjunctive adds -w/h- to the tense stem ending in -qe- or -e- and contracts: luqw=, -h=|s, -h=|, etc., from luqe/w, -e/h|s, -e/h|, etc.; fanw=, -h=|s, -h=| from fane/w, -e/h|s, -e/h|, etc.

Optative.—The optative adds -i_- or -ih- to the tense-stem ending in -qe- or -e-, and contracts. In the singular -ih- is regular; in the dual and plural -i_- is generally preferred. Thus luqei/hn from luqe-i/h-n, fanei/hn from fane-i/h-n, luqei=ton from luqe/-i_-ton, fanei=ton from fane/-i_-ton, luqei=men from luqe/-i_-men, fanei=en from fane/-ie-n. The inflection is like that of the present optative of a mi-verb. luqe-i/h-n tiqe-i/h-n luqe-i=-men tiqe-i=-men luqe-i/h-s tiqe-i/h-s luqe-i=-ton tiqe-i=-ton luqe-i=-te tiqe-i=-te luqe/-i/h tiqe-i/h luqe-i/-thn tiqe-i/-thn luqe-i=e-n tiqe-i=e-n a. -ei/hmen is used only in prose (but Plato and Isocrates have also -ei=men). -ei/hte is almost always found in the Mss. of prose writers; -ei=te occurs only in poetry (except from mi-verbs). -ei=en is more common in prose than -ei/hsan.

Imperative.—The endings of the imperative are added to the tense-stem ending in -qh- or -h-. Before -ntwn, -qh- and -h- become -qe- and -e- (luqe/ntwn, fane/ntwn). For -ti instead of -qi in the first aorist (lu/qhti) see 125 b.
Infinitive.—-nai is added to the tense-stem in -qh- or -h-: luqh=-nai, fanh=-nai.
Participle.—The participle adds -nt, as masc. luqei/s from luqent-s, fem. luqei=sa from luqent-[iglide]a, neut. luqe/n from luqen（t). See 301. So fanei/s, etc.
Most verbs in -w inflect the second aorist according to the w-conjugation; some inflect it according to the mi-conjugation.

The inflection of most second aorists of w-verbs is like that of an imperfect of w-verbs in the indicative, and like that of a present in the other moods. e)/-lipo-n e)/-lu_o-n li/pe lu=e e)-lipo/-mhn e)-lu_o/-mhn lipou= (424 b. 2) lu/_ou li/pw lu/_w lipei=n (lipe/-en, 424 c) lu/_ein (lu/_e-en） li/pw-mai lu/_w-mai lipe/-sqai lu/_e-sqai lipo-i/-mhn lu_o-i/-mhn lipw/n lu/_wn lipo/-menos lu_o/-menos For the loss of s in -so in the second person singular see 465 b.

A number of w-verbs form their second aorists without a thematic vowel, herein agreeing with the second aorists of mi-verbs. Cp. e)/du_n p. 140. The second aorist of gi-gnw/-skw know is inflected as follows.

The indicative is inflected like e)/sthn (p. 138); the subjunctive, like dw= (p. 138). e)/-gnw-n e)/-gnw-men gnw= gnw=-men e)/-gnw-s e)/-gnw-ton e)/-gnw-te gnw=-s gnw=-ton gnw=-te e)/-gnw e)-gnw/-thn e)/-gnw-san gnw= gnw=-ton gnw=-si a. We expect e)/gnoton, e)/gnomen, etc. (551), but the strong stem gnw- has been transferred to the dual and plural. So also in e)/bhn, e)/fqhn, e(a/_lwn.—Subjunctive bw=, bh=|s, bh=|, bh=ton, bw=men, bh=te, bw=si. On the formation of the subjunctive see 757 D.

The optative is inflected like doi/hn (p. 138). gnoi/hn gnoi=men or gnoi/hmen gnoi/hs gnoi=ton or gnoi/hton gnoi=te or gnoi/hte gnoi/h gnoi/thn or gnoih/thn gnoi=en or gnoi/hsan a. So bai/hn, bai=ton or bai/hton, bai=men or bai/hmen. In the 2 plur. the Mss. of prose writers have only -ihte (gnoi/hte, -bai/hte); but -ihte is not attested by the evidence of verse.

The imperative is inflected like sth=qi (p. 139). gnw=qi, gnw/tw gnw=ton, gnw/twn gnw=te, gno/ntwn a. In composition dia/gnwqi, a)na/bhqi (423). For bh=qi (from bai/nw) -ba_ in composition occurs in poetry, as a)na/ba_.
The infinitive adds -enai, as gnw=nai from gnw/-enai (like sth=nai from sth/-enai). In composition diagnw=nai (426 d).

The participle adds -nt-, as masc. gnou/s from gnont-s, fem. gnou=sa from gnont-[iglide]a, neut. gno/n from gnon（t). See 301. In composition diagnou/s (426 d). a. Before nt the long vowel w is regularly shortened to o by 40.

The following w-verbs have second aorists of the mi form. a(li/skomai (a(l-o-) am captured, e(a/_lwn or h(/lwn (a(lw=, a(loi/hn, a(lw=nai, a(lou/s). bai/nw (ba-<*> go, e)/bhn (bw=, bai/hn, bh=qi and also -ba_ in composition, bh=nai, ba/_s). bio/w (bio-) live, e)bi/wn (biw=, biw/|hn, biw=nai, biou/s). Hom. biw/tw imper. ghra/skw (ghra-) grow old, ghra=nai poet., ghra/_s Hom. gignw/skw (gno-, gnw-) know, e)/gnwn (gnw=, gnoi/hn, gnw=qi, gnw=nai, gnou/s). -didra/_skw (dra_-) run, only in composition, -e/dra_n (-drw=, -drai/hn, -dra=nai, -dra/_s). Hdt. has e)/drhn, drh=nai, dra/_s in composition. du/_w (du_-) enter e)/du_n entered inflected p. 140 (du/_w, opt. Hom. du/_h and e)/kdu_men for du-i/h, e)kdu/-i_-men; du=qi, du=nai, du/_s). e)/xw (sxe-) have, sxe/s imper. ktei/nw (kten-, kta-) kill, e)/kta^n, e)/kta^s, e)/kta^, e)/kta^men, 3 pl. e)/kta^n 551 D, subj. kte/wmen, inf. kta/menai kta/men, part kta/_s; e)kta/mhn was killed (kta/sqai, kta/menos); all poetic forms. pe/tomai (pet-, pte-, pta-) fly, poet. e)/pthn (ptai/hn, pta/_s), middle e)pta/mhn (pta/sqai, pta/menos). ptw=, pth=qi, pth=nai are late. pi/_nw (pi-) drink, pi=qi imper. ske/llw in a)poske/llw (skel-, skle-) dry up, a)posklh=nai. tla- endure, fut. tlh/somai, poetic e)/tlhn (tlw=, tlai/hn, tlh=qi, tlh=nai, tla/_s). fqa/nw (fqa-) anticipate, e)/fqhn (fqw=, fqai/hn, fqh=nai, fqa/_s). fu/_w (fu_^-) produce, e)/fu_n was produced, am (fu/w subj., fu=nai, fu/_s 308).

The following w-verbs have in poetry (especially in Homer) second aorists of the mi form: a(/llomai (a)=lso, a)=lto), a)paura/w (a)pou/ra_s), a)rari/skw (a)/rmenos), a)/w (a)/_menai), ba/llw (cumblh/thn, e)/blhto), bibrw/skw (e)/brwn), root gen- (ge/nto grasped), de/xomai (de/kto), Epic kixa/_nw (e)ki/xhn, kixh/w, kixei/h, kixh=nai and kixh/menai, kixei/s and kixh/menos; properly from ki/xhmi), kla/w (a)po/kla_s), klu/w (klu=qi, ke/kluqi), kti/zw (kti/menos), root lex- (e)/lekto laid himself to rest), lu/_w (lu/to), ou)ta/w (ou)=ta, ou)ta/menos), pa/llw (pa/lto), pela/zw (e)plh/mhn), pe/rqw (pe/rqai = perq-sqai), plw/w (e)/plwn), pnu_- (a)/mpnu_to revived), pth/ssw (katapth/thn), seu/w (e)ssu/mhn, e)/suto, su/menos), fqi/nw (e)fqi/mhn), xe/w (e)xu/mhn, xu/menos). e)/lekto, pa/lto are properly first aorists (for e)lek-s-to, pal-s-to), s being lost between two consonants (103).
All vowel and consonant verbs in -w inflect the first perfect alike. Some verbs in -w inflect the second perfect according to the w-conjugation, others inflect it according to the mi-conjugation.

Indicative.—Originally the endings were added to the stem without any thematic vowel. Of this unthematic formation a few traces survive (573). In the 2 p. sing. the ending is -s, but originally -qa; in the 3 pl. -ka_si stands for ka-nsi out of ka-nti (100). Thus le/luka, -as, -e, pe/pomfa, -as, -e, etc. The periphrastic combination occurs in the indicative (599 a).

Subjunctive.—The perfect subjunctive is commonly formed periphrastically by the perfect active participle and w)=, h)=|s, h)=|, etc. Thus lelukw\s (gegrafw\s) w)=, etc., leluko/tes (gegrafo/tes) w)=men, etc. Of the periphrastic forms only the 1 and 3 sing., 2 and 3 plur. are attested.

Instances of the simple perfect subjunctive (lelu/kw, gegra/fw) are very rare. The simple form is made by substituting the thematic vowel w/h for a in the tense-stem. Only the sing. and the 3 plur. are attested from w-verbs.

Besides ei)dw= (oi)=da) and e(sth/kh|, etc., Attic prose has only about 16 occurrences of the simple perf. subj., and from the following verbs only: bai/nw, de/dia, e)gei/rw, e)/oika, qnh/|skw, lamba/nw, lanqa/nw, pa/sxw, poiw=, fu/_w. Hippocr. has forms from bibrw/skw, ponw=, teu/xw. There are about 30 occurrences in the poetry. Attic prose writers show about 25 cases of the periphrasis from all w-verbs.

Optative.—The perfect optative is commonly formed periphrastically by the perfect active participle and ei)/hn, ei)/hs, ei)/h, etc. Thus lelukw\s (gegrafw\s) ei)/hn, etc., leluko/tes (gegrafo/tes) ei)=men, etc. The dual is exceedingly rare.

Occasionally the simple forms are used (lelu/koimi, gegra/foimi). These are formed by adding the mood-sign i_, and the endings, to the tense-stem with the thematic vowel (o). All the -ih-forms are attested; of the -i_-forms only the 3 sing. and 1 and 3 plur.

Of the simple optative there are about 25 occurrences in Attic prose, and from the following verbs only: a)poxwrw=, e)capatw=, ei)sba/llw, paradi/dwmi, e)/oika, -e(sth/koi, u(phretw=, qnh/|skw, lanqa/nw, katalei/pw, poiw=, pa/sxw, proe/rxomai, e)mpi/_ptw, fu/_w. In the poets there are about 16 occurrences. Prose writers show about 106 occurrences of the periphrastic forms.
Imperative.—The usual form of the first perfect imperative is periphrastic: lelukw\s i)/sqi, e)/stw, etc. No classical Attic writer uses the simple forms.

The second perfect is rare, and occurs only in the case of verbs which have a present meaning. From active verbs inflected according to the w- conjugation there occur kexh/nete gape, Ar. Ach. 133 (xa/skw, xan-), and kekra/_gete screech, Vesp. 415 (kra/_zw). Most second perfects show the mi form and have present meaning, as te/qnaqi (Hom.) teqna/tw from qnh/|skw die, de/diqi from de/dia fear, and ke/kra_xqi from kra/_zw in Aristophanes. Most such second perfects are poetical.
Infinitive.—The perfect infinitive adds -e/-nai, as leluke/nai, leloipe/nai.
Participle.—The suffixes of the perfect participle in the nominative are -(v）w/s, -ui=a, -(v）o/s, as lelukw/s, leloipw/s. See 301 c, d, 309.

sections.group: o/, h(, to/ AS AN ARTICLE (the) IN ATTIC (ESPECIALLY IN PROSE)
sections.en: The article o(, h(\, to/ marks objects as definite and known, whether individuals (the particular article) or classes (the generic article). The context must determine the presence of the generic article. a. There is no indefinite article in Greek, but a, an is often represented by ti\s (1267).

The particular article denotes individual persons or things as distinguished from others of the same kind. Thus, mai/netai a(/_nqrwpos the man is mad (a definite person, distinguished from other men) P. Phae. 268c.

Special uses of the particular article. The particular article defines a. Objects well known: o( tw=n e(pta\ sofw/tatos *so/lwn Solon the wisest of the Seven (Sages) P. Tim. 20d. b Objects already mentioned or in the mind of the speaker or writer (the anaphoric article): ei)=pon o(/ti ta/lanton a)rguri/ou e(/toimos ei)/hn dou=nai . . . o( de\ labw to\ ta/lanton k.t.l. I said that I was ready to give him a talent of silver . . . and he taking the talent, etc. L. 12.9-10. c. Objects specially present to the senses or mind (the deictic article): labe to\ bibli/on take the book P. Th. 143c , boulo/menos th ma/xhn poih=sai wishing to fight the battle T. 4.91 . Hence the article is regularly used with demonstrative pronouns (1176). N.—The foregoing (a - c) uses recall the old demonstrative force of the article. Words that ordinarily have no article may receive the article when this older force is present. d. Objects particularized by an attributive or by a following description: o( dh=mos o( *)aqhnai/wn the people of the Athenians Aes. 3.116 , le/ge th e)pistolh/n, h( e)/pemyen read the letter that he sent D. 18.39 . Cp. 1178 d. e. Objects marked as usual or proper under the circumstances: to\ me/ros tw=n yh/fwn o( diw/kwn ou)k e)/laben the prosecutor did not get the (requisite) part of the votes D. 18.103. f. Objects representative of their class (the distributive article, which resembles the generic use; often translated by a, each): u(pisxnei=tai dw/sein tri/a h(mida_reika\ tou= mhno\s tw=| stratiw/th| he promises to give each soldier three half-darics a month X. A. 1.3.21 . But the article may be omitted: kai\ ei(/lonto de/ka, e(/na a)po\ fu_lh=s and they chose ten, one from (each) tribe X. H. 2.4.23.

The article often takes the place of an unemphatic possessive pronoun when there is no doubt as to the possessor. *ku=ros kataphdh/sa_s a)po\ tou= a(/rmatos to qw/ra_ka e)ne/du_ Cyrus leaped down from his chariot and put on his breastplate X. A. 1.8.3 .

The generic article denotes an entire class as distinguished from other classes. Thus, o( a)/nqrwpos man (as distinguished from other beings), oi( ge/rontes the aged; dei= to stratiw/thn fobei=sqai ma=llon to a)/rxonta h)\ tou\s polemi/ous the (a) soldier should fear his commander rather than the enemy X. A. 2.6.10, ponhro o( su_kofa/nths the informer is a vile thing D. 18.242 .

In the singular the generic article makes a single object the representative of the entire class; in the plural it denotes all the objects belonging to a class. The generic article is especially common, in the plural, with adjectives used substantively: ou)k a)/n tis ei)/poi w(s tou\s kakou/rgous kai\ a)di/kous ei)/a_ katagela=n no one could say that he permitted the malefactor and the wrongdoer to deride him X. A. 1.9.13 .

The Article with Participles.—A participle with the article may denote an entire class: o( boulo/menos any one who wishes. Cp. 2050, 2052. o( tuxw/n any chance comer, o( h(ghso/menos a guide, ou)k a)porh/sete tw=n e)qelhso/ntwn u(pe\r u(_mw=n kindu_neu/ein you will not be in want of those who will be willing to encounter danger for you D. 20.166 , oi( logopoiou=ntes newsmongers 4. 49. The same sense is expressed by pa=s o( with a participle or adjective. On the article with a participle in the predicate, see 1152. a. When the reference is to a particular occasion, the article may be particular (2052); as o( le/gwn the speaker on a definite occasion.

sections.group: THE ARTICLE AND A PREDICATE NOUN
sections.en: A predicate noun has no article, and is thus distinguished from the subject: kalei=tai h( a)kro/polis e)/ti u(p' *)aqhnai/wn po/lis the acropolis is still called ‘city’ by the Athenians T. 2.15.

sections.group: THE ARTICLE AND A PREDICATE NOUN
sections.en: Predicate comparatives and superlatives, possessive pronouns, and ordinals have no article: w)/|mhn th e)mautou= gunai=ka pa_sw=n swfronesta/thn <*> I thought that my wife was (the) most virtuous of all L. 1.10, *xairefw=n <*> e(tai=ros h)=n Chaerephon was a friend of mine P. A. 21a. Cp. 1125 d.

sections.group: THE ARTICLE AND A PREDICATE NOUN
sections.en: Even in the predicate the article is used with a noun referring to a definite object (an individual or a class) that is well known, previously mentioned or hinted at, or identical with the subject: oi( d' a)/lloi e)pixeirou=si ba/llein <*> *de/cippon a)nakalou=ntes to prodo/thn the rest try to strike Dexippus calling him ‘the traitor’ X. A. 6.6.7, ou(=toi h)=san oi( feu/gontes to e)/legxon these men were those who (as I have said) avoided the inquiry Ant. 6.27. oi( tiqe/menoi tou\s no/mons <*> a)sqenei=s a)/nqrwpoi/ ei)si kai\ oi( polloi/ the enactors of the laws are the weak men and the multitude P. G. 483b, u(pw/pteue de\ ei)=nai to diaba/llonta *me/nwna he suspected that it was Menon who traduced him X. A. 2.5.28 (here subject and predicate could change places). So also with o( au)to/s the same (1209 a), qa)/_teron one of two (69), tou)nanti/on the opposite.

A word or group of words standing between the article and its noun, or immediately after the article if the noun, with or without the article, precedes, is an attributive. Thus, o( sofo\s a)nh/r, o( a)nh\r o( sofo/s, or a)nh\r o( sofo/s (cp. 1168).

This holds true except in the case of such post-positive words as me/n, de/, ge/, te/, ga/r, dh/, oi)=mai, ou)=n, toi/nun; and ti\s in Hdt.: tw=n tis *perse/wn one of the Persians 1. 85. In Attic, ti\s intervenes only when an attributive follows the article: tw=n barba/rwn tine\s i(ppe/wn some of the barbarian cavalry X. A. 2.5.32 .
Adjectives, participles, adverbs, and (generally) prepositions with their cases, if preceded by the article, have attributive position.

(1) Commonly, as in English, the article and the attributive precede the noun: o( sofo\s a)nh/r the wise man. In this arrangement the emphasis is on the attributive. Thus, th=| prw/th| h(me/ra| on the first day T. 3.96 , e)n tw=| pro\ tou= xro/nw| in former times D. 53.12 , to e)k tw=n *(ellh/nwn ei)s tou\s barba/rous fo/bon i)dw/n seeing the terror inspired by the Greeks in the barbarians X. A. 1.2.18 .

(2) Less often, the article and the attributive follow the noun preceded by the article: o( a)nh\r o( sofo/s the wise man. Thus, to\ stra/teuma to\ tw=n *)aqhnai/wn the army of the Athenians T. 8.50 , e)n th=| porei/a| th=| me/xri e)pi\ qa/lattan on the journey as far as the sea X. A. 5.1.1 . In this arrangement the emphasis is on the noun, as something definite or previously mentioned, and the attributive is added by way of explanation. So tou\s ku/nas tou\s xalepou\s dide/a_si they tie up the dogs, the savage ones (I mean) X. A. 5.8.24.

(3) Least often, the noun takes no article before it, when it would have none if the attributive were dropped: a)nh\r o( sofo/s the wise man (lit. a man, I mean the wise one). Thus, ma/xais tai=s plei/osi in the greater number of battles T. 7.11 , su/neimi me qeoi=s, su/neimi de\ a)nqrw/pois toi=s a)gaqoi=s I associate with gods, I associate with good men X. M. 2.1.32. In this arrangement the attributive is added by way of explanation; as in the last example: with men, the good (I mean).

A proper name, defining a preceding noun with the article, may itself have the article: o( a)delfo\s o( *)areqou/sios (his) brother Arethusius D. 53.10. Cp. 1142 c. An appositive to a proper name has the article when it designates a characteristic or something well known: o( *so/lwn o( palaio\s h)=n filo/dhmos Solon of ancient times was a lover of the people Ar. Nub. 1187 , *pa_si/wn o( *megareu/s Pasion, the Megarian X. A. 1.4.7.

The genitive of a substantive limiting the meaning of another substantive may take any one of four positions:— a. to\ tou= patro\s bibli/on the father's book (very common). Thus, h( <*> teqnew/twn a)reth/ the valour of the dead L. 12.36. b. to\ bibli/on to\ tou= patro/s (less common). Thus, h( oi)ki/a_ h( *si/mwnos the house of Simon L. 3.32 . c. tou= patro\s to\ bibli/on (to emphasize the genitive or when a genitive has just preceded). Thus, th=s vi/_khs to\ me/geqos the greatness of the victory X. H. 6.4.19 . d. to\ bibli/on tou= patro/s (very common). Thus, h( to/lma tw=n lego/ntwn the effrontery of the speakers L. 12.41 . The genitive of the divided whole (1306) is so placed or as in c. N. 1.—A substantive with no article is sometimes followed by the article and the attributive genitive: e)pi\ skhnh i)o/ntes th *cenofw=ntos going to the ten<*> (namely, that) of Xenophon X. A. 6.4.19. Cp. 1159.

The order bringing together the same forms of the article (peri\ tou= t<*> patro\s bibli/ou) is avoided, but two or three articles of different form may stand together: to\ th=s tou= cai/nontos te/xnhs e)/rgon the work of the art of the wool-carder P. Pol. 281a .

The attributive position is employed with the possessive pronouns and the possessive genitives of the reflexive and demonstrative pronouns (1184), au)to<*> meaning same (1173), and pa=s expressing the sum total (1174).

Two or more attributives of a substantive are variously placed: (1) ei)s ta\_s a)/lla_s *)arkadika\_s po/leis to the other Arcadian cities X. H. 7.4.38 . (2) to\ e)n *)arkadi/a| to\ tou= *dio\s tou= *lukai/ou i(ero/n the sanctuary of Lycean Zeus in Arcadia P. R. 565d . (3) e)s to e)pi\ tw=| sto/mati tou= lime/nos stenou= o)/ntos to e(/teron pu/rgon to the other tower at the mouth of the harbour which was narrow T. 8.90 . (4) e)n th=| oi)ki/a| th=| *xarmi/dou th=| para\ to\ *)olumpiei=on in the house of Charmides by the Olympieum And. 1.16 . (5) a)po\ tw=n e)n th=| *)asi/a| po/lewn *(ellhni/dwn from the Greek cities in Asia X. H. 4.3.15 . (6) pro\s th e)k th=s *sikeli/a_s tw=n *)aqhnai/wn mega/lhn kakopra_gi/a_n with regard to the great failure of the Athenians in Sicily T. 8.2 . (7) to\ tei=xos to\ makro to\ no/tion the long southern wall And. 3.7 .
A relative or temporal clause may be treated as an attributive: *so/lwn e)mi/_sei tou\s oi(=os ou(=tos a)nqrw/pous Solon detested men like this man here D. 19.254 .

Position of an attributive participle with its modifiers (A = article, N = noun, P = participle, D = word or words dependent on P): (1) APND: to e)festhko/ta ki/ndu_non th=| po/lei the danger impending over the State D. 18.176 . (2) APDN: tou\s periesthko/tas th=| po/lei kindu/_nous D. 18.179. (3) ADPN: to to/te th=| po/lei perista/nta ki/ndu_non D. 18.188. (4) NADP: e(/toimon e)/xei du/namin th . . . katadoulwsoue/nhn a)/pantas he has in readiness a force to enslave all D. 8.46 .

a. Especially after verbal substantives denoting an action or a state an attributive prepositional phrase is added without the article being repeated: th mega/lhn stratei/a_n *)aqhnai/wn kai\ tw=n cumma/xwn e)s *ai)/gupton the great expedition of the Athenians and their allies to Egypt T. 1.110 . b. A word defining a substantivized participle, adjective, or infinitive may be placed before the article for emphasis: kai\ tau=ta tou\s ei)do/tas kalou=men and we will summon those who have knowledge of this D. 57.65 , tou/twn toi=s e)nanti/ois with the opposite of these T. 7.75 .

A predicate adjective either precedes or follows the article and its noun: sofo\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r sofo/s the man is wise. Thus, a)telei= th=| ni/_kh| a)ne/sthsan they retired with their victory incomplete T. 8.27 , yi_lh e)/xwn th kefalh/n with his head bare X. A. 1.8.6 , ta\_s trih/reis a)fei/lkusan kena/_s they towed off the ships without their crews T. 2.93 . a. This is called the predicate position, which often lends emphasis.

A predicate adjective or substantive may thus be the equivalent of a clause of a complex sentence: a)qa/naton th peri\ au(tw=n mnh/mhn katalei/yousin they will leave behind a remembrance of themselves that will never die I. 9.3 , e)ph/reto po/son ti a)/goi to\ stra/teuma he asked about how large the force was that he was leading ( = po/son ti ei)/h to\ stra/teuma o(\ a)/goi 2647) X. C. 2.1.2, par' e(ko/ntwn tw=n cumma/xwn th h(gemoni/a_n e)/labon they received the leadership from their allies (being willing) who were willing to confer it I. 1.17.
