A predicate expression may stand inside an attributive phrase: o( deino\s (pred.) lego/menos gewrgo/s he who is called a skilful agriculturist X. O. 19.14 . This is common with participles of naming with the article.

The predicate position is employed with the demonstratives ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos, and a)/mfw, a)mfo/teros, e(ka/teros, and e(/kastos; with the possessive genitives of personal and relative pronouns (1185, 1196) and of au)to/s (1201); with au)to/s meaning self (1206 b); with the genitive of the divided whole (1306), as tou/twn oi( plei=stoi the most of these X. A. 1.5.13 , oi( a)/ristoi tw=n peri\ au)to/n the bravest of his companions 1. 8. 27; and with pa=s meaning all (1174 b). a. This wise man is ou(=tos o( sofo\s a)nh/r, o( sofo\s a)nh\r ou(=tos (and also o( sofo\s ou(=tos a)nh/r).

Adjectives of Place.—When used in the predicate position (1168) a)/kros (high) means the top of, me/sos (middle) means the middle of, e)/sxatos (extreme) means the end of. Cp. summus, medius, extremus. Attributive Position Predicate Position to\ a)/kron o(/ros the lofty mountain a)/kron to\ o)/ros ) the top of to\ o)/ros a)/kron ) the mountain h( me/sh a)gora/_ the central market me/sh h( a)gora/_ ) the centre of h( a)gora\_ me/sh ) the market h( e)sxa/th nh=sos the farthest island e)sxa/th h( nh=sos ) the verge of h( nh=sos e)sxa/th ) the island Thus, peri\ a)/krais tai=s xersi\ xeiri=des gloves on the fingers (points of the hands) X. C. 8.8.17, dia\ me/sou tou= paradei/sou r(ei= flows through the middle of the park X. A. 1.2.7 . The meaning of the predicate position is also expressed by (to\) a)/kron tou= o)/rous, (to\) me/son th=s a)gora=s, etc.

mo/nos, h(/misus.—(1) Attributive: o( mo/nos pai=s the only son, ai( h(mi/seiai xa/rites half-favours. (2) Predicate: mo/nos o( pai=s (or o( pai=s mo/nos) pai/zei the boy plays alone, h(/misus o( bi/os (or o( bi/os h(/misus) half of life, ta\ a(/rmata ta\ h(mi/sea half of the chariots. au)to/s: (1) Attributive: o( au)to\s a)nh/r the same man. (2) Predicate: au)to\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself.

pa=s (and in the strengthened forms a(/pa_s, su/mpa_s all together). a. In the attributive position pa=s denotes the whole regarded as the sum of all its parts (the sum total, the collective body): oi( pa/ntes poli=tai the whole body of citizens, h( pa=sa *sikeli/a_ the whole of Sicily, a)poktei=nai tou\s a(/pantas *mutilhnai/ous to put to death the entire Mitylenean population T. 3.36 . N.—Hence, with numbers, oi( pa/ntes, ta\ su/mpanta in all: e(cako/sioi kai\ xi/_lioi oi( pa/ntes 1600 in all T. 1.60 . b. In the predicate (and usual) position pa=s means all: pa/ntes oi( poli=tai or (often emphatic) oi( poli=tai pa/ntes all the citizens (individually), peri\ pa/ntas tou\s qeou\s h)sebh/ka_si kai\ ei)s a(/pa_san th po/lin h(marth/ka_sin they have committed impiety towards all the gods and have sinned against the whole State L. 14.42 . c. Without the article: pa/ntes poli=tai all (conceivable) citizens, misqwsa/menoi pa/ntas a)nqrw/pous hiring every conceivable person L. 12.60 . N. 1.—In the meaning pure, nothing but, pa=s is strictly a predicate and has no article: ku/klw| frourou/menos u(po\ pa/ntwn polemi/wn hemmed in by a ring of guards all of whom are his enemies ( = pa/ntes u(f' w(=n frourei=tai pole/mioi/ ei)si) P. R. 579b. So pa=sa kaki/a_ utter baseness. N. 2.—The article is not used with pa=s if the noun, standing alone, would have no article. N. 3.—In the singular, pa=s often means every: su soi\ pa=sa o(do\s eu)/poros with you every road is easy to travel X. A. 2.5.9 , pa=sa qa/lassa every sea T. 2.41 .

o(/los: (1) Attributive: to\ o(/lon stra/teuma the whole army; (2) Predicate: o(/lon to\ stra/teuma (or to\ stra/teuma o(/lon) the army as a whole, th nu/kta o(/lhn the entire night. With no article: o(/lon stra/teuma a whole army, o(/la strateu/mata whole armies.

The demonstrative pronouns ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos, and au)to/s self, in agreement with a noun, usually take the article, and stand in the predicate position (1168): ou(=tos o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r ou(=tos (never o( ou(=tos a)nh/r) this man, au)to\s o( a)nh/r or o( a)nh\r au)to/s the man himself (o( au)to\s a)nh/r the same man 1173).

One or more words may separate the demonstrative from its noun: o( tou/tou e)/rws tou= a)nqrw/pou the love of this man P. S. 213c . Note also tw=n oi)kei/wn tine\s tw=n e)kei/nwn some of their slaves (some of the slaves of those men) P. A. 33d.

ou(=tos, o(/de, e)kei=nos sometimes omit the article. a. Regularly, when the noun is in the predicate: au(/th e)/stw i(kanh\ a)pologi/a_ let this be a sufficient defence P. A. 24b , oi)=mai e)mh tau/thn patri/da ei)=nai I think this is my native country X. A. 4.8.4 . b. Usually, with proper names, except when anaphoric (1120 b): e)kei=nos *qouku_di/dhs that (well-known) Thucydides Ar. Ach. 708. c. Usually, with definite numbers: tau/ta_s tria/_konta mna=s these thirty minae D. 27.23 . d. Optionally, when a relative clause follows: e)pi\ gh=n th/nde h)/lqomen, e)n h(=| oi( pate/res h(mw=n *mh/dwn e)kra/thsan we have come against this land, in which our fathers conquered the Medes T. 2.74 . e. In the phrase (often contemptuous) ou(=tos a)nh/r P. G. 505c; and in other expressions denoting some emotion: a)/nqrwpos ou(tosi/_ D. 18.243. f. Sometimes, when the demonstrative follows its noun: e)pi/gramma to/de T. 6.59. So often in Hdt. g. Frequently, in poetry.

a)/mfw, a)mfo/teros both, e(ka/teros each (of two), e(/kastos each (of several) have the predicate position. But with e(/kastos the article is often omitted: kata\ th h(me/ra_n e(ka/sthn (day by day and) every day, kaq' e(ka/sthn h(me/ra_n every day.

The demonstratives of quality and quantity, toiou=tos, toio/sde, tosou=tos, toso/sde, thlikou=tos, when they take the article, usually follow it: tw=n tosou/twn kai\ toiou/twn a)gaqw=n of so many and such blessings D. 18.305 , tou=to to\ toiou=ton e)/qos such a practice as this 21. 123. o( dei=na such a one (336) regularly takes the article. a. But the predicate position occurs: tosau/th h( prw/th paraskeuh\ pro\s to po/lemon die/plei so great was the first armament which crossed over for the war T. 6.44 .

An attributive, following the article, may be separated from its noun by a pronoun: h( pa/lai h(mw=n fu/sis our old nature P. S. 189d , h( stenh\ au(/th o(do/s (for au(/th h( stenh\ o(do/s) this narrow road X. A. 4.2.6.

Possessive pronouns take the article only when a definite person or thing is meant, and stand between article and noun: to\ e)mo bibli/on my book, ta\ h(me/tera bibli/a our books. a. But names of relationship, po/lis, patri/s, etc., do not require the article (1140).

The article is not used with possessive pronouns or the genitive of personal and reflexive pronouns (cp. 1184, 1185): a. When no particular object is meant: e)mo bibli/on or bibli/on mou a book of mine. b. When these pronouns belong to the predicate: maqhth\s ge/gona so/s I have become a pupil of yours P. Euth. 5a , ou) lo/gous e)mautou= le/gwn not speaking words of my own D. 9.41 .

In the attributive position (1154) stands the genitive of the demonstrative, reflexive, and reciprocal pronouns. to\ tou/tou bibli/on or to\ bibli/on to\ tou/tou his book, to\ e)mautou= bibli/on or to\ bibli/on to\ e)mautou= my own book; metepe/myato th e(autou= qugate/ra kai\ to pai=da au)th=s he sent for his daughter and her child X. C. 1.3.1 . a. The type to\ bibli/on tou/tou is rare and suspected except when another attributive is added: th=| nu=n u(/brei tou/tou D. 4.3. The types to\ bibli/on e)mautou= (Hdt. 6.23) and to\ au)tou= bibli/on (T. 6.102) are rare.

In the predicate position stands a. The genitive of the personal pronouns (whether partitive or not): to\ bibli/on mou (sou, au)tou=, etc.), or mou sou, au)tou=. etc.) to\ bibli/on when other words precede, as o(\s e)/xei sou th a\delohn who has your sister to wife And. 1.50 . b. The genitive of the other pronouns used partitively. N. 1.—Homer does not use the article in the above cases, and often employs the orthotone forms ( sei=o me/ga kle/os thy great fame p 241 ). Even in Attic e)mou= for mou occurs ( e)mou= ta\ forti/a my wares Ar. Vesp. 1398 ). N. 2.—The differences of position between 1184 and 1185 may be thus illustrated: My book is pretty: kalo/n e)sti/ to\ bibli/on mou. kalo/n e)sti/ mou to\ bibli/on. My pretty book: to\ kalo/n mou bibli/on. They read their books: ta\ e/autw=n <*>bibli/a a)nagignw/skousi.

The interrogatives ti/s, poi=os may take the article when a question is asked about an object before mentioned: *s*w. nu=n d<*> e)ke <*>na, w)= *fai=dre, duna/meqa kri/_nein. *f*a*i. ta\ poi=a; SOCR. Now at last we can decide those questions. PH. The what questions? P. Phae. 277a.

So even with a personal pronoun: A. deu=ro dh\ eu)qu\ h(mw=n . . . B. poi= le/geis kai\ para\ ti/nas tou\s u(_ma=s; A. Come hither straight to us. B. Whither do you mean and who are you that I am to come to (you being who)? P. Lys. 203b.

a)/llos other.—o( a)/llos in the singular usually means the rest (h( a)/llh *(ella/s the rest of Greece); in the plural. the others (oi( a)/lloi *(/ellhnes the other (ceteri) Greeks, but a)/lloi *(/ellhnes other <*>lii) Greeks). A substantivized adjective or participle usually has the article when it stands in apposition to oi( a)/lloi: ta)=lla ta\ poli_tika/ the other civic affairs X. Hi. 9.5 . On a)/llos, o( a)/llos (sometimes e(/teros) besides, see 1272.

polu/s, o)li/gos: to\ polu/ usually means the great（er) part, oi( polloi/ the multitude, the vulgar crowd; plei/ones several, oi( plei/ones the majority, the mass; plei=stoi very many, oi( plei=stoi the most; o(li/goi few, oi( o)li/goi the oligarchs (as opposed to oi( polloi/). Note polu/s predicative: e)pei\ e(w/ra_ polla\ ta\ kre/a_ when he saw that there was abundance of meat X. C. 1.3.6 .

The nominative of the personal pronoun is usually omitted except when emphatic, e.g. in contrasts, whether expressed or implied: e)pei\ u(_mei=s e)moi\ ou) qe/lete pei/qesqai, e)gw su u(_mi=n e(/yomai since you are not willing to obey me, I will follow along with you X. A. 1.3.6. In contrasts the first pronoun is sometimes omitted (930).

Where there is no contrast the addition of the pronoun may strengthen the verb: ei) mhde\ tou=to bou/lei a)pokri/_nasqai, su\ de\ tou)nteu=qen le/ge if you do not wish to reply even to this, tell me then X. C. 5.5.21 .

The forms e)mou=, e)moi/, and e)me/ and the accented forms of the pronoun of the second person (325 a) are used when emphatic and usually after prepositions: kai\ pei/sa_s e)me\ pista\ e)/dwka/s moi kai\ e)/labes par' e)mou= and after prevailing on me you gave me pledges of faith and received them from me X. A. 1.6.7 . Cp. 187 N. 2. On the reflexive use of the personal pronouns of the first and second persons, see 1222-1224.
e)gw/, su/ (e)mo/s, so/s) are rarely used of an imaginary person (‘anybody’): D. 9.17, X. R. A. 1.11.

The nominative of the pronoun of the third person is replaced by e)kei=nos (of absent persons), o(/de, ou(=tos (of present persons), o( me/n . . . o( de/ (at the beginning of a sentence), and by au)to/s in contrasts. The oblique cases of the foregoing replace ou(=, etc., which in Attic prose are usually indirect reflexives (1228, 1229). ou(= and e(/ in Attic prose occur chiefly in poetical passages of Plato; in Attic poetry they are personal pronouns. The pronoun of the third person is very rare in the orators.

Homer uses e(/o, oi(=, etc., as personal pronouns ( = au)tou=, au)tw=|, etc., in Attic), in which case they are enclitic: dia\ mantosu/nhn, th/n oi( po/re *foi=bos by the art of divination, which Phoebus gave to him A 72. Homer also uses e(/o, oi(=, etc., either as direct ( = e(autou=, etc., 1218) or as indirect reflexives ( = au)tou=, etc., 1225). In the former case they are orthotone; in the latter, either enclitic or orthotone. Thus, oi/= pai=da e)oiko/ta gei/nato he begat a son like unto himself E 800, ou)/ tina/ fhsin o(moi=on oi)= e)/menai *danaw=n he says there is no one of the Danaans like unto himself I 306. Hdt. agrees with Hom. except that eu(=, oi(= are not direct reflexives and orthotone; sfi/si (not sfi/) is reflexive.

The possessive pronouns (330) of the first and second persons are the equivalents of the possessive genitive of the personal pronouns: e)mo/s = mou, so/s = sou, h(me/teros = h(mw=n, u(_me/teros = u(_mw=n. a. When the possessives refer to a definite, particular thing, they have the article, which always precedes (1182); the personal pronouns have the predicate position (1185). Distinguish o( e)mo\s fi/los, o( fi/los o( e)mo/s, o( fi/los mou my friend from fi/los e)mo/s, fi/los mou a friend of mine. b. A word may stand in the genitive in apposition to the personal pronoun implied in a possessive pronoun. See 977.

A possessive pronoun may have the force of an objective genitive (cp. 1331) of the personal pronoun: fili/a| th=| e)mh=| out of friendship for me X. C. 3.1.28 . (fili/a_ h( e)mh/ usually means my friendship (for others)).
The possessive pronouns of the first and second persons are sometimes reflexive (when the subject of the sentence and the possessor are the same person), sometimes not reflexive.

FIRST AND SECOND PERSONS SINGULAR 1. Not reflexive (adjective my, thy (your); pronoun mine, thine (yours)). e)mo/s, so/s: o(ra=| to e)mo fi/lon he sees my friend, o(ra=| to so pate/ra she sees your father, ste/rgei to e)mo pate/ra he loves my father (or to pate/ra to e)mo/n or pate/ra to e)mo/n; or to pate/ra mou or mou to pate/ra), oi( e)moi\ o)fqalmoi\ kalli/_ones a) tw=n sw=n ei)/hsan my eyes will prove to be more beautiful than yours X. S. 5 . 5. 2. Reflexive (my own, thine (your) own). a. e)mautou=, seautou=, in the attributive position (very common): e)/labon to e)mautou= misqo/n (or to misqo to e)mautou=) I received my (own) pay, to a)delfo to e)mautou= e)/pemya I sent my (own) brother Aes. 2.94, ka)_pi\ toi=s sauth=s kakoi=si ka)_pi\ toi=s e)moi=s gela=|s; art thou laughing at thine own misery and at mine? S. El. 879. b. e)mo/s, so/s (less common): ste/rgw to e)mo pate/ra I love my (own) father, ste/rgeis th sh mhte/ra you love your (own) mother, h( e)mh\ gunh\ my wife X. C. 7.2.28 , a)delfo\s th=s mhtro\s th=s e)mh=s brother of my mother And. 1.117 . c. e)mo\s au)tou=, so\s au)tou= (poetical): to e)mo au)tou= pate/ra (b 45, S. O. T. 416). d. mou, sou (rare): to pate/ra mou Ant. 1.23. N.—When the possessor is not to be mistaken, the article alone is placed before the substantive and the possessive or reflexive pronoun is omitted (cp. 1121). Thus, ste/rgeis to pate/ra you love your (own) father, ste/rgei to pate/ra he loves his (own) father, ste/rgousi to pate/ra they love their (own) father.

FIRST AND SECOND PERSONS PLURAL 1. Not reflexive (adjective our, your; pronoun ours, yours). a. h(me/teros, u(_me/teros: o( h(me/teros fi/los our friend (more common than o( fi/lo<*> h(mw=n), o( u(_me/teros fi/los your friend (more common than o( fi/los u(_mw=n), zh/thsin poiou/menoi h)\ u(_mw=n h)\ tw=n u(_mete/rwn tino/s making a search for you or for anything of yours L. 12.30 . 2. Reflexive (our own, your own). a. h(me/teros, u(_me/teros (common): ste/rgomen to h(me/teron fi/lon we love our own friend, ste/rgete to u(_me/teron fi/lon you love your own friend. b. Usually the intensive au)tw=n is used with h(me/teros, u(_me/teros in agreement with h(mw=n (u(_mw=n) implied in the possessive forms. This gives a stronger form of reflexive. Thus: h(me/teros au)tw=n, u(_me/teros au)tw=n: ste/rgomen to h(me/teron au)tw=n fi/lon we love our own friend, oi)kodo/mhma h)\ tw=n fi/lwn tini\ h)\ h(me/teron au)tw=n a house either for some one of our friends or our own P. G. 514b ; ste/rgete to u(_me/teron au)tw=n fi/lon you love your own friend, dida/skete tou\s pai=das tou\s u(_mete/rous au)tw=n teach your own children I. 3.57 . c. h(mw=n, u(_mw=n (rare): ai)tiw/meqatou\s pate/ras h(mw=n let us accuse our (own) fathers P. Lach. 179c. d. h(mw=n au)tw=n, u(_mw=n au)tw=n (very rare): di/kaion h(ma=s . . . fai/nesqai mh/te h(mw=n au)tw=n th=s do/chs e)ndeeste/rous it is not right for us to show ourselves inferior to our own fame T. 2.11 , ta\ tw=n i(/ppwn kai\ ta\ u(_mw=n au)tw=n o(/pla the equipments both of your horses and yourselves X. C. 6.3.21 .

THIRD PERSON SINGULAR 1. Not reflexive (his, her, its). a. au)tou=, au)th=s, au)tou= in the predicate position (very common): o(rw= to fi/lon au)tou= (au)th=s) I see his (her) friend, gignw/skwn au)tou= th a)ndrei/a_n knowing his courage P. Pr. 310d . b. e)kei/nou, etc., or tou/tou, etc. in the attributive position (very common): o(rw= to e)mo fi/lon, ou) to e)kei/nou I see my friend, not his, a)fiknou=ntai par' *)ariai=on kai\ th e)kei/nou stratia/_n they come up with Ariaeus and his army X. A. 2.2.8 , pareka/lese/ tinas tw=n tou/tou e)pithdei/wn he summoned some of his friends L. 3.11 . c. o(/s, h(/, o(/n, Hom. e(o/s, e(h/, e(o/n (poetical): th gh=men e(o dia\ ka/llos he married her because of her beauty l 282 . Hom. has eu(= rarely for au)tou=, au)th=s. 2. Reflexive (his own, her own). a. e(autou=, e(auth=s, in the attributive position (very common): ste/rgei to e(autou= fi/lon he loves his own friend, o:ra=| th e(auth=s mhte/ra she sees her own mother, th e(autou= a)delfh di/dwsi *seu/qh| he gives his own sister in marriage to Seuthes T. 2.101 , u(bri/zei gunai=ka th e(autou= he misuses his own wife And. 4.15 . This is the only way in prose to express his own, her own. b. o(/s (e(o/s): poetical. Sometimes in Homer o(/s (e(o/s) has the sense of own with no reference to the third person (1230 a). c. o(\s au)tou=, au)th=s (poetical): o( au)tou= pate/ra (K 204).

THIRD PERSON PLURAL 1. Not reflexive (their). a. au)tw=n in the predicate position (very common): o( fi/los au)tw=n their friend. b. e)kei/nwn, tou/twn in the attributive position (very common): o( tou/twn (e)kei/nwn) fi/los their friend, dia\ th e)kei/nwn a)pisti/a_n because of distrust of them And. 3.2 . c. sfe/wn (Ionic): Hdt. 5.58. 2. Reflexive (their own). a. e(autw=n (very common): ste/rgousi tou\s e(autw=n fi/lous they love their own friends, tw=n e(autw=n summa/xwn katefro/noun they despised their own allies X. H. 4.4.7 . b. sfe/teros au)tw=n, the intensive au)tw=n agreeing with sfw=n implied in sfe/teros (common): oi)ke/ta_s tou\s sfete/rous au)tw=n e)pikalou=ntai they call their own slaves as witnesses Ant. 1.30 . c. sfw=n au)tw=n, without the article (rare): ta\ o)no/mata diapra/_ttontai sfw=n au)tw=n prosgrafh=nai they contrived that their own names were added L. 13.72 . Cp. 1234. to sfw=n au)tw=n is not used. d. sfe/teros (rare in prose): *boiwtoi\ me/ros to\ sfe/teron parei/xonto the Boeotians furnished their own contingent T. 2.12 . e. sfw=n in the predicate position, occasionally in Thucydides, as tou\s cumma/xoui e)de/disan sfw=n they were afraid of their own allies 5. 14. Cp. 1228 N. 2.

Summary of possessive forms (poetical forms in parenthesis). a. Not reflexive my e)mo/s mou thy so/s sou his, her （o)/s Hom., rare) au)tou=, -h=s （eu(= Hom., rare) our h(me/teros h(mw=n your u(_me/teros u(_mw=n their au)tw=n （sfe/wn Ionic) N.—h(me/teros and u(_me/teros are more used than h(mw=n and u(_mw=n. b. Reflexive my own e)mo/s （e)mo\s au)tou=, -h=s） e)mautou=, -h=s thy own so/s （so\s au)tou=, -h=s） seautou=, -h=s his, her own (o(/s） （o(\s au)tou=, -h=s） e(autou=, -h=s (poet. and Ionic) our own h(me/teros h(me/teros au)tw=n your own u(_me/teros ume/teros au)tw=n their own sfe/teros sfe/teros au)tw=n (rare) e(autw=n, sfw=n (rare), sfw=n au)tw=n N.—In the plural h(mw=n au)tw=n, u(_mw=n au)tw=n are replaced by h(me/teros au)tw=n, u(_me/teros au)tw=n, and these forms are commoner than h(me/teros, u(_me/teros. sfe/teros au)tw=n is less common than e(autw=n. sfe/teros in poetry may mean mine own, thine own, your own.

Of the cases belonging to the Indo-European language, Greek has lost the free use of three: instrumental, locative, and ablative. A few of the forms of these cases have been preserved (341, 1449, 1535); the syntactical functions of the instrumental and locative were taken over by the dative; those of the ablative by the genitive. The genitive and dative cases are therefore composite or mixed cases. N.—The reasons that led to the formation of composite cases are either (1) formal or (2) functional. Thus (1) xw/ra| is both dat. and loc.; lo/gois represents the instr. lo/gois and the loc. lo/goisi; in consonantal stems both ablative and genitive ended in -os; (2) verbs of ruling may take either the dat. or the loc., hence the latter case would be absorbed by the former; furthermore the use of prepositions especially with loc. and instr. was attended by a certain indifference as regards the form of the case.

Through the influence of one construction upon another it often becomes impossible to mark off the later from the original use of the genitive and dative. It must be remembered that since language is a natural growth and Greek was spoken and written before formal categories were set up by Grammar, all the uses of the cases cannot be apportioned with definiteness.

The cases fall into two main divisions. Cases of the Subject: nominative (and vocative). Cases of the Predicate: accusative, dative. The genitive may define either the subject (with nouns) or the predicate (with verbs). On the nominative, see 938 ff.

The content of a thought may be expressed in different ways in different languages. Thus, pei/qw se, but persuadeo tibi (in classical Latin): and even in the same language, the same verb may have varying constructions to express different shades of meaning.

The vocative is used in exclamations and in direct address: w)= *zeu= kai\ qeoi/ oh Zeus and ye gods P. Pr. 310d , a)/nqrwpe my good fellow X. C. 2.2.7 . The vocative forms an incomplete sentence (904 d). a. The vocative is never followed immediately by de/ or ga/r.

In ordinary conversation and public speeches, the polite w)= is usually added. Without w)= the vocative may express astonishment, joy, contempt, a threat, or a warning, etc. Thus a)kou/eis *ai)sxi/nh; d'ye hear, Aeschines? D. 18.121. But this distinction is not always observed, though in general w)= has a familiar tone which was unsuited to elevated poetry.

The vocative is usually found in the interior of a sentence. At the beginning it is emphatic. In prose e)/fh, in poetry w)=, may stand between the vocative and an attributive or between an attributive and the vocative; in poetry w)= may be repeated for emphasis.

In late poetry a predicate adjective may be attracted into the vocative: o)/lbie kw=re ge/noio blessed, oh boy, mayest thou be Theocr. 17. 66. Cp. Matutine pater seu Iane libentius audis Hor. S. 2. 6. 20.

By the omission of su/ or u(_mei=s the nominative with the article may stand in apposition to a vocative: w)= a)/ndoes oi( paro/ntes you, gentlemen, who are present P. Pr. 337c, w)= *ku=re kai\ oi( a)/lloi *pe/rsai Cyrus and the rest of you Persians X. C. 3.3.20 ; and in apposition to the pronoun in the verb: o( pai=s, a)kolou/qei boy, attend me Ar. Ran. 521.

The nominative may be used in exclamations as a predicate with the subject unexpressed: w)= pikro\s qeoi=s oh loathed of heaven S. Ph. 254 , fi/los w)= *mene/la_e ah dear Menelaus *d 189 ; and connected with the vocative by and: w)= po/lis kai\ dh=me oh city and people Ar. Eq. 273 . In exclamations about a person: w)\ gennai=os oh the noble man P. Phae. 227c . a. ou(=tos is regular in address: ou(=tos, ti/ pa/sxeis, w)= *canqi/a_; ho there, I say, Xanthias, what is the matter with you? Ar. Vesp. 1; w)= ou(=tos, *ai)/a_s ho there, I say, Ajax S. Aj. 89.

The genitive most commonly limits the meaning of substantives, adjectives, and adverbs, less commonly that of verbs. Since the genitive has absorbed the ablative it includes (1) the genitive proper, denoting the class to which a person or thing belongs, and (2) the ablatival genitive. a. The name genitive is derived from casus genitivus, the case of origin, the inadequate Latin translation of genikh\ ptw=sis case denoting the class.
A substantive in the genitive limits the meaning of a substantive on which it depends.

The genitive limits for the time being the scope of the substantive on which it depends by referring it to a particular class or description, or by regarding it as a part of a whole. The genitive is akin in meaning to the adjective and may often be translated by an epithet. Cp. ste/fanos xru_si/ou with xru_sou=s ste/fanos, fo/bos polemi/ou with pole/mios fo/bos, to\ eu)=ros ple/qrou with to\ eu)=ros pleqriai=on (1035). But the use of the adjective is not everywhere parallel to that of the genitive.
In poetry a genitive is often used with bi/a_, me/nos, sqe/nos might, etc., instead of the corresponding adjective: bi/h *diomh/deos mighty Diomede E 781.
In poetry de/mas form, ka/ra_ and kefalh/ head, etc., are used with a genitive to express majestic or loved persons or objects: *)ismh/nhs ka/ra_ S. Ant. 1.
xrh=ma thing is used in prose with a genitive to express size, strength, etc.: sfendonhtw=n pa/mpolu/ ti xrh=ma a very large mass of slingers X. C. 2.1.5 . Cp. 1322.

The genitive with substantives denotes in general a connection or dependence between two words. This connection must often be determined (1) by the meaning of the words, (2) by the context, (3) by the facts presupposed as known (1301). The same construction may often be placed under more than one of the different classes mentioned below; and the connection between the two substantives is often so loose that it is difficult to include with precision all cases under specific grammatical classes. a. The two substantives may be so closely connected as to be equivalent to a single compound idea: teleuth\ tou= bi/ou ‘life-end’ (cp. life-time) X. A. 1.1.1. Cp. 1146. b. The genitive with substantives has either the attributive (1154), or, in the case of the genitive of the divided whole (1306), and of personal pronouns (1185), the predicate, position (1168).

Words denoting number, especially numerals or substantives with numerals, often agree in case with the limited word instead of standing in the genitive: fo/ros te/ssara ta/lanta a tribute of four talents T. 4.57 (cp. 1323), e)s ta\_s nau=s, ai(\ e)frou/roun du/o, katafugo/ntes fleeing to the ships, two of which were keeping guard 4. 113. So with oi( me/n, oi( de/ in apposition to the subject (981).

The genitive denotes ownership, possession, or belonging: h( oi)ki/a_ h( *si/mwnos the house of Simon L. 3.32 , o( *ku/_rou sto/los the expedition of Cyrus X. A. 1.2.5 . Cp. the dative of possession (1476).

Here may be classed the genitive of origin: oi( *so/lwnos no/moi the laws of Solon D. 20.103 , h( e)pistolh\ tou= *fili/ppou the letter of Philip 18. 37, ku/_mata pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn waves caused by all kinds of winds B 396.

The possessive genitive is used with the neuter article (singular or plural) denoting affairs, conditions, power, and the like: to\ tw=n e)fo/rwn the power of the ephors P. L. 712d , to\ th=s te/xnhs the function of the art P. G. 450c , to\ tou= *so/lwnos the maxim of Solon P. Lach. 188b , a)/dhla ta\ tw=n pole/mwn the chances of war are uncertain T. 2.11 , ta\ th=s po/lews the interests of the State P. A. 36c , ta\ tou= dh/mou fronei= is on the side of the people Ar. Eq. 1216 . Sometimes this is almost a mere periphrasis for the thing itself: to\ th=s tu/xhs chance D. 4.12 ta\ th=s swthri/a_s safety 23. 163, to\ th=s o(si/a_s, o(tidh/pot' e)sti/ the quality of holiness, whatever it is 21. 126, to\ tw=n presbute/rwn h(mw=n we elders P. L. 657d . So to\ tou/tou S. Aj. 124 is almost = ou(=tos, as tou)mo/n is = e)gw/ or e)me/. Cp. L. 8.19.
The genitive of possession may be used after a demonstrative or relative pronoun: tou=to/ mou diaba/llei he attacks this action of mine D. 18.28 .

With persons the genitive may denote the relation of child to parent, wife to husband, and of inferior to superior: *qouku_di/dhs o( *)olo/rou Thucydides, the son of Olorus T. 4.104 (and so uio/s is regularly omitted in Attic official documents), *dio\s *)/artemis Artemis, daughter of Zeus S. Aj. 172, h( *smi_kuqi/wnos *melisti/xh Melistiche wife of Smicythion Ar. Eccl. 46 , *au_do\s o( *ferekle/ous Lydus, the slave of Pherecles And. 1.17, oi( *me/nwnos the troops of Menon X. A. 1.5.13 (oi( tou= *me/nwnos stratiw=tai 1. 5. 11). a. In poetry we may have an attributive adjective: *telamw/nios *ai)/a_s ( = *ai)/a_s o( *telamw=nos) B 528. Cp. 846 f.

The word on which the possessive genitive depends may be represented by the article: a)po\ th=s e(autw=n from their own country (gh=s) T. 1.15 (cp. 1027 b). A word for dwelling (oi)ki/a_, do/mos, and also i(ero/n) is perhaps omitted after e)n, ei)s, and sometimes after e)c. Thus, e)n *)ari/fronos at Ariphron's P. Pr. 320a , e)n *dionu/_sou (scil. i(erw=|) at the shrine of Dionysus D. 5.7, ei)s didaska/lou foita=n to go to school X. C. 2.3.9 , e)k *patrokle/ous e)/rxomai I come from Patroclus's Ar. Plut. 84 . So, in Homer, ei)n（ei)s) *)ai/da_o.

Predicate Use.—The genitive may be connected with the noun it limits by means of a verb. *(ippokra/ths e)sti\ oi)ki/a_s mega/lhs Hippocrates is of an influential house P. Pr. 316b , *boiwtw=n h( po/lis e)/stai the city will belong to the Boeotians L. 12.58 , h( *ze/leia/ e)sti th=s *)asi/a_s Zelea is in Asia D. 9.43 , ou)de\ th=s au)th=s *qra/|khs e)ge/nonto nor did they belong to the same Thrace T. 2.29 , a(\ diw/kei tou= yhfi/smatos, tau=t' e)sti/n the clauses in the bill which he attacks, are these D. 18.56 .

The genitive with ei)mi/ may denote the person whose nature, duty, custom, etc., it is to do that set forth in an infinitive subject of the verb: peni/a_n fe/rein ou) panto/s, a)ll' a)ndro\s sofou= 'tis the sage, not every one, who can bear poverty Men. Sent. 463, dokei= dikai/ou tou=t' ei)=nai poli/_tou this seems to be the duty of a just citizen D. 8.72 , tw=n ni_kw/ntwn e)sti\ kai\ ta\ e(autw=n sw/|zein kai\ ta\ tw=n h(ttwme/nwn lamba/nein it is the custom of conquerors to keep what is their own and to take the possessions of the defeated X. A. 3.2.39 .

With verbs signifying to refer or attribute, by thought, word, or action, anything to a person or class. Such verbs are to think, regard, make, name, choose, appoint, etc. logi/zou . . . ta\ d' a)/lla th=s tu/xhs deem that the rest belongs to chance E. Alc. 789 , tw=n e)leuqerwta/twn oi)/kwn nomisqei=sa deemed a daughter of a house most free E. And. 12 , e)me\ gra/fe tw=n i(ppeu/ein u(perepiqu_mou/ntwn put me down as one of those who desire exceedingly to serve on horseback X. C. 4.3.21 , th=s prw/ths ta/cews tetagme/nos assigned to the first class L. 14.11 , th=s a)gaqh=s tu/xhs th=s po/lews ei)=nai ti/qhmi I reckon as belonging to the good fortune of the State D. 18.254 , ei) de/ tines th *)asi/a_n e(autw=n poiou=ntai but if some are claiming Asia as their own X. Ages. 1.33 , nomi/zei u(_ma=s e(autou= ei)=nai he thinks that you are in his power X. A. 2.1.11 .
The genitive may denote a whole, a part of which is denoted by the noun it limits. The genitive of the divided whole may be used with any word that expresses or implies a part.

Position.—The genitive of the whole stands before or after the word denoting the part: tw=n *qra|kw=n peltastai/ targeteers of the Thracians T. 7.27 , oi( a)/poroi tw=n poli_tw=n the needy among the citizens D. 18.104 ; rarely between the limited noun and its article: oi( tw=n a)di/kwn a)fiknou/menoi those of the unrighteous who come here P. G. 525c . Cp. 1161 N. 1.

When all are included there is no partition: so in ou(=toi pa/ntes all of these, all these, te/ttares h(mei=s h)=men there were four of us, to\ pa=n plh=qos tw=n o(pli_tw=n the entire body of the hoplites T. 8.93 , o(/soi e)ste\ tw=n o(moi/wn as many of you as belong to the ‘peers’ X. A. 4.6.14.
The idea of division is often not explicitly stated. See third example in 1310.

(I) The genitive of the divided whole is used with substantives. me/ros ti tw=n barba/rwn some part of the barbarians T. 1.1 , oi( *dwrih=s h(mw=n those of us who are Dorians 4. 61. The governing word may be omitted: *)arxi/a_s tw=n *(hra_kleidw=n Archias (one) of the Heraclidae T. 6.3. To an indefinite substantive without the article may be added a genitive denoting the special sort: *ferau/la_s *pe/rshs tw=n dhmotw=n Pheraulas, a Persian, one of the common people X. C. 2.3.7.

Chorographic Genitive.— th=s *)attikh=s e)s *oi)no/hn to Oenoë in Attica T. 2.18 (or e)s *oi)no/hn th=s *)attikh=s, not e)s th=s *)attikh=s *oi)no/hn), th=s *)itali/a_s *aokroi/ the Locrians in Italy 3. 86. The article, which is always used with the genitive of the country (as a place well known), is rarely added to the governing substantive ( to\ *kh/naion th=s *eu)boi/a_s Cenaeum in Euboea T. 3.93 ).

(II) With substantive adjectives and participles. oi( a)/dikoi tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the unjust among men D. 27.68 (but always oi( qnhtoi\ a)/nqrwpoi), mo/nos tw=n pruta/newn alone of the prytans P. A. 32b , o)li/goi au)tw=n few of them X. A. 3.1.3 , tw=n a)/llwn *(ellh/nwn o( boulo/menos whoever of the rest of the Greeks so desires T. 3.92 . So to\ katantikru\ au)tw=n tou= sphlai/ou the part of the cavern facing them P. R. 515a . For nihil novi the Greek says ou)de kaino/n.

Adjectives denoting magnitude, and some others, may conform in gender to the genitive, instead of appearing in the neuter: e)/temon th=s gh=s th pollh/n they ravaged most of the land T. 2.56 , th=s gh=s h( a)ri/sth the best of the land 1. 2. This construction occurs more frequently in prose than in poetry.

But such adjectives, especially when singular, may be used in the neuter: tw=n *)argei/wn loga/dwn to\ polu/ the greater part of the picked Argives T. 5.73 , e)pi\ polu\ th=s xw/ra_s over a great part of the land 4. 3.

(III) With comparatives and superlatives. h(mw=n o( gerai/teros the elder of us X. C. 5.1.6 (1066 b), oi( presbu/tatoi tw=n strathgw=n the oldest of the generals X. A. 3.3.11 , si/_tw| pa/ntwn a)nqrw/pwn plei/stw| xrw/meq' e)peisa/ktw| we make use of imported grain more than all other people D. 18.87 . So with a superlative adverb: h( nau=s a)/rista/ moi e)/plei panto\s tou= stratope/dou my ship was the best sailer of the whole squadron L. 21.6 .

In poetry this use is extended to positive adjectives: a)ridei/ketos a)ndrw=n conspicuous among men A 248, w)= fi/la_ gunaikw=n oh dear among women E. Alc. 460 . In tragedy an adjective may be emphasized by the addition of the same adjective in the genitive: a)/rrht' a)rrh/twn horrors unspeakable S. O. T. 465 . Cp. 1064.

(IV) With substantive pronouns and numerals. oi( me au)tw=n, oi( d' ou)/ some of them and not others P. A. 24e , oi(\ u(/steron e)lh/fqhsan tw=n polemi/wn those of the enemy who were taken later X. A. 1.7.13 , ou)dei\s a)nqrw/pwn no one in the world P. S. 220a , ti\ tou= tei/xous a part of the wall T. 7.4 , ti\s qew=n one of the gods E. Hec. 164 ( ti\s qeo/s a god X. C. 5.2.12 ), e( tw=n pollw=n one of the many things P. A. 17a ; rarely after demonstrative pronouns: tou/tois tw=n a)nqrw/pwn to these (of) men T. 1.71. a. With o)li/goi and with numerals a)po/ and e)c are rarely added: e)k triw=n e(/n one of three S. Tr. 734 . e)c with superlatives is also rare. See also 1688. 1 c.

The genitive of the divided whole may do duty as the subject of a finite verb (928 b) or of the infinitive: (e)/fasan) e)pimeignu/nai sfw=n pro\s e)kei/nous they said that some of their number associated with them X. A. 3.5.16.

Predicate Use.— h)=n d' au)tw=n *fali=nos and among them was Phalinus X. A. 2.1.7 , *so/lwn tw=n e(pta\ sofistw=n e)klh/qh Solon was called one of the Seven Sages I. 15.235, tw=n a)topwta/twn a) ei)/h it would be very strange D. 1.26 ; and often with verbs signifying to be, become, think, say, name, choose. With some of these verbs ei(=s with the genitive may be used instead of the genitive alone.

The genitive to denote quality occurs chiefly as a predicate. e)w tro/pou h(suxi/ou being of a peaceful disposition Hdt. 1.107 , oi( de/ tines th=s au)th=s gnw/mhs o)li/goi kate/fugon but some few of the same opinion fled T. 3.70 , tau=ta pampo/llwn e)sti\ lo/gwn this calls for a thorough discussion P. L. 642a , qewrh/sat' au)to/n, mh\ o(pote/rou tou= lo/gou, a)ll' o(pote/rou tou= bi/ou e)sti/n consider, not the manner of his speech, but the manner of his life Aes. 3.168, ei) dokei= tau=ta kai\ dapa/nhs mega/lhs kai\ po/nwn pollw=n kai\ pra_gmatei/a_s ei)=nai if these matters seem to involve great expense and much toil and trouble D. 8.48 . a. The attributive use occurs in poetry: xo/rtwn eu)de/ndrwn *eu)rw/pa_s Europe with its pastures amid fair trees E. I. T. 134 , leukh=s xio/nos pte/ruc a wing white as snow (of white snow) S. Ant. 114.

The use of the genitive to express quality, corresponding to the Latin genitive, occurs in the non-predicate position, only when age or size is exactly expressed by the addition of a numeral (genitive of measure, 1325). The Latin genitive of quality in mulier mirae pulchritudinis is expressed by gunh\ qaumasi/a_ ka/llos (or tou= ka/llous), gunh\ qaumasi/a_ i)dei=n, gunh\ e)/xousa qauma/sion sxh=ma, etc.

The genitive of an explicit word may explain the meaning of a more general word. *)i_li/ou po/lis E 642, as urbs Romae, a)/ellai pantoi/wn a)ne/mwn blasts formed of winds of every sort e 292 . This construction is chiefly poetic, but in prose we find u(o\s me/ga xrh=ma a monster (great affair, 1294) of a boar Hdt. 1.36, to\ o)/ros th=s *)istw/nhs Mt. Istone T. 4.46 (very rare, 1142 c). An articular infinitive in the genitive often defines the application of a substantive: a)maqi/a_ h( tou= oi)/esqai ei)de/nai a:\ ou)k oi)=den the ignorance of thinking one knows what one does not know P. A. 29b . a. But with o)/noma the person or thing named is usually in apposition to o)/noma: tw=| de\ newta/tw| e)qe/mhn o)/noma *kalli/straton I gave the youngest the name Callistratus D. 43.74 .

The genitive expresses material or contents. e(/rkos o)do/ntwn the fence (consisting) of the teeth *d 350, krh/nh h(de/os u(/datos a spring of sweet water X. A. 6.4.4 , swroi\ si/_tou, cu/lwn, li/qwn heaps of corn, wood, stones X. H. 4.4.12, e(cako/sia ta/lanta fo/rou six hundred talents in taxes T. 2.13 (cp. 1296).

Predicate Use: stefa/nous r(o/dwn o)/ntas, a)ll' ou' xru_si/ou crowns that were of roses, not of gold D. 22.70 , e)strwme/nh e)sti\ o(do\s li/qou a road was paved with stone Hdt. 2.138 , and often with verbs of making, which admit also the instrumental dative. Hdt. has poiei=sqai a)po/ and e)/k tinos.

The genitive denotes measure of space, time, or degree. o)ktw\ stadi/wn tei=xos a wall eight stades long T. 7.2 , pe/nte h(merw=n si_ti/a provisions for five days 7. 43 (cp. fossa pedum quindecim, exilium decem annorum Less commonly with a neuter adjective or pronoun: e)pi\ me/ga e)xw/rhsan duna/<*> they advanced to a great pitch of power T. 1.118, ti\ do/chs some honour (aliq<*> famae) 1. 5, a)mh/xanon eu)daimoni/a_s (something infinite in the way of happiness) infinite happiness P. A. 41c (with emphasis on the adj.). But the phrases ei)s tou=to, ei)s tosou=to a)fike/sqai (h)/kein, e)lqei=n, prosbai/nein, usually with a personal subject) followed by the genitive of abstracts are common: ei)s tou=to qra/sous a)fi/_keto he reached such a pitch of boldness D. 21.194 , e)n panti\ a)qu_mi/a_s in utter despondency T. 7.55 , e)n tou/tw| paraskeuh=s in this stage of preparation 2. 17, kata\ tou=to kairou= at that critical moment 7. 2. The article with this genitive is unusual in classical Greek: ei)s tou=to th=s h(liki/a_s to this stage of life L. 5.3 . Some of these genitives may also be explained by 1306.
Under the head of measure belongs amount: duoi=n mnai=n pro/sodos an income of two minae X. Vect. 3.10 . Cp. 1296, 1323.
Predicate Use.— e)peida e)tw=n h)=| tis tria/_konta when a man is thirty years old P. L. 721a , ta\ tei/xh h)=n stadi/wn o)ktw/ the walls were eight stades long T. 4.66 .

With a verbal noun the genitive may denote the subject or object of the action expressed in the noun. a. Many of these genitives derive their construction from that of the kindred verbs: tou= u(/datos e)piqu_mi/a_ desire for water T. 2.52 (1349), xo/los ui(o/s anger because of his son O 138 (1405). But the verbal idea sometimes requires the accusative, or (less commonly) the dative.
In poetry an adjective may take the place of the genitive: no/stos o( basi/leios the return of the king A. Pers. 8 . Cp. 1291.

The Subjective Genitive is active in sense: tw=n barba/rwn fo/bos the fear of the barbarians (which they feel: oi( ba/rbaroi fobou=ntai) X. A. 1.2.17, h( basile/ws e)piorki/a_ the perjury of the king (basileu\s e)piorkei=) 3. 2. 4, to\ o)rgizo/menon th=s gnw/mhs their angry feelings T. 2.59 (such genitives with substantive participles are common in Thucydides; cp. 1153 b, N. 2).

The Objective Genitive is passive in sense, and is very common with substantives denoting a frame of mind or an emotion: fo/bos tw=n *ei(lw/twn the fear of the Helots (felt towards them: fobou=ntai tou\s *ei(/lwtas) T. 3.54, h( tw=n *(ellh/nwn eu)/noia good-will towards the Greeks (eu)noei= toi=s *(/ellhsi) X. A. 4.7.20, h( tw=n kalw=n sunousi/a_ intercourse with the good (su/neisi toi=s kaloi=s) P. L. 838a. a. The objective genitive often precedes another genitive on which it depends: meta\ th=s cummaxi/a_s th=s ai)th/sews with the request for an alliance T. 1.32 .

Various prepositions are used in translating the objective genitive: o( qew=n po/lemos war with the gods X. A. 2.5.7 , o(/rkoi qew=n oaths by the gods E. Hipp. 657 , qew=n eu)xai/ prayers to the gods P. Phae. 244e , a)dikhma/twn o)rgh/ anger at injustice L. 12.20 , e)gkra/teia h(donh=s moderation in pleasure I. 1.21 , h( tw=n h(donw=n ni/_kh victory over pleasures P. L. 840c , tro/paia barba/rwn memorials of victory over barbarians X. A. 7.6.36 , paraine/seis tw=n cunallagw=n exhortations to reconciliation T. 4.59 , mu=qos fi/lwn tidings about friends S. Ant. 11 , sou= mu=qos speech with thee S. O. C. 1161 . In qana/tou lu/sis release from death i 421 , metapauswlh\ pole/moio respite from war T 201, it is uncertain whether the genitive is objective or ablatival (1392).

The objective genitive is often used when a prepositional expression, giving greater precision, is more usual: to\ *megare/wn yh/fisma the decree relating to (peri/) the Megarians T. 1.140, a)po/basis th=s gh=s a descent upon the land (e)s th gh=n) 1. 108, a)po/stasis tw=n *)aqhnai/wn revolt from the Athenians (a)po\ tw=n *)aqhnai/wn) 8. 5.

For the objective genitive a possessive pronoun is sometimes used: sh xa/rin for thy sake P. Soph. 242a , diabolh\ h( e)mh/ calumniation of me P. A. 20e . o( e)mo\s fo/bos is usually objective: the fear which I inspire. (But sou= mu=qos speech with thee S. O. C. 1161 .)
Predicate Use.—ou) tw=n kakou/rgwn oi)=ktos, a)lla\ th=s di/khs compassion is not for wrong-doers, but for justice E. fr. 270.
The genitive expresses value. i(era\ triw=n tala/ntwn offerings worth three talents L. 30.20 , xi_li/wn draxmw=n di/khn feu/gw I am defendant in an action involving a thousand drachmas D. 55.25 .
Predicate Use: tou\s ai)xmalw/tous tosou/twn xrhma/twn lu/_esqai to ransom the captives at so high a price D. 19.222 , triw=n draxmw=n ponhro\s w)/n a threepenny rogue 19. 200.

Two genitives expressing different relations may be used with one noun. oi( a)/nqrwpoi dia\ to\ au(tw=n de/os tou= qana/tou katayeu/dontai by reason of their fear of death men tell lies P. Ph. 85a , *dionu/_sou presbu_tw=n xoro/s a chorus of old men in honour of Dionysus P. L. 665b , h( tou= *aa/xhtos tw=n new=n a)rxh/ Laches' command of the fleet T. 3.115 , h( *faia/_kwn proenoi/khsis th=s *kerku/_ra_s the former occupation of Corcyra by the Phaeacians 1.25.
The genitive may serve as the immediate complement of a verb, or it may appear, as a secondary definition, along with an accusative which is the immediate object of the verb (920, 1392, 1405).

The subject of an active verb governing the genitive may become the subject of the passive construction: *ni_kh/ratos e)rw=n th=s gunaiko\s a)ntera=tai Niceratus, who is in love with his wife, is loved in return X. S. 8. 3. Cp. 1745 a.

A verb may be followed by the partitive genitive if the action affects the object only in part. If the entire object is affected, the verb in question takes the accusative. *)adrh/stoio d' e)/ghme qugatrw=n he married one of Adrastus' daughters *c 121, tw=n pw/lwn lamba/nei he takes some of the colts X. A. 4.5.35, labo/ntes tou= barbarikou= stratou= taking part of the barbarian force 1. 5. 7, kle/ptontes tou= o)/rous seizing part of the mountain secretly 4. 6. 15 (cp. tou= o)/rous kle/yai ti 4. 6. 11), th=s gh=s e)/temon they ravaged part of the land T. 2.56 (cp. th gh=n pa=san e)/temon 2. 57 and e)/temon th=s gh=s th pollh/n 2. 56), katea/_gh th=s kefalh=s he had a hole knocked somewhere in his head Ar. Vesp. 1428 ( th kefalh katea_ge/nai to have one's head broken D. 54.35 ).

With impersonals a partitive genitive does duty as the subject: pole/mou ou) meth=n au)th=| she had no share in war X. C. 7.2.28 , e)moi\ ou)damo/qen prosh/kei tou/tou tou= pra/_gmatos I have no part whatever in this affair And. 4.34 . Cp. 1318.

The genitive is used with verbs of sharing. pa/ntes metei=xon th=s e(orth=s all took part in the festival X. A. 5.3.9 , metedi/dosan a)llh/lois w(=n (= tou/twn a(\) ei)=xon e(/kastoi they shared with each other what each had 4. 5. 6, to\ a)nqrw/pinon ge/nos metei/lhfen a)qanasi/a_s the human race has received a portion of immortality P. L. 721b , si/_tou koinwnei=n to take a share of food X. M. 2.6.22 , dikaiosu/nhs ou)de u(_mi=n prosh/kei you have no concern in righteous dealing X. H. 2.4.40 , poli_tei/a_, e)n h(=| pe/nhsin ou) me/testin a)rxh=s a form of government in which the poor have no part in the management of affairs P. R. 550c . So with metalagxa/nein get a share (along with somebody else), sunai/resqai and koinou=sqai take part in, metaitei=n and metapoiei=sqai demand a share in.

The part received or taken, if expressed, stands in the accusative. oi( tu/rannoi tw=n megi/stwn a)gaqw=n e)la/xista mete/xousi tyrants have the smallest por- tion in the greatest blessings X. Hi. 2.6, tou/twn metaitei_ to\ me/ros he demands his share of this Ar. Vesp. 972 . a. With me/testi the part may be added in the nominative: me/testi xu)_mi=n tw=n pepra_gme/nwn me/ros ye too have had a share in these doings E. I. T. 1299 .

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to touch, take hold of, make trial of. （h( no/sos) h(/yato tw=n a)nqrw/pwn the plague laid hold of the men T. 2.48 , th=s gnw/mhs th=s au)th=s e)/xomai I hold to the same opinion 1. 140, e)n th=| e)xome/nh| e)mou= kli/_nh| on the couch next to me P. S. 217d , a)ntila/besqe tw=n pra_gma/twn take our public policy in hand D. 1.20 , o(/pws peirw=|nto tou= tei/xous to make an attempt on (a part of) the wall T. 2.81. So with yau/ein touch (rare in prose), a)nte/xesqai cling to, e)pilamba/nesqai and sullamba/nesqai lay hold of.

The genitive of the part, with the accusative of the person (the whole) who has been touched, is chiefly poetical: to de\ peso/nta podw=n e)/labe but him as he fell, he seized by his feet *d 463 , e)/labon th=s zw/nhs to *)oro/nta_n they took hold of Orontas by the girdle X. A. 1.6.10 (but mou= labo/menos th=s xeiro/s taking me by the hand P. Charm. 153b ), a)/gein th=s h(ni/a_s to i(/ppon to lead the horse by the bridle X. Eq. 6.9 (cp. bou=n d' a)ge/thn kera/wn they led the cow by the horns g 439 ).

Verbs of beseeching take the genitive by analogy to verbs of touching: e)me\ lisse/sketo gou/nwn she besought me by (clasping) my knees I 451 (cp. genei/ou a(ya/menos li/ssesqai beseech by touching his chin K 454).

The genitive is used with verbs of beginning. a. Partitive: e)/fh *ku=ron a)/rxein tou= lo/gou w(=de he said that Cyrus began the discussion as follows X. A. 1.6.5 , tou= lo/gou h)/rxeto w(=de he began his speech as follows 3. 2. 7. On a)/rxein as distinguished from a)/rxesqai see 1734. 5. b. Ablatival (1391) denoting the point of departure: se/o d' a)/rcomai I will make a beginning with thee I 97. In this sense a)po/ or e)c is usually added: a)rca/menoi a)po\ sou= D. 18.297, a)/rcomai a)po\ th=s i)_a_trikh=s le/gwn I will make a beginning by speaking of medicine P. S. 186b .

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to aim at, strive after, desire (genitive of the end desired). a)nqrw/pwn stoxa/zesqai to aim at men X. C. 1.6.29 , e)fi_e/menoi tw=n kerdw=n desiring gain T. 1.8 , pa/ntes tw=n a)gaqw=n e)piqu_mou=sin all men desire what is good P. R. 438a , to\ e)ra=n tw=n kalw=n the passionate love of what is noble Aes. 1.137 , peinw=si xrhma/twn they are hungry for wealth X. S. 4 . 36, po/lis e)leuqeri/a_s diyh/sa_sa a state thirsting for freedom P. R. 562c . So with o)i+steu/ein shoot at (poet.), lilai/esqai desire (poet.), gli/xesqai desire. filei=n love, poqei=n long for take the accusative.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to reach, obtain (genitive of the end attained). th=s a)reth=s e)fike/sqai to attain to virtue I. 1.5 , oi( a)kontistai\ braxu/tera h)ko/ntizon h)\ w(s e)ciknei=sqai tw=n sfendonhtw=n the javelin-throwers did not hurl far enough to reach the slingers X. A. 3.3.7 , spondw=n e)/tuxe he obtained a truce 3. 1. 28. So with kurei=n obtain (poet.), klhronomei=n inherit, a)potugxa/nein fail to hit. tugxa/nein, when compounded with e)n, e)pi/, para/, peri/, and su/n, takes the dative. lagxa/nein obtain by lot usually takes the accusative. a. This genitive and that of 1349 form the genitive of the goal.

The genitive of the thing obtained may be joined with an ablatival genitive (1410) of the person: ou(= de\ dh\ pa/ntwn oi)o/meqa teu/cesqai e)pai/nou in a case where we expect to win praise from all men X. A. 5.7.33 . But where the thing obtained is expressed by a neuter pronoun, the accusative is employed.

It is uncertain whether verbs signifying to miss take a partitive or an ablatival genitive: ou)dei\s h(ma/rtanen a)ndro/s no one missed his man X. A. 3.4.15 , sfale/ntes th=s do/chs disappointed in expectations T. 4.85 .

Verbs of approaching and meeting take the genitive according to 1343 or 1349. These verbs are poetical. Thus, a)ntio/wn tau/rwn for the purpose of obtaining (his share of) bulls a 25, a)nth/sw tou=d' a)ne/ros I will encounter this man II 423, pela/sai new=n to approach the ships S. Aj. 709 . In the meaning draw near to verbs of approaching take the dative (1463).
The genitive is used with verbs of smelling. o)/zw mu/rou I smell of perfume Ar. Eccl. 524 . So pnei=n mu/rou to breathe (smell of) perfume S. fr. 140.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to enjoy, taste, eat, drink. a)polau/omen pa/ntwn tw=n a)gaqw=n we enjoy all the good things X. M. 4.3.11 , eu)wxou= tou= lo/gou enjoy the discourse P. R. 352b , o)li/goi si/_tou e)geu/santo few tasted food X. A. 3.1.3 . So (rarely) with h(/desqai take pleasure in. a. Here belong e)sqi/ein, pi/_nein when they do not signify to eat up or drink up: w)mw=n e)sqi/ein au)tw=n to eat them alive X. H. 3.3.6 , pi/_nein oi)/noio drink some wine x 11 , as boire du vin (but pi/_nein oi)=non drink wine *c 5 , as boire le vin). Words denoting food and drink are placed in the accusative when they are regarded as kinds of nourishment.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to remember, remind, forget, care for , and neglect. tw=n a)po/ntwn fi/lwn me/mnhso remember your absent friends I. 1.26 , bou/lomai d' u(_ma=s a)namnh=sai tw=n e)moi\ pepra_gme/nwn I desire to remind you of my past actions And. 4.41 , de/doika mh\ e)pilaqw/meqa th=s oi)/kade o(dou= I fear lest we may forget the way home X. A. 3.2.25 , e)pimelo/menoi oi( me u(pozugi/wn, oi( de\ skeuw=n some taking care of the pack animals, others of the baggage 4. 3. 30, th=s tw=n pollw=n do/chs dei= h(ma=s fronti/zein we must pay heed to the world's opinion P. Cr. 48a , ti/ h(mi=n th=s tw=n pollw=n do/chs me/lei; what do we care for the world's opinion? 44 c, toi=s spoudai/ois ou)x oi(=o/n te th=s a)reth=s a)melei=n the serious cannot disregard virtue I. 1.48 , mhdeno\s o)ligwrei=te mhde\ katafronei=te (cp. 1385) tw=n prostetagme/nwn neither neglect nor despise any command laid on you 3. 48.

So with mnhmoneu/ein remember (but usually with the accus., especially of things), a)mnhmonei=n not to speak of, kh/desqai care for, e)ntre/pesqai give heed to, e)nqu_mei=sqai think deeply of, proora=n make provision for (in Hdt.), metame/lei moi it repents me, katamelei=n neglect.

Many of these verbs also take the accusative. With the accus. memnh=sqai means to remember something as a whole, with the gen. to remember something about a thing, bethink oneself. The accus. is usually found with verbs of remembering and forgetting when they mean to hold or not to hold in memory, and when the object is a thing. Neuter pronouns must stand in the accus. e)pilanqa/nesqai forget takes either the genitive or the accusative, lanqa/nesqai (usually poetical) always takes the genitive. me/lei it is a care, e)pime/lesqai care for, memnh=sqai think about may take peri/ with the genitive. oi)=da generally means I remember when it has a person as the object (in the accusative).
Verbs of reminding may take two accusatives: tau=q' u(pe/mnhs' u(_ma=s I have reminded you of this D. 19.25 (1628).

With me/lei, the subject, if a neuter pronoun, may sometimes stand in the nominative (the personal construction): tau=ta qew=| melh/sei God will care for this P. Phae. 238d . Except in poetry the subject in the nominative is very rare with other words than neuter pronouns: xoroi\ pa=si me/lousi P. L. 835e.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to hear and perceive: a)kou/ein, klu/ein (poet.) hear, a)kroa=sqai listen to, ai)sqa/nesqai perceive, punqa/nesqai hear, learn of, suni_e/nai understand, o)sfrai/nesqai scent. The person or thing, whose words, sound, etc. are perceived by the senses, stands in the genitive; the words, sound, etc. generally stand in the accusative. tino\s h)/kous' ei)po/ntos I heard somebody say D. 8.4 , a)kou/santes th=s sa/lpiggos hearing the sound of the trumpet X. A. 4.2.8 , a)kou/santes to qo/rubon hearing the noise 4. 4. 21, a)krow/menoi tou= a)/|dontos listening to the singer X. C. 1.3.10 , o(/soi a)llh/lwn cuni/_esan all who understood each other T. 1.3 , e)peida suni_h=| tis ta\ lego/mena when one understands what is said P. Pr. 325c (verbs of understanding, suni_e/nai and e)pi/stasqai, usually take the accus.), krommu/wn o)sfrai/nomai I smell onions Ar. Ran. 654 . a. A supplementary participle is often used in agreement with the genitive of the person from whom something is heard: le/gontos e)mou= a)kroa/_sontai oi( ne/oi the young men will listen when I speak P. A. 37d . b. The accusative is almost always used when the thing heard is expressed by a substantivized neuter adjective or participle, but the genitive plural in the case of ou(=tos, o(/de, au)to/s, and o(/s is frequent.
A double genitive, of the person and of the thing, is rare with a)kou/ein: tw=n u)pe\r th=s grafh=s dikai/wn a)kou/ein mou to listen to my just pleas as regards the indictment D. 18.9 .

a)kou/ein, ai)sqa/nesqai, punqa/nesqai, meaning to become aware of, learn, take the accusative (with a participle in indirect discourse, 2112 b) of a personal or impersonal object: oi( de/ *plataih=s, w(s h)/|sqonto e)/ndon te o)/ntas tou\s *qhbai/ous kai kateilhmme/nhn th po/lin but the Plataeans, when they became aware that the Thebans were inside and that the city had been captured T. 2.3, puqo/menoi *)artace/rchn teqnhko/ta having learned that Artaxerxes was dead 4. 50. a. To hear a thing is usually a)kou/ein ti when the thing heard is something definite and when the meaning is simply hear, not listen to.
a)kou/ein, a)kroa=sqai, punqa(nesqai, meaning to hear from, learn from, take the genitive of the actual source (1411).

a)kou/ein, klu/ein, punqa/nesqai/tinos may mean to hear about, hear of: ei) de/ ke teqnhw=tos a)kou/sh|s but if you hear that he is dead a 289 , klu/wn sou= hearing about thee S. O. C. 307 , w(s e)pu/qonto th=s *pu/lou kateilhmme/nhs when they heard of the capture of Pylos T. 4.6 . For the participle (not in indirect discourse) see 2112 a. peri/ is often used with the genitive without the participle.

In the meaning heed, hearken, obey, verbs of hearing generally take the genitive: a)/koue pa/ntwn, e)kle/gou d' a(\ sumfe/rei listen to everything, but choose that which is profitable Men. Sent. 566, tw=n polemi/wn a)kou/ein to submit to enemies X. C. 8.1.4 . pei/qesqai takes the genitive, instead of the dative, by analogy to this use (Hdt. 6.12, T. 7.73). (On the dative with a)kou/ein obey see 1465.)

ai)sqa/nesqai takes the genitive, or (less frequently) the accusative, of the thing immediately perceived by the senses: th=s kraugh=s h)/|sqonto they heard the noise X. H. 4.4.4 , h)/|sqeto ta\ gigno/mena he perceived what was happening X. C. 3.1.4 . The genitive is less common than the accusative when the perception is intellectual: w(s h)/|sqonto teixizo/ntwn when they heard that they were progressing with their fortification T. 5.83 . Cp. 1363.

Some verbs, ordinarily construed with the accusative, take the genitive by the analogy of ai)sqa/nesqai, etc.: e)/gnw a)/topa e)mou= poiou=ntos he knew that I was acting absurdly X. C. 7.2.18 , a)gnoou=ntes a)llh/lwn o(/ ti le/gomen each of us mistaking what the other says P. G. 517c . This construction of verbs of knowing (and showing) occurs in Attic only when a participle accompanies the genitive.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to fill, to be full of. The thing filled is put in the accusative. ou)k e)mplh/sete th qa/lattan trih/rwn ; will you not cover the sea with your triremes? D. 8.74 , a)naplh=sai ai)tiw=n to implicate in guilt P. A. 32c , trofh=s eu)porei=n to have plenty of provisions X. Vect. 6.1 , trih/rhs sesagme/nh a)nqrw/pwn a trireme stowed with men X. O. 8.8 , u(/brews mestou=sqai to be filled with pride P. L. 713c . So with plh/qein, plhrou=n, ge/mein, ploutei=n, bri/_qein (poet.), bru/ein (poet.). a. Here belong also xei\r sta/zei quhlh=s *)/areos his hand drips with sacrifice to Ares S. El. 1423 , mequsqei\s tou= ne/ktaros intoxicated with nectar P. S. 203b , h( phgh\ r(ei= yu_xrou= u(/o=atos the spring flows with cold water P. Phae. 230b . The instrumental dative is sometimes used.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to rule, command, lead. qei=on to\ e)qelo/ntwn a)/rxein it is divine to rule over willing subjects X. O. 21.12 , th=s qala/tths e)kra/tei he was master of the sea P. Menex. 239e , *)/erws tw=n qew=n basileu/ei Love is king of the gods P. S. 195c , h(gei=to th=s e)co/dou he led the expedition T. 2.10 , strathgei=n tw=n ce/nwn to be general of the mercenaries X. A. 2. 6. 28. So with turannei=n be absolute master of, a)na)ssein be lord of (poet.), h(gemoneu/ein be commander of. This genitive is connected with that of 1402.

Several verbs of ruling take the accusative when they mean to conquer, overcome (so kratei=n), or when they express the domain over which the rule extends; as th *pelopo/nnhson peira=sqe mh\ e)la/_ssw e)chgei=sqai try not to lessen your dominion over the Peloponnese T. 1.71 . h(gei=sqai/ tini means to be a guide to any one, show any one the way. Cp. 1537.

The genitive is used with verbs signifying to buy, sell, cost, value, exchange. The price for which one gives or does anything stands in the genitive. a)rguri/ou pri/asqai h)\ a)podo/sqai i(/ppon to buy or sell a horse for money P. R. 333b , *qemistokle/a_ tw=n megi/stwn dwrew=n h)ci/wsan they deemed Themistocles worthy of the greatest gifts I. 4.154 , ou)k a)ntallakte/on moi th filoti_mi/a_n ou)deno\s ke/rdous I must not barter my public spirit for any price D. 19.223 . So with ta/ttein rate, misqou=n let, misqou=sqai hire, e)rga/zesqai work, and with any verb of doing anything for a wage, as oi( th=s par' h(me/ra_n xa/ritos ta\ me/gista th=s po/lews a)polwleko/tes those who have ruined the highest interests of the State to purchase ephemeral popularity D. 8.70 , po/sou dida/skei; pe/nte mnw=n for how much does he teach? for five minae P. A. 20b , oi( *xaldai=oi misqou= strateu/ontai the Chaldaeans serve for pay X. C. 3.2.7 . a. The instrumental dative is also used. With verbs of exchanging, a)nti/ is usual (1683).

To value highly and lightly is peri\ pollou= (plei/onos, plei/stou) and peri\ o)li/gou (e)la/_ttonos, e)laxi/stou) ti_ma=sqai or poiei=sqai: ta\ plei/stou a)/cia peri\ e)laxi/stou poiei=tai, ta\ de\ faulo/tera peri\ plei/onos he makes least account of what is most important, and sets higher what is less estimable P. A. 30a . The genitive of value, without peri/, is rare: pollou= poiou=mai a)khkoe/nai a(\ a)kh/koa *prwtago/rou I esteem it greatly to have heard what I did from Protagoras P. Pr. 328d . a. The genitive of cause is rarely used to express the thing bought or that for which pay is demanded: ou)de/na th=s sunousi/a_s a)rgu/rion pra/_ttei you charge nobody anything for your teaching X. M. 1.6.11 , trei=s mnai= difri/skou three minae for a small chariot Ar. Nub. 31 .

In legal language ti_ma=n tini qana/tou is to fix the penalty at death (said of the jury, which is not interested in the result), ti_ma=sqai/ tini qana/tou to propose death as the penalty (said of the accuser, who is interested), and tima=sqai/ tinos to propose a penalty against oneself (said of the accused). Cp. ti_ma=tai/ moi o( a)nh\r qana/tou the man proposes death as my penalty P. A. 36b , a)lla\ dh\ fugh=s ti_mh/swmai; i)/sws ga\r a)/n moi tou/tou ti_mh/saite but shall I propose exile as my penalty? for perhaps you (the jury) might fix it at this 37 c. So qana/tou with kri/_nein, diw/kein, u(pa/gein. Cp. 1379.

With verbs of judicial action the genitive denotes the crime, the accusative denotes the person accused. ai)tia=sqai a)llh/lous tou= gegenhme/nou to accuse one another of what had happened X. Ages. 1.33 , diw/kw me kakhgori/a_s, th=| d' au)th=| yh/fw| fo/nou feu/gw I bring an accusation for defamation and at the same trial am prosecuted for murder L. 11.12 , e)me\ o( *me/lhtos a)sebei/a_s e)gra/yato Meletus prosecuted me for impiety P. Euth. 5c , dw/rwn e)kri/qhsan they were tried for bribery L. 27.3 . On verbs of accusing and condemning compounded with kata/, see 1385.

So with a)mu/_nesqai and kola/zein punish, ei)sa/gein and proskalei=sqai summon into court, ai(rei=n convict, ti_mwrei=sqai take vengeance on. With ti_mwrei=n avenge and lagxa/nein obtain leave to bring a suit, the person avenged and the person against whom the suit is brought are put in the dative. So with dika/zesqai/ tini/ tinos to go to law with a man about something.

Verbs of judicial action may take a cognate accusative (di/khn, grafh/n), on which the genitive of the crime depends: grafh u(/brews kai\ di/khn kakhgori/a_s feu/cetai he will be brought to trial on an indictment for outrage and on a civil action for slander D. 21.32 . From this adnominal use arose the construction of the genitive with this class of verbs.

a(li/skesqai (a(lw=nai) be convicted, o)fliska/nein lose a suit, feu/gein be prosecuted are equivalent to passives: e)a/_n tis a(lw=| kloph=s . . . ka)\_n a)stratei/a_s tis o)/flh| if any one be condemned for theft . . . and if any one be convicted of desertion D. 24.103 , a)sebei/a_s feu/gonta u(po\ *melh/tou being tried for impiety on the indictment of Meletus P. A. 35d . o)fliska/nein may take di/khn as a cognate accus. ( w)flhke/nai di/khn to be cast in a suit Ar. Av. 1457 ); the crime or the penalty may stand in the genitive (with or without di/khn), or in the accusative: o(po/soi kloph=s h)\ dw/rwn o)/floien all who had been convicted of embezzlement or bribery And. 1.74 , u(f' u(_mw=n qana/tou di/khn o)flw/n having incurred through your verdict the penalty of death, u(po\ th=s a)lhqei/a_s w)flhko/tes moxqhri/a_n condemned by the truth to suffer the penalty of wickedness P. A. 39b .

With verbs of judicial action the genitive of the penalty may be regarded as a genitive of value: qana/tou kri/_nousi they judge in matters of life and death X. C. 1.2.14 . So u(pa/gein tina\ qana/tou to impeach a man on a capital charge X. H. 2.3.12 ; cp. ti_ma=n qana/tou 1374. a. With many verbs of judicial action peri/ is used.

The genitive may express a more or less close connection or relation, where peri/ is sometimes added. With verbs of saying or thinking: ti/ de\ i(/ppwn oi)/ei; but what do you think of horses? P. R. 459b. Often in poetry: ei)pe\ de/ moi patro/s but tell me about my father l 174 , tou= kasignh/tou ti/ fh/|s; what dost thou say of thy brother? S. El. 317.

The genitive is often used loosely, especially at the beginning of a construction, to state the subject of a remark: i(/ppos h) kakourgh=|, to i(ppe/a_ kaki/zomen: th=s de\ gunaiko/s, ei) kakopoiei= ktl. if a horse is vicious, we lay the fault to the groom; but as regards a wife, if she conducts herself ill, etc. X. O. 3.11, w(sau/tws de\ kai\ tw=n a)/llwn texnw=n and so in the case of the other arts too P. Charm. 165d , ti/ de\ tw=n pollw=n kalw=n; what about the many beautiful things? P. Ph. 78d.

The genitive depends on the meaning of a compound verb as a whole (1) if the simple verb takes the genitive without a preposition, as u(pei/kein withdraw, paralu/_ein release, paraxwrei=n surrender (1392), e)fi/_esqai desire (1349); or (2) if the compound has acquired through the preposition a signification different from that of the simple verb with the preposition: thus a)pogno/ntes th=s e)leuqeri/a_s despairing of freedom L. 2.46 cannot be expressed by gno/ntes a)po\ th=s e)leuqeri/a_s. But it is often difficult to determine whether the genitive depends on the compound verb as a whole or on the preposition contained in it.

A verb compounded with a preposition taking the dative or accusative may take the genitive by analogy of another compound verb whose preposition requires the genitive: so e)mbai/nein o(/rwn to set foot on the boundaries S. O. C. 400 by analogy to e)pibai/nein tw=n o(/rwn P. L. 778e.

Many verbs compounded with a)po/, pro/, u(pe/r, e)pi/, and kata/ take the genitive when the compound may be resolved into the simple verb and the preposition without change in the sense: tou\s summa/xous a)potre/yantes th=s gnw/mhs dissuading the allies from their purpose And. 3.21 , proapesta/lhsan th=s a)posta/sews they were despatched before the revolt T. 3.5 , polloi=s h( glw=tta protre/xei th=s dianoi/a_s in many people the tongue outruns the thought I. 1.41 , (oi( pole/mioi) u(perka/qhntai h(mw=n the enemy are stationed above us X. A. 5.1.9 , tw=| e)piba/nti prw/tw| tou= tei/xous to the first one setting foot on the wall T. 4.116 . This use is most frequent when the prepositions are used in their proper signification. Many compounds of u(pe/r take the accusative. a. This use is especially common with kata/ against or at: mh/ mou katei/ph|s don't speak against me P. Th. 149a , kateyeu/sato/ mou he spoke falsely against me D. 18.9 , yeudh= kateglw/ttize/ mou he mouthed lies at me Ar. Ach. 380 . The construction in 1384 is post-Homeric.

The verbs of accusing and condemning (cp. 1375) containing kata/ in composition (katagignw/skein decide against, katadika/zein adjudge against, katayhfi/zesqai vote against, katakri/_nein give sentence against) take a genitive of the person, and an accusative of the penalty. kathgorei=n accuse, katagignw/skein and katayhfi/zesqai take a genitive of the person, an accusative of the crime: katagnw=nai dwrodoki/a_n e)mou= to pronounce me guilty of bribery L. 21.21 , tou/tou deili/a_n katayhfi/zesqai to vote him guilty of cowardice 14. 11, tw=n diafugo/ntwn qa/naton katagno/ntes having condemned the fugitives to death T. 6.60 ; person, crime, and penalty: pollw=n oi( pate/res mhdismou= qa/naton kate/gnwsan our fathers passed sentence of death against many for favouring the Persians I. 4.157 . The genitive is rarely used to express the crime or the penalty: parano/mwn au)tou= kathgorei=n to accuse him of proposing unconstitutional measures D. 21.5 ; cp. a)nqrw/pwn katayhfisqe/ntwn qa/naton men who have been condemned to death P. R. 558a .
In general, prose, as distinguished from poetry, repeats the preposition contained in the compound; but kata/ is not repeated.

Passive.—qa/natos au)tw=n kategnw/sqh sentence of death was passed on them L. 13.39 (so kateyhfisme/nos h)=n mou o( qa/natos X. Ap. 27 ), kathgorei=to au)tou= ou)x h(/kista mhdismo/s he was especially accused of favouring the Persians T. 1.95 .

Many verbs ordinarily construed with the accusative are also followed by a genitive of a person, apparently dependent on the verb but in reality governed by an accusative, generally a neuter pronoun or a dependent clause. Thus, ta/d' au)tou= a(/gamai I admire this in him X. Ages. 2.7 , tou=to e)painw= *)a_ghsila/_ou I praise this in Agesilaus 8. 4, au)tw=n e( e)qau/masa I was astonished at one thing in them P. A. 17a . *)aqhnai=oi sfw=n tau=ta ou)k a)pode/contai the Athenians will not be satisfied with them in this T. 7.48 , o)\ me/mfontai ma/lista h(mw=n which they most censure in us 1. 84, ei) a)/gasai tou= patro\s o(/sa pe/pra_xe if you admire in my father what he has done (the actions of my father) X. C. 3.1.15, diaqew/menos au)tw=n o(/shn xw/ra_n e)/xoien contemplating how large a country they possess X. A. 3.1.19 , qauma/zw tw=n strathgw=n o(/ti ou) peirw=ntai h(mi=n e)kpori/zein si_thre/sion I wonder that the generals do not try to supply us with money for provisions 6. 2. 4, e)neno/hse de\ au)tw=n kai\ w(s e)phrw/twn a)llh/lous he took note also how they asked each other questions X. C. 5.2.18 . So with qewrei=n observe, u(ponoei=n feel suspicious of, e)nqu_mei=sqai consider, etc.

From such constructions arose the use of the genitive in actual dependence on the verb without an accusative word or clause: a)/gasai au)tou= you admire him X. M. 2.6.33 , qauma/zw tw=n u(pe\r th=s i)di/a_s do/chs a)poqnh/|skein e)qelo/ntwn I wonder at those who are willing to die in defence of their personal opinions I. 6.93 . The use in 1389 recalls that with ai)sqa/nesqai (1367). On a)/gasqai, qauma/zein with the genitive of cause, see 1405.

A form of the genitive of possession appears in poetry with verbal adjectives and passive participles to denote the personal origin of an action (cp. 1298): kei/nhs didakta/ taught of her S. El. 344 , e)kdidaxqei\s tw=n kat' oi)=kon informed by those in the house S. Tr. 934 , plhgei\s qugatro/s struck by a daughter E. Or. 497 . Cp. dio/sdotos given of God; and “beloved of the Lord.” On the genitive absolute, see 2070.

The same verb may govern both a true genitive and an ablatival genitive. So a)/rxesqai to begin (1348 a) and to start from, e)/xesqai to hold to (1345) and to keep oneself from. In many cases it is difficult to decide whether the genitive in question was originally the true genitive or the ablatival genitive, or whether the two have been combined; e.g. in kune/h r(i_nou= poihth/ a cap made of hide K 262, ku/pellon e)de/cato h(=s a)lo/xoio he received a goblet from his wife *w 305 . So with verbs to hear from, know of (1364, 1411), and verbs of emotion (1405), the partitive idea, cause, and source are hard to distinguish. Other cases open to doubt are verbs of missing (1352), being deceived (1392), and the exclamatory genitive (1407).

With verbs signifying to cease, release, remove, restrain, give up, fail, be distant from, etc., the genitive denotes separation. lh/gein tw=n po/nwn to cease from toil I. 1.14 , e)pisth/mh xwrizome/nh dikaiosu/nhs knowledge divorced from justice P. Menex. 246e , metasta\_s th=s *)aqhnai/wn cummaxi/a_s withdrawing from the alliance with the Athenians T. 2.67 , pau/santes au)to th=s strathgi/a_s removing him from his office of general X. H. 6.2.13 , ei)/rgesqai th=s a)gora=s to be excluded from the forum L. 6.24 , sw=sai kakou= to save from evil S. Ph. 919 , e)kw/lu_on th=s porei/a_s au)to/n they prevented him from passing X. Ages. 2.2 , pa=s a)sko\s du/o a)/ndras e(/cei tou= mh\ katadu=nai each skin will keep two men from sinking X. A. 3.5.11 , lo/gou teleuta=n to end a speech T. 3.59 , th=s e)leuqeri/a_s paraxwrh=sai *fili/ppw| to surrender their freedom to Philip D. 18.68 , ou) po/nwn u(fi/_eto, ou) kindu/_nwn a)fi/_stato, ou) xrhma/twn e)fei/deto he did not relax his toil, stand aloof from dangers, or spare his money X. Ages. 7.1, yeusqe/ntes tw=n e)lpi/dwn disappointed of their expectations I. 4.58 (but cp. 1352), h( nh=sos ou) polu\ die/xousa th=s h)pei/rou the island being not far distant from the mainland T. 3.51 .
Several verbs of separation, such as e)leuqerou=n (especially with a personal subject), may take a)po/ or e)c when the local idea is prominent. Many take also the accusative.

The genitive, instead of the accusative (1628), may be used with verbs of depriving: a)posterei= me tw=n xrhma/twn he deprives me of my property I. 17.35 , tw=n a)/llwn a)fairou/menoi xrh/mata taking away property from others X. M. 1.5.3 .

The genitive of the place whence is employed in poetry where a compound verb would be used in prose: ba/qrwn i(/stasqe rise from the steps S. O. T. 142 (cp. u(pani/stantai qa/_kwn they rise from their seats X. S. 4 . 31), xqono\s a)ei/ra_s raising from the ground S. Ant. 417 .

The genitive with verbs signifying to want, lack, empty, etc. may be classed with the genitive of separation. tw=n e)pithdei/wn ou)k a)porh/somen we shall not want provisions X. A. 2.2.11 , e)pai/nou ou)/pote spani/zete you never lack praise X. Hi. 1.14 , a)ndrw=n ta/_nde po/lin kenw=sai to empty this city of its men A. Supp. 660 . So with e)llei/pein and ste/resqai lack, e)rhmou=n deliver from.

de/w I lack (the personal construction) usually takes the genitive of quantity: pollou= ge de/w nothing of the sort P. Phae. 228a , mi_krou= e)/deon e)n xersi\ tw=n o(pli_tw=n ei)=nai they were nearly at close quarters with the hoplites X. H. 4.6.11 , tosou/tou de/w zhlou=n I am so far from admiring D. 8.70 (also tosou=ton de/w).

de/omai I want, request may take the genitive, or the accusative (regularly of neuter pronouns and adjectives), of the thing wanted; and the genitive of the person: e)rwtw/menos o(/tou de/oito, *)askw=n, e)/fh, disxi_li/wn deh/somai being asked what he needed, he said ‘I shall have need of two thousand skins’ X. A. 3.5.9, tou=to u(_mw=n de/omai I ask this of you P. A. 17c . The genitive of the thing and of the person is unusual: deo/menoi *ku/_rou a)/llhs a)/llhs pra/_cews petitioning Cyrus about different matters X. C. 8.3.19 .

dei= (impersonal) is frequently used with genitives of quantity: pollou= dei= ou(/tws e)/xein far from that being the case P. A. 35d , ou)de\ pollou= dei= D. 8.42 (only in D.) and ou)d' o)li/gou dei= no, far from it D. 19.184. dei=n may be omitted (but not with pollou=), leaving o)li/gou and mi_krou= in the sense of almost, all but; <*>li/gou pa/ntes almost all P. R. 552d, o)li/gou ei(=lon th po/lin they all but. took the city T. 8.35 . On dei=n used absolutely, see 2012 d; on de/wn with numerals, 350 c.

dei= moi/ tinos means I have need of something. In place of the dative (1467) an accusative of the person is rarely allowed in poetry on the analogy of dei= with the infinitive (1985): ou) po/nou pollou= me dei= I have need of no great toil E. Hipp. 23 (often in E.). The thing needed is rarely put in the accusative: ei)/ ti de/oi tw=| xorw=| if the chorus need anything Ant. 6.12 (here some regard ti\ as nominative). Cp. 1562.
The active voice represents the subject as performing the action of the verb: lou/w I wash. a. Under action is included being, as h( o(do\s makra/_ e)sti the way is long.
Active verbs are transitive or intransitive (920).
The action of a transitive verb is directed immediately upon an object, as tu/ptw to pai=da I strike the boy.
The object of a transitive verb is always put in the accusative (1553).

The action of an intransitive verb is not directed immedi-ately upon an object. The action may be restricted to the subject, as a)lgw= I am in pain, or it may be defined by an oblique case or by a preposition with its case, as a)lgw= tou\s po/das I have a pain in my feet, a)fi/_keto ei)s th po/lin he arrived at the city.

Many verbs are used in the active voice both transitively and intransitively. So, in English, turn, move, change. Cp. 1557 ff. a. The distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs is a grammatical convenience, and is not founded on an essential difference of nature.

Active verbs ordinarily transitive are often used intransitively: a. By the ellipsis of a definite external object, which in some cases may be employed, as a)/gein (to\ stra/teuma) march, ai)/rein (th a)/gku_ran) hoist the anchor, (ta\_s nau=s) get under sail, start, a)pai/rein (ta\_s nau=s, to strato/n) sail away, march away, dia/gein (to bi/on) live, e)lau/nein (to i(/ppon) ride, (to\ a(/rma) drive, (to strato/n) march, katalu/_ein (tou\s i(/ppous, ta\ u(pozu/gia) halt, kate/xein (th=n nau=n) put in shore, prose/xein (to nou=n) pay attention, teleuta=n (to bi/on) die. The original sense has often been so completely forgotten that it becomes possible to say ai)/rein tw=| stratw=| set out with the army T. 2.12 , e)lau/nwn i(drou=nti tw=| i(/ppw| riding with his horse in a sweat X. A. 1.8.1 . b. pra/_ttein, e)/xein with adverbs often mean to keep, to be: eu)= pra/_ttein fare well, kalw=s e)/xein be well (bene se habere), e)/xein ou(/tws be so. So when a reflexive pronoun is apparently omitted: e)/x' au)tou= stop there! D. 45.26 . c. Many other transitive verbs may be used absolutely, i.e. with no definite object omitted, as ni_ka=n be a victor, a)dikei=n be guilty. Cp. ‘amare’ be in love, ‘drink’ be a drunkard. This is especially the case in compounds, e.g. of a)lla/ttein, a)nu/ein, dido/nai, kli/_nein, lamba/nein, lei/pein, meignu/nai. d. In poetry many uncompounded transitive verbs are used intransitively. Many intransitive verbs become transitive when compounded with a prep., especially when the compound has a transferred sense, 1559. In some verbs 1st aorist and 1st perfect are transitive, 2d aorist and 2d perfect are intransitive.

Instead of the active, a periphrasis with gi/gnesqai may be used, often to express solemnity. mhnu_tai\ gi/gnontai they turned informers T. 3.2 , mh\ u(bristh\s ge/vh| ‘do not be guilty of outrage’ S. Aj. 1092.

Causative Active.—The active may be used of an action performed at the bidding of the subject: *ku=ros ta\ basi/leia kate/kausen Cyrus burnt down the palace (i.e. had it burnt down) X. A. 1.4.10. So with a)poktei/nein put to death, qa/ptein bury, oi)kodomei=n build, paideu/ein instruct, a)nakhru+/ttein publicly proclaim.
An infinitive limiting the meaning of an adjective is usually active where English employs the passive (cp. 2006).
The middle voice shows that the action is performed with special reference to the subject: lou=mai I wash myself.
The middle represents the subject as doing something in which he is interested. He may do something to himself, for himself, or he may act with something belonging to himself.
The future middle is often (807), the first aorist middle is almost never, used passively.

The object of the middle (1) may belong in the sphere of the subject, as his property, etc.: lou/omai ta\_s xei=ras I wash my hands, or (2) it may be brought into the sphere of the subject: tou\s o(pli/_ta_s metepe/myanto they sent for the hoplites, or (3) it may be removed from the sphere of the subject: a)podi/doma\i th oi)ki/a_n I sell my house (lit. give away). Here the object is also the property of the subject.

The Direct Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting directly on himself. Self is here the direct object.
