So with verbs expressing external and natural acts, as the verbs of the toilet: a)lei/fesqai anoint oneself, lou=sqai wash oneself; and kosmei=sqai adorn oneself, stefanou=sqai crown oneself; gumna/zesqai exercise oneself. a. The direct reflexive idea is far more frequently conveyed by the active and a reflexive pronoun, 1723. b. The part affected may be added in the accusative: e)pai/sato to mhro/n he smote his thigh X. C. 7.3.6 .

So with many other verbs, as i(/stasqai stand (place oneself), tre/pesqai turn (lit. turn oneself), dhlou=sqai show oneself, ta/ttesqai post oneself, a)pologei=sqai defend oneself (argue oneself off), fai/nesqai show oneself, appear, paraskeua/zesqai prepare onself, a)po/llusqai destroy oneself, perish.

The Indirect Reflexive Middle represents the subject as acting for himself, with reference to himself, or with something belonging to himself. Self is often here the indirect object. So pori/zesqai provide for oneself (pori/zein provide), fula/ttesqai guard against (fula/ttein keep guard), ai(rei=sqai choose (take for oneself), pare/xesqai furnish (pare/xein offer, present).

Cases in which the object is to be removed from the sphere of the subject may be resolved into the dative for oneself (1483）: th r(a|qu_mi/a_n a)poqe/sqai to lay aside your indolence D. 8.46 , e)tre/yanto tou\s i(ppe/a_s they routed the cavalry T. 6.98 , tou\s e)xqrou\s a)mu/_nesqai to ward off the enemy for themselves, i.e. to defend themselves against the enemy 1. 144.

The middle often denotes that the subject acts with something belonging to himself (material objects, means, powers). It is often used of acts done willingly. Thus, pare/xesqai furnish from one's own resources, e)pagge/llesqai promise, make profession of, ti/qesqai th yh=fon give one's vote, ti/qesqai ta\ o(/pla ground arms, a)podei/casqai gnw/mhn set forth one's opinion, lamba/nesqai/ tinos put one's hand on (seize) something. Thus, e)spasme/noi ta\ ci/fh having drawn their swords X. A. 7.4.16 , pai=das e)kkekomisme/noi h)=san they had removed their children T. 2.78 , tropai=on sthsa/menoi having set up a trophy X. H. 2.4.7 , o(/pla pori/sasqai to procure arms for themselves T. 4.9 , o(pli/_ta_s metepe/myato he sent for hoplites 7. 31, gunai=ka h)gago/mhn I married L. 1.6 .

Under the indirect middle belong the periphrases of poiei=sqai with verbal nouns instead of the simple verb (cp. 1754). poiei=n with the same nouns means to bring about, effect, fashion, etc. ei)rh/nhn poiei=sqai make peace (of one nation at war with another). ei)rh/nhn poiei=n bring about a peace (between opponents, nations at war: of an individual). qh/ra_n poiei=sqai ( = qhra=n hunt, qh/ra_n poiei=n arrange a hunt. lo/gon poiei=sqai ( = le/gein) deliver a speech, lo/gon poiei=n compose a speech. naumaxi/a_n poiei=sqai ( = naumaxei=n) fight a naval battle. naumaxi/a_n poiei=n bring on a naval battle (of the commander). o(do poiei=sqai ( = o(deu/ein) make a journey, o(do poiei=n build a road. po/lemon poiei=sqai wage war, po/lemon poiei=n bring about a war. sponda\_s poiei=sqai conclude (make) a treaty , or truce. sponda\_s poiei=n bring about a treaty , or truce.

Active and Reflexive.—Instead of the direct middle the active voice with the reflexive pronoun is usually employed; often of difficult and unnatural actions (especially with au)to\s e(auto/n, etc.). ta\ o(/pla pare/dosan kai\ sfa=s au)tou/s they surrendered their arms and themselves T. 4.38 , misqw/sa_s au(to/n hiring himself out D. 19.29 (not misqwsa/menos, which means hiring for himself), katale/luke th au)to\s au(tou= dunastei/a_n he himself has put an end to his own sovereignty Aes. 3.233 , h)ti/_mwken e(auto/n he has dishonoured himself D. 21.103 . But regularly a)pa/gxesqai hang oneself (1717). a. The active and a reflexive pronoun in the gen. or dat. may be used for the simple middle when the reflexive notion is emphatic: katalei/pein suggra/mmata e(autw=n to leave behind them their written compositions P. Phae. 257d .

Middle and Reflexive.—The reflexive pronoun may be used with the middle: e(auto a)pokru/ptesqai to hide himself P. R. 393c ; often for emphasis, as in contrasts: oi( me/n fa_si basile/a_ keleu=sai/ tina e)pisfa/cai au)to *ku/_rw|, oi( d' e(auto e)pisfa/casqai some say that the king issued orders for some one to slay him (Artapates) over (the body of) Cyrus, while others say that he slew himself with his own hand X. A. 1.8.29, cp. also ti/ th po/lin prosh=ke poiei=n, a)rxh kai\ turanni/da tw=n *(ellh/nwn o)rw=san e(autw=| kataskeuaco/menon *fi/lippon; what did it beseem the city to do when it saw Philip compassing for himself dominion and despotic sway over the Greeks? D. 18.66.

The Causative Middle denotes that the subject has something done by another for himself: e)gw\ ga/r se tau=ta e)didaca/mhn for I had you taught this X. C. 1.6.2 , parati/qesqai si=ton to have food served up 8. 6. 12, o(/soi o(/pla a)fh/|rhntai, taxu\ a)/lla poih/sontai all who have had their arms taken from them will soon get others made 6. 1. 12, e(autw=| skhnh kateskeua/sato he had a tent prepared for himself 2. 1. 30. a. This force does not belong exclusively to the middle; cp. 1711.

Reciprocal Middle.—With a dual or plural subject the middle may indicate a reciprocal relation. So with verbs of contending, conversing (questioning, replying), greeting, embracing, etc. The reciprocal middle is often found with compounds of dia/. oi( a)_qlhtai\ h)gwni/zonto the athletes contended T. 1.6 , katasta/ntes e)ma/xonto when they had got into position they fought 1. 49, a)nh\r a)ndri\ diele/gonto they conversed man with man 8. 93, e)pimei/gnusqai a)llh/lois to have friendly intercourse with one another X. C. 7.4.5 , tau=ta dianemou=ntai they will divide this up among themselves L. 21.14 . So ai)tia=sqai accuse, lu_mai/nesqai maltreat, me/mfesqai blame, a(milla=sqai vie, parakeleu/esqai encourage one another. a. The active may also be employed, as polemei=n wage war. b. Some of these verbs have a passive aorist form, as diele/xqhn (812).

The reciprocal relation may also be expressed (1) by the use of the reflexive pronoun (cp. 1724) with the active: fqonou=sin e(autoi=s they are mutually envious X. M. 3.5.16 ; (2) by the use of a)llh/lwn, etc., with the active: a)mfisbhtou=men a)llh/lois we are at variance with one another P. Phae. 263a ; (3) by repetition of the noun: ptwxo\s ptwxw=| fqone/ei = beggars envy each other Hesiod W. D. 26. The reflexive pronouns and a)llh/lwn, etc., may also be added to the middle.

Differences between Active and Middle.—As contrasted with the active, the middle lays stress on the conscious activity, bodily or mental participation, of the agent. In verbs that possess both active and middle: bouleu/esqai deliberate, bouleu/ein plan, staqma=n measure, staqma=sqai calculate, skopei=n look at, skopei=sqai consider, e)/xesqai cling to, pau/esqai cease (1734. 14). The force of the middle often cannot be reproduced in translation (a)kou/esqai, ti_ma=sqai, a)riqmei=sqai, a)porei=sqai), and in some other cases it may not have been felt, as in o(ra=sqai in poetry (proora=sqai occurs in prose). a. Many such verbs form their futures from the middle: a)kou/somai, a)/|somai, a(marth/somai. See 805. b. In verbs in -euw, the middle signifies that the subject is acting in a manner appropriate to his state or condition: poli_teu/ein be a citizen, poli_teu/esqai act as a citizen, perform one's civic duties; presbeu/ein be an envoy, presbeu/esqai negotiate as envoy or send envoys (of the State in its negotiations). But this force of the middle is not always apparent.

Middle Deponents (810) often denote bodily or mental action (feeling and thinking): a(/llesqai jump, pe/tesqai fly, o)rxei=sqai dance, oi)/xesqai be gone, de/rkesqai look; bou/lesqai wish, ai)sqa/nesqai perceive, a)kroa=sqai listen, me/mfesqai blame, oi)/esqai conjecture, think (lit. take omens for oneself, from o)vis, Lat. avis, auspicium), h(gei=sqai consider; o)lofu/_resqai lament. a. Some of the verbs denoting a functional state or process have the middle either in all forms or only in the future. b. Verbs denoting bodily activity regularly have a middle future, 805-806.

Deponent verbs are either direct or indirect middles; direct: u(pisxnei=sqai undertake, promise (lit. hold oneself under); indirect: kta=sqai acquire for oneself, a)gwni/zesqai contend (with one's own powers).
The middle may denote more vigorous participation on the part of the subject than the active: seu/esqai dart, but qe/ein run.

The active is often used for the middle when it is not of practical importance to mark the interest of the subject in the action. The active implies what the middle expresses. So with metape/mpein send for T. 7.15 , dhlw/santes th gnw/mhn setting forth their opinion 3. 37, tropai=on sth/santes setting up a trophy 7. 5.

The passive form may have reflexive force, as ki_nhqh=nai set oneself in motion, a)pallagh=nai remove oneself, e)nantiwqh=nai oppose oneself, swqh=nai save oneself ( sw/qhti save yourself P. Cr. 44b ). Some of these middle passives may take the accusative, as ai)sxunqh=nai be ashamed before, fobhqh=nai be afraid of, kataplhgh=nai/ tina be amazed at some one. See 814 ff.

List of the chief verbs showing important differences of meaning between active and middle. It will be noted that the active is often transitive, the middle intransitive. 1. ai(rei=n take; ai(rei=sqai choose. 2. a)mu/_nein ti/ tini ward off something from some one, a)mu/_nein tini/ help some one; a)mu/_nesqai/ ti defend oneself against something, a)mu/_nesqai/ tina requite some one. 3. a)podou=nai give back; a)podo/sqai sell (give away for one's profit). 4. a(/ptein attach; a(/ptesqai/ tinos touch. 5. a)/rxein begin, contrasts one beginner of an action with another, as a)/rxein pole/mou take the aggressive, strike the first blow (bellum movere), a)/rxein lo/gou be the first to speak, h)=rxe xeirw=n a)di/kwn he began an unprovoked assault L. 4.11 ; a)/rxesqai make one's own beginning, as contrasted with the later stages, as a)/rxesqai pole/mou begin warlike operations (bellum incipere), a)/rxesqai tou= lo/gou begin one's speech. pole/mou ou)k a)/rcomen, a)rxome/nous de\ a)mu_nou/meqa we shall not take the initiative in the war, but upon those who take it up we shall retaliate T. 1.144 . 6. gamei=n marry (of the man, ducere); gamei=sqai marry (of the woman, nubere). 7. gra/fein no/mon propose a law (said of the maker of a law whether or not he is himself subject to it); gra/fesqai grafh/n draw up an indictment for a public offence, gra/fesqai/ tina bring suit against some one (have him written down in the magistrates' records). 8. danei/zein (make of anything a da/nos loan) i.e. put out at interest, lend; danei/zesqai (have a da/nos made to oneself) have lent to one, borrow at interest. 9. dika/zein give judgment; dika/zesqai (di/khn tini/) go to law with a person, conduct a case (properly get some one to give judgment). 10. e)piyhfi/zein put to vote (of the presiding officer); e)piyhfi/zesqai vote, decree (of the people). 11. e)/xein hold; e)/xesqai/ t<*>nos hold on to, be close to. 12. qu/_ein sacrifice; qu/_esqai take auspices (of a general, etc.). 13. misqou=n (pu

The passive voice represents the subject as acted on: e)w/qoun, e)wqou=nto, e)/paion, e)pai/onto they pushed, were pushed, they struck, were struck X. C. 7.1.38. a. The passive has been developed from the middle. With the exception of some futures and the aorist, the middle forms do duty as passives: ai(rei=tai takes for himself, i.e. chooses, and is chosen. (For this development of the passive, cp. the reflexive use in se trouver, sich finden.) So ke/xutai has poured itself, has been poured. In Homer there are more perfect middles used passively than any other middle tenses. Cp. 802. b. Uncompounded e)sxo/mhn sometimes retained its use as a passive. e)sxe/qhn is late.

The passive may have the sense allow oneself to be, get oneself: e)ca/gonte/s te kai\ e)cago/uenoi carrying and allowing ourselves to be carried across the border P. Cr. 48d , a)pexqh/sei *gorgi/a| you will incur the hatred of Gorgias P. Phil. 58c .
Many future middle forms are used passively (807 ff.).

The future middle forms in -somai are developed from the present stem, and express durative action; the (later) future passives in -h/somai, -qh/somai are developed from the aorists in -hn and -qhn, and are aoristic. This difference in kind of action is most marked when the future middle forms are used passively, but it is not always found. toi=s a)/llois cumma/xois para/deigma safe\s katasth/sate, o(\s a) a)fi/sthtai, qana/tw| zhmiwso/menon give to the rest of the allies a plain example that whoever revolts shall be punished (in each case) with death T. 3.40, e)a\_n a(lw=|, qana/tw| zhmiwqh/setai if he is convicted, he will be punished (a single occurrence) with death D. 23.80, o( di/kaios masti_gw/setai, streblw/setai, dedh/setai, e)kkauqh/setai tw)fqalmw/ the just man will be scourged, racked, fettered, will have his eyes burnt out P. R. 361e, ti_mh/somai I shall enjoy honour, ti_mhqh/somai I shall be honoured (on a definite occasion), w)felh/somai I shall receive lasting benefit, w)felhqh/somai I shall be benefited (on a definite occasion). Cp. 808, 809, 1911.

The second aorist passive was originally a second aorist active (of the -mi form) that was used intransitively to distinguish it from the transitive first aorist, as e)/fhna showed, e)fa/nhn appeared; e)/fqeira destroyed, e)fqa/rhn am destroyed; e)ce/plhca was terrified, e)cepla/ghn was alarmed. So e)da/hn learned, e)rru/hn flowed. Cp. e)/sthsa placed, e)/sthn stood (819).

In Hom. all the second aorist forms in -hn are intransitive except e)plh/ghn and e)tu/phn was struck. Most of the forms in -qhn are likewise intransitive in Hom., as e)fa/nqhn appeared (in Attic was shown).

The perfect passive in the third singular with the dative of the agent (1488) is often preferred to the perfect active of the first person. Thus pe/pra_ktai/ moi it has been done by me is more common than pe/pra_ga or pe/pra_xa I have done.

The passive may be passive of the middle as well as passive of the active: ai(rei=tai is taken or is chosen, bia/zetai does violence or suffers violence (is forced), h(|re/qh was taken or was chosen, e)gra/fh was written or was indicted (ge/grammai is commonly middle). The use of the passive as passive of the middle is post-Homeric. a. When deponent verbs have a passive force, the future and aorist have the passive form: e)bia/sqhn I suffered violence (was forced), but e)biasa/mhn I did violence. This holds when there was once an active form. Cp. also ti_mwrei=sqai, metape/mpesqai, yhfi/zesqai, kuklei=sqai. b. The aorist passive may have a middle sense (814).

The direct object of an active verb becomes the subject of the passive: h( e)pistolh\ u(po\ tou= didaska/lou gra/fetai the letter is written by the teacher (active o( dida/skalos gra/fei th e)pistolh/n).
The cognate accusative may become the subject of the passive: po/lemos e)polemh/qh war was waged P. Menex. 243e (po/lemon polemei=n, 1564).

Active or middle verbs governing the genitive or dative may form (unlike the Latin use) a personal passive, the genitive or dative (especially if either denotes a person) becoming the subject of the passive. a. With the genitive: a)/rxein, h(gemoneu/ein, katafronei=n, katagela=n, katayhfi/zein (katayhfi/zesqai), a)melei=n. b. With the dative: a)peilei=n, a)pistei=n, e)gkalei=n, e)pibouleu/ein, e)piti_ma=n, o)neidi/zein, pisteu/ein, polemei=n, fqonei=n. c. Examples: ou)k h)ci/oun ou(=toi h(gemoneu/esqai u(f' h(mw=n they did not think it right to be governed by us T. 3.61 , e)kei=nos kateyhfi/sqh he was condemned X. H. 5.2.36 , but qa/natos au)tw=n kategnw/sqh the penalty of death was pronounced against them L. 13.39 (pass. of katagnw=nai qa/naton au)tw=n), w(/ra_ h(mi=n bouleu/esqai u(pe\r h(mw=n au)tw=n mh\ katafronhqw=men it is time for us to take counsel for ourselves that we may not be brought into contempt X. A. 5.7.12 , polemou=ntai me u(po\ tw=n th xw/ra_n au)tw=n perioikou/ntwn, a)pistou=ntai d' u(f' a(pa/ntwn they are warred against by those who dwell around their country, and are distrusted by all I. 5.49 , pw=s a) e)pebou/leusa/ ti au)tw=|, o(/ ti mh\ kai\ e)pebouleu/qhn u(p' au)tou=; how could I have plotted against him, unless I had been plotted against by him? Ant. 4. b. 5, fqonhqei\s u(po\ tou=) *odusse/ws envied by Odysseus X. M. 4.2.33 (contrast Lat. invidetur mihi ab aliquo). N.—The above principle does not hold when the accusative of an external object intervenes between the verb and the dative.

A verb governing an oblique case rarely forms in Greek (unlike Latin) an impersonal passive: e)moi\ beboh/qhtai tw=| te teqnew=ti kai\ tw=| no/mw| my aid has been given to the deceased and to the law Ant. 1.31 . The tense used is one from the perfect stem.

An active verb followed by two accusatives, one of a person, the other of a thing, retains, when transferred to the passive, the accusative of the thing, while the accusative of the person becomes the nominative subject of the passive. Examples 1621, 1625, 1627, 1632.

An active verb followed by an accusative of the direct object (a thing) and an oblique case of a person, retains, when transferred to the passive, the accusative of the direct object, while the indirect object becomes the nominative subject of the passive. Cp. I have been willed a large estate. a. With verbs signifying to enjoin, entrust: oi( *boiwtoi\ tau=ta e)pestalme/noi a)nexw/roun the Boeotians having received these instructions withdrew T. 5.37 (pass. of e)piste/llein tau=ta toi=s *boiwtoi=s), a)/llo ti mei=zon e)pitaxqh/sesqe you will have some greater command laid upon you 1. 140 (pass. of e)pita/ttein a)/llo ti mei=zon u(_mi=n). Both accusatives are internal; and so, in oi( tw=n *)aqhnai/wn e)pitetramme/noi th fulakh/n those of the Athenians who had been entrusted with the watch T. 1.126 , fulakh/n is equivalent to an internal accusative. The nominative of the thing and the dative of the person sometimes occur ( *)/iwnes, toi=si e)pete/trapto h( fulakh/ the Ionians to whom the guard had been entrusted Hdt. 7.10 ). The dative is common when an inf. is used with the pass. verb: e)pete/takto toi=s skeuofo/rois i)e/nai the baggage-carriers had been commanded to go X. C. 6.3.3 . b. With other verbs: a)potmhqe/ntes ta\_s kefala/_s having been decapitated (had their heads cut off) X. A. 2.6.1 (pass. of a)pote/mnein ta\_s kefala/_s tisi or tinwn).

A passive may be formed in the case of verbs ordinarily intransitive but allowing a cognate accusative in the active: i(kana\ toi=s polemi/ois hu)tu/xhtai the enemy has had enough good fortune T. 7.77 (eu)tuxei=n i(kana/, 1573), kekindu_neu/setai the risk will have been run Ant. 5.75 . See 1746. This is common with neuter passive participles: ta\ h)sebhme/na au)tw=| the impious acts committed by him L. 6.5 , ta\ soi\ ka)_moi\ bebiwme/na the life led by you and by me D. 18.265 , ta\ pepoli_teume/na au)toi=s their political acts 1. 28, a(marthqe/nta errors committed X. A. 5.8.20 . a. Some verbs describing the action of the weather may be used in the passive: neifo/menoi a)ph=lqon ei)s to\ a)/stu they returned to the city covered with snow X. H. 2.4.3 .

The cognate subject may be implied, as in the case of impersonal passives, in the perfect and tenses derived from the perfect. Thus, e)peidh\ au)toi=s pareskeu/asto when their preparations were complete T. 1.46 . le/getai it is said, e)dhlw/qh it was made known, followed by the logical subject are not impersonal: e)dhlw/qh tw=| tro/pw| a)pwlw/lei ta\ xrh/mata it was shown how the money had been lost Ant. 5.70 . See 935.
Greek uses impersonals from intransitives (corresponding to Lat. ambulatur, itur, curritur) only when the active is itself intransitive; as de/doktai it has seemed good (cp. dokei=).

The active or the middle deponent of a transitive verb used transitively or of an intransitive verb may replace the passive of a transitive verb. a)kou/ein (poet. klu/ein) be called; be well (eu)=, kalw=s) or ill (kakw=s) spoken of, = pass. of le/gein: nu=n ko/lakes a)kou/ousin now they are called flatterers D. 18.46 , ti/s u(p' e)mou= kakw=s a)kh/koen h)\ pe/ponqe; who has been ill spoken of or suffered at my hands? L. 8.3. Cp. bene, male audire; Milton: “England hears ill abroad.” a(li/skesqai be caught = pass. of ai(rei=n, as e)a\_n a(lw=|s tou=to pra/_ttwn if you are caught doing this P. A. 29c . a)poqnh/skein (die) be killed = pass. of a)poktei/nein, as a)pe/qnh|skon u(po\ i(ppe/wn they were killed by the cavalry X. C. 7.1.48 . But not in the perfect, where the uncompounded te/qnhka is used. gi/gnesqai be born = pass. of ti/ktein beget, bring forth: pai=des au)tw=| ou)k e)gi/gnonto e)k tau/ths he had no children by her X. H. 6.4.37 . di/khn dou=nai be punished = pass. of zhmiou=n, as u(p' au)tw=n tou/twn di/khn e)/dosan they were punished by these very men X. C. 1.6.45 . h(tta=sqai be defeated = pass. of ni_ka=n conquer, as u(po\ tw=n summa/xwn h(ttw/menoi worsted by their allies And. 4.28 . katie/nai (kate/rxesqai) return from exile = pass. of kata/gein restore from exile, as u(p o)ligarxi/a_s katelqei=n to be restored by an oligarchy T. 8.68 . kei=sqai (lie) be placed = pass. of the perfect of tiqe/nai: pei/qou toi=s no/mois toi=s u(po\ tw=n basile/wn keime/nois obey the laws established by kings I. 1.36 . lagxa/nein (obtain by lot) be drawn by lot = pass. of klhrou=n: e)/laxon i(ereu/s I became priest by lot D. 57.47 . pa/sxein (suffer) be treated well (eu)=) or ill (kakw=s) = pass. of poiei=n (eu)=, kakw=s): eu)= paqo/ntes u(p' au)tw=n well treated by them P. G. 519c . pi/_ptein in e)kpi/_ptein (fall out) be expelled = pass. of e)kba/llein: oi( e)kpeptwko/tes <*> tou= dh/mou those who had been expelled by the people X. H. 4.8.20. feu/gein (flee) be prosecut

Other equivalents of passive forms are e)/xein, tugxa/nein, lamba/nein, used with a substantive of like meaning with the active verb: o)/noma e)/xein = o)no<*>sqai, suggnw/mhn e)/xein or suggnw/mhs tugxa/nein = suggignw/skesqai, e)/painon lamba/<*> or e)pai/nou tugxa/nein = e)painei=sqai. So with middle deponents: ai)ti/a_n e)/xein = <*>tia=sqai.
The passive of the periphrasis with poiei=sqai (1722) is made with <*>esqai: so ei)rh/nh gi/gnetai peace is made.
The agent of the passive is regularly expressed by u(po/ and the genitive; sometimes by a)po/, dia/, e)k, para/, pro/s with the genitive, or by u(po/ with the dative (in poetry). See 1678.
The instrument of an action, when regarded as the agent, is personified, and may be expressed by u(po/ with the genitive: a<*>li/sketai u(po\ trih/rous he is captured by a trireme D. 53.6.

The dative, or a prepositional phrase, is regularly used with the passive to denote the instrument, means, or cause (1506). The agent may be viewed as the instrument: in prose, when persons are regarded as instruments, the dative is usually that of military accompaniment (1526).
The dative of the agent used with the perfect passive and verbal adjective is a dative of interest (1488); on u(po/ with the genitive used instead of the dative, see 1493, 1494.
Mood designates by the form of the verb the mode or manner (modus) in which the speaker conceives of an assertion concerning the subject.

There are four moods proper in Greek: indicative, subjunctive, optative, and imperative. The infinitive (strictly a verbal noun) and the participle (strictly an adjective form of the verb) may be classed with the moods.

The particle a)/n (Hom. ke/n, ke/) limits the meaning of the moods. It has two distinct uses: a. In independent clauses: with the past tenses of the indicative and with the optative; also with the infinitive and participle representing the indicative or optative. b. In dependent clauses: with the subjunctive.

No separate word can be used to translate a)/n by itself; its force varies as it modifies the meaning of the moods. In general a)/n limits the force of the verb to particular conditions or circumstances (‘under the circumstances,’ ‘in that case,’ ‘then’).
In Homer a)/n is preferred in negative, ke/n, ke/ in relative, sentences.

Position of a)/n.—a)/n does not begin a sentence or a clause, except after a weak mark of punctuation, as ti/ ou)=n, a)/n tis ei)/poi, tau=ta le/geis h(mi=n nu=n; why then (some one might say) do you tell us this now? D. 1.14. In independent sentences with a)/n (indic. and opt.) the particle is often separated from its verb for emphasis, and is attached to negatives (ou)k a)/n), interrogatives (ti/s a)/n, pw=s a)/n), or to any emphatic modifier. It is commonly attached to verbs of saying or thinking: su u(_mi=n me a) oi)=mai ei)=nai ti/_mios if I should remain with you, I think I should be esteemed X. A. 1.3.6. a. So with ou)k oi)=d' a) ei) (or ou)k a) oi)=da ei)) followed by a verb to which a)/n belongs: ou)k oi)=d' a) ei) pei/saimi I do not know whether I could persuade E. Med. 941 (for pei/saimi a)/n).

Repetition of a)/n.—a)/n may be repeated once or twice in the same sentence. a. a)/n is placed early in a sentence which contains a subordinate clause, in order to direct attention to the character of the construction: dokou=men d' a)/n moi tau/th| prospoiou/menoi prosbalei=n e)rhmote/rw| a) tw=| o)/rei xrh=sqai if we should make a feint attack here it seems to me we should find the mountain to have fewer defenders X. A. 4.6.13 . b. For rhetorical emphasis a)/n is added to give prominence to particular words: ti/s ga\r toiau=t' a) ou)k a) o)rgi/zoit' e)/ph klu/wn; and who would not be angered upon hearing such words? S. O. T. 339, pw=s a) ou)k a) e)n di/kh| qa/noim' a)/n; how should I not justly die? S. fr. 673.

a)/n without a Verb.—a)/n sometimes stands without a verb, which is to be supplied from the context. So in the second member of a sentence with coördinate clauses: oi)=da o(/ti pollou\s me h(gemo/nas a) doi/h, pollou\s d' a) (doi/h) o(mh/rous I know that he would give many guides and many hostages X. A. 3.2.24 . Often with pw=s a)/n (ei)/h); how can (could) it be? P. R. 353c, ta/x' a)/n perhaps P. Soph. 255c . a. So with w(s a)/n, w(/sper a) ei) (2480): parh=n o( *gada/_ta_s dw=ra polla\ fe/rwn, w(s a) (scil. fe/roi tis) e)c oi)/kou mega/lou Gadatas came with many gifts, such as one might offer from large means X. C. 5.4.29 , fobou/menos w(/sper a) ei) pai=s fearing like a child (w(/sper a) e)fobei=to, ei) pai=s h)=n) P. G. 479a. b. ka)\_n ei) is often used for the simple kai\ ei) (2372) and without regard to the mood of the following verb; sometimes there is no verb in the apodosis to which the a)/n may be referred, as e)/stin a)/ra th=| a)lhqei/a|, ka)\_n ei) mh/ tw| dokei=, o( tw=| o)/nti tu/rannos tw=| o)/nti dou=los the very tyrant is then in truth a very slave even if he does not seem so to any one P. R. 579d (here kai\ ei) mh\ dokei=, ei)/h a)/n is implied). ka)\_n ei) may be also so used that a)/n belongs to the apodosis, while kai/, though going with ei) in translation (even if), affects the whole conditional sentence. Thus, nu=n de/ moi dokei=, ka) a\se/beian ei) (tis) katagignw/skoi, ta\ prosh/konta poiei=n but as it is, it seems to me that, even if any one should condemn his wanton assault, he would be acting properly D. 21.51 (here a)/n goes with poiei=n, i.e. poioi/h a)/n). ka)/_n if only, followed by a limiting expression, may generally be regarded as kai\ a)/_n ( = e)a/_n) with a subjunctive understood; as a)lla/ moi pa/res ka)\_n smi_kro ei)pei=n yet permit me to say but a word ( = kai\ e)a\_n parh=|s) S. El. 1482.

Omission of a)/n.—a)/n is sometimes omitted when it may be supplied from the preceding sentence or clause. So often with the second of two verbs that are connected or opposed: ti/ e)poi/hsen a)/n; h)\ dh=lon o(/ti w)/mose (a)/n); what would he have done? is it not clear that he would have taken an oath? D. 31.9, ou)/t' a) ou(=tos e)/xoi le/gein ou)/q' u(_mei=s peisqei/hte neither can he assert nor can you be made to believe D. 22.17 . By retention of earlier usage the subjunctive is sometimes used without a)/n where it is commonly employed in the later language (2327, 2339, 2565 b, 2567 b). Here the difference is scarcely appreciable except that the omission gives an archaic tone.

Subjunctive with a)/n.—Conditional, relative, and temporal clauses requiring the subjunctive must have a)/n, which is more closely attached to the conditional, relative, and temporal words than it is to the subjunctive. a. Hence the combinations e)a/_n (h)/n, a)/_n) on which cp. 2283; o(/tan, o(po/tan, e)ph/n (e)pa/_n), e)peida/n from ei), o(/te, o(po/te, e)pei/, e)peidh/ + a)/n. When the particle does not thus coalesce, it is usually separated only by such words as me/n, de/, te/, ga/r. b. The force of a)/n with the subjunctive cannot usually be expressed in English. For a)/n in final clauses with w(s, o(/pws, and o)/fra, see 2201. In Hom. a)/n (ke/n) is found in dependent clauses, 2334 c.

§§ 1770-1849 treat of the use of the moods in independent sentences and principal clauses. The dependent construction of the moods was developed from their independent use. The use of the moods in subordinate clauses was not originally different from that in independent sentences and in the principal clauses of complex sentences. For the uses of the indicative, see also 1875-1958.

The indicative mood makes a simple, direct assertion of fact; or asks a question anticipating such an assertion: h)=lqe he came, ou)k h)=lqe he did not come, e)leu/setai he will come, po/te tau=ta poih/sei; when will he do this?

The indicative states particular or general suppositions, makes affirmative or negative assertions, which may or may not be absolutely true. Thus, in assumptions, e)ch/marte/ tis a)/_kwn: suggnw/mh a)nti\ ti_mwri/a_s tou/tw| suppose some one involuntarily committed an offence; for him there is pardon rather than punish- ment D. 18.274, and often after kai\ dh/, as kai\ dh\ teqna=si and suppose they are dead E. Med. 386 .

The indicative may be used to express a doubtful assertion about a present or past action (negative mh/ or mh\ ou)): a)ll' a)/ra . . . mh\ o( *kth/sippos h)=n o( tau=t' ei)pw/n but I suspect (i.e. perhaps) after all it was Ctesippus who said this P. Eu. 290e, a)lla\ mh\ tou=to ou) kalw=s w(mologh/samen but perhaps we did not do well in agreeing to this P. Men. 89c . Such sentences are often regarded as questions with the effect of doubtful affirmation.

The indicative may be used alone where in English we employ an auxiliary verb: pisteu/wn de\ qeoi=s pw=s ou)k ei)=nai qeou\s e)no/mizen; since he trusted in the gods how could (or should) he believe there were no gods? X. M. 1.1.5, o)li/gou ei(=lon th po/lin a little more and they would have taken the city T. 8.35 , a)pwllu/meqa we might have perished (we were in danger of perishing) X. A. 5.8.2. Cp. 2319.

Unfulfilled Obligation (Propriety, Possibility).—With the imperfect indicative of impersonal expressions denoting obligation, propriety, necessity, or possibility, the action of a dependent infinitive is usually not realized. (Examples 1775-1776.) Such expressions are e)/dei, xrh=n (or e)xrh=n), prosh=ke, kairo\s h)=n, a)/cion h)=n, ei)ko\s h)=n, di/kaion h)=n, ai)sxro h)=n, e)ch=n, kalw=s ei)=xen, verbals in -to/n or -te/on with h)=n, etc. a. For the use of these expressions (also with a)/n) in the apodosis of unreal conditions, see 2313, 2315.

Present.—Thus, e)/dei se tau=ta poiei=n you ought to be doing this (but are not doing it), tou/sde mh\ zh=n e)/dei these men ought not to be alive S. Ph. 418 , ti/ si_ga=|s; ou)k e)xrh=n si_ga=n why art thou silent? Thou shouldst not be silent E. Hipp. 297 , ei)ko\s h)=n u(_ma=s . . . mh\ malakw=s, w(/sper nu=n, cummaxei=n you should not be slack in your alliance, as you are at present T. 6.78 .

Past.—e)/dei se tau=ta poih=sai (or poiei=n) you ought to have done this (but did not do it), e)ch=n soi e)lqei=n you might have gone (but did not go), e)nh=n au)tw=| tau=ta poih=sai he could have done this (almost equivalent to the potential indicative tau=ta e)poi/hsen a)/n, 1784), e)/dei ta\ e)ne/xura to/te labei=n I ought to have taken the pledges then X. A. 7.6.23 , a)/cion h)=n a)kou=sai it would have been worth hearing P. Eu. 304d , me/nein e)ch=n he might have remained D. 3.17 .

The Greek usage simply states the obligation (propriety, possibility) as a fact which existed in the past (and may continue to exist in the present). In English we usually express the non-fulfilment of the action.

Present or past time is denoted when the present infinitive is used. When the reference is to present time, the action of the present infinitive is always denied. Past time is denoted when the aorist infinitive is used.

The expressions in 1774 may also refer to simple past obligation (propriety, possibility) and have the ordinary force of past indicatives: e)/dei me/nein he had to remain (and did remain) D. 19.124. The context determines the meaning; thus ti/ to su/mboulon e)xrh=n poiei=n; (D. 18.190) by itself might mean either what was it the duty of the statesman to do or what was it the duty of the statesman to have done?

Unattainable Wish.—A wish, referring to the present or past, which cannot be realized, is expressed by a past tense of the indicative with ei)/qe or with ei) ga/r (negative mh/). The imperfect refers to present time, the aorist to past time (cp. 2304, 2305). ei)/q' ei)=xes belti(_ous fre/nas would that thou hadst (now) a better heart E. El. 1061, ei)/qe soi to/te sunegeno/mhn would that I had then been with thee X. M. 1.2.46 .

An unattainable wish may also be expressed by w)/felon (ought) with the present or aorist infinitive: w)/fele *ku=ros zh=n would that Cyrus were (now) alive (Cyrus ought to be alive) X. A. 2.1.4 (1775). The negative is mh/: mh/pot' w)/felon lipei=n th *sku=ron would that I had never left Scyros S. Ph. 969 . ei)/qe or ei) ga/r (poet. ai)/qe, w(s) may be used before w)/felon: ei) ga\r w)/felon oi(=oi/ te ei)=nai oi( polloi\ kaka\ e)rga/zesqai would that the multitude were able to do evil Pl. Cr. 44 d.

e)boulo/mhn followed by an infinitive may express an unattainable wish: e)boulo/mhn me ou)k e)ri/zein e)nqa/de I would that I were not contending here (as I am) Ar. Ran. 866. (e)boulo/mhn a)/n vellem, 1789.)

The indicative is also used in other than simple sentences: in final sentences (2203); in object sentences after verbs of effort (2211), of caution (2220 a), of fearing (2231, 2233); in consecutive sentences with w(/ste so that (2274), in conditional sentences (2300, 2303, 2323, 2326); in temporal sentences (2395); in object sentences after o(/ti and w(s with a verb of saying, etc. (2577 ff.).

Past Potential.—The past tenses (usually the aorist, less commonly the imperfect) of the indicative with a)/n (ke/n) denote past potentiality, probability (cautious statement), or necessity: o(\ ou)k a) w)/|onto which they could not have expected T. 7.55 , ti/s ga\r a) w)|h/qh tau=ta gene/sqai; for who would have expected these things to happen? D. 9.68 (note that a)/n does not go with gene/sqai by 1764), e)/gnw a)/n tis one might (could, would) have known X. C. 7.1.38, u(po/ ken talasi/frona/ per de/os ei(=len fear might have seized even a man of stout heart *d 421 . a. This is especially frequent with ti\s and with the ideal second person (cp. putares, crederes): e)pe/gnws a)/n you would (could, might) have observed X. C. 8.1.33. b. The potential optative (1829) in Homer refers also to the past.
A protasis may often be extracted from a participle, or is intimated in some other word; but there is no reference to any definite condition, hence a definite ellipsis is not to be supplied.

Unreal Indicative.—The indicative of the historical tenses with a)/n (ke/n) may denote unreality: to/te d' au)to\ to\ pra=gm' a) e)kri/_neto e)f' au(tou= but the case would then have been decided on its own merits D. 18.224 , kai/ ken polu\ ke/rdion h)=en and in that case it were far better *g 41 .

This use of the indicative with a)/n to denote unreality is not inherent in the meaning of the past tenses of that mood, but has been developed from the past potential with which the unreal indicative is closely connected. On the common use of this construction in the apodosis of unreal conditions see 2303. On e)/dei a)/n, etc., see 2315.
The imperfect refers to the present or the past, the aorist to the past (rarely to the present), the pluperfect to the present (less commonly to the past).

e)boulo/mhn a)/n (vellem) I should like or should have liked may express an unattainable wish: e)boulo/mhn a) *si/mwna th au)th gnw/mhn e)moi\ e)/xein I should have liked Simon to be (or I wish Simon were) of the same mind as myself L. 3.21. On e)boulo/mhn without a)/n, see 1782.

Iterative Indicative (repeated action).—The imperfect and aorist with a)/n are used to express repeated or customary past action (post-Homeric): dihrw/twn a)/n I used to ask P. A. 22b , a) e)/lecen he was wont to say X. C. 7.1.10 .

This construction is connected with the past potential and denoted originally what could or would take place under certain past circumstances. Thus, a)nalamba/nwn ou)=n au)tw=n ta\ poih/mata . . . dihrw/twn a) au)tou\s ti/ le/goien accordingly, taking up their poems, I used to (would) ask them (as an opportunity presented itself) what they meant P. A. 22b. In actual use, since the action of the verb did take place, this construction has become a statement of fact.

In Herodotus this construction is used with the iterative forms: klai/eske a)/n she kept weeping 3. 119, oi( de\ a) *pe/rsa<*> la/beskon ta\ pro/bata the Persians were wont to seize the cattle 4. 130.

Homer and the early poets use a)/n (ke/n) with the future indicative with a conditional or limiting force: kai/ ke/ tis w(=d' e)re/ei and in such a case some one will (may) say thus *d 176. This use is found also in conditional relative sentences (2565 b). In Attic a)/n is found with the future in a few passages which are now generally emended. In P. A. 29c there is an anacoluthon.
a)/n is not used with the present and perfect indicative.

The chief uses of the independent subjunctive are the hortatory (1797), the prohibitive (1800), and the deliberative (1805). a. The name subjunctive is due to the belief of the ancient grammarians that the mood was always subordinate. Thus, ei)/pw shall I speak? (1805) was explained as due to the omission of a preceding bou/lei, i.e. do you wish that I speak?

The independent subjunctive refers to future time. It has three main uses: (1) the voluntative, expressing the will of the speaker. This is akin to the imperative. (2) The deliberative. This is possibly a form of the voluntative. (3) The anticipatory (or futural). This anticipates an action as an immediate future possibility. Whether the anticipatory is a form of the voluntative is uncertain (cp. ich will sehen, je veux voir, dialectal il veut pleuvoir).

Hortatory Subjunctive.—The hortatory subjunctive (present or aorist) is used to express a request or a proposal (negative mh/). a. Usually in the first person plural: nu=n i)/wmen kai\ a)kou/swmen tou= a)ndro/s let us go now and hear the man P. Prot. 314 b, mh/pw e)kei=se i)/wmen let's not go there yet 311 a. a)/ge, fe/re (dh/), in Hom. a)/ge (dh/), sometimes precedes, as a)/ge skopw=men come, let us consider X. C. 5.5.15. i)/qi (dh/) rarely precedes. b. Less frequently in the first person singular, which is usually preceded (in affirmative sentences) by fe/re (dh/), in Hom. by a)/ge (dh/): fe/re dh\ peri\ tou= yhfi/smatos ei)/pw let me now speak about the bill D. 19.234 .

The first person singular in negative exhortations (rare and poetic) may convey a warning or a threat: mh/ se, ge/ron, koi/lh|sin para\ nhusi\ kixei/w old man, let me not find thee by the hollow ships A 26. This use is often regarded as prohibitive (1800).
The hortatory use of the subjunctive compensates for the absence of an imperative of the first person.

Prohibitive Subjunctive.—The subjunctive (in the second and third persons of the aorist) is often used to express prohibitions (negative mh/). a. Usually in the second person: mhde a)qu_mh/shte do not lose heart X. A. 5.4.19 . For the aorist subjunctive the present imperative may be employed (1840): mh\ poih/sh|s (or mh\ poi/ei) tau=ta do not do this (not mh\ poih=|s). b. Less commonly in the third person, which usually represents the second: u(pola/bh| de\ mhdei/s and let no one suppose T. 6.84 ( = mh\ u(pola/bhte do not suppose). c. The third person of the present subjunctive is rare: mh\ toi/nun tis oi)/htai ( = mh\ oi)w/meqa) let not any one think P. L. 861 E. N.—ou) mh/ with the subjunctive of the second person in the dramatic poets occasionally expresses a strong prohibition: ou) mh\ lhrh/sh|s don't talk nonsense Ar. Nub. 367 .

The infinitive is in part a verb, in part a substantive. a. Many substantives are closely related to verbs, but not all verbs can form substantives. All verbs can, however, form infinitives. b. The word infinitive denotes a verbal form without any limitations (finis) of number and person.

The infinitive is like a verb herein: a. It shows the distinctions of voice and tense (but not those of number and person). Having tenses, it can express different stages of action (action simply occurring, continuing, or finished); whereas the corresponding substantive sets forth the abstract idea without these distinctions. Contrast poiei=n, poih/sein, poih=sai, pepoihke/nai with poi/hsis making. b. It can have a subject before it and a predicate after it, and it can have an object in the genitive, dative, or accusative like the corresponding finite verb. Infinitives scarcely ever stand in the subjective genitive; and the object of an infinitive never stands in the objective genitive. c. It is modified by adverbs, not by adjectives. d. It may take a)/n and with that particle represent a)/n with the indicative (1784 ff.) or a)/n with the optative (1824). e. It forms clauses of result with w(/ste, and temporal clauses with pri/n, etc.

The infinitive is like a substantive herein: a. It may be the subject or object of a verb. b. With the (neuter) article it shows all the case forms (except the vocative): to\ (tou=, tw=|, to\) lu/_ein, lu/_sein, etc. c. It may be governed by prepositions: pro\ tou= lu/_ein.

The infinitive was originally a verbal noun in the dative (in part possibly also in the locative) case. The use to express purpose (2008) is a survival of the primitive meaning, from which all the other widely diverging uses were developed in a manner no longer always clear to us. But the to or for meaning seen in manqa/nein h(/komen we have come to learn (for learning) can also be discerned in du/namai i)dei=n I have power for seeing, then I can see. Cp. 2000, 2006 a. As early as Homer, when the datival meaning had been in part obscured, the infinitive was employed as nominative (as subject) and accusative (as object). After Homer, the infinitive came to be used with the neuter article, the substantive idea thus gaining in definiteness. The article must be used when the infinitive stands as an object in the genitive or dative, and when it depends on prepositions.
The infinitive is used as subject, as predicate, and to supplement the meaning of words and clauses.

The negative of the infinitive is mh/; but ou), used with a finite mood in direct discourse, is retained when that mood becomes infinitive in indirect discourse. Sometimes, however, mh/ is used in place of this ou) (2723 ff.).

In general the subject of the infinitive, if expressed at all, stands in the accusative; when the subject of the infinitive is the same as the subject or object of the governing verb, or when it has already been made known in the sentence, it is not repeated with the infinitive.

When the subject of the infinitive is the same as that of the governing verb, it is omitted, and a predicate noun stands in the nominative case. oi)=mai ei)de/nai I think that I know P. Pr. 312e , *pe/rshs e)/fh ei)=nai he said he was a Persian X. A. 4.4.17 , e)gw\ ou)x o(mologh/sw a)/klhtos h(/kein I shall not admit that I have come uninvited P. S. 174d , o(mologei=s peri\ e)me\ a)/dikos gegenh=sqai; do you admit that you have been guilty as regards me? X. A. 1.6.8 (cp. 4.2.27 in 2263). a. The nominative is used when the infinitive, expressing some action or state of the subject of the main verb, has the article in an oblique case. Thus, tou/twn a)ciwqei\s dia\ to\ patriko\s au)tw=| fi/los ei/=nai justifying these requests on the ground that he was his hereditary friend Aes. 3.52, tou=to d' e)poi/ei e)k tou= xalepo\s ei)=nai this he effected by reason of his being severe X. A. 2.6.9 , e)pi\ tw=| o(moi=oi toi=s leipome/nois ei)=nai e)kpe/mpontai (colonists) are sent out to be the equals of those who stay at home T. 1.34. b. The nominative stands usually in sentences with dei=n, xrh=nai etc., dependent on a verb of saying or thinking. Thus, h(gou/mhn . . . periei=nai dei=n au)tw=n kai\ megaloyu_xo/teros fai/nesqai I thought I ought to surpass them and to show myself more magnificent D. 19.235 . Here h(gou/mhn dei=n is equivalent to I thought it proper. c. When the governing verb is a participle in an oblique case, a predicate noun usually agrees with the participle, and rarely stands in the nominative. Thus, a)pallagei\s tou/twn tw=n fasko/ntwn dikastw=n ei)=nai being rid of those who profess to be judges P. A. 41a , ta\_s a)rxa\_s di/dwsi . . . toi=s a)ei\ do/ca_sin a)ri/stois ei)=nai it dispenses the offices to those who always seem to be the most deserving P. Menex. 238d .

A pronoun subject of the infinitive, if (wholly or partially) identical with the subject of the main verb, is generally expressed when emphatic, and stands in the accusative (cases of the nominative are rare and suspected); but the indirect reflexive sfei=s stands in the nominative or accusative. oi)=mai e)me\ plei/w xrh/mata ei)rga/sqai h)\ a)/llous su/nduo I think I have made more money than any two others together P. Hipp. M. 282e , h(ghsa/menos e)mauto e)pieike/steron ei)=nai (emphatic for h(ghsa/menos e)pieike/steros ei)=nai) deeming myself to be too honest P. A. 36b, tou\s de\ *qhbai/ous h(gei=to . . . e)a/_sein o(/pws bou/letai pra/_ttein e(auto/n he thought the Thebans would let him have his own way D. 6.9 , ou) sfei=s a)dikei=sqai, a)ll' e)kei/nous ma=llon he said that not they (the speaker and the other Lacedaemonians), but they (the Toroneans) rather had been wronged 4. 114 (but sfa=s in 1228 b). a. After a preceding accusative with the infinitive, a second pronoun referring to a different person, and also subject of an infinitive, must also stand in the accusative whether or not it denotes the same person as the subject of the governing verb. Thus, a)lla\ nomi/zeis h(ma=s me a)ne/cesqai/ sou, au)to\s (see below) de\ tuph/sein; kai\ h(ma=s me a)poyhfiei=sqai/ sou, de\ (not su\) d' ou' pau/sesqai but do you think that we are going to put up with you, while you strike us yourself? and that we are going to acquit you, while you will not cease your outrageous conduct? D. 21.204. au)to/s, above and in *kle/wn ou)k e)/fh au)to/s, a)ll' e)kei=non strathgei=n Cleon said that not he himself, but that Nicias was in command T. 4.28, is not the expressed subject of the infinitive, but au)to/s of direct discourse (au)to\s tuph/seis, au)to\s ou) strathgw=); hence au)to/s is not used here for seauto/n (e(auto/n).

When the subject of the infinitive is different from that of the governing verb, it stands in the accusative; and a predicate noun stands also in the accusative. nomi/zw ga\r u(_ma=s e)moi\ ei)=nai kai\ patri/da kai\ fi/lous for I think you are to me both fatherland and friends X. A. 1.3.6 , to ga\r kalo ka)_gaqo a)/ndra eu)dai/mona ei)=nai/ fhmi for I maintain that the noble and good man is happy P. G. 470e .

A predicate noun takes the case of the subject of an infinitive itself dependent on a subjectless infinitive. Thus, h(mi=n de\ poiou=si dokei=n sfa=s pantodapou\s fai/nesqai they manage it so that they seem to us to appear in various forms P. R. 381e .

Several infinitives may be used in succession, one infinitive being the subject of another: peri\ pollou= poiou/menos mhdeni\ do/cai u(bri/zein bou/lesqai regarding it of great importance not to seem to any one to wish to behave outrageously L. 23.5 .

When the subject of the infinitive is the same as the object (in the genitive or dative) of the governing verb, it is often omitted, and a predicate noun is either attracted into the genitive or dative, or stands in the accusative in agreement with the omitted subject of the infinitive. See 1060-1062. e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqoi=s ei)=nai or e)/cestin h(mi=n a)gaqou\s ei)=nai it is in our power to be good (lit. to be good is possible for us). Thus, deo/meq' ou)=n u(_mw=n . . . a)kroa/_sasqai tw=n legome/nwn, e)nqu_mhqe/ntas o(/ti ktl. we ask you therefore to listen to what is said, considering that, etc. 1. 14. 6. Cp. nu=n soi e)/cestin a)ndri\ gene/sqai quoted in 1062 with *lakedaimoni/ois e)/cestin u(_mi=n fi/lous gene/sqai it is in your power to become friends to the Lacedaemonians T. 4.29 . The latter construction may be explained as abbreviated for e)/cestin u(_mi=n (u(_ma=s) fi/lous gene/sqai.

The subject of the infinitive is often retained when it is the same as the (omitted) oblique object of the governing verb. Thus, parh/ggeile ta\ o(/pla ti/qesqai tou\s *(/ellhnas he issued orders that the Greeks should get under arms X. A. 2.2.21 .

An indefinite or general subject of the infinitive (tina/, tina/s, a)nqrw/pous) is commonly omitted; and a predicate noun stands in the accusative. Thus, fila/nqrwpon ei)=nai dei= one (tina/) must be humane I. 2.15 (cp. 1984), r(a=|on parainei=n h)\ paqo/nta karterei=n it is easier for a man to give advice than to endure suffering Men. Sent. 471, drw=ntas ga\r h)\ mh\ drw=ntas h(/di_on qanei=n for it is preferable to die in action rather than doing nothing E. Hel. 814 .

The construction of the accusative with the infinitive seems to have originated from the employment of the infinitive to complement the meaning of transitive verbs; as in keleu/w se a)pelqei=n I command you to depart. Here the accusative was separated from the transitive verb and felt to be the independent subject of the infinitive (I command that you depart). Gradually the accusative with the infinitive was used even after verbs incapable of taking an object-accusative.

Instead of an impersonal passive verb with the accusative and infinitive as subject, Greek often uses the personal passive construction, the accusative becoming the nominative, subject to the leading verb. Thus, *ku=ros h)gge/lqh ni_kh=sai Cyrus was reported to have conquered instead of h)gge/lqh *ku=ron ni_kh=sai it was reported that Cyrus had conquered, and di/kaio/s ei)mi a)pelqei=n I am justified in going away instead of di/kaio/n e)stin e)me\ a)pelqei=n it is right for me to go away. English sometimes has to use the impersonal construction in place of the Greek personal construction (cp. 2107). a. The personal construction is more common with le/getai, a)gge/lletai, o(mologei=tai and other passive verbs of saying (regular with passive verbs of thinking); with sumbai/nei it happens; with a)nagkai=os necessary, a)/cios worthy, di/kaios just, dunato/s possible, e)pith/deios fit, etc., followed by a form of ei)=nai, instead of a)nagkai=on, a)/cion, etc. Thus, o( *)assu/rios ei)s th xw/ra_n au)tou= e)mbalei=n a)gge/lletai the Assyrian is reported to be about to make an incursion into his country X. C. 5.3.30 , pollh/ tis a)logi/a_ cumbai/nei gi/gnesqai much absurdity would result P. Phil. 55a , di/kaios ei)= ei)pei=n it is right for you to speak P. S. 214c , th ai)ti/a_n ou(=to/s e)sti di/kaios e)/xein it is right for him to bear the blame D. 18.4 . Both constructions together: soi\ ga\r dh\ le/getai pa/nu ge teqerapeu=sqai o( *)apo/llwn, kai/ se pa/nta e)kei/nw| peiqo/menon pra)_ttein for Apollo is said to have been greatly served by you, and (it is said) that you do everything in obedience to him X. C. 7.2.15. Cp. 2104. N.—dh=lo/s e)sti and fanero/s e)sti take o(/ti or the participle (2107); dh=lo/n e)sti and fanero/n e)sti take o(/ti, not the infinitive.

The personal constructions dokw=, e)/oika (2089 c), de/w are regular instead of dokei=, e)/oike it seems, dei= it lacks (much or little). So with fai/nomai for fai/netai. dokw= ga/r moi a)/dunatos ei)=nai for I seem to be unable P. R. 368b , dokou=me/n moi kaqh=sqai it seems to me that we are encamped X. A. 1.3.12 , nu=n ge h(mw=n e)/oikas basileu\s ei)=nai now at least you seem to be our king X. C. 1.4.6 , pollou= de/w e)gw\ u(pe\r e)mautou= a)pologei=sqai I am far from speaking in my own defence P. A. 30d , mi_krou= e)de/hsen *ku/pron a(/pa_san katasxei=n he almost (lacked a little) occupied the whole of Cyprus I. 9.62, eu)= su\ le/gein fai/nei you seem to speak well Ar. Nub. 403 . a. dokei= moi/ tina e)lqei=n for dokei= ti/s moi e)lqei=n it seems to me that some one came is very rare. dokei= meaning it seems good, it is decreed always takes the infinitive (1984, 1991). dokw= believe has the construction of 1992 c. Cp. 1998.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: As Subject.—The infinitive may be used as subject, especially with quasi-impersonal verbs and expressions (933 a). gra/mmata maqei=n dei= to learn to read is necessary Men. Sent. 96 , ti/ xrh\ poiei=n; what must be done? X. A. 2.1.16, ko/smos (e)sti\) kalw=s tou=to dra=n to perform this well is a credit T. 1.5 , pa=sin a(dei=n xalepo/n (e)sti) to please everybody is difficult Solon 7, e)/docen au)toi=s proi+e/nai it seemed best to them to proceed X. A. 2.1.2 , sumfe/rei au)toi=s fi/lous ei)=nai it is for their interest to be friends X. O. 11.23 . Cp. 1062, 1978.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Such quasi-impersonal verbs and expressions are dei= it is necessary, xrh/ (properly a substantive with e)sti/ omitted, 793) it is necessary, dokei= it seems good, e)/sti it is possible, e)/cesti it is in one's power, oi(=o/n te/ e)sti it is possible, pre/pei and prosh/kei it is fitting, sumbai/nei it happens; and many expressions formed by e)sti/ and a predicate noun, as a)/cion it is right, di/kaion it is just, a)nag- kai=on it is necessary, dunato/n it is possible, a)du/naton (or a)du/nata) it is impossible, ai)sxro/n it is disgraceful, kalo/n it is honourable, w(/ra_ and kairo/s it is time. With the last two expressions the old dative use of the infinitive is clear: w(/ra_ bouleu/esqai it is time for considering P. Soph. 241b . a. On the personal a)/cio/s ei)mi, di/kaio/s ei)mi, dokw=, see 1982. For dei= me tou=to le/gein we find the personal de/omai tou=to le/gein. Note the attraction in to\ plh=qos tw=n e)no/ntwn ei)pei=n the number of the things it is possible to mention I. 5.110 (for tou/twn a(\ e)/nestin). b. dei= and xrh/ regularly take the accusative and infinitive (cp. 1562); a)na/gkh it is necessary takes the accusative or dative with the infinitive. c. The subject of the infinitive is expressed or omitted according to the sense. d. Homer shows only the beginnings of the use of the infinitive as a real subject, i.e. not a grammatical subject, as in 1984.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: As Predicate.—In definitions the infinitive may be used as a predicate noun with e)sti/. to\ ga\r gnw=nai e)pisth/mhn labei=n e)stin for to learn is to get knowledge P. Th. 209e .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: As an Appositive.—The infinitive may stand in apposition to a preceding substantive, pronoun, or adverb. ei(=s oi)wno\s a)/ristos, a)mu/_nesqai peri\ pa/trhs one omen is best, to fight for our country M 243, ei)=pon . . . tou=to mo/non o(ra=n pa/ntas, tw=| pro/sqen e(/pesqai I told all to pay heed to this only, viz., to follow their leader X. C. 2.2.8, kai\ u(_ma=s de\ ou(/tws, w)= pai=des, . . . e)pai/deuon, tou\s me geraite/rous proti_ma=n, tw=n de\ newte/rwn proteti_mh=sqai and I have instructed you, too, my children (to this effect) to honour your elders in preference to yourselves and to receive honour from the younger in preference to them X. C. 8.7.10.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive not in indirect discourse, and in indirect discourse, is often used as the object of a verb.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive as object not in indirect discourse is used after almost any verb that requires another verb to complete its meaning. The tenses of this infinitive are timeless, and denote only stage of action.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive may be the only expressed object, or it may be one of two expressed objects, of the leading verb. pai/deusis kalh\ dida/skei xrh=sqai no/mois a good education teaches obedience to the laws X. Ven. 12.14 , diagignw/skein se tou\s a)gaqou\s kai\ tou\s kakou\s e)di/dacen he taught you to distinguish the good and the bad X. M. 3.1.9 . a. Verbs signifying to ask, bid, forbid, permit, teach, etc., allow an infinitive as one of two objects. b. Many verbal expressions, formed by a substantive and a verb, take the infinitive. Thus, tou\s a)/llous dida/skein te/xnhn e)/xousin they possess the skill to teach (the) others I. 16.11. Cp. 2000. A. Object Infinitive after Verbs of Will or Desire Verbs of will or desire (and their opposites) are often followed by an infinitive. The infinitive with a subject accusative denotes that something should (may) be or be done. The negative is mh/ (see 2719-2721). h)/qelon au)tou= a)kou/ein they were willing to listen to him X. A. 2.6.11 , e)bouleu/onto e)klipei=n th po/lin they planned to leave the city Hdt. 6.100 , ta\ h(/dista . . . zhtei= poiei=n he seeks to do what he likes best X. M. 4.5.11 , basileu\s a)cioi= se\ a)poplei=n the king asks that you sail away X. H. 3.4.25 , i(_ke/teue mh\ a)poktei=nai he entreated that they should not put him (self) to death L. 1.25, pe/mpousin . . . strateu/esqai e)pi\ *ka_ri/a_n they send orders that he shall march upon Caria X. H. 3.1.7, e)/doce plei=n to *)alkibia/dhn it was decided that Alcibiades should sail T. 6.29 . a. Verbs of will or desire with an accusative subject of the infinitive form one of the classes of substantive clauses introduced in English by that, though the infinitive in English is often more idiomatic. Of verbs of will or desire that take the infinitive some have an object a. In the accusative (or are intransitive), e.g.: ai(rou=mai choose, ai)tw=, ai)tou=mai ask, a)ciw= claim, ask, bouleu/omai resolve, bou/lomai wish, will, dikaiw= deem right, dianoou=mai intend,
