sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Of verbs of will or desire that take the infinitive some have an object a. In the accusative (or are intransitive), e.g.: ai(rou=mai choose, ai)tw=, ai)tou=mai ask, a)ciw= claim, ask, bouleu/omai resolve, bou/lomai wish, will, dikaiw= deem right, dianoou=mai intend, e)qe/lw (poet. qe/lw), wish, will, ei)/wqa am wont to, e)pixeirw= attempt, e)w= permit, zhtw= seek, keleu/w command, suggest, invite, me/llw delay, peirw=mai try, pe/mpw send, proqu_mou=mai am zealous, prokalou=mai invite, protre/pw urge, speu/dw hasten, am eager, spouda/zw am eager, tolmw= dare, filw= am wont to, yhfi/zomai vote. b. In the genitive, e.g.: de/omai ask, e)piqu_mw= and o)re/gomai desire. c. In the dative, e.g.: eu)/xomai pray, paragge/llw and prosta/ttw command, e)pibouleu/w purpose, sumbouleu/w advise, e)pitre/pw and sugxwrw= permit, parainw= exhort, dokw= moi I have a mind to; and le/gw, ei)=pon, fwnw=, fra/zw tell (and bow= shout) in the sense of command. N.—pei/qw urge to a course of action, takes the infinitive, pei/qw convince generally has w(s, rarely the accusative with the infinitive. Thus, e)/peiqen au)to kaq' au(to poreu/esqai he urged him to go by himself X. A. 6.2.13 , ou) ga\r pei/sontai oi( polloi/, w(s su\ au)to\s ou)k h)qe/lhsas a)pie/nai for most people will not be convinced that of your own free will you did not desire to go away P. Cr. 44c (infinitive X. M. 1.1.20).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs of will or desire not to do anything are e.g.: de/doika, fobou=mai fear, feu/gw avoid, o)knw= scruple, ai)sxu/_nomai, ai)dou=mai (2126) feel shame to, a)pagoreu/w forbid, kwlu/_w hinder, a)pe/xomai abstain from, eu)labou=mai, fula/ttomai beware of. Thus, fobou=mai diele/gxein se I fear to refute you P. G. 457e , ai)sxu/_nomai u(_mi=n ei)pei=n ta)_lhqh= I am ashamed to tell you the truth P. A. 22b .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Under verbs of will or desire are included verbs expressing an activity to the end that something shall or shall not be done. Thus, di/dwmi offer, give, diama/xomai struggle against, poiw=, diapra/_ttomai, katerga/zomai manage, effect, pare/xw offer (others in 1992, 1993).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Several verbs of will or desire take o(/pws with the future or the subjunctive (verbs of effort, 2211, 2214); or mh/ with the subjunctive (verbs of fear, 2225); some take the participle (2123 ff.).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive may be used with the a. Genitive or dative when the expression of desire is addressed to a person and the genitive or dative depends on the leading verb. Here the sentence is simple. Thus, de/omai u(_mw=n . . . ta\ di/kaia yhfi/sasqai I ask you to render a just verdict I. 19.51 , toi=s a)/llois pa=si parh/ggellen e)copli/zesqai he ordered all the rest to arm themselves X. A. 1.8.3 . b. Accusative when the action of a person is desired (example in 1979). Such sentences are complex. N.—Verbs of commanding allow either a or b; but only keleu/w with the accusative permits either meaning: keleu/w se\ tau=ta mh\ poiei_n I tell you not to do this and I command that you shall not do this. Cp. 1981.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Several verbs signifying to say are also used as verbs of will and then mean command. The agent commanded usually stands in the accusative subject of the infinitive. So with le/gw, ei)=pon, fra/zw, fwnw=. Thus le/gw s' e)gw\ do/lw| *filokth/thn labei=n I say that thou shalt take Philoctetes by craft S. Ph. 101 , tou/tois e)/legon plei=n I told them that they should sail D. 19.150 , pa/ntes e)/legon tou\s tou/twn a)/rcantas dou=nai di/khn all said that the ringleaders should suffer punishment X. A. 5.7.34 , ei)=pon th qu/ra_n keklei=sqai they commanded that the door should be shut (and stay shut) X. H. 5.4.7, basileu\s e)/graye pa/_sa_s ta\_s e)n th=| *(ella/di po/leis au)tono/mous ei)=nai the king issued a written order that all the cities in Greece should be independent (not: wrote that they were independent) X. H. 6.3.12. a. The agent may stand in the dative as xala=n le/gw soi I bid thee let go S. O. C. 840 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The present and aorist infinitive (both timeless) are the usual tenses of the infinitive after verbs of will or desire (see 1869). The perfect is rare; as ei)=pon th qu/ra_n keklei=sqai (1997). dokw= and dokw= moi signifying I have a mind to or I am determined to take the present or aorist like dokei=: to o)/non e)ca/gein dokw= I have a mind to bring out the ass Ar. Vesp. 177 , e)gw\ ou)=n moi dokw= . . . u(fhgh/sasqai ktl. now I have a mind to show, etc. P. Eu. 288c. Cp. 1983 a. When it is clearly denoted that the action resolved on is to follow without delay the future is used; as in a)lla/ moi dokw= . . . ou) pei/sesqai au)tw=| but I am determined that I will not accept his opinion P. Th. 183d . a. Some verbs, as keleu/w, which might be held to introduce indirect discourse, are classed under ver<*>s of will or desire, because, like these verbs, they do not regularly take the future infinitive; and because, unlike verbs of saying and thinking (which admit all the tenses of the infinitive) they introduce infinitives which do not show differences of time. The future infinitive does not express a command. For a few cases of the future after verbs of will or desire, see 1869.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs signifying to hope, expect, promise, threaten , and swear, when followed by the aorist (less often the present) infinitive (1868), have the construction of verbs of will or desire. When such verbs take the future infinitive they have the construction of indirect discourse.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive follows many verbs, especially such as denote ability, fitness, necessity, etc. (and their opposites). ou)ke/ti e)du/nato . . . bioteu/ein he was no longer able to live T. 1.130 , nei=n e)pista/menos knowing how to swim X. A. 5.7.25 , pefu/_ka_si/ te a(/pantes . . . a(marta/nein and all men are by nature prone to err T. 3.45 , manqa/nousin a)/rxein te kai\ a)/rxesqai they learn how to govern and be governed X. A. 1.9.4 ; also after the impersonals of 1985. a. e)/xw I can is derived from the meaning I have especially with a verb of saying. Thus, *dio\s pla_ga\_n e)/xousin ei)pei=n they can proclaim a stroke of Zeus A. Ag. 367 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive serves to define the meaning of adjectives, adverbs, and substantives, especially those denoting ability, fitness, capacity, etc. (and their opposites), and generally those analogous in meaning to verbs which take the infinitive (2000). Here the datival meaning (purpose, destination) is often apparent. Cp. 1969.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Adjectives and Adverbs.— i(kanoi\ h(ma=s w)felei=n able to assist us X. A. 3.3.18 , deino\s le/gein, kako\s biw=nai skilled in speaking, evil in life Aes. 3.174 , oi(=oi filei=n able to love D. 25.2 , e(/toimoi/ ei)si ma/xesqai they are ready to fight X. C. 4.1.1 , a)/rxein a)ciw/tatos most worthy to govern X. A. 1.9.1 , o(do\s . . . a)mh/xanos ei)selqei=n strateu/mati a road impracticable for an army to enter 1. 2. 21, xalepo diabai/nein hard to cross 5. 6. 9, e)pinoh=sai o)cei=s quick to conceive T. 1.70 . So also after r(a/|dios easy, h(du/s pleasant, di/kaios just, a)nagkai=os necessary, e)pith/deios suitable, a)gaqo/s good, ai)/tios responsible for, malako/s incapable of; cp. o)li/gos 1063. After adverbs: ka/llista i)dei=n most splendid to behold X. C. 8.3.5 . a. Some of these adjectives take the infinitive by analogy to the related verbs, as pro/qu_mos zealous (proqu_mou=mai), e)pisth/mwn knowing how (e)pi/stamai).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: oi(=os fit, o(/sos sufficient take the infinitive like the fuller expressions toiou=tos oi(=os, tosou=tos o(/sos. Thus, ou) ga\r h)=n w(/ra_ oi(/a_ to\ pedi/on a)/rdein for it was not the proper season to irrigate the plain X. A. 2.3.13 , o(/son a)pozh=n sufficient to live off of T. 1.2 , toiou=tos oi(=os . . . pei/qesqai the kind of a man to be convinced P. Cr. 46b . On tosou=tos w(/ste (w(s) see 2263. Hom. has the infinitive after toi=os, to/sos, etc.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Substantives.—As, oi( pai=des u(_mi=n o)li/gou h(liki/a_n e)/xousi paideu/esqai your children are almost of an age to be educated P. Lach. 187c . With e)sti/ omitted: sxolh/ ge h(mi=n manqa/nein we have leisure to learn X. C. 4.3.12 , a)na/gkh pei/qesqai there is need to obey X. H. 1.6.8 , perai/nein h)/dh w(/ra_ it is high time to finish X. A. 3.2.32 . Cp. 1985.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive is added, like an accusative of respect (1601, 1602), to intransitive verbs (especially in poetry), to adjectives (more frequently in poetry), and to substantives (rarely). Thus, toi=os i)dei=n such in aspect (lit. to look on) Theognis 216, o(ra=n stugno/s of a repulsive expression X. A. 2.6.9 , a)kou=- sai pagka/lws e)/xei it is very fine to hear D. 19.47 , qau=ma kai\ a)kou=sai a marvel even to hear of P. L. 656d .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive limiting the meaning of an adjective is commonly active (or middle) in cases where the passive is more natural in English. Thus, lo/gos dunato\s katanoh=sai a speech capable of being understood P. Ph. 90c , a)/cios qauma/sai worthy to be admired T. 1.138 (but a)/cios qauma/zesqai X. C. 5.1.6). a. The active use is due to the old datival function of the infinitive: dunato\s katanoh=sai capable for understanding.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive, with or without w(/ste or w(s, may be used with h)/ than after comparatives, depending on an (implied) idea of ability or inability. h)\ w(/ste is more common than h)/ or h)\ w(s. Cp. 2264. to\ ga\r no/shma mei=zon h)\ fe/rein for the disease is too great to be borne S. O. T. 1293 , fobou=mai mh/ ti mei=zon h)\ w(/ste fe/rein du/nasqai kako th=| po/lei sumbh=| I fear lest some calamity befall the State greater than it can bear X. M. 3.5.17 , braxu/tera h)\ w(s e)ciknei=sqai too short to reach X. A. 3.3.7 . a. The force of h)\ w(/ste may be expressed by the genitive; as, krei=sson lo/gou (T. 2.50) = krei=sson h)\ w(/ste le/gesqai. Cp. 1077. b. Words implying a comparison may take the infinitive with w(/ste or w(s (1063).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Infinitive of Purpose.—The infinitive may express purpose (usually only with verbs taking the accusative). tau/thn th xw/ra_n e)pe/treye diarpa/sai toi=s *(/ellhsin he gave this land over to the Greeks to plunder X. A. 1.2.19 , to\ h(/misu (tou= strateu/matos) kate/lipe fula/ttein to\ strato/pedon he left half (of the army) behind to guard the camp 5. 2. 1, i)e/nai e)pi\ basile/a_ ou)k e)gi/gneto ta\ i(era/ the sacrifices did not turn out (favourable) for going against the king 2. 2. 3, *)arista/rxw| . . . e)/dote h(me/ra_n a)pologh/sasqai you granted a day to Aristarchus to make his defence X. H. 1.7.28 , h( qu/ra_ h( e)mh\ a)ne/w|kto . . . ei)sie/nai tw=| deome/nw| ti e)mou= my door stood open for any petitioner of mine to enter 5. 1. 14, pare/xw e)mauto e)rwta=n I offer myself to be questioned P. A. 33b , ta\_s gunai=kas piei=n ferou/sa_s the women bringing (something) to drink X. H. 7.2.9. Cp. also 2032 e.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive of purpose is used in prose especially after verbs meaning to give, entrust, choose, appoint, take, receive. Verbs signifying to send, go, come usually take the future active participle (2065); but T. 6.50 has de/ka tw=n new=n prou/pemyan e)s to me/gan lime/na pleu=sai they sent ahead ten ships to sail into the great harbour; and in poetry the infinitive often denotes purpose after these verbs, and after ei)=nai in Homer (*l 20) and Hdt. (5. 25).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: After verbs meaning to have (or be) at one's disposition: oi( stratiw=tai a)rgu/rion ou)k ei)=xon e)pisi_ti/zesqai the soldiers did not have money by means of which they could provision themselves X. A. 7.1.7 , e)kei= skia/_ t' e)sti\ kai\ po/a_ kaqi/zesqai there is shade and grass to sit down in P. Phae. 229b .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Infinitive of Result.—The infinitive may be used with w(/ste (sometimes with w(s) to denote a result, often an intended result. See 2260 ff. a. Several verbs, substantives, and adjectives usually taking the infinitive also admit w(/ste with the infinitive (2271); and the infinitive is found where w(/ste with the infinitive might be expected: mnhmoneu/ousin a)feqe/nta tou=ton e)leu/qeron ei)=nai they recall that he was emancipated (lit. released so as to be free) D. 29.25. Here the redundant infinitive expresses an intended result. N.—This redundant use of ei)=nai is common in Hom. and Hdt.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Certain idiomatic infinitives are used absolutely in parenthetical phrases to limit the application of a single expression or of the entire sentence. a. Verbs of Saying.—w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n, w(s ei)pei=n so to speak, almost; (w(s) a(plw=s ei)pei=n, w(s sunelo/nti (1497) ei)pei=n, w(s (e)n braxei= or) sunto/mws ei)pei=n to speak briefly, concisely; w(s e)pi\ pa=n ei)pei=n, to\ su/mpan ei)pei=n speaking generally; sxedo ei)pei=n so to say, almost (paene dixerim); su qew=| ei)pei=n in God's name; and so w(s with le/gein, fra/zein, ei)rh=sqai, as w(s e)n tu/pw| ei)rh=sqai in general. Examples: a)lhqe/s ge w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n ou)de ei)rh/ka_sin not one word of truth, I may say, did they utter P. A. 17a, a)gaqo me a(plw=s ei)pei=n ou)de ge/gone th=| po/lei in a word the State gained no advantage Dinarchus 1.33. b. w(s (e)/pos) ei)pei=n is often used to limit too strict an application of a general statement, especially pa=s or ou)dei/s. Thus, pa/ntes w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n nearly every one, ou)dei\s w(s e)/pos ei)pei=n almost no one. It is thus used like paene dixerim; rarely, like ut ita dicam, to soften the strength of a metaphor. c. Especially common is the absolute ei)=nai in e(kw willingly, intentionally, if you can help it, usually in negative or quasi-negative statements (e(kw/n may be inflected). Also in to\ kata\ tou=ton (e)pi\ tou/tw|) ei)=nai as far as he is concerned, w(s . . . ei)=nai as far as . . . is concerned, to\ nu=n ei)=nai at present. Examples: ou)de\ ce/nois e(kw ei)=nai ge/lwta pare/xeis nor do you intentionally cause strangers to laugh X. C. 2.2.15 , e(kou=sa ei)=nai ou)k a)polei/petai it is not willingly separated P. Phae. 252a , to/ ge e)p' e)kei=non ei)=nai e)sw/qhs (a)/n) so far, at least, as it depended on him you would have been saved L. 13.58. d. Other expressions: e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ dokei=n, w(s e)moi\ kri=nai as it seems to me, in my opinion, (w(s) ei)ka/sai to make a guess, (w(s) sumba/llein to compare, (w(s) a)kou=sai to the ear, w(s

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Infinitive in Commands.—The infinitive may be used for the second person of the imperative. The person addressed is regarded as the subject. This infinitive is commoner in poetry than in prose (where it has a solemn or formal force). qarsw=n nu=n, *dio/mhdes, e)pi\ *trw/essi ma/xesqai with good courage now, Diomed, fight against the Trojans E 124, su\ de/, *kleari/da_ . . . ta\_s pu/la_s a)noi/ca_s e)pekqei=n but do you, Clearidas, open the gates and sally forth T. 5.9. a. This infinitive may be used in conjunction with an imperative: a)kou/ete lew/|: kata\ ta\ pa/tria tou\s xo/as pi/_nein hear ye, good people! drink the Pitchers as our sires drank! Ar. Ach. 1000 . b. The infinitive for the third person of the imperative often occurs in legal language (laws, treaties, etc.), and does not necessarily depend on the principal verb. Thus, e)/th de\ ei)=nai ta\_s sponda\_s penth/konta and the treaty shall continue for fifty years T. 5.18 . In this construction the infinitive has the force of an infinitive dependent on e)/doce (it was voted that) or the like. So in medical language, as pi/_nein de\ u(/dwr it is well for the patient to drink water Hippocrates 1. 151. c. The infinitive (with subject accusative) is rarely used for the third person of the imperative when there is an unconscious ellipsis of a word like do/s grant, or eu)/xomai I pray. Thus, teu/xea su_lh/sa_s fere/tw koi/la_s e)pi\ nh=as, sw=ma de\ oi)/kad' e)mo do/menai pa/lin let him strip off my arms and carry them to the hollow ships, but let him give back my body to my home H 78. d. In negative commands (prohibitions) mh/ with the infinitive is poetic and Ionic: oi(=s mh\ pela/zein do not approach these ( = mh\ pe/laze) A. Pr. 712, mhde\ kalei=n pw o)/lbion and do not call him happy yet Hdt. 1.32 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Infinitive in Wishes.—The infinitive with a subject accusative may be used in the sense of the optative of wish, usually with the same ellipsis as in 2013 c. qeoi\ poli=tai, mh/ me doulei/a_s tuxei=n ye gods of my country, may bondage not be my lot! A. Sept. 253 , w)= *zeu=, e)kgene/sqai moi *)aqhnai/ous tei/sasqai oh Zeus, that it be granted to me to punish the Athenians! Hdt. 5.105 (cp. w)= *zeu=, do/s me tei/sasqai mo/ron patro/s oh Zeus, grant that I may avenge my father's murder! A. Ch. 18). This construction is very rare in Attic prose: to kunhge/thn e)/xonta e)cie/nai . . . e)lafra\_n e)sqh=ta the hunter should go forth in a light dress X. Ven. 6.11 . Here no definite verb can be supplied. a. The nominative with the infinitive (instead of the optative) after ai' ga/r occurs in Homer (h 311, w 376).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Infinitive in Exclamations.—The infinitive is often used in exclamations of surprise or indignation. The subject stands in the accusative. e)me\ paqei=n ta/de that I should suffer this! A. Eum. 837 , toioutoni\_ tre/fein ku/na to keep a dog like that! Ar. Vesp. 835 . On the infinitive with e)f' w(=| (e)f' w(=|te) see 2279; with pri/n, see 2453.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive is used as the object of verbs of saying and thinking. Such infinitives denote both time and stage of action (cp. 1866). a. The finite verb of a sentence placed in dependence on a verb of saying or thinking that requires the infinitive, becomes infinitive, which infinitive stands in the relation of a substantive as subject or object of the leading verb. Commonly as object: thus, *ku=ros ni_ka=| Cyrus is victorious, when made the object of fhsi/ he says, becomes a part of a new sentence fhsi\ *ku=ron ni_ka=n, in which *ku=ron nika=n is the object of fhsi/. As subject, when the verb of saying is passive: thus, in le/getai *ku=ron ni_ka=n, the last two words form the subject of le/getai.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs of saying are e.g.: say fhmi/, fa/skw, le/gw; confess o(mologw=; promise u(pisxnou=mai, u(pode/xomai, e)pagge/llomai, u(fi/stamai; pretend prospoiou=mai; swear o)/mnu_mi; deny a)parnou=mai; gainsay a)ntile/gw; dispute a)mfisbhtw=, etc. Some verbs of saying admit other constructions than the infinitive, and especially o(/ti or w(s (2579). le/gw, ei)=pon, fra/zw, fwnw= with o(/ti or w(s mean say, with the infinitive command (1997). a. fhmi/ say, assert, express the opinion that in classical Greek is almost always followed by the infinitive, but by o(/ti very often in the later language. fhmi\ o(/ti occurs in X. A. 7.1.5 (fhmi\ w(s in L. 7.19, X. H. 6.3.7; D. 4.48, 27. 19 by anacoluthon). b. le/gw state (impart a fact) takes either the infinitive or o(/ti or w(s. The infinitive occurs usually with the passive (le/getai, etc.) either in the personal or impersonal construction (1982 a). The active forms of le/gw with the infinitive mean command (1997). c. ei)=pon said usually takes o(/ti or w(s; with the infinitive, it commonly means commanded (1997). Cp. the double use of told. N.—ei)=pon meaning said with the infinitive is rare, but occurs in good Attic prose: And. 1.57, 80; Thuc. 7. 35; Lys. 10. 6, 10. 9, 10. 12; Xen. H. 1. 6. 7, 2. 2. 15, C. 5. 5. 24, S. 2. 13; Is. 2.29; Lyc. 50; Aes. 3.37, 3. 59; Dem. 15. 18; Plato, G. 473 a, 503 d, Lach. 192 b, Charm. 174 a, Hipp. Maj. 291 b, Pol. 263 c, 290 b, L. 654 a, Clitoph. 409 a, 410 b. In poetry this use is frequent.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs of thinking almost always take the infinitive. Such are: think h(gou=mai, oi)/omai, dokw=, nomi/zw; hope e)lpi/zw; suppose u(polamba/nw; suspect u(popteu/w; guess ei)ka/zw; feel confident pisteu/w; disbelieve a)pistw=. The use of w(s is rare, while o(/ti is very rare (2580). a. Verbs of perceiving sometimes take the infinitive by analogy to verbs of thinking; as a)kou/w, ai)sqa/nomai, punqa/nomai (2144).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Each tense of direct discourse is retained (with its proper meaning as regards stage of action) when it becomes infinitive in indirect discourse; but an imperfect is represented by the present infinitive; a pluperfect, by the perfect infinitive. See 1866, 1867.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: An original ou) of direct discourse is generally, an original mh/ is always, retained in indirect discourse. But in some cases ou) becomes mh/ (2723 ff.).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive is the subject of the passive of verbs of saying and thinking (1982 a). So with dokei= it seems, fai/netai it is plain, etc.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive represents a finite verb after verbs of saying and thinking. a. eu)=noi/ fa_sin ei)=nai they assert that they are loyal L. 12.49 , ou)dei\s e)/fasken gignw/skein au)to/n nobody said that he knew him 23. 3, oi( h(gemo/nes ou)/ fa_sin (2692) ei)=nai a)/llhn o(do/n the guides say there is no other road X. A. 4.1.21 , pa/ntes e)rou=si to\ loipo mhde ei)=nai kerdalew/teron th=s a)reth=s everybody in time to come will say that there is nothing more profitable than bravery X. C. 7.1.18 . Other examples 1867. b. basileu\s ni_ka=n h(gei=tai the king thinks he is victorious ( = ni_kw=, cp. 1887) X. A. 2.1.11, oi)/omai be/ltiston ei)=nai I think it is best 5. 1. 8, u(pw/pteuon e)pi\ basile/a_ i)e/nai they suspected that they were to go against the king 1. 3. 1, (*swkra/ths) to\ a)gnoei=n e(auto e)gguta/tw . . . mani/a_s e)logi/zeto ei)=nai Socrates was of the opinion that for a man not to know himself was very near to madness X. M. 3.9.6 . c. When a word of saying is expressed or implied in what precedes, several infinitives may be used where the indicative is employed in translation. So in the narration in X. C. 1.3.5-6.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The infinitive with a)/n represents an indicative with a)/n or a potential optative with a)/n. See 1846, 1848, 1849, 2270.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs signifying to hope, expect, promise, threaten , and swear take the future infinitive in indirect discourse, and the aorist (less often the present) infinitive not in indirect discourse (like verbs of will or desire, 1868, 1999). e)lpi/zw tau=ta poih/sein I hope that I shall do this, e)lpi/zw tau=ta poih=sai or poiei=n I hope to do this.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The articular infinitive, while having the character of a substantive, retains the functions of a verb. In its older use the articular infinitive is a subject or object; the nearest approach to this use in Homer is a)ni/_h kai\ to\ fula/ssein to watch is also trouble u 52 . In the tragic poets the genitive and dative are rarely used; in the speeches in Thucydides and in Demosthenes all of its four cases appear with great frequency. The articular infinitive may take dependent clauses.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The articular infinitive admits the constructions of an ordinary substantive. Nom. to\ poiei=n making or to make, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, to\ pepoihke/nai Gen. tou= poiei=n of making, tou= poih/sein, tou= poih=sai, etc. Dat. tw=| poiei=n for making, by making, tw=| poih/sein, tw=| poih=sai, etc. Acc. to\ poiei=n, to\ poih/sein, to\ poih=sai, etc.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The articular infinitive is treated as subject, predicate noun, and object like the simple infinitive (1984-1986).

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The negative of the articular infinitive is mh/.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The articular infinitive may indicate time (after verbs of saying or thinking, 2034 g), or may be timeless.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: The articular infinitive is in general used like the infinitive without the article, and may take a)/n; as regards its constructions it has the value of a substantive. The article is regularly used when the connection uniting the infinitive to another word has to be expressed by the genitive, the dative, or a preposition. a. The articular infinitive is rarely used, like a true substantive, with the subjective genitive: to/ g' eu)= fronei=n au)tw=n mi_mei=sqe imitate at least their wisdom D. 19.269 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: NOMINATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE Subject (1984): ne/ois to\ si_ga=n krei=tto/n e)sti tou= lalei=n in the young silence is better than speech Men. Sent. 387 , to\ *peloponnhsi/ous au)toi=s mh\ bohqh=sai pare/sxen u(_mi=n . . . *sami/wn ko/lasin the fact that the Peloponnesians did not come to their assistance enabled you to punish the Samians T. 1.41 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: GENITIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE a. The genitive of the articular infinitive is used to limit the meaning of substantives, adjectives, and verbs. b. Adnominal (1290): tou= piei=n e)piqu_mi/a| from desire to drink T. 7.84 , pro\s th po/lin prosbalo/ntes e)s e)lpi/da h)=lqon tou= e(lei=n they attacked the city and entertained hopes of taking it 2.56. c. Partitive (1306): tou= qarsei=n to\ plei=ston ei)lhfo/tes having gained the greatest amount of courage T. 4.34 . After comparatives (1431): ti/ ou)=n e)stin . . . tou= toi=s fi/lois a)rh/gein ka/lli_on; what then is nobler than to help one's friends? X. C. 1.5.13. d. After verbs: e)pe/sxomen tou= dakru/_ein we desisted from weeping P. Ph. 117e (cp. 1392). e. Purpose (cp. 1408), often a negative purpose: tou= mh\ ta\ di/kaia poiei=n in order not to do what was just D. 18.107 , e)teixi/sqh *)atala/nth . . . tou= mh\ lh|sta\_s . . . kakourgei=n th *eu)/boian Atalante was fortified to prevent pirates from ravaging Euboea T. 2.32 . More common is the use with u(pe/r (2032 g) or e(/neka. f. Genitive Absolute (2070): e)p' e)kei/nois de\ o)/ntos ai)ei\ tou= e)pixeirei=n kai\ e)f' h(mi=n ei)=nai dei= to\ proamu/_nasqai since the power of attack is always in their hands, so in our hands should lie the power of repelling it in advance T. 3.12. g. After prepositions, e.g. a)nti\ tou= e)pi\ *ka_ri/a_n i)e/nai . . . e)pi\ *frugi/a_s e)poreu/eto instead of going against Caria, he marched toward Phrygia X. H. 3.4.12, a)/neu tou= swfronei=n without exercising self-control X. M. 4.3.1 . To express purpose the genitive with u(pe/r is very common: u(pe\r tou= tou/twn gene/sqai ku/_rios . . . pa/nta pra_gmateu/etai he devotes his every effort that he may become master of these D. 8.45 , u(pe\r tou= mh\ to\ keleuo/menon poih=sai in order not to do what was commanded 18. 204. Furthermore, after a)po/, pro/, dia/, meta/, peri/, u(po/, e(/neka, xa/rin, xwri/s, plh/n, me/xri; and after adverbs. In Hdt. tou= may be omitted after a)nti/.

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: DATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE a. With verbs, adjectives, and adverbs: thus, i(/na . . . a)pistw=si tw=| e)me\ teti_mh=sqai u(po\ daimo/nwn that they may distrust my having been honoured by divine powers X. Ap. 14 , tw=| zh=n e)sti/ ti e)nanti/on, w(/sper tw=| e)grhgore/nai to\ kaqeu/dein; is it something opposed to living, as sleeping to waking? P. Ph. 71c, ou)deni\ tw=n pa/ntwn ple/on kekra/thke *fi/lippos h)\ tw=| pro/teros pro\s toi=s pra/_gmasi gi/gnesqai Philip has conquered us by nothing so much as by being beforehand in his operations D. 8.11 , a(/ma tw=| ti_ma=n at the same time that we honour P. R. 468e, i)/son de\ tw=| proste/nein equal to sorrowing beforehand A. Ag. 252 . b. After prepositions: e.g. ou) ga\r e)pi\ tw=| dou=loi, a)ll' e)pi\ tw=| o(moi=oi toi=s leipome/nois ei)=nai e)kpe/mpontai (a)/poikoi) for colonists are not sent out on the basis of being inferiors, but on the basis of being the equals of those who are left at home T. 1.34, o( me pro\s tw=| mhde e)k th=s presbei/a_s labei=n, tou\s ai)xmalw/tous . . . e)lu/_sato the one, in addition to gaining nothing from the embassy, ransomed the prisoners of war D. 19.229 , e)n tw=| fronei=n ga\r mhde h(/distos bi/os for life is sweetest in being conscious of nothing S. Aj. 553 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: ACCUSATIVE OF THE ARTICULAR INFINITIVE a. Object (cp. 1989): dei/sa_s to\ zh=n fearing to live P. A. 28d , mei=zon me/n famen kako to\ a)dikei=n, e)/la_tton de\ to\ a)dikei=sqai we call doing wrong a greater evil, being wronged a lesser P. G. 509c . b. After prepositions: e.g. me/giston a)gaqo to\ peiqarxei=n fai/netai ei)s to\ katapra/_ttein ta)_gaqa/ obedience appears to be an advantage of the greatest importance with regard to the successful accomplishment of excellent objects X. C. 8.1.3 , tw=n a(pa/ntwn a)peri/optoi/ ei)si para\ to\ ni_ka=n they are indifferent to everything in comparison with victory T. 1.41 , pro\s to\ metri/wn dei=sqai pepaideume/nos schooled to moderate needs X. M. 1.2.1 , pw=s e)/xeis pro\s to\ e)qe/lein a) i)e/nai a)/klhtos e)pi\ dei=pnon; how do you feel about being willing to go uninvited to supper? P. S. 174a (cp. e)qe/lois a) i)e/nai). Furthermore, after dia/, e)pi/, kata/, meta/, peri/. c. The accusative of the infinitive with to/ appears after many verbs and verbal expressions which usually take only the simple infinitive. Such verbal expressions may be followed also by a genitive of a noun. Thus, to\ speu/dein de/ soi parainw= I commend speed to thee S. Ph. 620 , kardi/a_s d' e)ci/stamai to\ dra=n I withdraw from my resolution so as to ( = and) do this thing S. Ant. 1105, maqw ga\r ou)k a) a)rnoi/mhn to\ dra=n when I am informed, I will not refuse the deed S. Ph. 118, to\ proqu_mei=sqai de\ sunau/cein to oi)=kon e)paideu/omen au)th/n we trained her to show zeal in assisting to increase our estate X. O. 9.12 (cp. 1628), to\ e)ra=n e)/carnos ei)= you refuse to love P. Lys. 205a . d. So after adjectives. Thus, makro\s to\ kri=nai tau=ta xw( loipo\s xro/nos the future is long (i.e. time enough) to decide this S. El. 1030. e. This object infinitive after verbs is often an internal accusative. The accusative after verbs and nouns is, in many cases, like an accusative of respect (1600); as to\ dra=n ou)k h)qe/lhsan they refused to do it S

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Apposition (cp. 1987). The articular infinitive, in any case, is often used in apposition to a preceding word, especially a demonstrative. tou=to/ e)sti to\ a)dikei=n, to\ ple/on tw=n a)/llwn zhtei=n e)/xein injustice is this: to seek to have more than other people P. G. 483c , ti/ ga\r tou/tou makariw/teron, tou= gh= mixqh=nai ktl. for what is more blessed than this: to be commingled with the earth, etc. X. C. 8.7.25, dokei= tou/tw| diafe/rein a)nh\r tw=n a)/llwn zw/|wn, tw=| ti_mh=s o)re/gesqai man differs herein from other creatures that he aspires after honour X. Hi. 7.3 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: In Exclamation (cp. 2015).—Thus, th=s tu/xhs: to\ e)me\ nu=n klhqe/nta deu=ro tuxei=n my ill-luck! that I should happen now to have been summoned hither! X. C. 2.2.3 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: With Adjuncts.—The articular infinitive may take various adjuncts including dependent clauses, the whole forming one large substantival idea. to\ me ga\r po/ll' a)polwleke/nai kata\ to po/lemon the fact that we have lost much in the war D. 1.10 , pe/peismai . . . ta\ plei/w tw=n pra_gma/twn h(ma=s e)kpefeuge/nai tw=| mh\ bou/lesqai ta\ de/onta poiei=n, h)\ tw=| mh\ suni_e/nai I am persuaded that more of your advantages have escaped you from your not being willing to do your duty than from your ignorance 3. 3, kai\ ga\r pa/nu moi dokei= a)/fronos a)nqrw/pou ei)=nai to\ (mega/lou e)/rgou o)/ntos tou= e(autw=| ta\ de/onta paraskeua/zein) mh\ a)rkei=n tou=to, a)lla\ prosanaqe/sqai to\ kai\ toi=s a)/llois poli/_tais w(=n de/ontai pori/zein and in fact, since it is a serious business to provide for one's own necessities, it seems to me to be the part of an utter fool not to rest content with that, but in addition to take upon himself the burden of providing for the needs of the rest of the community X. M. 2.1.8 .

sections.group: THE INFINITIVE WITHOUT THE ARTICLE: AS SUBJECT, PREDICATE, AND APPOSITIVE
sections.en: Verbs signifying (or suggesting) to hinder take both the simple infinitive and the articular infinitive. Such verbs may take the strengthening but redundant negative mh/ (2739); and some, when themselves negatived or appearing in a question expecting a negative answer, admit the addition of the sympathetic ou) (2742). Hence we have a variety of constructions (described in 2744 ff.)
